clozeText: Staphylococci are spherical {{c1::gram-positive}} cocci arranged in irregular {{c2::grapelike clusters}}.
extraNote: Gram-positive bacteria retain the crystal violet stain. The grapelike arrangement differentiates them from streptococci, which form chains.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, whereas no streptococci do.
extraNote: Catalase degrades hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) into oxygen (O2) and water (H2O), serving as an important virulence factor.

clozeText: Staphylococci are characterized by being {{c1::nonmotile}} and do not form {{c2::spores}}.
extraNote: These characteristics distinguish them from other gram-positive organisms like Bacillus or Clostridium species which may form spores.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci primarily by {{c1::coagulase}} production.
extraNote: Coagulase causes plasma to clot by activating prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to fibrin.

clozeText: Unlike coagulase-negative species, S. aureus usually ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and {{c2::hemolyzes}} red blood cells.
extraNote: Mannitol salt agar is a selective and differential medium used to identify S. aureus based on fermentation.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin and nafcillin in S. aureus is caused by changes in {{c1::penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)}}.
extraNote: The mecA gene encodes an altered PBP called PBP2a, which can perform transpeptidation but does not bind penicillins.

clozeText: Vancomycin-resistant S. aureus (VRSA) encodes enzymes that substitute {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This substitution reduces the binding affinity of vancomycin for the peptidoglycan precursor.

clozeText: {{c1::Protein A}} is the major cell wall protein of S. aureus and acts by binding to the {{c2::Fc portion}} of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents phagocytosis by neutrophils and macrophages because the Fc receptor cannot bind the occupied antibody.

clozeText: In the cell wall of staphylococci, {{c1::teichoic acids}} mediate adherence to mucosal cells.
extraNote: They are polymers of ribitol phosphate and also serve as part of the receptors for bacteriophages.

clozeText: {{c1::Lipoteichoic acids}} in staphylococci can induce septic shock by stimulating the release of {{c2::IL-1 and TNF}} from macrophages.
extraNote: This mechanism is similar to the action of endotoxin found in gram-negative bacteria.

clozeText: The main site of colonization for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of the population are chronic nasal carriers, which increases the risk of skin infections.

clozeText: The classic pyogenic lesion caused by S. aureus is an {{c1::abscess}}.
extraNote: Coagulase contributes to abscess formation by creating a fibrin clot that walls off the bacteria from neutrophils.

clozeText: S. aureus enterotoxin acts as a {{c1::superantigen}} in the gut to stimulate the release of {{c2::serotonin}} from mast cells.
extraNote: The serotonin stimulates the vagus nerve, which activates the vomiting center in the brain.

clozeText: S. aureus enterotoxin is fairly {{c1::heat-resistant}} and is not inactivated by brief cooking.
extraNote: It is also resistant to stomach acid and digestive enzymes in the jejunum.

clozeText: Toxic shock syndrome toxin (TSST) is a superantigen that triggers a massive release of {{c1::IL-1, IL-2, and TNF}}.
extraNote: Toxic shock occurs most commonly in tampon-using menstruating women or patients with nasal packing.

clozeText: The S. aureus toxin {{c1::exfoliatin}} causes scalded skin syndrome by cleaving {{c2::desmoglein}} in desmosomes.
extraNote: This protease activity leads to the separation of the epidermis at the granular cell layer.

clozeText: {{c1::P-V leukocidin}} is a pore-forming toxin that is an important virulence factor for {{c2::CA-MRSA}}.
extraNote: It is associated with severe skin and soft tissue infections and necrotizing pneumonia.

clozeText: Coagulase-negative staphylococci include S. epidermidis, which is sensitive to {{c1::novobiocin}}, and S. saprophyticus, which is {{c2::resistant}}.
extraNote: Novobiocin sensitivity is a key laboratory test to differentiate these two species.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections.
extraNote: CGD is characterized by a defect in the ability of neutrophils to kill bacteria using oxidative bursts.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylokinase}} is an enzyme produced by S. aureus that functions as a fibrinolysin to lyse thrombi.
extraNote: This enzyme assists the bacteria in spreading through tissues.

clozeText: The {{c1::USA300}} strain is the most common strain of MRSA in the United States.
extraNote: It is a prominent cause of both healthcare-acquired and community-acquired infections.

clozeText: The peptidoglycan of S. aureus can stimulate macrophages to produce cytokines, giving it {{c1::endotoxin-like}} properties.
extraNote: This explains why S. aureus can cause signs of septic shock despite lacking true endotoxin.

clozeText: Staphylococcal {{c1::capsule}} types {{c2::5 and 8}} cause approximately 85% of infections.
extraNote: The polysaccharide capsule is poorly immunogenic, making vaccine production difficult.

clozeText: The gene for P-V leukocidin is carried on a {{c1::lysogenic phage}}.
extraNote: This toxin specifically kills white blood cells by forming pores in their membranes.

clozeText: S. aureus utilizes {{c1::hemolysins}} to recover {{2::iron}} from hemoglobin for the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes.
extraNote: Iron is a critical requirement for the growth of the organism.

clozeText: The most common cause of skin abscesses in the United States is {{c1::Methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA)}}.
extraNote: MRSA is also a frequent cause of pneumonia, necrotizing fasciitis, and sepsis.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}.
extraNote: This population is at high risk for endocarditis and skin/soft tissue infections.

clozeText: Localized production of exfoliatin by S. aureus results in {{c1::bullous impetigo}}.
extraNote: Impetigo is characterized by vesicles with a honey-colored crust.

clozeText: S. aureus is a common cause of {{c1::bacterial conjunctivitis}}.
extraNote: It is also a major cause of surgical-wound infections and hospital-acquired pneumonia.

clozeText: {{c1::Diabetes}} is a major predisposing factor to infections by S. aureus.
extraNote: Compromised immune systems and reduced humoral immunity also increase susceptibility.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, an enzyme that degrades H2O2 into O2 and H2O.
extraNote: Catalase is a key biochemical test used to distinguish staphylococci (positive) from streptococci (negative).

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is primarily distinguished from other staphylococci by the production of {{c1::coagulase}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: S. aureus usually ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and hemolyzes red blood cells, whereas coagulase-negative species do not.
extraNote: Mannitol salt agar is a selective and differential medium often used for S. aureus.

clozeText: The major protein in the cell wall of S. aureus is {{c1::Protein A}}, which binds to the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG.
extraNote: By binding the Fc region, Protein A prevents the immunoglobulin from binding to Fc receptors on phagocytes, inhibiting phagocytosis.

clozeText: In S. aureus, {{c1::teichoic acids}} mediate adherence to mucosal cells and serve as part of the receptors for bacteriophages.
extraNote: These are polymers of ribitol phosphate found in the cell wall.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin and nafcillin in MRSA is caused by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a retains its transpeptidase function but does not bind beta-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus involves genes that encode enzymes substituting {{c1::d-lactate}} for {{c2::d-alanine}} in peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This modification is the same mechanism found in vancomycin-resistant enterococci.

clozeText: Staphylococcal {{c1::enterotoxin}} acts as a superantigen in the GI tract to stimulate the release of {{c2::IL-1 and IL-2}}.
extraNote: The toxin is heat-resistant and causes food poisoning characterized by vomiting and nonbloody diarrhea.

clozeText: The vomiting in staphylococcal food poisoning is caused by {{c1::serotonin}} released from mast cells, which stimulates the vagus nerve.
extraNote: This activates the vomiting center in the brain.

clozeText: Toxic shock syndrome toxin (TSST) is a superantigen that stimulates the release of {{c1::IL-1, IL-2, and TNF}}.
extraNote: TSST is associated with tampon use and nasal packing; blood cultures for S. aureus are typically negative in these cases.

clozeText: {{c1::Exfoliatin}} is a protease produced by S. aureus that cleaves {{c2::desmoglein}} in desmosomes, causing scalded skin syndrome.
extraNote: This lead to separation of the epidermis at the granular cell layer.

clozeText: {{c1::P-V leukocidin}} is a pore-forming toxin that is an important virulence factor for community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA).
extraNote: It targets white blood cells and is linked to severe skin and soft tissue infections and necrotizing pneumonia.

clozeText: The typical lesion of S. aureus pyogenic infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which is walled off by a fibrin clot formed by {{c2::coagulase}}.
extraNote: This fibrin wall prevents neutrophils from reaching the site of infection.

clozeText: The main site of S. aureus colonization in humans is the {{c1::nose}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of people are chronic carriers in the anterior nares.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil killing.
extraNote: CGD involves a defect in the NADPH oxidase system.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is distinguished from S. saprophyticus by its {{c1::sensitivity}} to the antibiotic novobiocin.
extraNote: S. epidermidis is sensitive, while S. saprophyticus is resistant.

clozeText: S. saprophyticus is a common cause of {{c1::urinary tract infections}} in young women.
extraNote: It is one of the coagulase-negative staphylococci.

clozeText: S. aureus recovers iron from {{c1::hemoglobin}} for use in the synthesis of {{c2::cytochrome}} enzymes.
extraNote: Hemolysins produce the hemolysis necessary to release this iron.

clozeText: The {{c1::peptidoglycan}} of S. aureus can stimulate macrophages to produce cytokines and activate complement, mimicking {{c2::endotoxin}}.
extraNote: This explains how gram-positive S. aureus causes septic shock despite lacking true endotoxin (LPS).

clozeText: Almost all strains of community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) produce {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}.
extraNote: This is a major differentiator from healthcare-acquired MRSA (HCA-MRSA).

clozeText: Staphylokinase is a {{c1::fibrinolysin}} produced by S. aureus that can lyse thrombi.
extraNote: This enzyme assists the bacteria in breaking out of clots.

clozeText: The S. aureus polysaccharide capsule has {{c1::11}} serotypes, but types {{c2::5 and 8}} cause the majority of infections.
extraNote: The capsule is often referred to as a microcapsule and is poorly immunogenic.

clozeText: Alpha toxin causes necrosis and hemolysis by creating {{c1::holes (pores)}} in the cell membrane.
extraNote: This leads to the loss of low-molecular-weight substances and cell death.

clozeText: Infections of prosthetic heart valves and prosthetic joints are commonly caused by {{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis}}.
extraNote: It is a frequent member of the normal skin flora.

clozeText: {{c1::Lipoteichoic acids}} in staphylococci can induce the release of IL-1 and TNF from macrophages, contributing to septic shock.
extraNote: They play a role similar to the lipid A component of gram-negative endotoxin.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by honey-colored crusts, can be caused by either {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}} or Streptococcus pyogenes.
extraNote: It involves the formation of crops of vesicles.

clozeText: MRSA currently accounts for more than {{c1::50%}} of S. aureus strains isolated from hospital patients in the United States.
extraNote: USA300 is the most common MRSA strain in the US.

clozeText: Staphylococci are differentiated from streptococci biochemically by the production of {{c1::catalase}}, which degrades hydrogen peroxide.
extraNote: Catalase-positive organisms can survive the killing effect of H2O2 within neutrophils. Streptococci are catalase-negative.

clozeText: Microscopically, staphylococci appear in {{c1::grapelike clusters}} while streptococci appear in chains.
extraNote: Staphylococci are gram-positive, nonmotile, and do not form spores.

clozeText: The classic lesion caused by a pyogenic Staphylococcus aureus infection is an {{c1::abscess}}.
extraNote: Abscesses often undergo central necrosis and drain pus; they are walled off by fibrin clots induced by coagulase.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci by its ability to produce {{c1::coagulase}}, which clots plasma.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: Methicillin resistance in S. aureus (MRSA) is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein.
extraNote: The altered protein, PBP2a, performs transpeptidase functions but does not bind penicillins.

clozeText: The major protein in the S. aureus cell wall is {{c1::Protein A}}, which binds to the Fc portion of IgG to prevent phagocytosis.
extraNote: By occupying the Fc portion, it prevents the antibody from binding to Fc receptors on neutrophils and macrophages.

clozeText: In S. aureus, {{c1::teichoic acids}} are polymers of ribitol phosphate that mediate adherence to mucosal cells.
extraNote: Teichoic acids also form part of the surface receptors for staphylococcal bacteriophages.

clozeText: S. aureus can cause septic shock without endotoxin because its {{c1::peptidoglycan}} can stimulate macrophages to produce cytokines.
extraNote: The peptidoglycan possesses endotoxin-like properties, activating complement and coagulation cascades.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose}}, with approximately 30% of the population colonized.
extraNote: Chronic carriers in the nose have an increased risk of subsequent skin infections.

clozeText: S. aureus enterotoxin acts as a {{c1::superantigen}} to stimulate the release of IL-1 and IL-2.
extraNote: The toxin is heat-resistant and acid-resistant, making it stable during brief cooking and stomach transit.

clozeText: The prominent vomiting seen in S. aureus food poisoning is caused by {{c1::serotonin}} released from mast cells.
extraNote: Serotonin stimulates the enteric nervous system via the vagus nerve to activate the brain's vomiting center.

clozeText: Toxic shock syndrome toxin (TSST) stimulates the massive release of cytokines, specifically {{c1::IL-1, IL-2, and TNF}}.
extraNote: TSST is produced locally (e.g., in the vagina or nose) and enters the bloodstream to cause toxemia.

clozeText: S. aureus exfoliatin causes scalded skin syndrome by acting as a protease that cleaves {{c1::desmoglein}} in desmosomes.
extraNote: This leads to the separation of the epidermis at the granular cell layer.

clozeText: Unlike S. aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci do not produce {{c1::exotoxins}}.
extraNote: This lack of toxins explains why they do not cause food poisoning or toxic shock syndrome.

clozeText: S. aureus is distinguished from S. epidermidis by the fermentation of {{c1::mannitol}} and the hemolysis of red blood cells.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides the bacteria with iron required for energy-producing cytochrome enzymes.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is sensitive to the antibiotic {{c1::novobiocin}}, while S. saprophyticus is resistant.
extraNote: This test is used to differentiate coagulase-negative staphylococci in the laboratory.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is a major cause of infections related to {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}} and prosthetic joints.
extraNote: It is a common member of the normal skin flora that becomes pathogenic on foreign bodies.

clozeText: S. aureus is a common cause of skin infections such as {{c1::impetigo}}, which presents as vesicles with a honey-colored crust.
extraNote: Impetigo can be caused by either S. aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes.

clozeText: Streptococci are {{c1::spherical::shape}} gram-positive cocci arranged in {{c2::chains::arrangement}} or pairs.
extraNote: This arrangement distinguishes them from staphylococci, which appear in grapelike clusters.

clozeText: Unlike staphylococci, all streptococci are {{c1::catalase-negative}}.
extraNote: Catalase degrades hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen; its absence is a key biochemical marker for Streptococci.

clozeText: Streptococci are {{c1::nonmotile}} and do not form {{c2::spores}}.
extraNote: These properties are shared with the genus Staphylococcus.

clozeText: {{c1::α-Hemolytic::Hemolysis type}} streptococci form a green zone around colonies due to the incomplete lysis of red blood cells.
extraNote: The green color results from the oxidation of hemoglobin to biliverdin by hydrogen peroxide produced by the bacteria.

clozeText: In α-hemolysis, the green color is formed when hydrogen peroxide oxidizes hemoglobin to {{c1::biliverdin}}.
extraNote: This represents incomplete lysis of red blood cells in the agar.

clozeText: Streptococcus pyogenes belongs to Lancefield {{c1::Group A}} and exhibits {{c2::β-hemolysis::hemolysis type}}.
extraNote: It is a leading bacterial cause of pharyngitis and cellulitis.

clozeText: A key diagnostic feature of Streptococcus pyogenes is that it is {{c1::bacitracin-sensitive::antibiotic sensitivity}}.
extraNote: This sensitivity differentiates it from other β-hemolytic streptococci like S. agalactiae.

clozeText: Streptococcus agalactiae is classified as Lancefield {{c1::Group B}} and is {{c2::bacitracin-resistant}}.
extraNote: It is the leading cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis.

clozeText: Streptococcus agalactiae can be identified by its ability to hydrolyze {{c1::hippurate}}.
extraNote: This is a characteristic diagnostic feature used for Group B streptococci.

clozeText: Enterococcus faecalis is an important cause of hospital-acquired {{c1::urinary tract infections::infection site}} and endocarditis.
extraNote: It belongs to Lancefield Group D.

clozeText: Enterococcus faecalis can be distinguished from Streptococcus bovis by its ability to grow in {{c1::6.5% NaCl}}.
extraNote: Both are Group D organisms and grow on bile-esculin agar, but only Enterococci tolerate high salt concentrations.

clozeText: Both Enterococcus faecalis and Streptococcus bovis grow on {{c1::bile-esculin::media}} agar, producing a black discoloration.
extraNote: The black color results from the hydrolysis of esculin.

clozeText: Streptococcus pneumoniae is α-hemolytic and is uniquely {{c1::bile-soluble}}.
extraNote: Bile solubility and optochin sensitivity distinguish it from viridans group streptococci.

clozeText: Streptococcus pneumoniae is inhibited by the drug {{c1::optochin}}.
extraNote: Viridans group streptococci are not inhibited by optochin.

clozeText: {{c1::Viridans group::Group name}} streptococci are the most common cause of endocarditis.
extraNote: Species in this group include S. sanguinis, S. mutans, and S. mitis.

clozeText: Streptococcus pyogenes is the inciting factor for two immunologic diseases: {{c1::rheumatic fever}} and {{c2::acute glomerulonephritis}}.
extraNote: These are nonsuppurative post-streptococcal sequelae.

clozeText: Streptococcus pyogenes is the leading bacterial cause of {{c1::pharyngitis}} and cellulitis.
extraNote: Other clinical manifestations include scarlet fever and necrotizing fasciitis.

clozeText: Streptococcus agalactiae is the leading cause of {{c1::neonatal sepsis::condition}} and meningitis.
extraNote: Transmission typically occurs during birth from the maternal genital tract.

clozeText: Streptococcus bovis is also known by the name {{c1::Streptococcus gallolyticus}}.
extraNote: It is a nonenterococcal group D streptococcus and an uncommon cause of endocarditis.

clozeText: Group D streptococci like S. bovis and E. faecalis cause a characteristic {{c1::black::color}} discoloration on bile-esculin agar.
extraNote: This occurs because the organisms hydrolyze esculin.

clozeText: Viridans group streptococci are α-hemolytic, but unlike S. pneumoniae, they are {{c1::not::inhibited/not inhibited}} inhibited by optochin.
extraNote: They are also not bile-soluble.

clozeText: S. pyogenes can cause {{c1::necrotizing fasciitis}}, a severe infection sometimes referred to as 'flesh-eating' disease.
extraNote: It is also a cause of erysipelas and streptococcal toxic shock syndrome.

clozeText: In α-hemolysis, the lysis of red blood cells is described as {{c1::incomplete::complete/incomplete}}.
extraNote: In contrast, β-hemolysis involves complete lysis, leaving a clear zone.

clozeText: The species {{c1::Streptococcus mutans::species}} is a member of the viridans group.
extraNote: Other members include S. sanguinis and S. mitis.

clozeText: Streptococci are differentiated from staphylococci microscopically because streptococci appear in {{c1::chains}}, whereas staphylococci appear in clusters.
extraNote: This chain-like arrangement is a classic morphological feature.

clozeText: Streptococcus pyogenes is a leading cause of {{c1::impetigo}}, characterized by skin crusts.
extraNote: It shares this clinical presentation with Staphylococcus aureus.

clozeText: Catalase-negative status means streptococci cannot degrade {{c1::hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)}}.
extraNote: Staphylococci use catalase as a virulence factor to survive within neutrophils.

clozeText: Enterococcus faecalis is frequently associated with {{c1::hospital-acquired::setting}} urinary tract infections.
extraNote: It is a common nosocomial pathogen.

clozeText: Streptococcus pyogenes is the primary bacterial agent responsible for {{c1::scarlet fever}}.
extraNote: This is often associated with streptococcal pharyngitis.

clozeText: The Lancefield classification system for streptococci is based on the {{c1::group::feature}} of medical importance.
extraNote: Common groups include A, B, and D.

clozeText: Microscopically, {{c1::streptococci}} are gram-positive cocci arranged in {{c2::chains}}.
extraNote: This arrangement differentiates them from staphylococci, which appear in grapelike clusters.

clozeText: Biochemically, all streptococci are {{c1::catalase-negative}}, whereas staphylococci produce catalase.
extraNote: Catalase degrades hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.

clozeText: {{c1::$\alpha$-Hemolytic}} streptococci form a green zone around their colonies due to {{c2::incomplete}} lysis of red blood cells.
extraNote: The green color results from the oxidation of hemoglobin to biliverdin.

clozeText: In $\alpha$-hemolysis, the green color is formed when {{c1::hydrogen peroxide}} produced by the bacteria oxidizes hemoglobin to {{c2::biliverdin}}.
extraNote: This process involves chemical modification of the red pigment into a green pigment.

clozeText: Streptococcus pyogenes is a member of Lancefield {{c1::Group A}} and typically exhibits {{c2::$\beta$-hemolysis}}.
extraNote: Group A streptococci are major human pathogens causing both pyogenic and immunologic diseases.

clozeText: A key diagnostic feature of Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A) is its sensitivity to {{c1::bacitracin}}.
extraNote: Bacitracin sensitivity is used in the clinical lab to differentiate S. pyogenes from other $\beta$-hemolytic streptococci.

clozeText: Streptococcus agalactiae belongs to Lancefield {{c1::Group B}} and is resistant to {{c2::bacitracin}}.
extraNote: Group B streptococci are a leading cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis.

clozeText: Unlike S. pyogenes, Streptococcus agalactiae has the biochemical ability to hydrolyze {{c1::hippurate}}.
extraNote: Hippurate hydrolysis is a diagnostic test for Group B streptococci.

clozeText: Enterococcus faecalis (Group D) is distinguished by its ability to grow in {{c1::6.5% NaCl}}.
extraNote: Salt tolerance differentiates Enterococci from nonenterococcal Group D organisms like S. bovis.

clozeText: Both Enterococcus faecalis and Streptococcus bovis can grow on {{c1::bile-esculin agar}}, producing a {{c2::black}} discoloration.
extraNote: The black color results from the hydrolysis of esculin.

clozeText: Streptococcus bovis (Group D) is also known as {{c1::Streptococcus gallolyticus}}.
extraNote: It is a nonenterococcal Group D organism that does not grow in 6.5% NaCl.

clozeText: Streptococcus pneumoniae is $\alpha$-hemolytic and is uniquely {{c1::bile-soluble}}.
extraNote: Bile solubility is a primary diagnostic test to identify S. pneumoniae.

clozeText: Growth of Streptococcus pneumoniae is inhibited by {{c1::optochin}}.
extraNote: This sensitivity differentiates it from Viridans group streptococci, which are optochin-resistant.

clozeText: Viridans group streptococci are characterized as being $\alpha$-hemolytic and are {{c1::not}} inhibited by optochin.
extraNote: They are also not bile-soluble.

clozeText: Two important immunologic diseases incited by Streptococcus pyogenes are {{c1::rheumatic fever}} and {{c2::acute glomerulonephritis}}.
extraNote: These are post-streptococcal sequelae that occur after the initial infection.

clozeText: Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B) is the leading cause of {{c1::neonatal sepsis}} and {{c2::meningitis}}.
extraNote: This pathogen is typically transmitted to the newborn during childbirth.

clozeText: Streptococcus pyogenes can cause {{c1::scarlet fever}} and {{c2::streptococcal toxic shock syndrome}}.
extraNote: These conditions involve systemic effects and toxin production.

clozeText: The hydrolysis of esculin on bile-esculin agar results in a characteristic {{c1::black}} discoloration.
extraNote: This is a key identifying feature for Group D streptococci and Enterococci.

clozeText: Streptococci are gram-positive and arranged in pairs or chains, which is often observed in {{c1::smears}} of clinical specimens.
extraNote: Microscopic morphology is one of the two main criteria for differentiating them from staphylococci.

clozeText: Viridans group streptococci include species such as {{c1::S. mutans}}, S. sanguinis, and S. mitis.
extraNote: These organisms are often found as part of the normal oral flora.

clozeText: Streptococcus pyogenes is also known as {{c1::Group A Streptococcus}}.
extraNote: It is the most common bacterial cause of throat infections.

clozeText: Among the streptococci, {{c1::S. pneumoniae}} is the species characterized as being bile-soluble.
extraNote: Bile solubility tests are specific to this species among the $\alpha$-hemolytic streptococci.

clozeText: Enterococcus faecalis and {{c1::Streptococcus bovis}} are both Lancefield Group D organisms.
extraNote: They are differentiated by their growth (or lack thereof) in 6.5% NaCl broth.

clozeText: S. pyogenes causes a wide variety of skin infections, including {{c1::impetigo}}, erysipelas, and necrotizing fasciitis.
extraNote: It is also a leading cause of cellulitis.

clozeText: In the Lancefield classification, S. agalactiae belongs to {{c1::Group B}}.
extraNote: It is often screened for in pregnant women to prevent neonatal infection.

clozeText: Biochemically, the conversion of {{c1::hemoglobin}} to biliverdin is the cause of the green color in $\alpha$-hemolysis.
extraNote: This incomplete lysis is characteristic of S. pneumoniae and Viridans streptococci.

clozeText: Biochemically, all streptococci are {{c1::catalase-negative}}, whereas staphylococci are catalase-positive.
extraNote: Catalase is an enzyme that degrades hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) into oxygen and water.

clozeText: Microscopically, streptococci are gram-positive cocci arranged in {{c1::chains}} or pairs.
extraNote: In contrast, staphylococci typically appear in irregular grapelike clusters.

clozeText: Streptococci and staphylococci are both {{c1::nonmotile}} and do not form {{c2::spores}}.
extraNote: These characteristics are shared among the medically important gram-positive cocci.

clozeText: Streptococcus pyogenes is an important cause of {{c1::necrotizing fasciitis}}, scarlet fever, and streptococcal toxic shock syndrome.
extraNote: It is also a significant cause of impetigo and erysipelas.

clozeText: The two important immunologic sequelae following Streptococcus pyogenes infections are {{c1::rheumatic fever}} and acute glomerulonephritis.
extraNote: These are non-pyogenic diseases that occur after the initial infection has resolved.

clozeText: The most common cause of bacterial endocarditis is the {{c1::Viridans group}} streptococci.
extraNote: This group includes species such as S. sanguinis, S. mutans, and S. mitis.

clozeText: In incomplete lysis (alpha-hemolysis), the green color in the agar is caused by the oxidation of hemoglobin to {{c1::biliverdin}}.
extraNote: This oxidation is triggered by hydrogen peroxide produced by the bacteria.

clozeText: Streptococcus pyogenes is characteristically {{c1::bacitracin-sensitive}}, which distinguishes it from other beta-hemolytic streptococci.
extraNote: It is also classified as Lancefield Group A.

clozeText: Streptococcus agalactiae is {{c1::bacitracin-resistant}} and has the ability to hydrolyze {{c2::hippurate}}.
extraNote: These two tests help differentiate it from Group A streptococci.

clozeText: Group D streptococci, such as Enterococcus faecalis and S. bovis, are identified by their ability to grow on {{c1::bile-esculin}} agar.
extraNote: The hydrolysis of esculin results in a characteristic black discoloration of the agar.

clozeText: {{c1::Enterococcus faecalis}} can be differentiated from S. bovis by its ability to grow in {{c2::6.5% NaCl}}.
extraNote: S. bovis (S. gallolyticus) is a nonenterococcal group D organism that cannot grow in high salt concentrations.

clozeText: {{c1::Streptococcus pneumoniae}} is characterized as being {{c2::bile-soluble}} and inhibited by optochin.
extraNote: These features distinguish it from the Viridans group streptococci, which are not bile-soluble.

clozeText: Viridans group streptococci are {{c1::not inhibited}} by optochin and are not bile-soluble.
extraNote: They typically exhibit alpha-hemolysis on blood agar.

clozeText: Streptococcus pyogenes, the Group A strep, typically produces {{c1::beta-hemolysis}} on blood agar.
extraNote: Beta-hemolysis is characterized by a clear zone of complete lysis around the colonies.

clozeText: {{c1::Streptococcus bovis}} (also known as Streptococcus gallolyticus) is an uncommon cause of endocarditis.
extraNote: It is a nonenterococcal Group D organism.

clozeText: The green zone formed around colonies of alpha-hemolytic streptococci is a result of {{c1::incomplete lysis}} of red blood cells.
extraNote: Hydrogen peroxide produced by the bacteria mediates this effect.

clozeText: Streptococci of medical importance are often categorized by their {{c1::Lancefield Group}}, which is based on cell wall antigens.
extraNote: Examples include Group A (S. pyogenes) and Group B (S. agalactiae).

clozeText: Pharyngitis caused by Streptococcus pyogenes is characterized by {{c1::swelling of the uvula}} and erythema of the posterior pharynx.
extraNote: Streptococcus pyogenes is the most common bacterial cause of this condition.

clozeText: {{c1::Streptococcus mutans}} and S. sanguinis are members of the Viridans group that can cause endocarditis.
extraNote: Other members include S. mitis, S. gordonii, and S. salivarius.

clozeText: All medically important Clostridia species are {{c1::anaerobic}}, spore-forming, gram-positive rods.
extraNote: Clostridia cannot grow in the presence of oxygen, unlike the aerobic Bacillus species.

clozeText: Clostridia species are characterized by their ability to form {{c1::spores}}, which allow them to survive in soil and harsh environments.
extraNote: Spores are highly resistant to environmental stressors and are often found in soil.

clozeText: The toxin produced by Clostridium botulinum is a protease that {{c1::blocks release of acetylcholine}} at peripheral nerve synapses.
extraNote: This inhibition of acetylcholine release leads to flaccid paralysis.

clozeText: Botulinum toxin is a polypeptide encoded by a {{c1::lysogenic phage}}.
extraNote: This is a key example of a bacterial toxin whose genetic information is carried by a virus (bacteriophage).

clozeText: In adults, botulism is typically caused by the ingestion of {{c1::preformed}} toxin, often found in canned or vacuum-packed foods.
extraNote: The organism germinates in anaerobic conditions within the food and releases the toxin before ingestion.

clozeText: High-risk foods for botulism include {{c1::alkaline vegetables::type of food}} (such as green beans, peppers, and mushrooms) and smoked fish.
extraNote: These foods provide the necessary environment for Clostridium botulinum spores to germinate.

clozeText: The botulinum toxin is relatively {{c1::heat-labile}}, meaning it can be inactivated by boiling for several minutes.
extraNote: Proper cooking is a primary prevention method because heat destroys the toxin.

clozeText: Botulism clinical findings include {{c1::descending}} weakness and paralysis of cranial nerves, such as diplopia, dysphagia, and ptosis.
extraNote: This contrast with Guillain-Barré syndrome, which typically presents as ascending paralysis.

clozeText: In infant botulism, the organism is transmitted through the ingestion of {{c1::honey}}.
extraNote: In infants, the spores germinate in the gut and produce toxin locally, unlike the adult form where toxin is preformed in food.

clozeText: Wound botulism is frequently associated with drug abuse, specifically {{c1::skin-popping}} with black tar heroin.
extraNote: Spores contaminate the wound, germinate, and produce toxin at the site of infection.

clozeText: The definitive laboratory diagnosis for botulinum toxin involves the {{c1::mouse protection test}}.
extraNote: Mice are inoculated with the specimen and only survive if they are also given specific antitoxin.

clozeText: The preferred treatment for botulism is the {{c1::heptavalent}} antitoxin containing all seven types (A–G).
extraNote: Antitoxin should be administered immediately without waiting for laboratory confirmation.

clozeText: For the treatment of infant botulism, a {{c1::bivalent}} antitoxin (types A and B) purified from human plasma is used.
extraNote: Human-derived antitoxin is used to reduce the risk of serum sickness compared to horse-derived antitoxins.

clozeText: Swollen cans must be discarded because clostridial {{c1::proteolytic enzymes}} form gas that causes the swelling.
extraNote: Gas production is a sign of clostridial growth and potential toxin presence.

clozeText: Clostridium perfringens causes two distinct diseases: {{c1::gas gangrene}} and food poisoning.
extraNote: The clinical presentation depends entirely on the route of entry into the body.

clozeText: Vegetative cells of Clostridium perfringens are members of the normal flora of the {{c1::colon}} and vagina.
extraNote: While spores are found in soil, the bacteria naturally inhabit these human mucosal sites.

clozeText: Besides C. perfringens, gas gangrene can also be caused by {{c1::Clostridium septicum}} and Clostridium novyi.
extraNote: Other histotoxic clostridia can cause similar necrotizing myonecrosis.

clozeText: {{c1::Clostridium sordellii}} causes toxic shock syndrome in postpartum and postabortion women.
extraNote: This specific clostridial species is associated with severe maternal complications.

clozeText: When managing a contaminated wound to prevent tetanus, the administration of both tetanus immune globulin and toxoid is an example of {{c1::passive–active}} immunity.
extraNote: The immune globulin provides immediate (passive) protection, while the toxoid stimulates long-term (active) immunity.

clozeText: The pediatric vaccine for tetanus is the {{c1::DTaP}} vaccine, which also covers diphtheria and acellular pertussis.
extraNote: Tetanus toxoid is the immunogenic component used to prevent tetanus.

clozeText: Tetanus immune globulin is made in {{c1::humans}} to avoid serum sickness reactions.
extraNote: Equine (horse) antitoxins are more likely to cause adverse hypersensitivity reactions.

clozeText: Commercial preparations of Clostridium botulinum exotoxin A, known as {{c1::Botox}}, are used to treat spasmodic muscle disorders like torticollis.
extraNote: Minute, controlled amounts of the toxin can be used therapeutically to relax overactive muscles.

clozeText: Botulinum toxin types {{c1::A, B, and E}} are the most common causes of human illness.
extraNote: There are eight immunologic types (A-G) in total.

clozeText: Unlike botulism, {{c1::no fever}} is present in the clinical findings of Clostridium botulinum infection.
extraNote: The lack of fever helps distinguish botulism from many other neurological infections.

clozeText: Clostridium perfringens is a large {{c1::gram-positive}} rod.
extraNote: Gram staining typically reveals large, thick rods.

clozeText: Clostridial gas gangrene is also known as {{c1::myonecrosis}}.
extraNote: This condition involves the death and destruction of muscle tissue.

clozeText: If a wound is grossly contaminated, {{c1::penicillin}} should be administered along with tetanus prophylaxis.
extraNote: Antibiotics are used to target the vegetative cells of Clostridium tetani.

clozeText: In cases of botulism, {{c1::respiratory support}} is a critical component of treatment due to potential muscle failure.
extraNote: Death in botulism often occurs from respiratory arrest.

clozeText: The four medically important species of Clostridium are {{c1::C. tetani, C. botulinum, C. perfringens, and C. difficile}}.
extraNote: These four species cause the majority of clostridial diseases in humans.

clozeText: Clostridium perfringens can cause necrotizing fasciitis, which is often referred to as {{c1::flesh-eating}} disease.
extraNote: S. pyogenes and MRSA are other common causes of this clinical presentation.

clozeText: All clostridia are {{c1::anaerobic}}, {{c2::spore-forming}}, and {{c3::gram-positive}} rods.
extraNote: These three characteristics define the genus morphologically and metabolically.

clozeText: In foodborne botulism, Clostridium botulinum toxin is produced within canned food and is {{c1::ingested preformed}}.
extraNote: This differentiates it from infant botulism where the organism grows in the gut.

clozeText: Clostridium botulinum toxin acts by blocking the release of {{c1::acetylcholine}} at peripheral nerve synapses.
extraNote: This leads to flaccid paralysis due to the lack of neurotransmitter at the neuromuscular junction.

clozeText: Mechanistically, botulinum toxin is a {{c1::protease}} that cleaves the proteins involved in neurotransmitter release.
extraNote: The toxin specifically targets SNARE proteins necessary for vesicle fusion.

clozeText: The polypeptide toxin of Clostridium botulinum is encoded by a {{c1::lysogenic phage}}.
extraNote: This is an example of specialized transduction conferring virulence to the bacterium.

clozeText: The most common immunologic types of botulinum toxin in human illness are types {{c1::A, B, and E}}.
extraNote: There are eight immunologic types in total (A-G).

clozeText: Botulism typically presents as {{c1::descending}} weakness and paralysis of cranial nerves.
extraNote: Symptoms include diplopia, dysphagia, and ptosis; this direction of paralysis contrast with Guillain-Barré syndrome.

clozeText: Unlike many bacterial infections, botulism is characterized by {{c1::no fever}} being present.
extraNote: The lack of fever helps differentiate it from other causes of paralysis or central nervous system infections.

clozeText: In infant botulism, the organisms grow in the gut and produce the toxin there, often following the ingestion of {{c1::honey}}.
extraNote: Infants lack the competing gut flora to prevent the germination of C. botulinum spores.

clozeText: In the United States, wound botulism is frequently associated with drug abuse, especially {{c1::skin-popping with black tar heroin}}.
extraNote: Contaminated wounds provide the anaerobic environment necessary for spore germination and toxin production.

clozeText: The standard diagnostic laboratory test for botulinum toxin is the {{c1::mouse protection test}}.
extraNote: Mice are inoculated with the specimen and only survive if protected by specific antitoxin.

clozeText: The preferred treatment for botulism is a {{c1::heptavalent}} antitoxin containing types A through G.
extraNote: Antitoxin should be administered immediately without waiting for laboratory confirmation.

clozeText: Swollen food cans should be discarded because clostridial {{c1::proteolytic enzymes}} form gas, which causes the swelling.
extraNote: Gas production is a marker of clostridial growth and potential toxin presence in anaerobic conditions.

clozeText: Clostridium perfringens causes gas gangrene, also known as {{c1::myonecrosis}} or necrotizing fasciitis.
extraNote: This condition is characterized by rapid tissue destruction and gas production in muscle.

clozeText: Besides C. perfringens, other histotoxic clostridia that cause gas gangrene include Clostridium {{c1::histolyticum}}, C. {{c2::septicum}}, and C. {{c3::novyi}}.
extraNote: Multiple species within the genus possess the enzymatic machinery to cause necrotizing disease.

clozeText: Clostridium {{c1::sordellii}} is known to cause toxic shock syndrome in postpartum and postabortion women.
extraNote: This species is also grouped with the histotoxic clostridia causing gas gangrene.

clozeText: If a wound is grossly contaminated, management includes {{c1::tetanus immune globulin}}, toxoid booster, and {{c2::penicillin}}.
extraNote: This combination provides immediate passive immunity, stimulates active immunity, and targets vegetative cells.

clozeText: Tetanus immune globulin is made in {{c1::humans}} to avoid the {{c2::serum sickness}} reactions seen with horse-derived antitoxin.
extraNote: Serum sickness is a type III hypersensitivity reaction to foreign proteins.

clozeText: The administration of both immune globulins and tetanus toxoid at different sites is an example of {{c1::passive–active}} immunity.
extraNote: Passive immunity provides immediate protection, while active immunity provides long-term memory.

clozeText: Botulinum toxin is relatively {{c1::heat-labile}} and is inactivated by boiling for several minutes.
extraNote: Adequate cooking of canned or vacuum-packed food can prevent disease.

clozeText: Botox is a commercial preparation of {{c1::exotoxin A}} used to treat muscle disorders like torticollis and writer’s cramp.
extraNote: It is also widely used in cosmetic procedures to remove facial wrinkles.

clozeText: In Clostridium botulinum transmission, spores are widespread in the {{c1::soil}} and contaminate vegetables and meats.
extraNote: Soil acts as the primary reservoir for most clostridial spores.

clozeText: The highest-risk foods for foodborne botulism are {{c1::alkaline}} vegetables and {{c2::smoked fish}}.
extraNote: Examples of high-risk vegetables include green beans, peppers, and mushrooms.

clozeText: Botulism clinical findings include ocular and throat symptoms such as {{c1::diplopia}}, {{c2::dysphagia}}, and {{c3::ptosis}}.
extraNote: These cranial nerve palsies are early hallmarks of the descending paralysis.

clozeText: Wound botulism occurs when {{c1::spores}} contaminate a wound, germinate, and produce toxin at the site.
extraNote: This requires an anaerobic environment within the tissue for the vegetative cells to grow.

clozeText: While mice tests and EIA are standard for botulinum toxin, {{c1::PCR}} tests can be used to detect the DNA encoding the toxin.
extraNote: PCR targets the genetic potential for toxin production rather than the toxin itself.

clozeText: All clostridia are {{c1::anaerobic::oxygen requirement}}, {{c2::spore-forming::survival mechanism}}, gram-positive rods.
extraNote: The four medically important species are C. tetani, C. botulinum, C. perfringens, and C. difficile.

clozeText: For grossly contaminated wounds at risk of tetanus, both {{c1::tetanus immune globulin}} and the {{c2::toxoid booster}} should be administered.
extraNote: Penicillin should also be administered for grossly contaminated wounds.

clozeText: When treating tetanus with immune globulin, half of the dose should be {{c1::infiltrated into the wound}} and the other half given intramuscularly.
extraNote: The intramuscular portion must be given at a site separate from the tetanus toxoid.

clozeText: The toxin of Clostridium botulinum is usually {{c1::ingested preformed}} from canned or vacuum-packed foods.
extraNote: Spores survive inadequate sterilization in anaerobic environments and germinate to produce toxin.

clozeText: Highest-risk foods for botulism include {{c1::alkaline vegetables::pH type}} (e.g., green beans, mushrooms) and {{c2::smoked fish}}.
extraNote: Clostridial proteolytic enzymes produce gas which causes cans to swell; such cans should be discarded.

clozeText: Botulinum toxin is relatively {{c1::heat-labile}}, meaning it can be inactivated by boiling for several minutes.
extraNote: Adequate cooking of food is a primary prevention method.

clozeText: Botulinum toxin acts by {{c1::blocking release of acetylcholine}} at peripheral nerve synapses.
extraNote: It is a protease that cleaves proteins involved in neurotransmitter release.

clozeText: Botulinum toxin is a polypeptide encoded by a(n) {{c1::lysogenic phage}}.
extraNote: It is among the most toxic substances known.

clozeText: Botulism is characterized by a(n) {{c1::descending}} weakness and paralysis of cranial nerves.
extraNote: In contrast, Guillain-Barré syndrome is an ascending paralysis.

clozeText: The classic cranial nerve symptoms of botulism include {{c1::diplopia::vision}}, {{c2::dysphagia::swallowing}}, and {{c3::ptosis::eyelids}}.
extraNote: Respiratory muscle failure is a severe life-threatening complication.

clozeText: A distinguishing clinical feature of botulism is that {{c1::no fever}} is present.
extraNote: This helps differentiate it from other infectious neurological conditions.

clozeText: Infant botulism is associated with the ingestion of {{c1::honey}} containing the organism.
extraNote: In this form, Clostridia grow in the gut and produce toxin locally.

clozeText: In the United States, {{c1::wound}} botulism is associated with drug abuse, specifically {{c2::black tar heroin}}.
extraNote: This involves spores germinating and producing toxin at the site of a contaminated wound.

clozeText: Botulinum toxin is demonstrated in the lab using {{c1::mouse protection tests}} on uneaten food or patient serum.
extraNote: Mice are inoculated and will die unless protected by specific antitoxin.

clozeText: The preferred treatment for botulism (types A–G) is the {{c1::heptavalent}} antitoxin.
extraNote: Antitoxin treatment should not be delayed while waiting for lab results.

clozeText: Infant botulism is treated with a(n) {{c1::human-derived bivalent}} antitoxin (types A and B).
extraNote: Using human-derived antitoxin helps avoid serum sickness associated with horse-derived versions.

clozeText: Gas gangrene (myonecrosis) can be caused by C. perfringens, {{c1::C. septicum}}, C. histolyticum, C. novyi, and C. sordellii.
extraNote: Necrotizing fasciitis is also colloquially known as "flesh-eating" disease.

clozeText: While clostridial spores are found in soil, vegetative cells are members of the normal flora of the {{c1::colon}} and {{c2::vagina}}.
extraNote: Normal flora status explains internal sources of infection for C. perfringens.

clozeText: Clostridium perfringens food poisoning features a long incubation period (18 hours) and {{c1::watery, nonbloody}} diarrhea.
extraNote: The symptoms resemble the long-incubation syndrome of Bacillus cereus.

clozeText: {{c1::Bacillus}} and Clostridium are the two medically important genera of gram-positive rods that form {{c2::spores}}.
extraNote: Corynebacterium, Listeria, and Gardnerella do not form spores.

clozeText: Members of the genus {{c1::Bacillus}} are aerobic, whereas those of the genus Clostridium are anaerobic.
extraNote: Respiration requirements distinguish these two spore-forming genera.

clozeText: Bacillus species are {{c1::longer}} and more {{c2::deeply staining}} than Corynebacterium and Listeria species on Gram stain.
extraNote: Size and staining intensity help differentiate these gram-positive rods.

clozeText: Bacillus anthracis is a large gram-positive rod with {{c1::square ends}}, often appearing in long chains.
extraNote: This is frequently referred to as a "box car-like" appearance.

clozeText: The antiphagocytic capsule of Bacillus anthracis is unique because it is composed of {{c1::D-glutamate}}.
extraNote: Most other bacterial capsules are made of polysaccharides.

clozeText: Unlike most other members of its genus, Bacillus anthracis is {{c1::nonmotile}}.
extraNote: Motility is a key differentiator between B. anthracis and other Bacillus species.

clozeText: The anthrax toxin is encoded on one {{c1::plasmid}}, and the enzymes for capsule synthesis are encoded on a different {{c2::plasmid}}.
extraNote: Both primary virulence factors of B. anthracis are plasmid-mediated.

clozeText: Human infection by Bacillus anthracis occurs most often via the {{c1::cutaneous}} route through skin trauma.
extraNote: Spores on animal products like hides, bristles, and wool enter through wounds.

clozeText: Inhalation anthrax is characterized by the organism moving rapidly to the {{c1::mediastinal}} lymph nodes, causing hemorrhagic inflammation.
extraNote: This rapid movement explains why inhalation anthrax is not communicable from person to person.

clozeText: The {{c1::edema factor}} component of anthrax toxin is an {{c2::adenylate cyclase}} that increases cyclic AMP levels.
extraNote: Its mechanism of action is similar to that of cholera toxin.

clozeText: {{c1::Lethal factor}} is a protease that cleaves phosphokinase, inhibiting the {{c2::MAPK}} signal transduction pathway.
extraNote: This inhibition leads to cell death, necrosis, and the characteristic black eschar.

clozeText: {{c1::Protective antigen}} binds to human cell membranes and forms pores to allow edema factor and lethal factor to enter.
extraNote: It is the binding (B) subunit for both anthrax exotoxins.

clozeText: The typical lesion of cutaneous anthrax is a painless ulcer with a {{c1::black eschar}}.
extraNote: This necrotic crust is also referred to as a "malignant pustule."

clozeText: A critical diagnostic criterion for pulmonary anthrax seen on chest X-ray is {{c1::mediastinal widening}}.
extraNote: This results from hemorrhagic mediastinitis rather than typical pneumonia.

clozeText: Pulmonary anthrax is commonly referred to as {{c1::wool-sorter’s disease}}.
extraNote: This name originates from its association with inhaling spores from animal products.

clozeText: On blood agar, Bacillus anthracis forms {{c1::nonhemolytic}} colonies with a characteristic {{c2::"comet’s tail"}} appearance.
extraNote: Growth is typically performed under aerobic conditions.

clozeText: Spores of Bacillus anthracis are usually NOT seen in clinical exudate because {{c1::nutrients}} are plentiful in infected tissue.
extraNote: Spore formation is triggered by nutrient insufficiency.

clozeText: {{c1::Ciprofloxacin}} is the drug of choice for the treatment of anthrax infections.
extraNote: Doxycycline serves as the primary alternative drug.

clozeText: The anthrax vaccine (BioThrax) contains purified {{c1::protective antigen}} as the immunogen.
extraNote: Antibodies against this protein protect against the disease.

clozeText: To prevent soil contamination, animals that die of anthrax should be {{c1::incinerated}}.
extraNote: Spores can persist in the soil for many years if not destroyed.

clozeText: Bacillus cereus food poisoning is commonly associated with spores germinating in reheated {{c1::rice}}.
extraNote: The spores survive steaming and germinate when the rice is kept warm for long periods.

clozeText: One enterotoxin of Bacillus cereus acts by adding {{c1::ADP-ribose}} to a G protein, which stimulates adenylate cyclase.
extraNote: This mechanism increases cyclic AMP within enterocytes, similar to cholera toxin.

clozeText: One of the enterotoxins produced by Bacillus cereus acts as a {{c1::superantigen}}.
extraNote: This mechanism is similar to staphylococcal enterotoxin.

clozeText: The Bacillus cereus syndrome with a {{c1::short}} incubation period (4 hours) primarily features nausea and vomiting.
extraNote: This emetic syndrome resembles staphylococcal food poisoning.

clozeText: The Bacillus cereus syndrome with a {{c1::long}} incubation period (18 hours) features watery, nonbloody diarrhea.
extraNote: This diarrheal syndrome resembles clostridial gastroenteritis.

clozeText: Diagnosis of Bacillus cereus food poisoning is usually {{c1::not performed}} in the laboratory.
extraNote: Treatment is typically restricted to symptomatic care.

clozeText: A monoclonal antibody preparation called {{c1::raxibacumab}} (Anthrasil) is used for the prevention of inhalational anthrax.
extraNote: It is an immune globulin targeting the protective antigen.

clozeText: Gastrointestinal anthrax symptoms include vomiting, abdominal pain, and {{c1::bloody diarrhea}}.
extraNote: This form occurs following the ingestion of contaminated meat.

clozeText: For rapid diagnosis in bioterror attacks, {{c1::PCR}}-based assays are used to detect Bacillus anthracis.
extraNote: Direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) tests can also detect antigens in lesions.

clozeText: Bacillus anthracis spores can enter the body via the respiratory tract, gastrointestinal tract, or through {{c1::trauma}} to the skin.
extraNote: The cutaneous route is the most common portal of entry.

clozeText: Bacillus anthracis is a large gram-positive rod with {{c1::square ends::shape}}, frequently found in {{c2::chains::arrangement}}.
extraNote: These are often described as having a "box car-like" appearance.

clozeText: Bacillus anthracis is {{c1::nonmotile}}, whereas other members of the genus Bacillus are motile.
extraNote: Lack of motility is a key distinguishing feature of B. anthracis within its genus.

clozeText: In Bacillus anthracis, the anthrax toxin is encoded on one {{c1::plasmid}}, and the enzymes for the capsule are encoded on a different {{c1::plasmid}}.
extraNote: The organism requires two distinct plasmids for full virulence.

clozeText: The B, or binding, subunit of anthrax toxin is called {{c1::protective antigen}}.
extraNote: Protective antigen forms pores in human cell membranes to allow other toxin components to enter.

clozeText: The active (A) subunit of anthrax toxin known as {{c1::edema factor}} acts as an {{c2::adenylate cyclase}}.
extraNote: This increases intracellular cyclic AMP, causing an outpouring of fluid and subsequent edema.

clozeText: Lethal factor, a component of anthrax toxin, is a {{c1::protease}} that cleaves the phosphokinase in the {{c2::MAPK}} signal transduction pathway.
extraNote: Cleavage inhibits cell growth and leads to apoptosis and the formation of a black eschar.

clozeText: The typical skin lesion of cutaneous anthrax is a painless ulcer with a {{c1::black eschar}}, also known as a {{c2::malignant pustule}}.
extraNote: The eschar is a necrotic lesion covered by a crust caused by lethal factor.

clozeText: Pulmonary anthrax, or "wool-sorter’s disease," is characterized by {{c1::hemorrhagic mediastinitis}} rather than classic pneumonia.
extraNote: The organism moves rapidly from the lungs to the mediastinal lymph nodes.

clozeText: An important diagnostic criterion for inhalation anthrax seen on chest X-ray is {{c1::mediastinal widening}}.
extraNote: This is due to hemorrhagic mediastinitis and is often accompanied by bloody pleural effusions.

clozeText: Bacillus anthracis colonies on blood agar typically show a characteristic flared {{c1::comet’s tail::appearance}}.
extraNote: The colonies are nonhemolytic and form aerobically.

clozeText: The drug of choice for the treatment of Bacillus anthracis is {{c1::ciprofloxacin}}.
extraNote: Doxycycline is the primary alternative drug.

clozeText: The Bacillus anthracis vaccine (BioThrax) contains purified {{c1::protective antigen}} as the immunogen.
extraNote: It is used for people at high risk and requires multiple doses and annual boosters.

clozeText: Bacillus cereus causes food poisoning traditionally associated with spores germinating in {{c1::reheated fried rice}}.
extraNote: Spores survive steaming and frying, then germinate when rice is kept warm.

clozeText: One Bacillus cereus enterotoxin acts similarly to {{c1::cholera toxin}} by increasing cyclic AMP via ADP-ribosylation.
extraNote: This mechanism leads to watery, nonbloody diarrhea.

clozeText: The second enterotoxin of Bacillus cereus acts as a {{c1::superantigen}}, resembling the mechanism of staphylococcal enterotoxin.
extraNote: This leads to a short-incubation syndrome of nausea and vomiting.

clozeText: The short-incubation (4 hours) syndrome of Bacillus cereus features {{c1::nausea and vomiting}}, similar to staphylococcal food poisoning.
extraNote: This is distinct from the long-incubation syndrome which features diarrhea.

clozeText: The long-incubation (18 hours) syndrome of Bacillus cereus features {{c1::watery, nonbloody diarrhea}}.
extraNote: This clinical presentation resembles clostridial gastroenteritis.

clozeText: Anthrax spores enter the body via three main routes: cutaneous trauma, inhalation, and {{c1::ingestion}} of contaminated meat.
extraNote: Gastrointestinal anthrax presents with symptoms including vomiting, abdominal pain, and bloody diarrhea.

clozeText: In the laboratory diagnosis of Bacillus anthracis, spores are usually {{c1::not seen}} in smears of infected tissue.
extraNote: Spores form when nutrients are insufficient; nutrients are plentiful in infected tissue.

clozeText: For rapid diagnosis of Bacillus anthracis in bioterror attacks, laboratories use {{c1::PCR}}-based assays.
extraNote: Direct fluorescent antibody tests can also detect organism antigens in lesions.

clozeText: The edema factor of Bacillus anthracis causes an increase in {{c1::cyclic AMP::molecule}} within cells.
extraNote: This matches the action of cholera toxin.

clozeText: {{c1::Raxibacumab}} is a monoclonal antibody against protective antigen used for the prevention of inhalational anthrax.
extraNote: This immune globulin preparation is used for people at risk of exposure.

clozeText: To prevent soil contamination with Bacillus anthracis spores, animals that die of anthrax should be {{c1::incinerated}}.
extraNote: Burying carcasses allows spores to persist in the soil for years.

clozeText: Bacillus species are described as being {{c1::longer}} and more deeply staining than Corynebacterium or Listeria.
extraNote: This morphological difference is visible on Gram stain.

clozeText: The incubation period for the vomiting-type food poisoning of Bacillus cereus is approximately {{c1::4 hours}}.
extraNote: This short timeframe is due to preformed toxin or rapid toxin production.

clozeText: Bacillus anthracis causes {{c1::hemorrhagic meningitis}} as a severe life-threatening complication of systemic infection.
extraNote: This can occur following bacteremia from cutaneous or pulmonary forms.

clozeText: Treatment for Bacillus cereus food poisoning is primarily {{c1::symptomatic}}.
extraNote: Specific antibiotic treatment is usually not required for the gastroenteritis syndromes.

clozeText: Unlike many other bacteria, the capsule of Bacillus anthracis is not composed of {{c1::polysaccharides}}.
extraNote: It is made of a polymer of D-glutamic acid.

clozeText: Bacillus anthracis possesses a unique antiphagocytic capsule composed of {{c1::D-glutamate}}.
extraNote: Most other bacteria have polysaccharide capsules; this protein-based capsule is a distinguishing feature.

clozeText: Unlike other members of its genus, Bacillus anthracis is {{c1::nonmotile}}.
extraNote: Other Bacillus species are generally motile.

clozeText: The anthrax toxin and the enzymes for the polyglutamate capsule are both encoded on {{c1::plasmids}}.
extraNote: Loss of these plasmids results in loss of virulence.

clozeText: Inhalation anthrax causes {{c1::hemorrhagic mediastinitis}} after the organism moves to the mediastinal lymph nodes.
extraNote: This occurs rapidly after inhalation and explains why the disease is not communicable person-to-person via the respiratory route.

clozeText: The {{c1::protective antigen}} subunit of anthrax toxin forms pores in the human cell membrane to allow entry of other toxin components.
extraNote: Antibody against this specific protein protects against the disease.

clozeText: The {{c1::edema factor}} component of anthrax toxin is an adenylate cyclase that increases intracellular {{c2::cyclic AMP::cAMP}}.
extraNote: This mechanism is similar to that of cholera toxin and leads to fluid outpouring into the extracellular space.

clozeText: Lethal factor is a protease that cleaves the phosphokinase in the {{c1::MAPK::abbreviation}} signal transduction pathway.
extraNote: This inhibition of cell growth leads to apoptosis and the formation of the necrotic black eschar.

clozeText: The typical skin lesion of cutaneous anthrax is a painless ulcer with a {{c1::black eschar}}.
extraNote: This lesion is also known as a malignant pustule.

clozeText: A critical diagnostic finding on a chest X-ray for pulmonary anthrax is {{c1::mediastinal widening}}.
extraNote: Classic features and X-ray evidence of pneumonia are usually absent in wool-sorter's disease.

clozeText: Severe life-threatening complications of pulmonary anthrax include hemorrhagic mediastinitis and {{c1::hemorrhagic meningitis}}.
extraNote: The disease progresses rapidly to septic shock and death.

clozeText: On blood agar, Bacillus anthracis colonies typically have a flared {{c1::comet's tail}} appearance.
extraNote: The colonies are nonhemolytic and grow aerobically.

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating anthrax is {{c1::ciprofloxacin}}.
extraNote: Doxycycline is the primary alternative drug.

clozeText: The BioThrax vaccine for high-risk individuals contains purified {{c1::protective antigen}}.
extraNote: The vaccine requires six doses over 18 months plus annual boosters.

clozeText: Bacillus cereus food poisoning is classically associated with spores germinating in {{c1::reheated fried rice}}.
extraNote: Spores survive initial steaming and frying, then germinate if the rice is kept warm for hours.

clozeText: One of the Bacillus cereus enterotoxins acts as a {{c1::superantigen}}, similar to staphylococcal enterotoxin.
extraNote: This syndrome typically presents with a short incubation period (4 hours).

clozeText: The long-incubation syndrome of Bacillus cereus features {{c1::watery, nonbloody}} diarrhea.
extraNote: This syndrome has an 18-hour incubation period and resembles clostridial gastroenteritis.

clozeText: The short-incubation syndrome of Bacillus cereus consists primarily of {{c1::nausea and vomiting}}.
extraNote: It has a 4-hour incubation period, mimicking staphylococcal food poisoning.

clozeText: Corynebacteria are gram-positive rods that appear {{c1::club-shaped::shape}} and are arranged in palisades or in V- or L-shaped formations.
extraNote: The club shape refers to the organism being wider at one end than the other.

clozeText: Corynebacterium species are distinguished from Bacillus and Clostridium because they are {{c1::non–spore-forming::spore status}}.
extraNote: Bacillus and Clostridium are the medically important gram-positive rods that do form spores.

clozeText: The beads seen in Corynebacterium diphtheriae consist of granules of highly polymerized {{c1::polyphosphate::chemical composition}}.
extraNote: These granules serve as a storage mechanism for high-energy phosphate bonds.

clozeText: The polyphosphate granules of C. diphtheriae stain {{c1::metachromatically::staining property}}.
extraNote: Metachromatic staining means a dye that stains the rest of the cell blue will stain the granules red.

clozeText: In the genus Corynebacterium, {{c1::humans::host}} are the only natural host.
extraNote: Transmission occurs via airborne droplets or contact with skin lesions.

clozeText: Diphtheria toxin inhibits protein synthesis by {{c1::ADP-ribosylation::biochemical mechanism}} of elongation factor-2 (EF-2).
extraNote: This inactivation of EF-2 affects all eukaryotic cells but has no effect on prokaryotic EF-2.

clozeText: The {{c1::binding (B)::toxin domain}} domain of diphtheria toxin mediates binding to glycoprotein receptors on the cell membrane.
extraNote: The toxin is a single polypeptide with two functional domains (A and B).

clozeText: The {{c1::active (A)::toxin domain}} domain of diphtheria toxin cleaves nicotinamide from NAD and transfers ADP-ribose to EF-2.
extraNote: This enzymatic activity is responsible for inactivating the translation machinery.

clozeText: The DNA coding for diphtheria toxin is carried by a temperate bacteriophage called {{c1::beta phage::virus name}}.
extraNote: The toxin is synthesized only when the DNA of this virus integrates into the bacterial chromosome during lysogeny.

clozeText: Local inflammation in the throat by C. diphtheriae results in a fibrinous exudate that forms a tough, adherent, {{c1::gray pseudomembrane::clinical sign}}.
extraNote: The pseudomembrane is characteristic of the disease and can extend into the larynx and trachea.

clozeText: The immune status of a person regarding diphtheria can be assessed by the {{c1::Schick’s test::diagnostic test}}.
extraNote: This involves an intradermal injection of purified toxin; inflammation indicates a lack of antitoxin.

clozeText: A prominent non-respiratory complication of diphtheria is {{c1::myocarditis::complication}}, often accompanied by arrhythmias.
extraNote: Other major complications include airway obstruction and nerve paralysis.

clozeText: Paralysis of the muscles of the soft palate and pharynx in diphtheria can lead to {{c1::regurgitation of fluids through the nose::symptom}}.
extraNote: Nerve weakness frequently affects the cranial nerves in severe cases.

clozeText: To isolate C. diphtheriae, a throat swab should be cultured on Loeffler’s medium, a blood agar plate, and a {{c1::tellurite plate::culture media}}.
extraNote: The tellurite plate is specific for identifying the organism based on its reduction of tellurium salts.

clozeText: C. diphtheriae colonies appear {{c1::gray-black::color}} on a tellurite plate.
extraNote: This color is due to the reduction of tellurium salt to elemental tellurium within the organism.

clozeText: The {{c1::methylene blue::stain name}} stain is excellent for revealing the typical metachromatic granules of C. diphtheriae.
extraNote: While Gram stain shows gram-positive rods, methylene blue highlights the polymerized polyphosphate storage granules.

clozeText: The treatment of choice for diphtheria is {{c1::antitoxin::treatment}}, which must be given immediately based on clinical impression.
extraNote: Antitoxin only neutralizes unbound toxin in the blood and cannot neutralize toxin already bound to cells.

clozeText: Because diphtheria antitoxin is made in {{c1::horses::source}}, patients must be tested for hypersensitivity to prevent anaphylaxis.
extraNote: Serum sickness may occur as a delayed reaction to the equine-derived antiserum.

clozeText: Antibiotics such as {{c1::penicillin G::drug}} or erythromycin are recommended for C. diphtheriae, but they are not substitutes for antitoxin.
extraNote: Antibiotics reduce the burden of the organism but do not neutralize the circulating exotoxin.

clozeText: Prevention of diphtheria is achieved by administration of the {{c1::toxid::vaccine type}} vaccine.
extraNote: The vaccine contains inactivated toxin that induces protective antibodies.

clozeText: Other Corynebacterium species, often referred to as {{c1::diphtheroids::group name}}, are typically implicated in opportunistic infections.
extraNote: They are part of the normal flora but can cause disease in certain clinical contexts.

clozeText: Cutaneous diphtheria typically presents as {{c1::ulcerating skin lesions::clinical sign}} covered by a gray membrane.
extraNote: This form of the disease occurs primarily in the tropics or in indigent populations with poor hygiene.

clozeText: The gel diffusion precipitin test, used to document toxin production in C. diphtheriae, is also known as the {{c1::Elek::test name}} test.
extraNote: This antibody-based test detects the presence of the exotoxin in isolated cultures.

clozeText: Corynebacterium species are described as being {{c1::aerobic::respiration}} and nonmotile.
extraNote: This distinguishes them from anaerobic gram-positive rods like Clostridium.

clozeText: In diphtheria pathogenesis, the toxin binds specifically to {{c1::glycoprotein receptors::target}} on the host cell membrane.
extraNote: The B domain of the A-B toxin facilitates this specific binding.

clozeText: Diphtheria toxin is a {{c1::single polypeptide::structure}} with two functional domains.
extraNote: Despite being one chain, it has distinct binding (B) and active (A) regions.

clozeText: Extension of the pseudomembrane into the {{c1::larynx and trachea::anatomical location}} can cause airway obstruction in diphtheria patients.
extraNote: This is one of the three major life-threatening complications of the infection.

clozeText: A PCR assay can be used to detect the presence of the {{c1::toxin gene::diagnostic target}} in organisms isolated from patients suspecting of diphtheria.
extraNote: This molecular method provides documentation of the organism's toxigenic potential.

clozeText: One of the predisposing factors for diphtheria is the {{c1::failure to immunize::risk factor}}.
extraNote: The toxoid vaccine is highly effective at preventing the disease.

clozeText: Diphtheria toxin inactivates EF-2 by transferring the ADP-ribose from {{c1::nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD)::substrate}}.
extraNote: The active domain cleaves nicotinamide and uses the remaining ADP-ribose to modify the target protein.

clozeText: Corynebacterium species are gram-positive rods that are characteristically {{c1::club-shaped}} and arranged in palisades or V- or L-shaped formations.
extraNote: The club-shaped appearance means they are wider at one end than the other.

clozeText: Members of the genus Corynebacterium do {{c1::not}} form spores.
extraNote: Unlike Bacillus and Clostridium, Corynebacterium is a non-spore-forming gram-positive rod.

clozeText: The rods of C. diphtheriae have a beaded appearance due to granules of highly polymerized {{c1::polyphosphate}}.
extraNote: These granules serve as a storage mechanism for high-energy phosphate bonds.

clozeText: The granules of C. diphtheriae stain {{c1::metachromatically}}, meaning a blue dye will stain the granules red.
extraNote: Methylene blue stain is specifically used to reveal these metachromatic granules.

clozeText: The only natural host of C. diphtheriae is {{c1::humans}}.
extraNote: Organisms reside in the upper respiratory tract of both toxigenic and nontoxigenic carriers.

clozeText: C. diphtheriae is primarily transmitted by {{c1::airborne droplets}}.
extraNote: It can also infect the skin at the site of preexisting lesions, particularly in tropical climates or areas with poor hygiene.

clozeText: The specific target of the diphtheria toxin is {{c1::elongation factor-2 (EF-2)}}.
extraNote: The toxin has no effect on the EF-2 of prokaryotic cells.

clozeText: The {{c1::binding (B)}} domain of the diphtheria toxin mediates attachment to glycoprotein receptors on the cell membrane.
extraNote: The toxin is a single polypeptide with two functional domains (A and B).

clozeText: The enzymatic activity of the diphtheria toxin is located in the {{c1::active (A)}} domain.
extraNote: The A domain cleaves nicotinamide from NAD and transfers ADP-ribose to EF-2.

clozeText: The DNA coding for diphtheria toxin is provided by a temperate bacteriophage called {{c1::beta phage}}.
extraNote: Only C. diphtheriae cells lysogenized by this phage produce the exotoxin and are pathogenic.

clozeText: C. diphtheriae causes a local inflammation in the throat characterized by a tough, adherent, gray {{c1::pseudomembrane}}.
extraNote: The membrane is formed from a fibrinous exudate.

clozeText: A prominent complication of diphtheria is {{c1::myocarditis}}, which may be accompanied by arrhythmias.
extraNote: Circulatory collapse is also a risk associated with this complication.

clozeText: C. diphtheriae can be cultured on {{c1::Loeffler’s}} medium, a tellurite plate, or a blood agar plate.
extraNote: Tellurite plates are selective and differential for Corynebacterium.

clozeText: On a tellurite plate, C. diphtheriae colonies appear {{c1::gray-black}}.
extraNote: This color results from the reduction of tellurium salts to elemental tellurium within the organism.

clozeText: The clinical decision to treat diphtheria with {{c1::antitoxin}} must be made without waiting for laboratory results.
extraNote: The toxin binds rapidly and irreversibly to cells, so unbound toxin must be neutralized early.

clozeText: Diphtheria antitoxin only neutralizes {{c1::unbound}} toxin in the blood.
extraNote: Once the toxin is bound to cell receptors, it cannot be neutralized by the antiserum.

clozeText: The recommended antibiotics for treating C. diphtheriae infection are {{c1::penicillin G}} or erythromycin.
extraNote: Antibiotics serve as an adjunct to antitoxin but are not a substitute for it.

clozeText: Prevention of diphtheria is achieved by immunization with the {{c1::toxoid}} vaccine.
extraNote: The toxoid is typically administered in combination with tetanus toxoid and acellular pertussis vaccine (DTaP).

clozeText: Other Corynebacterium species that are often part of the normal flora are collectively called {{c1::diphtheroids}}.
extraNote: These species are typically implicated in opportunistic infections.

clozeText: Diphtheria toxin cleaves nicotinamide from {{c1::NAD}} to facilitate the ribosylation of EF-2.
extraNote: NAD stands for nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide.

clozeText: The host response to C. diphtheriae includes antibody production that blocks the {{c1::binding}} domain of the toxin.
extraNote: This prevents the toxin from entering eukaryotic cells.

clozeText: In the Schick’s test, inflammation at the site 4 to 7 days later indicates the patient {{c1::has no antitoxin}}.
extraNote: If no inflammation occurs, it means the patient is immune.

clozeText: Cutaneous diphtheria causes ulcerating skin lesions covered by a {{c1::gray membrane}}.
extraNote: These lesions are often indolent and usually do not invade surrounding tissue.

clozeText: Laboratory documentation of toxin production in C. diphtheriae can be done via {{c1::PCR}} assay for the toxin gene.
extraNote: Other methods include animal inoculation or an antibody-based gel diffusion precipitin test.

clozeText: Because diphtheria antitoxin is made in {{c1::horses}}, patients must be tested for hypersensitivity before administration.
extraNote: Serum sickness may occur as a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to the horse-derived serum.

clozeText: Extension of the pseudomembrane into the larynx and trachea can cause {{c1::airway obstruction}}.
extraNote: This is a critical clinical complication of respiratory diphtheria.

clozeText: C. diphtheriae rods are described as {{c1::pleomorphic}} gram-positive rods.
extraNote: Gram stains may show many tapered or club-shaped forms.

clozeText: Corynebacterium species are {{c1::non-spore-forming::spore status}} gram-positive rods.
extraNote: Unlike Bacillus and Clostridium, Corynebacterium does not form spores.

clozeText: Corynebacterium species characteristically appear as {{c1::V- or L-shaped::shape}} rods on Gram stain.
extraNote: This arrangement is a hallmark microscopic finding for this genus.

clozeText: Corynebacterium species are often {{c1::club-shaped::appearance}}, meaning they are thinner on one end than the other.
extraNote: This morphology is why they are often described as pleomorphic or club-shaped.

clozeText: The granules in C. diphtheriae stain {{c1::metachromatically::stain reaction}}, appearing red when the rest of the cell is blue.
extraNote: This specific staining reaction is used to identify the characteristic polyphosphate granules.

clozeText: The natural host for Corynebacterium diphtheriae is {{c1::humans only}}.
extraNote: There is no animal reservoir for C. diphtheriae.

clozeText: The gene for diphtheria toxin is carried by a temperate bacteriophage called {{c1::beta phage}}.
extraNote: The toxin is synthesized during the lysogenic phase of viral growth.

clozeText: A characteristic clinical sign of diphtheria is a thick, gray, adherent {{c1::pseudomembrane}} over the tonsils and throat.
extraNote: This is formed by a fibrinous exudate resulting from local inflammation.

clozeText: The immune status of a person regarding diphtheria can be assessed using {{c1::Schick’s test}}.
extraNote: The test involves intradermal injection of purified toxin; inflammation at the site indicates a lack of antitoxin.

clozeText: A prominent cardiac complication of diphtheria is {{c1::myocarditis}}, which can lead to arrhythmias and circulatory collapse.
extraNote: This occurs due to the systemic effects of the diphtheria exotoxin.

clozeText: Nerve paralysis in diphtheria often affects the {{c1::soft palate::anatomical site}} and pharynx, leading to fluid regurgitation through the nose.
extraNote: Cranial nerves are frequently targeted in severe cases.

clozeText: For laboratory diagnosis, C. diphtheriae should be cultured on a {{c1::tellurite plate}}, where it forms gray-black colonies.
extraNote: The color is produced by the reduction of tellurium salt to elemental tellurium within the organism.

clozeText: {{c1::Loeffler’s medium::specific media}} is used to culture throat swabs when diphtheria is suspected.
extraNote: This is one of the classic primary isolation media for C. diphtheriae.

clozeText: The most important immediate treatment for suspected diphtheria is the administration of {{c1::antitoxin}}.
extraNote: It must be given based on clinical impression because it only neutralizes unbound toxin in the blood.

clozeText: Diphtheria toxin targets and inactivates {{c1::elongation factor-2 (EF-2)}}.
extraNote: This specifically blocks protein synthesis in eukaryotic cells.

clozeText: Cutaneous diphtheria is characterized by {{c1::ulcerating skin lesions}} covered by a gray membrane.
extraNote: This form occurs primarily in indigent persons or in tropical climates.

clozeText: To document toxin production in C. diphtheriae, an antibody-based {{c1::gel diffusion precipitin test}} (Elek test) can be performed.
extraNote: PCR assays for the toxin gene are also utilized for confirmation.

clozeText: Antibiotics recommended for treating C. diphtheriae infections include {{c1::penicillin G}} or erythromycin.
extraNote: These are used to stop organism growth but are not a substitute for antitoxin.
