clozeText: The mechanism of diarrhea caused by Campylobacter jejuni is classified as {{c1::invasive-inflammatory}}.
extraNote: This typically results in fever and inflammatory cells in the stool.

clozeText: Appropriate antibiotic therapy for enteric gram-negative rods like Campylobacter must be tailored to the {{c1::antibiotic sensitivity}} of the specific isolate.
extraNote: Testing is necessary because many enteric rods have developed high levels of resistance.

clozeText: Enteric gram-negative rods can acquire multiple drug resistance through the transfer of {{c1::plasmids}} (R factors) during the process of {{c2::conjugation}}.
extraNote: This genetic exchange allows for the rapid spread of resistance to drugs like penicillins and cephalosporins.

clozeText: Resistance in enteric gram-negative rods is often mediated by the production of {{c1::β-lactamases}}, including extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs).
extraNote: These enzymes can modify or deactivate a wide range of antimicrobial agents.

clozeText: Campylobacter staining results in a {{c1::gram-negative}} reaction.
extraNote: As a member of the enteric rods, it possesses a gram-negative cell wall structure containing endotoxin.

clozeText: Antimicrobial agents that are potentially effective against enteric rods, depending on sensitivity, include {{c1::quinolones::drug class}} and {{c2::aminoglycosides::drug class}}.
extraNote: Other options include tetracyclines, sulfonamides, and certain cephalosporins.

clozeText: Infections caused by {{c1::Campylobacter}} are among the most common causes of bacterial diarrhea in the United States.
extraNote: It shares this high frequency with Salmonella and Shigella.

clozeText: The curved morphology of Campylobacter can be visualized on a {{c1::Gram stain}}.
extraNote: They appear as thin, curved rods that may form S-shapes or spiral patterns.

clozeText: Campylobacter is associated with the autoimmune condition {{c1::Reiter syndrome}}, which often follows an episode of enterocolitis.
extraNote: Reiter syndrome is characterized by arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis.

clozeText: The high incidence of autoimmune disease following Campylobacter infection is shared with the genus {{c1::Yersinia::other enteric genus}}.
extraNote: Shigella and Salmonella also predispose to reactive arthritis.

clozeText: Spirochetes are morphologically described as thin-walled, flexible {{c1::spiral rods}}.
extraNote: They are motile through the undulation of axial filaments located under the outer sheath.

clozeText: Spirochetes are motile through the undulation of {{c1::axial filaments}} that lie under the outer sheath.
extraNote: These filaments enable movement without external flagella.

clozeText: Treponema and Leptospira are so thin that they are only visible using {{c1::dark-field microscopy}}, silver impregnation, or immunofluorescence.
extraNote: They are too thin to be seen on a standard Gram-stained smear.

clozeText: Unlike other spirochetes, {{c1::Borreliae}} are larger, accept Giemsa or blood stains, and can be seen with a standard light microscope.
extraNote: This genus includes the agents of Lyme disease and relapsing fever.

clozeText: Treponema pallidum cannot be grown on {{c1::bacteriologic media}} or in cell culture.
extraNote: Nonpathogenic treponemes of the normal flora can be cultured, but the pathogen for syphilis cannot.

clozeText: Treponema pallidum grows {{c1::very slowly}}, which necessitates that antibiotics be present at effective levels for several weeks for treatment.
extraNote: This slow growth explains why long-acting benzathine penicillin is used for treatment.

clozeText: The primary stage of syphilis is characterized by a local, nontender ulcer called a {{c1::chancre}}.
extraNote: This lesion typically forms 2 to 10 weeks after inoculation and heals spontaneously.

clozeText: Secondary syphilis often presents with a maculopapular rash notably found on the {{c1::palms}} and {{c1::soles}}.
extraNote: This stage occurs 1 to 3 months after the primary lesion.

clozeText: Moist papules on the genitals during secondary syphilis are called {{c1::condylomata lata}}.
extraNote: These lesions are rich in spirochetes and are highly infectious.

clozeText: The pathogenesis of Treponema pallidum involves the infection of small blood vessel endothelium, causing {{c1::endarteritis}}.
extraNote: This occurs during all stages but is critical for the brain and cardiovascular lesions in tertiary syphilis.

clozeText: Tertiary syphilis may present with granulomatous lesions of the skin and bones known as {{c1::gummas}}.
extraNote: Treponemes are rarely seen within these tertiary lesions.

clozeText: Neurosyphilis manifestations in the tertiary stage include {{c1::tabes}} and paresis.
extraNote: Cardiovascular lesions like aortitis and aneurysms of the ascending aorta are also common in this stage.

clozeText: Congenital syphilis may result in dental abnormalities such as {{c1::Hutchinson’s teeth}} and mulberry molars.
extraNote: Other bone findings include saber shins and saddle nose.

clozeText: Nonspecific serologic tests for syphilis (VDRL/RPR) detect antibodies called {{c1::reagin}}.
extraNote: Reagin reacts with cardiolipin extracted from normal mammalian tissues like beef heart.

clozeText: Nonspecific serologic test titers for syphilis {{c1::decrease}} with effective treatment, whereas specific tests remain positive for life.
extraNote: This makes VDRL/RPR useful for monitoring the response to therapy.

clozeText: The {{c1::prozone phenomenon}} can cause false-negative VDRL results due to antibody excess.
extraNote: Diluting the serum will result in a positive test if this phenomenon is present.

clozeText: Specific serologic tests like {{c1::FTA-ABS}} involve the use of treponemal antigens.
extraNote: These tests are used for confirmation and remain positive for life after infection.

clozeText: {{c1::Benzathine penicillin G}} is used to treat primary and secondary syphilis because it is released slowly from a depot preparation.
extraNote: A single injection can eradicate the organism due to its slow growth rate.

clozeText: In neurosyphilis, high doses of {{c1::aqueous penicillin G}} are administered because the benzathine form penetrates the CNS poorly.
extraNote: Effective CNS penetration is required for treating tabes or paresis.

clozeText: The {{c1::Jarisch-Herxheimer}} reaction is an acute influenza-like response occurring hours after starting syphilis treatment.
extraNote: It is attributed to the lysis of treponemes and the release of endotoxin-like substances.

clozeText: {{c1::Tumor necrosis factor (TNF)}} is an important mediator of the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction.
extraNote: Passive immunization with antibody against this mediator can prevent reaction symptoms.

clozeText: Borrelia burgdorferi is the causative agent of {{c1::Lyme disease}} and is transmitted via a tick bite.
extraNote: Diagnosis involves clinical observations and microscopy with Giemsa stain.

clozeText: The mode of transmission for Borrelia recurrentis (relapsing fever) is a {{c1::louse}} bite.
extraNote: Borrelia hermsii and Borrelia miyamotoi also cause relapsing fever via different vectors.

clozeText: Leptospira interrogans is transmitted through food or drink contaminated with the {{c1::urine}} of infected animals.
extraNote: Common reservoirs include rats, dogs, pigs, and cows.

clozeText: Treponema pallidum is a {{c1::human}} organism only, with no known animal reservoir.
extraNote: Transmission is primarily through intimate sexual contact or across the placenta.

clozeText: During the {{c1::late latent}} period of syphilis, which can last for years, patients are not infectious and show no symptoms.
extraNote: In contrast, patients in the early latent period can still infect others.

clozeText: Early stage Lyme disease is typically treated with {{c1::doxycycline}} or amoxicillin.
extraNote: Late stage Lyme disease may require penicillin G.

clozeText: Leptospira species are characterized morphologically as {{c1::thin, tight spirals}} seen by dark-field illumination.
extraNote: They can be grown in certain bacteriologic media, unlike Treponema pallidum.

clozeText: Nonvenereal treponematoses are transmitted by {{c1::direct contact}} and are endemic in certain populations.
extraNote: The causative spirochetes are virtually indistinguishable from T. pallidum.

clozeText: For diagnosing syphilis in a neonate, a higher titer of antibody in the {{c1::VDRL}} test compared to the mother suggests true infection.
extraNote: If the result is due to maternal antibody transfer, the titer will decline over time.

clozeText: Treponemes and leptospirae are so thin that they are seen only by {{c1::dark-field}} microscopy, silver impregnation, or immunofluorescence.
extraNote: They are too thin to be visualized by standard light microscopy or Gram staining.

clozeText: Unlike other spirochetes, {{c1::Borreliae::genus}} are larger and can be seen in the standard light microscope using Giemsa or other blood stains.
extraNote: This genus includes the agents of Lyme disease and relapsing fever.

clozeText: Treponema pallidum has {{c1::not::grown/not grown}} been grown on bacteriologic media or in cell culture.
extraNote: In contrast, nonpathogenic treponemes of the normal flora can be cultured.

clozeText: Treponema pallidum grows {{c1::very slowly}}, requiring antibiotics to be present at effective levels for several weeks for a cure.
extraNote: The slow growth rate dictates the use of long-acting depot penicillin preparations.

clozeText: {{c1::Benzathine penicillin G}} is used to treat primary and secondary syphilis because it is a depot preparation released very slowly over weeks.
extraNote: This ensures bactericidal concentrations are maintained long enough to kill the slow-growing T. pallidum.

clozeText: Nonspecific antibodies in syphilis, termed {{c1::reagin}}, are detected by the flocculation of {{c2::cardiolipin}} extracted from mammalian tissues.
extraNote: Cardiolipin is typically extracted from beef heart for use in these tests.

clozeText: T. pallidum often infects the endothelium of small blood vessels, causing {{c1::endarteritis}} during all stages of syphilis.
extraNote: This vascular damage is particularly important in the pathogenesis of tertiary syphilis lesions.

clozeText: The primary stage of syphilis is characterized by the formation of a local, nontender ulcer called a {{c1::chancre}}.
extraNote: The chancre typically heals spontaneously in 2 to 10 weeks even without treatment.

clozeText: Secondary syphilis often presents with a maculopapular rash, notably on the {{c1::palms}} and {{c2::soles}}.
extraNote: Moist papules on the genitals called condylomata lata may also appear during this stage.

clozeText: Highly infectious, moist perianal or genital lesions seen in secondary syphilis are known as {{c1::condylomata lata}}.
extraNote: These lesions are rich in spirochetes and heal spontaneously.

clozeText: Tertiary syphilis may manifest as granulomas of the skin and bones known as {{c1::gummas}}.
extraNote: Treponemes are rarely seen within these tertiary lesions.

clozeText: Cardiovascular lesions of tertiary syphilis include {{c1::aortitis}} or an aneurysm of the {{c2::ascending}} aorta.
extraNote: This is a consequence of the underlying endarteritis caused by the spirochete.

clozeText: Congenital syphilis may result in neonates developing dental deformities such as {{c1::Hutchinson’s teeth}} or {{c2::mulberry molars}}.
extraNote: Other findings include saber shins, saddle nose, and eighth nerve deafness.

clozeText: The forward bowing of the tibias in congenital syphilis is referred to as {{c1::saber shins}}.
extraNote: This is one of several characteristic bone and skin lesions of infected neonates.

clozeText: Nonspecific serologic tests for syphilis, such as {{c1::VDRL::acronym}} and {{c1::RPR::acronym}}, detect antibodies to cardiolipin.
extraNote: These tests are inexpensive and used for population screening.

clozeText: The titer of nonspecific syphilis antibodies (e.g., VDRL) {{c1::decreases}} with effective treatment.
extraNote: In contrast, specific treponemal antibodies usually remain positive for life.

clozeText: A false-negative result in nonspecific syphilis tests due to excessively high antibody titers is called the {{c1::prozone phenomenon}}.
extraNote: Diluting the serum will cause the test result to become positive.

clozeText: Specific treponemal tests like {{c1::FTA-ABS::acronym}} and TPPA remain {{c2::positive for life}} after effective treatment.
extraNote: Because they remain positive, they cannot be used to monitor response to treatment or diagnose reinfection.

clozeText: While benzathine penicillin G is standard for early syphilis, {{c1::aqueous penicillin G}} is used for neurosyphilis because it penetrates the CNS better.
extraNote: High doses are required to reach therapeutic levels in the central nervous system.

clozeText: The {{c1::Jarisch-Herxheimer}} reaction is a flu-like response occurring hours after syphilis treatment due to the lysis of spirochetes.
extraNote: It is caused by the release of endotoxin-like substances and is mediated by TNF.

clozeText: The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is primarily mediated by {{c1::tumor necrosis factor (TNF)}}.
extraNote: Passive immunization with anti-TNF antibodies can prevent the symptoms.

clozeText: Borrelia burgdorferi, the cause of Lyme disease, is transmitted to humans via a {{c1::tick}} bite.
extraNote: The organism is large enough to be seen with Giemsa stain on a standard light microscope.

clozeText: The spirochete responsible for relapsing fever, which is transmitted by a louse bite, is {{c1::Borrelia recurrentis}}.
extraNote: Like other Borreliae, it is large and loosely coiled.

clozeText: Leptospirosis is caused by {{c1::Leptospira interrogans}}, which is transmitted via food or drink contaminated with the {{c2::urine}} of infected animals.
extraNote: Common animal reservoirs include rats, dogs, pigs, and cows.

clozeText: Treponema pallidum is a human organism only, meaning there is no {{c1::animal reservoir}}.
extraNote: This differs from Leptospira and some Borrelia species which have animal hosts.

clozeText: Neurosyphilis manifests in the tertiary stage as conditions like {{c1::tabes}} or {{c2::paresis}}.
extraNote: These represent central nervous system involvement by the spirochetes.

clozeText: The diagnosis of congenital syphilis in an infant is suggested if the infant has a {{c1::higher}} VDRL titer than the mother.
extraNote: If the titer remains high over time, it indicates active infection rather than passive transfer of maternal antibodies.

clozeText: Unlike other spirochetes, {{c1::Borreliae}} are larger and can be seen in the standard light microscope using Giemsa or blood stains.
extraNote: This genus includes the causative agents of Lyme disease and relapsing fever.

clozeText: The three genera of spirochetes that cause human infection are {{c1::Treponema}}, {{c1::Borrelia}}, and {{c2::Leptospira}}.
extraNote: Treponema causes syphilis; Borrelia causes Lyme disease/relapsing fever; Leptospira causes leptospirosis.

clozeText: Effective treatment of syphilis requires antibiotics to be present for several weeks because T. pallidum grows {{c1::very slowly}}.
extraNote: Bactericidal concentrations must be maintained for long durations to achieve a cure.

clozeText: T. pallidum often infects the endothelium of small blood vessels, causing {{c1::endarteritis}}.
extraNote: This vascular pathology is especially important in the development of tertiary syphilis lesions.

clozeText: In primary syphilis, the spirochetes multiply at the site of inoculation and form a local, nontender ulcer called a {{c1::chancre}}.
extraNote: The lesion typically forms in 2 to 10 weeks and heals spontaneously.

clozeText: The maculopapular rash of secondary syphilis is notable for appearing on the {{c1::palms}} and {{c1::soles}}.
extraNote: This occurs 1 to 3 months after the primary lesion heals.

clozeText: Highly infectious moist papules found on the genitals during secondary syphilis are called {{c1::condylomata lata}}.
extraNote: These lesions are rich in spirochetes and are distinct from viral warts.

clozeText: Tertiary syphilis may manifest as chronic granulomas called {{c1::gummas}}, especially of the skin and bones.
extraNote: Treponemes are rarely seen within these tertiary lesions.

clozeText: Cardiovascular lesions in tertiary syphilis often involve {{c1::aortitis}} or an aneurysm of the ascending aorta.
extraNote: This results from the long-term effects of small vessel endarteritis.

clozeText: Dental abnormalities in congenital syphilis include {{c1::Hutchinson’s teeth}} and mulberry molars.
extraNote: These are part of a wider constellation of findings in infected neonates.

clozeText: Neonatal bone deformities associated with congenital syphilis include {{c1::saber shins}}, saddle nose, and frontal bossing.
extraNote: The organism is transmitted across the placenta, typically after the third month of pregnancy.

clozeText: Nonspecific serologic tests for syphilis (VDRL and RPR) detect antibodies called {{c1::reagin}}.
extraNote: These antibodies react with cardiolipin (beef heart extract).

clozeText: The titer of {{c1::nonspecific (nontreponemal)}} antibodies decreases with effective treatment, while specific antibodies remain positive for life.
extraNote: Decreasing VDRL/RPR titers are used to monitor the patient's response to therapy.

clozeText: False-negative VDRL or RPR results can occur due to the {{c1::prozone phenomenon::antibody excess}}.
extraNote: When the antibody titer is too high, flocculation does not occur until the serum is diluted.

clozeText: Specific treponemal tests like the {{c1::FTA-ABS}} and TPPA involve the use of Treponema pallidum antigens.
extraNote: These tests are used to confirm positive results from nonspecific screening tests.

clozeText: The preferred treatment for primary and secondary syphilis is a single injection of {{c1::benzathine penicillin G}}.
extraNote: This depot preparation releases the drug slowly over several weeks.

clozeText: In the treatment of neurosyphilis, {{c1::aqueous penicillin G}} is used because benzathine penicillin penetrates poorly into the CNS.
extraNote: High doses are required to reach the central nervous system.

clozeText: The {{c1::Jarisch-Herxheimer}} reaction, characterized by fever and chills after antibiotic administration, is attributed to the release of endotoxin-like substances from lysed spirochetes.
extraNote: This reaction is mediated by tumor necrosis factor (TNF) and can occur in syphilis, Lyme disease, and leptospirosis.

clozeText: Mycobacteria are aerobic, {{c1::acid-fast}} bacilli (rods) that are stained poorly by the dyes used in Gram stain.
extraNote: Mycobacteria are virtually the only bacteria that are acid-fast, with Nocardia being a rare exception.

clozeText: The term {{c1::acid-fast}} refers to an organism’s ability to retain {{c2::carbol fuchsin}} stain despite treatment with an ethanol–hydrochloric acid mixture.
extraNote: This property is a hallmark of the genus Mycobacterium.

clozeText: The high lipid content, approximately {{c1::60%}}, of the cell wall makes mycobacteria acid-fast.
extraNote: This high lipid concentration contributes to their staining properties and environmental resistance.

clozeText: {{c1::Löwenstein-Jensen}} medium, which contains complex nutrients like egg yolk and dyes such as malachite green, is used for the growth of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
extraNote: The malachite green dye inhibits the growth of unwanted normal flora in sputum samples.

clozeText: M. tuberculosis is an {{c1::obligate aerobe}}, which explains its predilection for oxygenated tissues like the upper lobe of the lung and the kidney.
extraNote: This explains the specific anatomical locations where clinical disease is often most severe.

clozeText: The acid-fast property of Mycobacterium is attributed to long-chain (C78–C90) fatty acids called {{c1::mycolic acids}} in the cell wall.
extraNote: These long-chain fatty acids are essential structural components unique to this genus.

clozeText: {{c1::Cord factor}} (trehalose dimycolate) is correlated with the virulence of M. tuberculosis, causing it to grow in a serpentine pattern.
extraNote: Avirulent strains of M. tuberculosis do not exhibit this serpentine growth pattern.

clozeText: A lipid in the bacterial cell wall called {{c1::phthiocerol dimycocerosate}} is required for the pathogenesis of M. tuberculosis in the lung.
extraNote: This specific lipid is a key factor for the establishment of pulmonary infection.

clozeText: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is relatively resistant to acids and alkalis; {{c1::NaOH}} is often used to concentrate clinical specimens by destroying unwanted bacteria and human cells.
extraNote: This resistance allows the laboratory to selectively isolate mycobacteria from contaminated sputum samples.

clozeText: Resistance to isoniazid (INH) in M. tuberculosis is often due to a mutation in the gene for {{c1::catalase-peroxidase}}, which is required to activate the drug within the bacterium.
extraNote: INH is a prodrug that must be activated by this specific enzyme to be effective.

clozeText: Resistance to {{c1::rifampin}} in M. tuberculosis is caused by mutations in the gene encoding the bacterial RNA polymerase.
extraNote: This is a common mechanism for multidrug-resistant (MDR) strains.

clozeText: The natural reservoir of M. tuberculosis is {{c1::humans}}.
extraNote: While animals like cattle can be infected, they are not the primary reservoir for human infection.

clozeText: In tissue, M. tuberculosis resides chiefly within {{c1::macrophages}} (reticuloendothelial cells).
extraNote: The organism can survive and multiply within these immune cells if they fail to kill the pathogen.

clozeText: {{c1::Mycobacterium bovis}} can cause gastrointestinal tuberculosis in humans when ingested in unpasteurized cow’s milk.
extraNote: This is a significant cause of TB in developing countries without mandatory milk pasteurization.

clozeText: The tuberculin skin test (PPD) is evaluated by measuring the diameter of {{c1::induration::thickening}} rather than simple erythema (reddening).
extraNote: A positive test is based on the palpable thickening of the skin, mediated by cellular immunity.

clozeText: {{c1::Scrofula}} is mycobacterial cervical lymphadenitis that presents as swollen, nontender lymph nodes, usually unilaterally.
extraNote: While M. tuberculosis is the most common cause, nontuberculous mycobacteria like M. scrofulaceum can also be responsible.

clozeText: {{c1::Erythema nodosum}}, characterized by tender nodules along the extensor surfaces of the tibia, is a manifestation of primary M. tuberculosis infection.
extraNote: This finding indicates a potent cell-mediated immune response against the infection.

clozeText: {{c1::Miliary}} tuberculosis is characterized by multiple disseminated lesions throughout the body that resemble millet seeds.
extraNote: This occurs during hematogenous or lymphatic dissemination of the organism.

clozeText: Vertebral osteomyelitis caused by M. tuberculosis is also known as {{c1::Pott’s disease}}.
extraNote: This is a significant form of disseminated extrapulmonary tuberculosis.

clozeText: Renal tuberculosis often presents with dysuria and hematuria, specifically exhibiting {{c1::sterile pyuria}} where WBCs are present but standard cultures are negative.
extraNote: Standard urinary cultures will not grow Mycobacterium; specific mycobacterial cultures are required.

clozeText: The IGRA test for latent tuberculosis measures the amount of {{c1::interferon-gamma}} released from a patient’s lymphocytes after exposure to M. tuberculosis antigens.
extraNote: This test requires only a single blood specimen and uses an ELISA for detection.

clozeText: The BCG vaccine contains a strain of live, attenuated {{c1::Mycobacterium bovis}}.
extraNote: It is used primarily in high-incidence areas to prevent clinical disease in children.

clozeText: Mycobacterium tuberculosis grows slowly, with a doubling time of approximately {{c1::18 hours}}.
extraNote: Most common bacteria double in 1 hour or less, making TB culture a lengthy process.

clozeText: The proteins in the {{c1::purified protein derivative (PPD)}} test elicit a delayed hypersensitivity response when combined with waxes in the cell wall.
extraNote: This response is the basis for the tuberculin skin test.

clozeText: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is resistant to {{c1::dehydration}}, which allows it to survive in dried expectorated sputum for aerosol transmission.
extraNote: This environmental stability facilitates spread through respiratory droplets.

clozeText: The atypical mycobacterium {{c1::Mycobacterium kansasii}} can cause a tuberculosis-like disease in humans but is less frequent than M. tuberculosis.
extraNote: It is typically found in soil and water sources.

clozeText: {{c1::Mycobacterium leprae}} is a major pathogen that causes leprosy and, unlike M. tuberculosis, cannot be cultured on bacteriologic media.
extraNote: Its inability to grow in vitro distinguishes it from most other mycobacteria.

clozeText: Rapidly growing mycobacteria, such as {{c1::Mycobacterium chelonae}}, occasionally cause disease in immunocompromised patients or those with prosthetic devices.
extraNote: These species grow in days rather than the weeks required for M. tuberculosis.

clozeText: Tuberculin reactivity (the PPD response) is mediated by the cellular arm of the immune system and can be transferred by {{c1::CD4-positive T cells}}.
extraNote: Serum cannot transfer this reactivity, confirming it is a cell-mediated rather than humoral response.

clozeText: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is highly resistant to {{c1::chromosomal}} mutations that lead to drug resistance because it lacks plasmids.
extraNote: Resistance to isoniazid and rifampin is specifically due to these chromosomal changes.

clozeText: The high {{c1::lipid}} content, approximately 60%, of the Mycobacterium cell wall is responsible for its acid-fast staining property.
extraNote: Acid-fastness refers to the ability to retain carbol fuchsin stain despite treatment with an ethanol-hydrochloric acid mixture.

clozeText: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is an {{c1::obligate aerobe}}, which explains its predilection for highly oxygenated tissues like the upper lobe of the lung and the kidney.
extraNote: The organism requires oxygen for growth; its doubling time is slow, approximately 18 hours.

clozeText: The virulence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis is correlated with {{c1::cord factor::trehalose dimycolate}}, which causes the organism to grow in a serpentine pattern.
extraNote: Virulent strains exhibit this characteristic cordlike growth, while avirulent strains do not.

clozeText: The cell wall of Mycobacterium contains long-chain fatty acids called {{c1::mycolic acids}} (C78–C90).
extraNote: These fatty acids are a primary contributor to the acid-fast property of the genus.

clozeText: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is cultured on {{c1::Löwenstein-Jensen}} medium, which contains egg yolk and malachite green.
extraNote: Malachite green is a dye added to inhibit the growth of unwanted normal flora in sputum samples.

clozeText: Resistance to isoniazid (INH) in M. tuberculosis is often due to mutations in the gene for {{c1::catalase-peroxidase}}, the enzyme required to activate the drug.
extraNote: INH is a prodrug that must be activated within the bacterium to inhibit mycolic acid synthesis.

clozeText: Chromosomal mutations, rather than {{c1::plasmids}}, are responsible for antibiotic resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
extraNote: No plasmids have been found in this organism; multidrug resistance (MDR) is exclusively chromosomal.

clozeText: Resistance to rifampin in M. tuberculosis is caused by mutations in the gene encoding {{c1::RNA polymerase}}.
extraNote: Rifampin targets the bacterial RNA polymerase to inhibit transcription.

clozeText: A lipid in the cell wall called {{c1::phthiocerol dimycocerosate}} is specifically required for Mycobacterium tuberculosis pathogenesis in the lung.
extraNote: This is a key lipid virulence factor for pulmonary infection.

clozeText: In tissue, Mycobacterium tuberculosis resides primarily within {{c1::macrophages::immune cell type}}.
extraNote: It is an intracellular pathogen that can survive and replicate within the reticuloendothelial system.

clozeText: {{c1::Mycobacterium bovis}} can cause gastrointestinal tuberculosis in humans if ingested via unpasteurized cow's milk.
extraNote: This species is found in cattle and was a major cause of TB before the advent of pasteurization.

clozeText: Mycobacterial cervical lymphadenitis, presenting as swollen and nontender lymph nodes, is known as {{c1::scrofula}}.
extraNote: While M. tuberculosis is the most common cause, atypical mycobacteria like M. scrofulaceum can also be responsible.

clozeText: Renal tuberculosis often presents with {{c1::sterile pyuria}}, where white blood cells are present in urine but standard cultures show no growth.
extraNote: Mycobacterial cultures are required to detect the organism in these cases.

clozeText: Vertebral osteomyelitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis is specifically referred to as {{c1::Pott’s disease}}.
extraNote: This is a form of disseminated extrapulmonary tuberculosis affecting the spine.

clozeText: The {{c1::IGRA::test name}} measures the amount of interferon-γ released from a patient's lymphocytes to detect latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection.
extraNote: This test only requires a single blood specimen and is an alternative to the PPD skin test.

clozeText: The BCG vaccine is a live, attenuated strain of {{c1::Mycobacterium bovis}}.
extraNote: BCG stands for Bacillus Calmette-Guérin; it provides partial resistance and is used mainly in high-incidence areas.

clozeText: Positive results for a PPD skin test are determined by measuring the diameter of {{c1::induration::physical sign}}, not erythema.
extraNote: Induration refers to the thickening or hardening of the skin at the injection site.

clozeText: {{c1::Mycobacterium leprae}} is unique among important mycobacteria because it cannot be grown on bacteriologic media.
extraNote: It requires living systems or specialized animal models (like armadillos) for growth.

clozeText: The atypical {{c1::Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare}} complex (MAC) can cause tuberculosis-like disease, particularly in immunocompromised patients.
extraNote: MAC is often soil- and water-borne and is a frequent pathogen in AIDS patients.

clozeText: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is relatively resistant to {{c1::NaOH::chemical}}, which is used to concentrate clinical specimens by destroying other bacteria and mucus.
extraNote: This property allows for the selective isolation of the organism from sputum samples.

clozeText: {{c1::Erythema nodosum::skin sign}} is a manifestation of primary M. tuberculosis infection, appearing as tender nodules on the extensor surfaces of the tibia.
extraNote: It indicates a potent cell-mediated immune response to the infection.

clozeText: Disseminated tuberculosis lesions that resemble millet seeds are characteristic of {{c1::miliary}} tuberculosis.
extraNote: This form represents widespread hematogenous spread of the bacilli.

clozeText: The purified protein derivative (PPD) used in skin testing consists of proteins from the organism combined with {{c1::waxes}}.
extraNote: These components elicit a delayed hypersensitivity reaction in previously infected individuals.

clozeText: Tuberculin reactivity (PPD response) is mediated by {{c1::CD4-positive T cells}}.
extraNote: This cellular immunity can be transferred by T cells but not by serum/antibodies.

clozeText: Rapidly growing mycobacteria, such as {{c1::Mycobacterium chelonae}}, occasionally cause disease associated with prosthetic device implants.
extraNote: Unlike M. tuberculosis, these species grow within days rather than weeks.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::90}}% of individuals infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis remain asymptomatic.
extraNote: These asymptomatic cases are considered latent tuberculosis infections.

clozeText: The preferred in vivo growth temperature for Mycobacterium leprae is {{c1::32}}°C, which explains its predilection for skin and nerves.
extraNote: Most other pathogenic mycobacteria prefer 37°C.

clozeText: The primary site of infection for both M. tuberculosis and M. avium-intracellulare is the {{c1::lungs}}.
extraNote: While both affect the lungs, M. leprae primarily affects the skin and nerves.

clozeText: BCG vaccine can be used to treat {{c1::bladder cancer}} by nonspecifically stimulating cell-mediated immunity.
extraNote: The vaccine is instilled directly into the bladder for this therapeutic purpose.

clozeText: The initial site of infection for Mycobacterium tuberculosis is the respiratory tract, specifically the {{c1::lung}}.
extraNote: Transmission occurs via respiratory aerosols produced by coughing.

clozeText: Acid-fastness is due to the high {{c1::lipid}} content (approximately 60%) in the cell wall of Mycobacterium.
extraNote: The organism retains carbol fuchsin stain even after treatment with ethanol–hydrochloric acid due to these cell wall lipids.

clozeText: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is an {{c1::obligate aerobe}}, which explains its predilection for oxygenated tissues like the {{c2::upper lobe}} of the lung and the kidney.
extraNote: This high oxygen requirement drives the tropism for specific organs and anatomical sites.

clozeText: The acid-fast property of mycobacteria is specifically attributed to long-chain fatty acids called {{c1::mycolic acids}} (C78–C90) found in the cell wall.
extraNote: These long-chain fatty acids are structural hallmarks of the genus Mycobacterium.

clozeText: {{c1::Cord factor::Virulence factor}} (trehalose dimycolate) is correlated with the virulence of M. tuberculosis and causes virulent strains to grow in a serpentine pattern.
extraNote: Avirulent strains do not exhibit this characteristic serpentine growth pattern.

clozeText: M. tuberculosis cultures on {{c1::Löwenstein-Jensen}} medium must be held for {{c2::6 to 8::timeframe}} weeks before being recorded as negative.
extraNote: The slow growth (doubling time of 18 hours) necessitates long incubation periods compared to most bacteria.

clozeText: {{c1::Scrofula}} is mycobacterial cervical lymphadenitis that typically presents as unilaterally swollen, nontender lymph nodes.
extraNote: While M. tuberculosis is the most common cause, nontuberculous mycobacteria like M. scrofulaceum can also be responsible.

clozeText: {{c1::Pott’s disease}} refers to tuberculous osteomyelitis specifically involving the {{c2::vertebral body}}.
extraNote: This is a significant disseminated form of the disease.

clozeText: Renal tuberculosis characteristically presents with {{c1::sterile pyuria}}, where urine contains white blood cells but cultures for common bacterial pathogens show no growth.
extraNote: Mycobacterial cultures should be requested if standard cultures are negative despite symptoms of dysuria and hematuria.

clozeText: {{c1::Erythema nodosum}}, characterized by tender nodules along the extensor surfaces of the tibia, is a manifestation of primary infection seen in patients with a potent {{c2::cell-mediated}} response.
extraNote: It is an immunological manifestation of the host attempting to control the infection.

clozeText: Gastrointestinal tuberculosis can be caused by the ingestion of {{c1::Mycobacterium bovis}} in unpasteurized milk.
extraNote: It can also be caused by M. tuberculosis if the organism is swallowed after being coughed up from a lung lesion.

clozeText: In reactivation tuberculosis, chest X-ray findings typically include an infiltrate in the {{c1::upper lobe}} with or without a {{c2::cavity}}.
extraNote: Reactivation typically occurs in adult life and favors the well-oxygenated upper lobes.

clozeText: The {{c1::Interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA)}} measures the amount of IFN-γ released from lymphocytes to detect latent infections.
extraNote: This test requires only a single blood specimen and is used as a laboratory alternative to the skin test.

clozeText: {{c1::Miliary}} tuberculosis is characterized by multiple disseminated lesions that resemble millet seeds.
extraNote: This occurs following severe bacteremia and hematogenous dissemination.

clozeText: The primary site of involvement in gastrointestinal tuberculosis is the {{c1::ileocecal}} region.
extraNote: Common symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, fever, and weight loss.

clozeText: The {{c1::Purified protein derivative (PPD)}} skin test involves the injection of proteins which, when combined with waxes, elicit {{c2::delayed hypersensitivity}}.
extraNote: A positive test is determined by induration (thickening), not just erythema (reddening).

clozeText: Nongonococcal conjunctivitis in infants is caused by {{c1::Chlamydia trachomatis}} and is acquired during passage through the birth canal.
extraNote: This organism is a major cause of neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) alongside Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

clozeText: Infants acquire nongonococcal conjunctivitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis during {{c1::passage through the birth canal}}.
extraNote: Transmission occurs from the infected mother to the newborn during delivery.

clozeText: {{c1::Chlamydia trachomatis::Organism}} is a common cause of nongonococcal urethritis and can often coexist with gonorrhea infections.
extraNote: Appropriate diagnostic and therapeutic measures must be taken for both infections when they coexist.

clozeText: To treat a possible coinfection with Chlamydia trachomatis, {{c1::doxycycline}} should be added to the single-dose ceftriaxone used for gonorrhea.
extraNote: Coinfection is common, necessitating a dual-antibiotic approach in many treatment guidelines.

clozeText: If a patient is pregnant and requires treatment for a suspected chlamydial infection, {{c1::azithromycin}} can be used instead of doxycycline.
extraNote: Azithromycin serves as a safe and effective alternative for chlamydial coverage during pregnancy.

clozeText: The treatment of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) typically includes a combination of cefoxitin and {{c1::doxycycline}} to provide coverage for Chlamydia trachomatis.
extraNote: PID is often an ascending infection that requires hospitalization and complex antibiotic regimens.

clozeText: Partner therapy for individuals exposed to gonorrhea frequently involves a combination of oral cefixime and {{c1::doxycycline}} to cover potential {{c2::Chlamydia}} infection.
extraNote: The addition of doxycycline specifically targets the nongonococcal component of the infection.

clozeText: Neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) has two primary bacterial causes: Neisseria gonorrhoeae and {{c1::Chlamydia trachomatis}}.
extraNote: Chlamydial conjunctivitis is considered nongonococcal and is acquired during birth.

clozeText: {{c1::Chlamydia trachomatis}} is a leading cause of nongonococcal conjunctivitis, which infants acquire during passage through the birth canal.
extraNote: Nongonococcal conjunctivitis is a significant cause of neonatal eye infection alongside Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

clozeText: Neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) is commonly caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae or {{c1::Chlamydia trachomatis}}.
extraNote: Infections are typically acquired from the mother during delivery through the birth canal.

clozeText: To treat possible coinfection with Chlamydia trachomatis in a patient with gonorrhea, {{c1::doxycycline}} should be added to the regimen.
extraNote: Doxycycline is routinely added to ceftriaxone to cover potential chlamydial infection due to high rates of coexistence.

clozeText: {{c1::Chlamydia trachomatis}} is a primary cause of nongonococcal urethritis, which can coexist with gonorrhea.
extraNote: Clinicians must take appropriate diagnostic and therapeutic measures for both organisms when treating sexually transmitted infections.

clozeText: In cases of uncomplicated gonorrhea, ceftriaxone is the drug of choice, but {{c1::doxycycline}} must be added to address suspected chlamydial infection.
extraNote: Azithromycin may be used as an alternative if the patient is pregnant.

clozeText: {{c1::Nongonococcal}} conjunctivitis is typically caused by Chlamydia trachomatis.
extraNote: In infants, this is acquired during passage through the birth canal.

clozeText: Infants acquire Chlamydia trachomatis conjunctivitis during passage through the {{c1::birth canal}}.
extraNote: This condition is often contrasted with gonococcal conjunctivitis acquired via the same route.

clozeText: Along with Neisseria gonorrhoeae, {{c1::Chlamydia trachomatis}} is a common cause of neonatal conjunctivitis.
extraNote: Neonatal conjunctivitis is also known as ophthalmia neonatorum.

clozeText: Chlamydia trachomatis is a primary cause of {{c1::nongonococcal urethritis::syndrome}}.
extraNote: This infection frequently coexists with gonorrhea, requiring simultaneous diagnostic and therapeutic measures.

clozeText: When treating gonorrhea with ceftriaxone, {{c1::doxycycline}} should be added to treat a possible chlamydial infection.
extraNote: Dual therapy is common due to high rates of coinfection between these two organisms.

clozeText: If a patient with a suspected chlamydial infection is {{c1::pregnant}}, azithromycin can be used for treatment.
extraNote: Azithromycin is an alternative to doxycycline in this specific patient population.

clozeText: Partner therapy for suspected chlamydial and gonococcal infection may involve oral {{c1::cefixime}} plus doxycycline.
extraNote: Prompt treatment of sex partners is a key prevention strategy.

clozeText: One of the two most important causes of {{c1::ophthalmia neonatorum::condition}} is Chlamydia trachomatis.
extraNote: The other common cause is Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

clozeText: Doxycycline is indicated for possible {{c1::coinfection}} with Chlamydia trachomatis in patients diagnosed with gonorrhea.
extraNote: Appropriate measures must be taken because both sexually transmitted infections can coexist.

clozeText: For the treatment of uncomplicated urogenital gonorrhea, a single dose of ceftriaxone is used, and {{c1::doxycycline}} is added for possible chlamydial coverage.
extraNote: This regimen covers both Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis.

clozeText: {{c1::Chlamydia trachomatis}} is the primary cause of nongonococcal conjunctivitis in infants.
extraNote: In contrast, gonococcal conjunctivitis is caused by N. gonorrhoeae.

clozeText: In cases of gonorrhea, {{c1::doxycycline}} is added to the treatment regimen to address possible coinfection with Chlamydia trachomatis.
extraNote: Ceftriaxone is used for the gonococcal portion, while doxycycline covers Chlamydia.

clozeText: For pregnant patients with a chlamydial infection, {{c1::azithromycin}} is the recommended alternative to doxycycline.
extraNote: Azithromycin is used when doxycycline is contraindicated due to pregnancy.

clozeText: Chlamydia trachomatis is the causative agent of {{c1::nongonococcal urethritis}}, which often coexists with gonorrhea.
extraNote: Patients should be tested for both pathogens when presenting with urethral symptoms.

clozeText: The recommended partner therapy for gonorrhea and potential chlamydial coinfection is oral cefixime plus {{c1::doxycycline}}.
extraNote: This combination ensures both N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis are treated in asymptomatic partners.

clozeText: Along with Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis is a major cause of {{c1::ophthalmia neonatorum}} (neonatal conjunctivitis).
extraNote: Prophylactic erythromycin eye ointment is typically used at birth to prevent these infections.

clozeText: To treat pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), {{c1::doxycycline}} is typically added to cefoxitin to provide coverage for Chlamydia trachomatis.
extraNote: PID treatment requires broad coverage for both gonococci and chlamydiae.

clozeText: Nongonococcal urethritis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis can coexist with other sexually transmitted infections, such as {{c1::syphilis}} and gonorrhea.
extraNote: Comprehensive STI screening is necessary when one infection is identified.

clozeText: A single dose of ceftriaxone is used for gonorrhea, but {{c1::doxycycline::drug}} must be added to treat possible chlamydial infection.
extraNote: Dual therapy has been standard due to high rates of coinfection.

clozeText: {{c1::Chlamydia trachomatis}} is identified as a common cause of neonatal conjunctivitis that presents with purulent discharge.
extraNote: It is one of the two most common bacterial causes alongside N. gonorrhoeae.

clozeText: In neonatal conjunctivitis, the presence of {{c1::Chlamydia trachomatis}} is a differential diagnosis when purulent exudate is observed shortly after birth.
extraNote: Passage through the birth canal is the route of infection.

clozeText: When treating uncomplicated urogenital gonorrhea, adding {{c1::doxycycline}} is necessary specifically to cover {{c2::Chlamydia}}.
extraNote: Ceftriaxone alone does not provide adequate coverage for C. trachomatis.

clozeText: For patients allergic to penicillins or cephalosporins being treated for gonorrhea and possible chlamydia, a regimen of {{c1::gentamicin}} plus {{c2::azithromycin}} may be used.
extraNote: Azithromycin provides the necessary chlamydial coverage in this alternative regimen.

clozeText: Rickettsia are {{c1::obligate intracellular::lifestyle}} bacteria because they are unable to produce sufficient {{c2::energy::ATP}} to replicate extracellularly.
extraNote: They must be grown in cell culture, embryonated eggs, or experimental animals.

clozeText: Rickettsia species divide by {{c1::binary fission}} within the host cell.
extraNote: This distinguishes them from Chlamydia, which has a more complex intracellular cycle.

clozeText: The cell wall of Rickettsia structurally resembles that of {{c1::gram-negative}} rods, although they stain poorly with the standard Gram stain.
extraNote: Morphologically, they appear as very short rods barely visible by light microscopy.

clozeText: The {{c1::Weil-Felix}} test is a serologic assay based on the cross-reactivity between rickettsial antigens and the OX strains of {{c2::Proteus vulgaris}}.
extraNote: Antigens OX-2, OX-19, and OX-K are commonly used to detect antirickettsial antibodies.

clozeText: Rickettsia primarily infect the {{c1::endothelium::cell type}} of the blood vessel walls, leading to bacteremia.
extraNote: This infection pattern causes the characteristic vasculitis observed in rickettsial diseases.

clozeText: The typical pathological lesion in rickettsial infection is {{c1::vasculitis}}, which causes increased capillary permeability, edema, and hemorrhage.
extraNote: Damage to the blood vessels in the skin results in the characteristic rash.

clozeText: With the exception of epidemic typhus, all rickettsial diseases are {{c1::zoonoses}}, meaning they have an animal reservoir.
extraNote: Epidemic typhus is the only rickettsial disease that occurs strictly in humans.

clozeText: Rickettsia rickettsii is the causative agent of {{c1::Rocky Mountain spotted fever}}.
extraNote: Despite the name, it is most common in southeastern states like North Carolina.

clozeText: The primary vector for Rickettsia rickettsii in the Eastern United States is the {{c1::dog tick}} ({{c2::Dermacentor variabilis}}).
extraNote: In the Western U.S., the wood tick (Dermacentor andersoni) is the primary vector.

clozeText: Rickettsia rickettsii is maintained in tick populations through {{c1::transovarian}} transmission.
extraNote: The organism is passed from the adult tick to its eggs, resulting in a lifetime infection of the tick.

clozeText: The rash of Rocky Mountain spotted fever typically begins on the {{c1::hands and feet}} and moves {{c2::inward::direction}} toward the trunk.
extraNote: The rash usually appears 2 to 6 days after the onset of fever and headache.

clozeText: Rickettsia prowazekii causes {{c1::epidemic typhus}}, a disease associated with crowded and unsanitary conditions.
extraNote: It is a life-threatening disease often seen during wartime or famine.

clozeText: The vector for Rickettsia prowazekii is the {{c1::human body louse}} ({{c2::Pediculus::genus}}).
extraNote: The organism is excreted in louse feces and enters the human via scratching the bite.

clozeText: The rash of epidemic typhus begins on the {{c1::trunk}} and spreads {{c2::peripherally::direction}}.
extraNote: Unlike Rocky Mountain spotted fever, this rash typically spares the face, palms, and soles.

clozeText: {{c1::Brill-Zinsser}} disease is a recurrent, milder form of epidemic typhus that can occur decades after the primary infection.
extraNote: The organism persists in the body and can be reactivated by intercurrent disease.

clozeText: Rickettsia typhi is the causative agent of {{c1::endemic (murine) typhus}}.
extraNote: It is found in small numbers in the southern regions of California and Texas.

clozeText: The vector for Rickettsia typhi is the {{c1::flea}}, and the primary mammalian reservoir is the {{c2::rat}}.
extraNote: This disease is also known as murine typhus.

clozeText: Rickettsia akari is transmitted by {{c1::mites}} and causes {{c2::rickettsial pox}}.
extraNote: The mammalian reservoir for Rickettsia akari is the mouse.

clozeText: Rickettsia tsutsugamushi (Orientia tsutsugamushi) is transmitted by {{c1::mites (chiggers)}} and causes {{c2::scrub typhus}}.
extraNote: It is primarily found in developing countries and Asia.

clozeText: Laboratory diagnosis of Rickettsia usually relies on a {{c1::fourfold}} or greater rise in antibody titer between acute and convalescent serum samples.
extraNote: Diagnosis is often retrospective since the convalescent sample is taken 2 weeks after the acute phase.

clozeText: The most commonly used serologic tests for Rickettsia are {{c1::indirect immunofluorescence}} and {{c2::ELISA}}.
extraNote: The Weil-Felix test is now considered of historic interest due to low specificity.

clozeText: A single acute-phase antibody titer of {{c1::1:128}} or greater is accepted as presumptive evidence of a rickettsial infection if the clinical picture is typical.
extraNote: Prompt treatment is essential and should not be delayed for laboratory confirmation.

clozeText: In the acute phase of Rocky Mountain spotted fever, a diagnosis can be made using an immunofluorescence assay on tissue from the {{c1::petechial rash}}.
extraNote: This provides a faster diagnosis than waiting for antibody titer rises.

clozeText: Rocky Mountain spotted fever symptoms include the sudden onset of fever, severe headache, and {{c1::myalgias}}.
extraNote: CNS changes like delirium and coma can occur in severe cases.

clozeText: The severe headache in rickettsial diseases is caused by {{c1::vasculitis}} of the blood vessels in the {{c2::brain}}.
extraNote: Endothelial damage in the CNS leads to neurologic symptoms.

clozeText: Rickettsial diseases may lead to {{c1::disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)}}, edema, and circulatory collapse in severe cases.
extraNote: These complications are often due to systemic vascular damage.

clozeText: Rocky Mountain spotted fever accounts for {{c1::95}}% of rickettsial diseases in the United States.
extraNote: There are approximately 1000 cases reported per year.

clozeText: Outbreaks of endemic typhus in large U.S. cities have been reported among the {{c1::homeless}} population.
extraNote: This is caused by Rickettsia typhi and associated with rat and flea exposure.

clozeText: Rickettsia prowazekii is transmitted to humans when the louse bite is {{c1::scratched}}, leading to autoinoculation of louse {{c2::feces}}.
extraNote: The infected louse dies after a few weeks; humans are a required stage in its life cycle.

clozeText: The primary method of Rickettsia replication is {{c1::binary fission}}, occurring inside the host cell {{c2::cytoplasm::location}}.
extraNote: They are unable to grow on non-living media.

clozeText: Rickettsiae are {{c1::obligate intracellular}} parasites because they are unable to produce sufficient energy to replicate extracellularly.
extraNote: This characteristic requires the organism to be grown in cell culture, embryonated eggs, or experimental animals.

clozeText: Rickettsiae divide by {{c1::binary fission}} within the host cell, distinguishing them from the replication cycle of Chlamydiae.
extraNote: Unlike Chlamydiae, Rickettsiae do not follow a complex life cycle with different forms like elementary bodies.

clozeText: The {{c1::Weil-Felix}} test detects antirickettsial antibodies in a patient's serum by agglutination of {{c2::Proteus vulgaris::organism}} OX strains.
extraNote: This test is based on the cross-reaction between rickettsial antigens and Proteus O antigens (OX-2, OX-19, and OX-K).

clozeText: Rickettsiae primarily infect the {{c1::endothelium}} of blood vessel walls.
extraNote: This tropism leads to the characteristic vasculitis seen in rickettsial diseases.

clozeText: Virtually all rickettsial diseases are zoonoses, with the prominent exception of {{c1::epidemic typhus::disease}}, which occurs only in humans.
extraNote: Humans are the only reservoir for Rickettsia prowazekii.

clozeText: Rickettsia rickettsii causes {{c1::Rocky Mountain spotted fever}}, which occurs primarily in the southeastern United States.
extraNote: Despite the name, states like North Carolina, Virginia, and Georgia have high incidence rates.

clozeText: Rickettsia prowazekii causes {{c1::epidemic typhus}}, a disease often associated with crowded, unsanitary conditions during wartime.
extraNote: It is transmitted via the human body louse.

clozeText: Structurally, rickettsial cell walls resemble {{c1::gram-negative rods}}, although they stain poorly with the standard Gram stain.
extraNote: They are very short rods and are barely visible under light microscopy.

clozeText: The typical lesion caused by pathogenic rickettsiae is {{c1::vasculitis}}, particularly in the endothelial lining of vessel walls.
extraNote: Damage results in increased capillary permeability, leading to edema and hemorrhage.

clozeText: Rickettsial vasculitis of the vessels in the {{c1::brain}} leads to the prominent headache seen in these patients.
extraNote: Severe cases can progress to delirium and coma.

clozeText: The rash in Rocky Mountain spotted fever typically begins on the {{c1::hands and feet}} and then moves inward to the trunk.
extraNote: This centripetal spread is characteristic and often progresses from macules to petechiae.

clozeText: In the eastern United States, Rickettsia rickettsii is transmitted by the dog tick, {{c1::Dermacentor variabilis}}.
extraNote: In the western United States, the vector is the wood tick, Dermacentor andersoni.

clozeText: The rash in epidemic typhus begins on the {{c1::trunk}} and spreads peripherally, specifically sparing the {{c2::face, palms, and soles}}.
extraNote: This spread pattern is the opposite of that seen in Rocky Mountain spotted fever.

clozeText: Epidemic typhus is transmitted by the human body louse, {{c1::Pediculus}}.
extraNote: The organism is excreted in louse feces and autoinoculated when the host scratches the bite.

clozeText: {{c1::Brill-Zinsser::disease}} is a recurrent form of epidemic typhus that can appear up to 50 years after the primary infection.
extraNote: It is less severe and rarely fatal compared to the primary infection.

clozeText: Rickettsia typhi causes {{c1::endemic (murine)}} typhus, which is transmitted by fleas.
extraNote: The primary mammalian reservoir for this organism is rats.

clozeText: Rickettsia akari causes {{c1::rickettsialpox}}, a rare disease transmitted by mites with a mouse reservoir.
extraNote: It is typically found in densely populated cities in the United States.

clozeText: Laboratory diagnosis of Rickettsia is primarily based on {{c1::serologic analysis}} rather than isolation of the organism.
extraNote: Isolation is hazardous and generally not performed in standard clinical labs.

clozeText: A diagnostic rise in antibody titer for Rickettsia is typically defined as a {{c1::fourfold}} or greater increase between acute and convalescent samples.
extraNote: Convalescent samples are usually obtained two weeks after the acute phase.

clozeText: During the acute phase of a rickettsial infection, a diagnosis can be made using an {{c1::immunofluorescence}} assay on tissue from the petechial rash site.
extraNote: This provides a faster alternative to waiting for convalescent serology.

clozeText: Severe cases of Rocky Mountain spotted fever can progress to {{c1::disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)}}, edema, and circulatory collapse.
extraNote: Prompt clinical diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent fatality.

clozeText: The primary mammalian reservoirs for Rickettsia rickettsii include {{c1::dogs and rodents}}.
extraNote: Humans are accidental hosts and are not required for the organism's perpetuation in nature.

clozeText: Endemic typhus outbreaks in the United States occur most frequently among the {{c1::homeless}} in large cities.
extraNote: This involves the flea-rat-human transmission cycle of Rickettsia typhi.

clozeText: Although their exact role is unconfirmed, {{c1::endotoxins}} are thought to contribute to rickettsial pathogenesis, including fever and petechiae.
extraNote: no exotoxins or cytolytic enzymes have been found in Rickettsiae.

clozeText: Rocky Mountain spotted fever accounts for {{c1::95}}% of rickettsial disease in the United States.
extraNote: There are approximately 1000 cases reported per year.

clozeText: Rickettsial infections often present with a sudden onset of nonspecific symptoms like fever, severe headache, and {{c1::myalgias::symptom}}.
extraNote: Prostration is also common during the initial acute onset.

clozeText: In epidemic typhus, the infected louse {{c1::dies}} after a few weeks, and there is no louse-to-louse transmission.
extraNote: This makes human infection an obligatory stage in the Rickettsia prowazekii life cycle.

clozeText: Rickettsia are distinct from the cause of Q fever (Coxiella burnetii) because the latter is transmitted by {{c1::aerosol}} rather than arthropod bite.
extraNote: Rickettsiae almost exclusively rely on arthropod vectors for human transmission.

clozeText: Rickettsiae primarily infect the {{c1::endothelium::specific tissue type}} of the blood vessel walls.
extraNote: The organisms circulate in the bloodstream (bacteremia) before targeting these cells.

clozeText: The characteristic rash of rickettsial diseases is caused by damage to the {{c1::vessels of the skin}}.
extraNote: Damage leads to edema and hemorrhage due to increased capillary permeability.

clozeText: The prominent headache seen in rickettsial infections is due to {{c1::vasculitis}} of the vessels in the brain.
extraNote: This is a direct result of the organism's tropism for vascular endothelial cells.

clozeText: Rocky Mountain spotted fever is caused by {{c1::Rickettsia rickettsii}}.
extraNote: It is a life-threatening disease occurring primarily in the Southeastern United States.

clozeText: The typical rash of Rocky Mountain spotted fever appears {{c1::2 to 6 days}} after the onset of symptoms.
extraNote: The rash begins as macules and frequently progresses to petechiae.

clozeText: The rash of Rocky Mountain spotted fever usually appears first on the {{c1::hands and feet}} and then moves inward to the trunk.
extraNote: This inward (centripetal) movement is a classic diagnostic feature.

clozeText: In the Southeastern United States, Rocky Mountain spotted fever is transmitted by the dog tick, {{c1::Dermacentor variabilis}}.
extraNote: Commonly occurs in Virginia, North Carolina, and Georgia.

clozeText: In the Western United States, Rocky Mountain spotted fever is transmitted by the wood tick, {{c1::Dermacentor andersoni}}.
extraNote: Ticks serve as both vectors and reservoirs.

clozeText: Rickettsia rickettsii is passed within tick populations via the {{c1::transovarian}} route.
extraNote: This allows the organism to persist in the tick population for a lifetime.

clozeText: Epidemic typhus is caused by {{c1::Rickettsia prowazekii}} and is transmitted by the human body louse.
extraNote: It is the only rickettsial disease that is not a zoonosis (occurs only in humans).

clozeText: The vector for Rickettsia prowazekii (epidemic typhus) is {{c1::Pediculus::genus}}, also known as the human body louse.
extraNote: Transmission occurs when louse feces are autoinoculated by scratching.

clozeText: In epidemic typhus, the maculopapular rash begins on the {{c1::trunk}} and spreads peripherally.
extraNote: This centrifugal spread is the opposite of the Rocky Mountain spotted fever rash.

clozeText: The rash of epidemic typhus typically {{c1::spares}} the face, palms, and soles.
extraNote: In contrast, the RMSF rash often involves the palms and soles.

clozeText: A recurrent form of epidemic typhus that can appear up to 50 years after the initial infection is called {{c1::Brill-Zinsser}} disease.
extraNote: It is less severe than the primary infection but the patient remains a reservoir.

clozeText: Endemic (murine) typhus is caused by {{c1::Rickettsia typhi}} and is transmitted by fleas.
extraNote: Rats serve as the primary reservoir for this disease.

clozeText: Rickettsial pox is caused by {{c1::Rickettsia akari}} and is transmitted by mites.
extraNote: The primary reservoir for R. akari is mice.

clozeText: The {{c1::Weil-Felix}} test uses Proteus vulgaris antigens to detect antirickettsial antibodies through a cross-reaction.
extraNote: It is based on the O antigens of Proteus strains OX-2, OX-19, and OX-K.

clozeText: Actinomyces israelii is a strict {{c1::anaerobe}} that is part of the normal flora of the oral cavity.
extraNote: A. israelii is notable for requiring anaerobic conditions for growth, unlike Nocardia which is aerobic.

clozeText: The natural habitat of Actinomyces israelii is the {{c1::oral cavity}}.
extraNote: Infection typically occurs when the organism is introduced into deeper tissues via trauma.

clozeText: Actinomyces may invade tissues after local trauma such as a {{c1::broken jaw}} or dental extraction.
extraNote: Invasion leads to the formation of filaments surrounded by inflammation.

clozeText: Actinomyces forms long, {{c1::branching filaments}} that resemble the hyphae of fungi.
extraNote: Despite their fungal-like appearance, they are true bacteria.

clozeText: On Gram stain, Actinomyces species are {{c1::gram-positive}}.
extraNote: They appear as branching rods or filaments.

clozeText: In contrast to Nocardia asteroides, Actinomyces is {{c1::not acid-fast}}.
extraNote: This is a critical diagnostic distinction as both form branching filaments.

clozeText: The typical lesion of actinomycosis is a {{c1::hard, non-tender::characteristic}} swelling that develops slowly.
extraNote: The chronic nature of the swelling is a hallmark of the disease.

clozeText: Actinomycosis lesions eventually drain pus through {{c1::sinus tracts}}.
extraNote: These tracts can connect the deep infection to the skin surface.

clozeText: Pus from Actinomyces infections often contains hard, yellow granules called {{c1::sulfur granules}}.
extraNote: These granules are actually masses of bacterial filaments, not actual sulfur.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::50%}} of actinomycosis cases involve the face and neck.
extraNote: The remaining cases typically involve the chest or abdomen.

clozeText: Pelvic actinomycosis can occur in women who have retained an {{c1::intrauterine device (IUD)}} for a long period.
extraNote: Long-term IUD use is a specific risk factor for pelvic involvement.
