clozeText: The Giardia lamblia trophozoite is surrounded by a {{c1::flexible cell membrane}}.
extraNote: This distinguishes the motile trophozoite form from the thick-walled cyst form.

clozeText: The Giardia lamblia cyst is surrounded by a {{c1::thick wall}}, allowing it to survive well in the environment.
extraNote: Environmental stability of the cyst is critical for its role in transmission.

clozeText: Giardia lamblia is a member of the {{c1::flagellate}} group of intestinal protozoa.
extraNote: It is frequently listed alongside Entamoeba (ameba) and Cryptosporidium (sporozoan) as a major intestinal pathogen.

clozeText: Within the intestinal tract, Giardia is categorized alongside {{c1::Entamoeba histolytica}} and Cryptosporidium as one of the three most important organisms.
extraNote: These three represent the major intestinal protozoan pathogens.

clozeText: The clinical presentation of Giardia lamblia in AIDS patients primarily involves the {{c1::intestinal tract}}.
extraNote: Diarrhea is the primary symptom associated with intestinal infection in this population.

clozeText: Giardia is categorized as a {{c1::protozoon::type of parasite}}, distinguishing it from multicellular metazoa (helminths).
extraNote: Protozoa are single-celled organisms, whereas metazoa (helminths) are multicellular.

clozeText: The infective stage of Giardia lamblia that survives environmental exposure is the {{c1::cyst}}.
extraNote: Cysts are the resistant form of the parasite's life cycle.

clozeText: {{c1::Giardia lamblia}} is a medically important protozoan specifically classified as a(n) {{c2::intestinal::location}} pathogen.
extraNote: It is grouped with other major intestinal protozoa such as Entamoeba histolytica and Cryptosporidium hominis.

clozeText: In the classification of protozoa by motility, {{c1::Giardia lamblia}} belongs to the {{c2::Mastigophora::group}} group, also known as {{c3::flagellates}}.
extraNote: The Mastigophora are the flagellated group of protozoa.

clozeText: {{c1::Giardia lamblia}} is frequently associated with {{c2::traveler’s diarrhea::clinical syndrome}} (also known as "turista").
extraNote: While ETEC is the most common cause, protozoa like Giardia are also involved.

clozeText: In patients with {{c1::AIDS}}, {{c2::Giardia lamblia}} is a common causative organism for diarrhea in the intestinal tract.
extraNote: It is listed among other AIDS-related opportunistic intestinal pathogens like Salmonella and Cryptosporidium.

clozeText: The life cycle of {{c1::Giardia lamblia}} consists of a {{c2::trophozoite}}, which is the motile, feeding, and reproducing form.
extraNote: This form is surrounded by a flexible cell membrane.

clozeText: The {{c1::trophozoite}} form of Giardia lamblia is characterized by having a {{c2::flexible cell membrane}}.
extraNote: This is the active, feeding stage of the protozoan.

clozeText: The {{c1::cyst}} form of {{c2::Giardia lamblia}} is nonmotile, nonmetabolizing, and nonreproducing.
extraNote: The cyst is the form that survives well in the environment.

clozeText: The {{c1::cyst}} form of Giardia lamblia is surrounded by a {{c2::thick wall}}, which facilitates its survival in the environment.
extraNote: This protective wall makes the cyst the primary stage involved in transmission.

clozeText: Transmission of {{c1::Giardia lamblia}} typically occurs via the {{c2::ingestion}} of cysts.
extraNote: This is the standard transmission route for intestinal protozoa.

clozeText: Within the intestinal tract, {{c1::Giardia lamblia}} is considered one of the three most important protozoan pathogens, alongside {{c2::Entamoeba histolytica}} and {{c3::Cryptosporidium}}.
extraNote: These three represent the ameba, flagellate, and sporozoan groups respectively.

clozeText: The {{c1::cyst}} stage of Giardia lamblia is responsible for {{c2::transmission}} because it survives environmental stress better than the trophozoite.
extraNote: Environmental survival is due to the thick wall of the cyst.

clozeText: The {{c1::trophozoite}} of Giardia lamblia is the form responsible for {{c2::reproducing}} and feeding within the host.
extraNote: In contrast, the cyst is nonmetabolizing.

clozeText: {{c1::Giardia lamblia}} is classified as a {{c2::Mastigophora::biological group}}, which means it moves using flagella.
extraNote: Other groups include Sarcodina (amebas), Sporozoa, and Ciliata.

clozeText: Entamoeba histolytica causes {{c1::amebic dysentery}} and {{c1::liver abscess}}.
extraNote: Major protozoan pathogen in the intestinal tract.

clozeText: The life cycle of E. histolytica has two stages: the motile {{c1::trophozoite::ameba}} and the nonmotile {{c1::cyst}}.
extraNote: Trophozoites are found in lesions and diarrheal stools; cysts predominate in non-diarrheal stools.

clozeText: The cyst of Entamoeba histolytica has {{c1::four}} nuclei, which is a critical diagnostic criterion.
extraNote: Distinguishes it from Entamoeba coli, which has eight nuclei.

clozeText: Upon excystation in the intestinal tract, a single ameba with four nuclei divides to form {{c1::eight}} trophozoites.
extraNote: Excystation occurs after ingestion of the cyst.

clozeText: The mature trophozoite of E. histolytica has a single nucleus with fine peripheral chromatin and a prominent {{c1::central nucleolus::karyosome}}.
extraNote: Distinctive nuclear morphology is used for laboratory identification.

clozeText: E. histolytica cysts are resistant to {{c1::chlorination}} of water supplies but are readily killed by {{c1::boiling}}.
extraNote: Filtration is required to remove cysts from municipal water.

clozeText: The organism is primarily acquired via the {{c1::fecal–oral}} route through contaminated food and water.
extraNote: No animal reservoir exists for Entamoeba histolytica.

clozeText: In the colon, E. histolytica trophozoites invade the epithelium to form characteristic {{c1::flask-shaped}} ulcers.
extraNote: The ulcers undermine and destroy large areas of intestinal epithelium.

clozeText: By far, the most frequent site of systemic/extraintestinal E. histolytica disease is the {{c1::liver}}.
extraNote: Trophozoites reach the liver via the portal circulation.

clozeText: Aspiration of an amebic liver abscess yields brownish-yellow pus described as having the consistency of {{c1::anchovy paste}}.
extraNote: Liver abscesses are characterized by RUQ pain, weight loss, fever, and a tender liver.

clozeText: Acute intestinal amebiasis is characterized by {{c1::dysentery}}, which is bloody, mucus-containing diarrhea.
extraNote: Associated with lower abdominal discomfort, flatulence, and tenesmus.

clozeText: A granulomatous lesion called an {{c1::ameboma}} may form in the cecal or rectosigmoid areas and resemble adenocarcinoma.
extraNote: Occurs in some patients with chronic amebiasis.

clozeText: E. histolytica trophozoites in stool specimens characteristically contain {{c1::ingested red blood cells}}.
extraNote: This feature is key for distinguishing them from non-pathogenic amebas or fecal leukocytes.

clozeText: The most common diagnostic error in identifying E. histolytica is mistaking {{c1::fecal leukocytes}} for trophozoites.
extraNote: Microscopic examination must be done carefully to identify true ameboid motility.

clozeText: Stool specimens should be examined within {{c1::one hour}} of collection to observe the motile trophozoites.
extraNote: Trophozoites are fragile and lose motility quickly outside the body.

clozeText: The {{c1::indirect hemagglutination}} test is a serologic assay that is usually positive in patients with invasive amebiasis.
extraNote: Often negative in asymptomatic individuals who are only passing cysts.

clozeText: The treatment of choice for symptomatic intestinal amebiasis or hepatic abscesses is {{c1::metronidazole::Drug class}} or tinidazole.
extraNote: Hepatic abscesses typically do not need to be surgically drained.

clozeText: Asymptomatic cyst carriers of E. histolytica should be treated with {{c1::iodoquinol}} or paromomycin.
extraNote: Prevents the spread of cysts to others even in the absence of patient symptoms.

clozeText: {{c1::Entamoeba dispar}} is a nonpathogenic species that is morphologically indistinguishable from E. histolytica.
extraNote: Diagnosis of E. histolytica often requires PCR or antigen detection to differentiate from E. dispar.

clozeText: A fixed, {{c1::trichrome-stained}} preparation is used for complete stool examination to bring out cyst morphology.
extraNote: Other examination methods include saline wet mounts and iodine-stained wet mounts.

clozeText: In E. histolytica infection, previous infection {{c1::does not}} prevent reinfection.
extraNote: Antibodies are formed against trophozoite antigens but are not protective.

clozeText: E. histolytica trophozoites secrete enzymes that cause {{c1::localized necrosis}} with little inflammation at the site.
extraNote: This occurs during initial invasion of the colonic epithelium.

clozeText: Anal–oral transmission of E. histolytica is common among {{c1::male homosexuals}}.
extraNote: This population is identified as a group with higher prevalence in the United States.

clozeText: Prevention of E. histolytica involves the prohibition of using {{c1::human feces::night soil}} for fertilization of crops.
extraNote: A key measure for preventing food contamination in endemic areas.

clozeText: Unlike bacillary dysentery, amebic dysentery typically shows {{c1::few}} inflammatory cells (leukocytes) in the stool.
extraNote: Helps distinguish amebic infection from bacterial causes of dysentery.

clozeText: E. histolytica trophozoites reach systemic sites by invading the {{c1::submucosa}} and then the portal circulation.
extraNote: Progression past the muscularis layer allows systemic spread.

clozeText: Roughly {{c1::90}}% of individuals infected with E. histolytica remain asymptomatic.
extraNote: However, these individuals can still serve as carriers and transmit cysts to others.

clozeText: Chronic amebiasis symptoms include {{c1::weight loss}}, fatigue, and occasional diarrhea.
extraNote: Lower-grade symptoms contrasted with acute amebic dysentery.

clozeText: Liver abscesses in the {{c1::right}} lobe can penetrate the diaphragm and cause lung disease.
extraNote: Right-lobe abscesses are the most common manifestation of extraintestinal amebiasis.

clozeText: Tests for E. histolytica in the stool can be specific by detecting either Nucleic Acids (PCR) or {{c1::antigen}}.
extraNote: Used to differentiate E. histolytica from the nonpathogenic E. dispar.

clozeText: Entamoeba histolytica is the primary protozoan pathogen that causes {{c1::amebic dysentery}} and {{c2::liver abscess}}.
extraNote: Amebiasis is often categorized into intestinal (dysentery) and extraintestinal (most commonly hepatic) disease.

clozeText: The life cycle of Entamoeba histolytica consists of two stages: the motile {{c1::trophozoite}} and the nonmotile {{c2::cyst}}.
extraNote: Trophozoites are the active, feeding stage found in lesions, while cysts are the infective stage found in the environment.

clozeText: Mature cysts of Entamoeba histolytica are characterized by having {{c1::four}} nuclei, which serves as a critical diagnostic criterion.
extraNote: This distinguishes it from Entamoeba coli, which typically has eight nuclei in its mature cyst stage.

clozeText: Entamoeba histolytica cysts are resistant to {{c1::chlorination}} of water supplies but are readily killed by {{c2::boiling}}.
extraNote: Water purification requires filtration or boiling to effectively remove or kill the cysts.

clozeText: Upon excystation in the intestinal tract, an Entamoeba histolytica ameba with four nuclei emerges and then divides to form {{c1::eight}} trophozoites.
extraNote: The initial quadrinucleate ameba undergoes division to produce the active trophozoite population.

clozeText: The mature trophozoite of Entamoeba histolytica has a single nucleus with a prominent {{c1::central nucleolus::karyosome}} and an even lining of peripheral chromatin.
extraNote: Nuclear morphology is a key feature used to distinguish E. histolytica from other nonpathogenic amebas.

clozeText: Although antibodies are formed against {{c1::trophozoite}} antigens in invasive amebiasis, they are {{c2::not protective}} against reinfection.
extraNote: Serologic testing is useful for diagnosis, but previous infection does not confer immunity.

clozeText: Entamoeba histolytica is primarily acquired via the {{c1::fecal–oral}} route, often through contaminated food and water.
extraNote: Anal–oral transmission is also noted, particularly among men who have sex with men.

clozeText: In the human host, there is {{c1::no animal reservoir}} for Entamoeba histolytica.
extraNote: Humans are the primary host and source of infection via cyst shedding.

clozeText: Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites invade the colonic epithelium by secreting {{c1::enzymes}} that cause localized necrosis.
extraNote: This enzymatic activity facilitates the invasion of the intestinal mucosa with minimal initial inflammation.

clozeText: As Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites reach the muscularis layer of the colon, they form characteristic {{c1::flask-shaped}} ulcers.
extraNote: These ulcers can undermine and destroy large areas of the intestinal epithelium.

clozeText: Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites can reach the liver by invading the {{c1::portal circulation}}.
extraNote: The liver is the most frequent site of systemic (extraintestinal) disease.

clozeText: Amebic dysentery is clinically characterized by {{c1::bloody, mucus-containing}} diarrhea.
extraNote: This is often accompanied by lower abdominal discomfort, flatulence, and tenesmus.

clozeText: A granulomatous lesion called an {{c1::ameboma}} may form in the colon, which can be mistaken for {{c2::adenocarcinoma}}.
extraNote: These lesions typically occur in the cecal or rectosigmoid areas.

clozeText: Amebic liver abscesses are characterized by the aspiration of brownish-yellow pus that has the appearance of {{c1::anchovy paste}}.
extraNote: This pus is formed by necrotic liver tissue and usually contains trophozoites.

clozeText: In the laboratory diagnosis of amebic dysentery, trophozoites characteristically contain {{c1::ingested red blood cells}}.
extraNote: This phenomenon, known as erythrophagocytosis, is a hallmark of invasive E. histolytica.

clozeText: The most common error in identifying Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites is mistaking {{c1::fecal leukocytes}} for the organism.
extraNote: True trophozoites must be distinguished from inflammatory cells in the stool.

clozeText: A major morphological difference between E. histolytica and Entamoeba coli is that E. coli cysts contain {{c1::eight}} nuclei.
extraNote: E. histolytica cysts are also generally smaller than E. coli cysts.

clozeText: The nonpathogenic species {{c1::Entamoeba dispar}} is morphologically indistinguishable from E. histolytica.
extraNote: Specific tests like PCR or antigen detection are required to differentiate the two species.

clozeText: Two highly specific tests for E. histolytica in stool include {{c1::antigen}} detection and {{c2::nucleic acid (PCR)}} assays.
extraNote: These tests are superior to stool microscopy for distinguishing E. histolytica from nonpathogenic amebas.

clozeText: In amebic dysentery, stool examination typically shows a lack of {{c1::polymorphonuclear leukocytes::PMNs}}, unlike bacillary dysentery.
extraNote: Bacillary dysentery (e.g., Shigella) is associated with a robust inflammatory response and many white blood cells in the stool.

clozeText: Asymptomatic cyst carriers of Entamoeba histolytica should be treated with luminal agents such as {{c1::iodoquinol}} or {{c2::paromomycin}}.
extraNote: These drugs are used to eliminate the cyst stage from the intestinal lumen.

clozeText: Entamoeba histolytica liver abscesses generally {{c1::do not need::need vs. do not need}} to be surgically drained.
extraNote: Drug therapy with metronidazole is typically sufficient for resolution.

clozeText: In endemic areas, preventative measures include prohibiting the use of {{c1::night soil}} (human feces) as fertilizer.
extraNote: Night soil is a major contributor to the contamination of crops and the spread of amebic cysts.

clozeText: Roughly {{c1::90}}% of individuals infected with Entamoeba histolytica have asymptomatic infections.
extraNote: These individuals act as carriers, shedding infectious cysts in their feces.

clozeText: Amebic liver abscesses are characterized by {{c1::right-upper-quadrant}} pain, weight loss, fever, and a tender liver.
extraNote: Right-lobe abscesses may occasionally penetrate the diaphragm to cause lung disease.

clozeText: Diarrheal stools must be examined within {{c1::one hour}} of collection to observe the ameboid motility of trophozoites.
extraNote: Trophozoites are fragile and lose their characteristic motility quickly after leaving the body.

clozeText: Because Entamoeba histolytica cysts are passed intermittently, at least {{c1::three}} stool specimens should be examined.
extraNote: A single stool O&P test is often insensitive, leading to false-negative results.

clozeText: Entamoeba histolytica causes two primary clinical conditions: {{c1::amebic dysentery}} and {{c2::liver abscess}}.
extraNote: These are the hallmark intestinal and extraintestinal manifestations of the infection.

clozeText: The {{c1::trophozoite}} is the motile stage found within intestinal and extraintestinal lesions, as well as in diarrheal stools.
extraNote: Trophozoites are the stage responsible for causing tissue damage and disease.

clozeText: In non-diarrheal stools, the {{c1::cyst}} is the predominating stage of Entamoeba histolytica.
extraNote: Cysts are the infectious stage and are found in formed stools of carriers.

clozeText: The mature cyst of Entamoeba histolytica contains {{c1::four}} nuclei, which is a key diagnostic criterion.
extraNote: This distinguishes it from Entamoeba coli, which contains eight nuclei in its mature cyst stage.

clozeText: The trophozoite of Entamoeba histolytica possesses a single nucleus with a {{c1::prominent central nucleolus::karyosome}} and an even lining of peripheral chromatin.
extraNote: The central nucleolus and chromatin pattern are specific morphological features used in laboratory identification.

clozeText: Entamoeba histolytica is primarily transmitted via the {{c1::fecal–oral}} route through contaminated food and water.
extraNote: Humans are the only source; there is no animal reservoir for this organism.

clozeText: When trophozoites invade the colonic mucosa and reach the muscularis layer, they form a characteristic {{c1::flask-shaped}} ulcer.
extraNote: These ulcers can undermine and destroy large areas of the colonic epithelium.

clozeText: Progression of Entamoeba histolytica into the submucosa leads to invasion of the {{c1::portal circulation}}, allowing the parasite to reach the liver.
extraNote: The liver is the most frequent site of systemic/extraintestinal disease.

clozeText: Acute intestinal amebiasis typically presents as dysentery, which is characterized by {{c1::bloody, mucus-containing}} diarrhea.
extraNote: This is often accompanied by lower abdominal discomfort, flatulence, and tenesmus.

clozeText: A granulomatous lesion called an {{c1::ameboma}} may form in the cecal or rectosigmoid areas, potentially mimicking adenocarcinoma of the colon.
extraNote: Differential diagnosis is critical to distinguish this inflammatory lesion from malignancy.

clozeText: Amebic liver abscesses are characterized by {{c1::right-upper-quadrant}} pain, weight loss, fever, and a tender, enlarged liver.
extraNote: Most patients with liver abscesses do not have concurrent overt intestinal amebiasis.

clozeText: Aspiration of an amebic liver abscess yields pus that has the appearance and consistency of {{c1::anchovy paste}}.
extraNote: The pus is described as brownish-yellow in color.

clozeText: Liver abscesses in the right lobe can penetrate the {{c1::diaphragm}}, leading to lung disease.
extraNote: This represents a direct extension complication of hepatic involvement.

clozeText: A critical diagnostic finding in diarrheal stools is the presence of trophozoites containing {{c1::ingested red blood cells}}.
extraNote: This finding is highly characteristic of invasive Entamoeba histolytica.

clozeText: In laboratory diagnosis, the most common error is mistaking {{c1::fecal leukocytes}} for trophozoites.
extraNote: True trophozoites must be distinguished from inflammatory cells in stool samples.

clozeText: Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites are morphologically indistinguishable from {{c1::Entamoeba dispar}}, which is a nonpathogenic species.
extraNote: Because of this, specific PCR or antigen tests are required for definitive identification.

clozeText: The {{c1::indirect hemagglutination}} test is a serologic assay usually positive in patients with invasive amebiasis.
extraNote: Serology is often negative in asymptomatic cyst carriers.

clozeText: The flagellated forms of {{c1::Leishmania}} are known as {{c2::promastigotes::form name}}.
extraNote: Leishmania also possesses a nonflagellated form called an amastigote.

clozeText: The nonflagellated forms of {{c1::Leishmania}} are known as {{c2::amastigotes::form name}}.
extraNote: These forms are characteristic of the organism's life cycle in the host tissue.

clozeText: In the classification of protozoa, {{c1::Leishmania}} is categorized within the group {{c2::Mastigophora::biological group}} (flagellates).
extraNote: This group is distinguished by the presence of flagella in certain life stages.

clozeText: Based on the site of infection, {{c1::Leishmania}} is classified as a {{c2::blood and tissue::location type}} protozoan.
extraNote: This differentiates it from intestinal or urogenital protozoa.

clozeText: The insect vector responsible for transmitting {{c1::Leishmania donovani}} is the {{c2::sandfly}}.
extraNote: Leishmania donovani specifically causes visceral leishmaniasis.

clozeText: {{c1::Leishmania donovani}} is the causative agent of {{c2::visceral leishmaniasis}} (also known as kala-azar).
extraNote: Visceral leishmaniasis is a serious systemic form of the disease.

clozeText: {{c1::Kala-azar}} is the clinical name for the disease caused by {{c2::Leishmania donovani}}.
extraNote: It is synonymously known as visceral leishmaniasis.

clozeText: {{c1::Leishmania tropica}} causes {{c2::cutaneous leishmaniasis}} in the Old World.
extraNote: Old World cutaneous leishmaniasis is primarily associated with L. tropica.

clozeText: {{c1::Leishmania mexicana}} causes {{c2::cutaneous leishmaniasis}} in the New World.
extraNote: New World cutaneous leishmaniasis is specifically linked to L. mexicana.

clozeText: Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis is caused by {{c1::Leishmania braziliensis}}.
extraNote: This species primarily affects the mucous membranes and skin.

clozeText: For the diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), samples are typically taken from the {{c1::bone marrow}}, {{c2::spleen}}, or lymph node.
extraNote: These sites contain the tissue-dwelling amastigote forms.

clozeText: Laboratory diagnosis of {{c1::cutaneous leishmaniasis}} (L. tropica or L. mexicana) involves examining {{c2::fluid from the lesion}}.
extraNote: Microscopic examination of lesion fluid identifies the presence of the parasite.

clozeText: The drug used for the treatment of all medically important species of {{c1::Leishmania}} is {{c2::stibogluconate}}.
extraNote: Stibogluconate is the standard therapy for L. donovani, L. tropica, L. mexicana, and L. braziliensis.

clozeText: Prevention of {{c1::Leishmania}} involves interrupting transmission via {{c2::insect control}} and personal protection.
extraNote: Targeting the sandfly vector is critical for disease prevention.

clozeText: Personal protection measures against the {{c1::Leishmania}} vector include the use of {{c2::insect repellent}} and {{c3::bed nets}}.
extraNote: These barriers prevent the sandfly from biting and transmitting the parasite.

clozeText: An {{c1::intermediate host}} in the parasite life cycle is defined as the host in which the {{c2::asexual cycle}} occurs.
extraNote: For Leishmania, humans serve as the host for asexual reproduction.

clozeText: A {{c1::definitive host}} is defined as the one in which the {{c2::sexual cycle}} occurs.
extraNote: This terminology differentiates hosts based on the reproductive stage of the parasite.

clozeText: Transmission of blood and tissue protozoa like {{c1::Leishmania}} usually occurs via {{c2::insect vectors}}.
extraNote: Unlike intestinal protozoa transmitted by cysts, Leishmania requires a biting insect.

clozeText: {{c1::Leishmania}} is a single-celled organism categorized as a {{c2::protozoa}}.
extraNote: Parasites are broadly divided into protozoa (single-celled) and metazoa (multicellular).

clozeText: While {{c1::L. tropica}} causes leishmaniasis in the {{c2::Old World}}, {{c1::L. mexicana}} causes it in the {{c3::New World}}.
extraNote: The geographical origin is a key diagnostic and classification feature for cutaneous species.

clozeText: In the human host, {{c1::Leishmania}} typically exists in the {{c2::nonflagellated::flagellar status}} form.
extraNote: This nonflagellated form is specifically called the amastigote.

clozeText: The {{c1::sandfly}} is the common vector for all species of {{c2::Leishmania}}.
extraNote: All pathogenic species listed in the text utilize this specific insect for transmission.

clozeText: Prevention of leishmaniasis requires {{c1::interrupting the chain of transmission}}.
extraNote: This is a general principle for controlling parasitic infections transmitted by insects.

clozeText: Regarding occurrence in the United States, {{c1::Leishmania}} species are generally categorized as {{c2::not::yes or no}} occurring in the US.
extraNote: While cases may be imported, the organism is traditionally considered absent in standard US epidemiological tables.

clozeText: {{c1::Leishmania}} and Trypanosoma are both examples of flagellated {{c2::blood and tissue}} protozoa.
extraNote: They are grouped together because of their motility structure and primary infection site.

clozeText: In a diagnostic sample of lymph node tissue from a patient with kala-azar, the clinician expects to find {{c1::Leishmania donovani}}.
extraNote: Lymph node involvement is a common feature of visceral leishmaniasis.

clozeText: The motile form of {{c1::Leishmania}} found in the insect vector is the {{c2::promastigote}}.
extraNote: The promastigote contains the flagellum used for movement within the sandfly.

clozeText: {{c1::Leishmania braziliensis}} is associated with {{c2::mucocutaneous}} leishmaniasis.
extraNote: This form involves both skin lesions and destructive mucosal involvement.

clozeText: One of the three major diagnostic sites for {{c1::Leishmania donovani}} is the {{c2::spleen}}.
extraNote: The spleen is a primary organ affected in the visceral form of the disease.

clozeText: The classification of {{c1::Leishmania}} as a flagellate means it belongs to the group {{c2::Mastigophora}}.
extraNote: Protozoa classification includes Mastigophora, Sarcodina, Sporozoa, and Ciliata.

clozeText: For medical purposes, {{c1::Leishmania}} is classified as a blood and tissue protozoan.
extraNote: Protozoa are often categorized by their primary site of infection, with Leishmania specifically targeting blood and tissue.

clozeText: The flagellated form of Leishmania is called a {{c1::promastigote::stage name}}.
extraNote: Leishmania and Trypanosoma are unique among protozoa for having distinct flagellated promastigote/trypomastigote forms.

clozeText: The nonflagellated form of Leishmania is called an {{c1::amastigote::stage name}}.
extraNote: The amastigote is the intracellular, nonflagellated stage of the parasite's life cycle.

clozeText: The insect vector responsible for the transmission of Leishmania donovani is the {{c1::sandfly}}.
extraNote: Transmission occurs when the sandfly bites a host, introducing the parasite into the blood or tissue.

clozeText: Leishmania donovani is the causative agent of {{c1::kala-azar}}, also known as visceral leishmaniasis.
extraNote: Kala-azar is a severe systemic form of leishmaniasis involving internal organs.

clozeText: {{c1::Leishmania tropica}} is a species that causes Old World cutaneous leishmaniasis.
extraNote: Cutaneous leishmaniasis typically presents as skin lesions at the site of the sandfly bite.

clozeText: {{c1::Leishmania mexicana}} is a species that causes New World cutaneous leishmaniasis.
extraNote: New World cutaneous leishmaniasis is geographically distinct from the Old World form caused by L. tropica.

clozeText: {{c1::Leishmania braziliensis}} is the primary species associated with mucocutaneous leishmaniasis.
extraNote: This form of the disease involves the mucous membranes, often leading to significant tissue destruction.

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating various forms of leishmaniasis is {{c1::stibogluconate}}.
extraNote: Stibogluconate is the standard treatment for both visceral and cutaneous forms of the disease.

clozeText: Diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) often requires the examination of the {{c1::bone marrow}}, spleen, or lymph nodes.
extraNote: These sites are sampled to detect the presence of amastigotes in systemic infections.

clozeText: In cases of cutaneous leishmaniasis, the parasite is typically diagnosed by examining {{c1::fluid from the lesion}}.
extraNote: Aspirates or scrapings from the skin ulcer are used to visualize the organism.

clozeText: Leishmania species belong to the group of protozoa known as {{c1::Mastigophora::biological group}}, or flagellates.
extraNote: This group is characterized by the presence of flagella at certain stages of the life cycle.

clozeText: Leishmania donovani specifically causes {{c1::visceral}} leishmaniasis.
extraNote: Visceral leishmaniasis affects internal organs like the liver, spleen, and bone marrow.

clozeText: Leishmania is considered a {{c1::blood and tissue}} protozoan because it does not typically infect the intestinal or urogenital tracts.
extraNote: This differentiates it from organisms like Giardia or Trichomonas.

clozeText: A spleen biopsy or aspirate is a diagnostic method used for {{c1::Leishmania donovani}} infections.
extraNote: Spleen sampling is highly sensitive for detecting the amastigotes in visceral disease.

clozeText: Old World cutaneous leishmaniasis is caused by {{c1::Leishmania tropica}}.
extraNote: Old World refers to geographic regions including parts of Asia, Africa, and the Mediterranean.

clozeText: New World cutaneous leishmaniasis is caused by {{c1::Leishmania mexicana}}.
extraNote: New World refers to regions within the Americas.

clozeText: The nonmotile, intracellular stage of Leishmania is the {{c1::amastigote}}.
extraNote: Unlike the promastigote, the amastigote lacks a visible external flagellum.

clozeText: The {{c1::promastigote}} stage is the flagellated form of Leishmania found in the sandfly vector.
extraNote: This is the infective stage transmitted to humans during the sandfly's blood meal.

clozeText: Examination of the {{c1::lymph node}} is a diagnostic option for detecting Leishmania donovani.
extraNote: Along with the spleen and bone marrow, lymph nodes are a key tissue site for visceral leishmaniasis.

clozeText: Certain protozoa, such as {{c1::Leishmania}} and Trypanosoma, have flagellated forms called {{c2::promastigotes::non-blood form}} and nonflagellated forms called amastigotes.
extraNote: Leishmania transition between flagellated and nonflagellated stages during their life cycle.

clozeText: Leishmania and Trypanosoma have nonflagellated forms called {{c1::amastigotes}}.
extraNote: The amastigote is the intracellular, nonflagellated stage of Leishmania.

clozeText: Transmission of {{c1::Leishmania donovani}} usually occurs via the {{c2::sandfly::insect vector}}.
extraNote: The sandfly is the essential vector for the transmission of visceral leishmaniasis.

clozeText: Prevention of leishmaniasis involves interrupting the chain of transmission, particularly via {{c1::insect control}}.
extraNote: Because the parasite is blood-borne via a vector, controlling the sandfly population is the primary preventive measure.

clozeText: In the classification of protozoa, Leishmania is categorized as a {{c1::tissue::site of infection}} protozoan and a {{c2::flagellate::motility type}}.
extraNote: Other flagellates include Trypanosoma, Giardia, and Trichomonas.

clozeText: The blood and tissue protozoa consist of a varied group including the flagellates {{c1::Leishmania}} and Trypanosoma, and the sporozoans Plasmodium and Toxoplasma.
extraNote: Leishmania is specifically classified under the blood and tissue group despite its complex morphology.

clozeText: Leishmania tropica and Leishmania mexicana cause {{c1::cutaneous::lesion type}} leishmaniasis.
extraNote: These species typically cause localized skin ulcers rather than systemic disease.

clozeText: Leishmania tropica is associated with {{c1::Old World}} cutaneous leishmaniasis.
extraNote: Geographic distribution is a key factor in differentiating species causing cutaneous leishmaniasis.

clozeText: Leishmania mexicana is associated with {{c1::New World}} cutaneous leishmaniasis.
extraNote: Geographic distribution helps distinguish L. mexicana from L. tropica.

clozeText: Leishmania braziliensis is the causative agent of {{c1::mucocutaneous}} leishmaniasis.
extraNote: This form involves the destruction of mucous membranes in the nose and mouth.

clozeText: Diagnosis of Leishmania donovani is achieved by sampling {{c1::bone marrow}}, {{c2::spleen}}, or {{c3::lymph node}}.
extraNote: These sites are targeted because visceral leishmaniasis infects the reticuloendothelial system.

clozeText: The laboratory diagnosis for cutaneous leishmaniasis (e.g., L. tropica, L. mexicana) involves examining {{c1::fluid from the lesion}}.
extraNote: Parasites can be visualized in the fluid or scrapings taken directly from the skin ulcer.

clozeText: The primary drug used for the treatment of various Leishmania species is {{c1::stibogluconate}}.
extraNote: Stibogluconate is the standard treatment for both visceral and cutaneous forms of leishmaniasis.

clozeText: Leishmania belongs to the group of flagellates known as {{c1::Mastigophora}}.
extraNote: This group includes all medically important protozoa that use flagella for motility.

clozeText: While intestinal protozoa are transmitted by ingestion of cysts, tissue protozoa like Leishmania are typically transmitted via {{c1::insect vectors}}.
extraNote: For Leishmania, the sandfly is the vector; for Plasmodium, it is the mosquito.

clozeText: Leishmania is grouped with {{c1::Pneumocystis}}, Plasmodium, and Toxoplasma as a blood and tissue protozoan.
extraNote: These organisms infect locations outside of the intestinal or urogenital tracts.

clozeText: Kala-azar, caused by {{c1::Leishmania donovani}}, does not occur in {{c2::the United States}}.
extraNote: Leishmaniasis is primarily a tropical and subtropical disease not native to the US.

clozeText: Diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis often involves {{c1::spleen::organ}} sampling, as it is a major site of infection.
extraNote: Splenomegaly is a common clinical feature of L. donovani infection.

clozeText: The infectious stage of Leishmania transmitted by the sandfly is the flagellated {{c1::promastigote}}.
extraNote: Promastigotes are the form found in the insect vector, while amastigotes are found in human tissues.

clozeText: Certain protozoa, such as {{c1::Leishmania}} and Trypanosoma, have flagellated forms called promastigotes.
extraNote: Leishmania is classified as a flagellate within the group Mastigophora.

clozeText: Leishmania donovani is transmitted to humans via the bite of the {{c1::sandfly}}.
extraNote: The sandfly serves as the insect vector for visceral leishmaniasis.

clozeText: Visceral leishmaniasis, caused by Leishmania donovani, is also known as {{c1::kala-azar}}.
extraNote: This condition involves systemic infection of the reticuloendothelial system.

clozeText: To diagnose visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), samples are typically obtained from the {{c1::bone marrow}}, spleen, or lymph nodes.
extraNote: Diagnostic examination involves looking for amastigotes in tissue samples.

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating infections caused by Leishmania species is {{c1::stibogluconate}}.
extraNote: This treatment is used for both visceral and cutaneous forms of the disease.

clozeText: {{c1::Leishmania tropica::Species}} is a primary cause of Old World cutaneous leishmaniasis.
extraNote: Cutaneous leishmaniasis typically presents with localized skin ulcers.

clozeText: {{c1::Toxoplasma gondii}} is an important protozoan that is transmitted transplacentally from mother to offspring.
extraNote: Transplacental transmission occurs in utero across the placenta and is a form of vertical transmission.

clozeText: In patients with AIDS, *Toxoplasma gondii* is a common causative organism of {{c1::brain abscesses}} in the central nervous system.
extraNote: Central nervous system involvement is a major opportunistic manifestation of toxoplasmosis in advanced HIV infection.

clozeText: The drug {{c1::Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole}} is used for the prevention of toxoplasmosis in patients with AIDS.
extraNote: This medication is also used for the prevention of Pneumocystis pneumonia in the same patient population.

clozeText: {{c1::Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS)}} may occur in HIV-infected patients coinfected with *Toxoplasma gondii* who are treated with HAART.
extraNote: IRIS results from the restored capacity of the immune system to produce an inflammatory response against existing pathogens.

clozeText: To avoid IRIS in HIV patients, a coinfection with *Toxoplasma gondii* should ideally be treated {{c1::prior to::timing}} instituting HAART.
extraNote: Managing the opportunistic infection before starting antiretroviral therapy helps minimize the inflammatory exacerbation.

clozeText: *Toxoplasma gondii* is classified as a {{c1::protozoan}} that is transmitted transplacentally.
extraNote: It is grouped with bacteria like Treponema pallidum and Listeria monocytogenes as important pathogens transmitted across the placenta.

clozeText: Transmission of *Toxoplasma gondii* from mother to offspring in utero is a form of {{c1::vertical}} transmission.
extraNote: Vertical transmission can occur transplacentally, at the time of delivery, or during breast-feeding.

clozeText: In the context of HIV, *Toxoplasma gondii* infection of the {{c1::central nervous system}} typically presents as a brain abscess.
extraNote: Neurological opportunistic infections become more frequent as the CD4 count declines.

clozeText: Symptoms of a *Toxoplasma gondii* infection may become more pronounced during HAART because the drugs restore the {{c1::inflammatory response}}.
extraNote: This enhancement of inflammation is the underlying mechanism of Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS).

clozeText: The risk of opportunistic infections such as *Toxoplasma gondii* significantly increases when the CD4 count falls below {{c1::200/μL}}.
extraNote: A CD4 count of 200/μL or below is the diagnostic threshold for an AIDS-defining condition.

clozeText: Chemoprophylaxis for {{c1::toxoplasmosis::disease}} is indicated for patients in the advanced stages of AIDS to prevent neurological complications.
extraNote: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the standard agent used for this prophylactic purpose.

clozeText: *Toxoplasma gondii* is one of the important {{c1::opportunistic}} organisms that requires management in patients with low CD4 counts.
extraNote: The severity of these infections increases as the immune system (specifically CD4 T cells) is depleted.

clozeText: Along with *Treponema pallidum* and *Listeria monocytogenes*, {{c1::Toxoplasma gondii}} is a key pathogen capable of transplacental transmission.
extraNote: These organisms are distinct from viruses like CMV and Rubella that also share the transplacental route.

clozeText: While AIDS patients with low CD4 counts have a reduced capacity for inflammation, {{c1::HAART}} restores this response, potentially exacerbating *Toxoplasma gondii* symptoms.
extraNote: This occurs during the clinical phenomenon known as IRIS.

clozeText: Brain abscesses caused by {{c1::Toxoplasma gondii}} are categorized as opportunistic infections of the central nervous system.
extraNote: Other CNS infections in AIDS include meningitis by Cryptococcus neoformans and PML by JC virus.

clozeText: Toxoplasma gondii is classified as a(n) {{c1::protozoan}} that can be transmitted transplacentally.
extraNote: Toxoplasma gondii is listed alongside Treponema pallidum and Listeria monocytogenes as important non-viral pathogens transmitted across the placenta.

clozeText: Along with Treponema pallidum and Listeria monocytogenes, {{c1::Toxoplasma gondii}} is an important pathogen transmitted transplacentally to cause fetal and neonatal infections.
extraNote: Transplacental transmission is a form of vertical transmission from mother to offspring.

clozeText: In patients with AIDS, Toxoplasma gondii is a common cause of {{c1::brain abscesses}}.
extraNote: Brain abscesses are the specific clinical manifestation of Toxoplasma gondii in the central nervous system of HIV-infected patients.

clozeText: The {{c1::central nervous system}} is the primary site of infection for Toxoplasma gondii in AIDS patients.
extraNote: Toxoplasma gondii is an opportunistic pathogen that targets the CNS when the immune system is severely compromised.

clozeText: The drug combination {{c1::trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole}} is used for the prevention of toxoplasmosis in AIDS patients.
extraNote: This medication is also used as prophylaxis for Pneumocystis pneumonia in advanced stages of AIDS.

clozeText: Co-infection with Toxoplasma gondii can lead to {{c1::Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS)}} in HIV patients starting HAART.
extraNote: IRIS occurs because the restoration of the immune system by antiretroviral drugs enhances the inflammatory response against the pathogen.

clozeText: To avoid IRIS, a coinfection with Toxoplasma gondii should be {{c1::treated}} prior to instituting HAART.
extraNote: Treating the opportunistic infection first reduces the risk of an exacerbated inflammatory response when antiretroviral therapy begins.

clozeText: The frequency and severity of opportunistic infections like Toxoplasma gondii significantly increase when CD4 counts fall below {{c1::200}} cells/μL.
extraNote: A CD4 count of 200 cells/μL or below is an AIDS-defining condition.

clozeText: In IRIS involving Toxoplasma gondii, an exacerbation of clinical symptoms occurs because antiretroviral drugs enhance the capacity to mount a(n) {{c1::inflammatory response}}.
extraNote: Patients with low CD4 counts initially have a reduced capacity for inflammation, which is restored by HAART.

clozeText: Toxoplasma gondii is an opportunistic infection that typically occurs during the {{c1::late stage}} of HIV infection.
extraNote: Late-stage HIV is manifested by a decline in CD4 cells below 200/μL and increased susceptibility to opportunistic pathogens.

clozeText: In the context of fetal and neonatal infections, Toxoplasma gondii transmission occurs via the {{c1::transplacental::route}} route.
extraNote: This is distinct from perinatal transmission (at the time of birth) or transmission via breast-feeding.

clozeText: Chemoprophylaxis for {{c1::Toxoplasma gondii::pathogen}} is indicated for HIV-infected patients to prevent opportunistic brain abscesses.
extraNote: Management of infected patients involves determining if they need chemoprophylaxis based on CD4 counts.

clozeText: The protozoan {{c1::Toxoplasma gondii}} is an important pathogen transmitted to the fetus {{c2::transplacentally}}.
extraNote: Toxoplasma gondii is specifically noted as a protozoan capable of crossing the placenta to cause congenital infection.

clozeText: In the central nervous system of AIDS patients, {{c1::Toxoplasma gondii}} is a common cause of {{c2::brain abscess}}.
extraNote: Central nervous system involvement in advanced AIDS often manifests as localized brain abscesses due to Toxoplasma gondii.

clozeText: Prophylaxis for {{c1::toxoplasmosis}} in patients with advanced AIDS is achieved using {{c2::trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole}}.
extraNote: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a high-yield prophylactic agent used to prevent both Pneumocystis pneumonia and toxoplasmosis.

clozeText: {{c1::Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS)}} may occur in HIV-infected patients coinfected with {{c2::Toxoplasma gondii}} after starting HAART.
extraNote: IRIS represents a clinical worsening of a pre-existing infection as the immune system recovers its inflammatory capacity.

clozeText: IRIS symptoms in patients with toxoplasmosis become more pronounced because antiretroviral drugs {{c1::enhance}} the ability to mount an {{c2::inflammatory response}}.
extraNote: The recovery of the immune system under HAART allows for a vigorous inflammatory response against pathogens like Toxoplasma gondii.

clozeText: To avoid the development of IRIS, a coinfection with {{c1::Toxoplasma gondii}} should be treated {{c2::prior}} to instituting HAART whenever possible.
extraNote: Standard clinical management involves controlling the opportunistic infection before restoring immune function with HAART.

clozeText: HIV-infected patients with a {{c1::low CD4 count}} have a reduced capacity to produce an inflammatory response against {{c2::Toxoplasma gondii}}.
extraNote: The lack of inflammation in severely immunocompromised patients can mask the clinical signs of a Toxoplasma infection.

clozeText: The drug {{c1::trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole}} provides dual prophylaxis for both {{c2::toxoplasmosis}} and Pneumocystis pneumonia in AIDS patients.
extraNote: Sulfonamide-based combinations are foundational for preventing multiple opportunistic infections in advanced HIV.

clozeText: The characteristic central nervous system lesion associated with {{c1::Toxoplasma gondii}} in the context of AIDS is a {{c2::brain abscess}}.
extraNote: Toxoplasma gondii is listed as a primary causative organism for brain abscesses in the late stages of HIV infection.

clozeText: Toxoplasma gondii is categorized as an important {{c1::protozoan}} that can cross the {{c2::placenta}}.
extraNote: Identifying the pathogen type is critical; Toxoplasma is a protozoan, distinguishing it from bacteria or viruses transmitted transplacentally.

clozeText: In the syndrome known as {{c1::IRIS}}, an {{c2::exacerbation}} of Toxoplasma symptoms occurs as the immune system is restored.
extraNote: IRIS symptoms are often more severe than the baseline infection symptoms due to the newly restored inflammatory power.

clozeText: Besides certain viruses, the protozoan Toxoplasma gondii is frequently transmitted via the {{c1::transplacental}} route.
extraNote: Vertical transmission of this protozoan can occur in utero across the placenta.

clozeText: Toxoplasma gondii is an opportunistic pathogen that typically affects the {{c1::central nervous system (CNS)}} in AIDS patients.
extraNote: It is listed alongside Cryptococcus neoformans and JC virus as a primary CNS opportunistic infection in advanced HIV.

clozeText: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) can occur in HIV-infected patients coinfected with {{c1::Toxoplasma gondii}} after starting HAART.
extraNote: IRIS results from the restored immune system's heightened inflammatory response to pre-existing opportunistic infections.

clozeText: In the context of Toxoplasma gondii coinfection, IRIS occurs because antiretroviral drugs enhance the ability of the host to mount an {{c1::inflammatory response}}.
extraNote: Patients with low CD4 counts initially have a reduced capacity for inflammation, which HAART restores.

clozeText: To avoid the development of IRIS, a coinfection with Toxoplasma gondii should be {{c1::treated}} prior to instituting HAART.
extraNote: Treating the opportunistic pathogen first reduces the risk of an exaggerated inflammatory response when the immune system recovers.

clozeText: The drug combination {{c1::trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole}} is used for the prevention of toxoplasmosis in patients with advanced AIDS.
extraNote: This medication provides dual prophylaxis for both Pneumocystis pneumonia and Toxoplasma gondii.

clozeText: Chemoprophylaxis against Toxoplasma gondii with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is indicated during the {{c1::late (or advanced)}} stage of HIV infection.
extraNote: The late stage of HIV is defined by a decline in CD4 cells below 200/μL and increased opportunistic infections.

clozeText: Toxoplasma gondii is classified as a(n) {{c1::protozoan}}, distinguishing it from other transplacental pathogens like Rubella (virus) or Syphilis (bacteria).
extraNote: It is the primary protozoan mentioned in the context of transplacental vertical transmission.

clozeText: In AIDS patients, brain abscesses caused by {{c1::Toxoplasma gondii}} must be clinically differentiated from meningitis caused by Cryptococcus or PML caused by JC virus.
extraNote: T. gondii specifically targets the brain parenchyma causing abscesses rather than meningitis.

clozeText: The risk of IRIS associated with Toxoplasma gondii is highest in patients who start HAART with a {{c1::low CD4 count}}.
extraNote: A low CD4 count indicates a severely suppressed inflammatory capacity that reacts sharply upon HAART initiation.

clozeText: Schistosoma species are classified as {{c1::Trematodes::class}} (flukes) within the phylum Platyhelminthes.
extraNote: Trematodes and Cestodes (tapeworms) are the two major classes of flatworms.

clozeText: Unlike most other trematodes which are hermaphrodites, adult Schistosoma exist as {{c1::separate sexes}}.
extraNote: They are dioecious; the female lives within the male's gynecophoric canal.

clozeText: The female Schistosoma fluke resides in a groove in the male known as the {{c1::gynecophoric canal}}.
extraNote: The term schist means split, referring to this canal where the male continuously fertilizes the female's eggs.

clozeText: Schistosoma mansoni eggs are distinguished by the presence of a {{c1::large lateral spine}}.
extraNote: The spine's location and size are diagnostic for identifying the species in stool or urine samples.

clozeText: The eggs of {{c1::Schistosoma haematobium}} have a terminal spine.
extraNote: These eggs are typically recovered from urine samples.

clozeText: Schistosoma japonicum eggs are characterized by a {{c1::very small lateral spine}}.
extraNote: The spine may appear rudimentary compared to S. mansoni.

clozeText: The infective stage of Schistosoma for humans is the free-swimming, fork-tailed {{c1::cercaria}}.
extraNote: Cercariae leave the snail host and penetrate human skin in freshwater.

clozeText: The essential intermediate host for all medically important Schistosoma species is the {{c1::freshwater snail}}.
extraNote: Different species of snails serve as hosts for S. mansoni, S. japonicum, and S. haematobium.

clozeText: The ciliated, swimming larvae released from Schistosoma eggs that infect snails are called {{c1::miracidia}}.
extraNote: Miracidia must find a snail host in freshwater to continue the life cycle.

clozeText: Adult S. mansoni and S. japonicum reside primarily in the {{c1::mesenteric veins}}.
extraNote: Specifically, S. mansoni affects the inferior mesenteric venules (colon) and S. japonicum affects both small and large intestine venules.

clozeText: Adult Schistosoma haematobium flukes live in the {{c1::venous plexus}} draining the urinary bladder.
extraNote: This location facilitates the passage of eggs into the bladder lumen for excretion in urine.

clozeText: In the liver, Schistosoma eggs induce the formation of {{c1::granulomas}}, leading to fibrosis and portal hypertension.
extraNote: Granulomas form in response to antigens secreted by the eggs; hepatocytes usually remain undamaged.

clozeText: Chronic Schistosoma infection leads to portal hypertension, which in turn causes {{c1::splenomegaly}}.
extraNote: The liver function tests often remain normal despite the hepatomegaly and splenomegaly.

clozeText: Chronic infection with Schistosoma haematobium is a known risk factor for {{c1::carcinoma of the bladder}}.
extraNote: The cancer risk results from chronic inflammation, granulomas, and fibrosis in the bladder wall.

clozeText: Schistosoma evades the host immune system by {{c1::coating its surface with host antigens}}.
extraNote: This molecular mimicry prevents the immune system from recognizing the fluke as foreign.

clozeText: The primary drug of choice for treating all three major Schistosoma species is {{c1::praziquantel}}.
extraNote: Praziquantel is effective against S. mansoni, S. japonicum, and S. haematobium.

clozeText: Schistosoma japonicum is unique among the blood flukes because {{c1::domestic animals}} (e.g., water buffalo, pigs) act as significant reservoirs.
extraNote: This zoonotic component makes eradication of S. japonicum more difficult.

clozeText: After cercariae penetrate human skin, they differentiate into larvae called {{c1::schistosomula}}.
extraNote: Schistosomula enter the bloodstream and travel to the portal circulation to mature into adults.

clozeText: Laboratory diagnosis of S. mansoni and S. japonicum is typically performed by stool examination for {{c1::ova::eggs}}.
extraNote: Ova and parasites (O&P) examination is the standard diagnostic tool.

clozeText: Schistosoma infections characteristically elicit a high peripheral blood count of {{c1::eosinophils}}.
extraNote: Eosinophilia and elevated IgE are common host responses to helminthic tissue invasion.

clozeText: The acute stage of schistosomiasis, appearing 2-3 weeks after infection with fever and chills, is often associated with {{c1::migrating larvae}}.
extraNote: This acute stage usually resolves spontaneously before the chronic stage begins.

clozeText: The most common cause of death in patients with chronic S. mansoni or S. japonicum is {{c1::exsanguination}} from ruptured esophageal varices.
extraNote: Varices result from portal hypertension caused by egg-induced liver fibrosis.

clozeText: The chief early clinical finding in Schistosoma haematobium infection is {{c1::hematuria}}.
extraNote: Blood in the urine occurs as eggs penetrate the bladder wall and enter the lumen.

clozeText: Schistosoma eggs damage tissue through the host inflammatory response and the release of {{c1::proteolytic enzymes}} by the egg.
extraNote: These enzymes help the egg digest through the vascular endothelium and wall of the gut or bladder.

clozeText: Schistosoma mansoni is endemic in {{c1::Africa and Latin America}}.
extraNote: It is frequently found in the Caribbean (e.g., Puerto Rico) and parts of South America.

clozeText: Prevention of schistosomiasis involves avoiding {{c1::bathing or swimming}} in contaminated freshwater sources.
extraNote: Proper sewage disposal and snail control are also vital public health measures.

clozeText: Schistosoma flukes are collectively known as {{c1::blood flukes}}.
extraNote: They are named such because the adults live within the venous system of the host.

clozeText: During the laboratory diagnosis of Schistosoma, the term used to refer to the eggs in stool or urine is {{c1::ova}}.
extraNote: Stool for O&P (Ova and Parasites) is a standard order for helminth diagnosis.

clozeText: Host defense against Schistosoma involves both eosinophils and elevated levels of {{c1::Immunoglobulin E::IgE}}.
extraNote: IgE-mediated responses are typical for helminthic infections.

clozeText: In the Schistosoma life cycle, humans serve as the {{c1::definitive host}}.
extraNote: The definitive host is where the parasite undergoes sexual reproduction or the adult stage is present.

clozeText: Schistosoma belongs to the class {{c1::Trematoda::class}} within the phylum Platyhelminthes.
extraNote: Commonly known as flukes; distinct from Cestoda (tapeworms) and Nematoda (roundworms).

clozeText: Unlike most other trematodes which are hermaphroditic, Schistosoma adults exist as {{c1::separate sexes}}.
extraNote: The female resides in a groove in the male called the gynecophoric canal.

clozeText: The infective stage of Schistosoma for humans is the {{c1::cercaria::specific larval form}}, which is free-swimming and has a forked tail.
extraNote: Cercariae penetrate human skin directly when in contact with contaminated freshwater.

clozeText: The intermediate host for all medically important Schistosoma species is the {{c1::freshwater snail}}.
extraNote: Asexual reproduction and development from miracidia to cercariae occur within the snail.

clozeText: Schistosoma mansoni eggs are characterized by a {{c1::large lateral spine}}.
extraNote: These eggs are primarily found in the stool and the adult worms reside in the mesenteric veins of the colon.

clozeText: Schistosoma japonicum eggs are distinguished by having a {{c1::small lateral spine}}.
extraNote: Adults reside in the mesenteric veins of the small intestine and liver.

clozeText: Schistosoma haematobium eggs are characterized by a {{c1::terminal spine}}.
extraNote: These eggs are typically recovered from the urine; the adults live in the veins draining the urinary bladder.

clozeText: The ciliated larval stage that hatches from Schistosoma eggs and infects snails is the {{c1::miracidium}}.
extraNote: The miracidium must find and penetrate a suitable snail host in freshwater to continue the cycle.

clozeText: After penetrating the skin, Schistosoma cercariae differentiate into larvae called {{c1::schistosomula}} before entering the blood.
extraNote: These larvae travel through the venous and arterial circulation to reach the portal system.

clozeText: Most pathologic findings in schistosomiasis are caused by the host's reaction to {{c1::eggs}} in tissues, resulting in {{c2::granulomas}}.
extraNote: Granulomas form in response to antigens secreted by the eggs in the liver, spleen, gut, or bladder wall.

clozeText: In the liver, Schistosoma eggs induce granulomas that lead to {{c1::fibrosis::pathological state}}, hepatomegaly, and portal hypertension.
extraNote: Hepatocytes usually remain undamaged, and liver function tests typically stay normal.

clozeText: The most common cause of death in chronic S. mansoni or S. japonicum infection is {{c1::exsanguination}} from ruptured {{c2::esophageal varices}}.
extraNote: This is a direct consequence of severe portal hypertension and splenomegaly.

clozeText: Chronic infection with Schistosoma haematobium in the bladder wall can eventually lead to {{c1::carcinoma of the bladder}}.
extraNote: Granulomas and fibrosis in the bladder wall predispose patients to malignancy.

clozeText: Schistosomes evade the host immune system by coating their surface with {{c1::host antigens}}.
extraNote: This process limits the immune system's ability to recognize the flukes as foreign invaders.

clozeText: Schistosoma eggs damage tissue in the gut and bladder using {{c1::proteolytic enzymes}} they produce.
extraNote: The damage is a combination of enzymatic digestion and the host's inflammatory response.

clozeText: The early clinical finding for Schistosoma haematobium infection is {{c1::hematuria::symptom}}.
extraNote: Blood in the urine occurs as eggs penetrate the bladder mucosa.

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating all three major species of Schistosoma is {{c1::praziquantel}}.
extraNote: Treatment targets the adult flukes to resolve the infection.

clozeText: Schistosoma infections characteristically elicit {{c1::eosinophilia}} and an elevation in {{c2::IgE::antibody}}.
extraNote: High eosinophil counts are especially common during the migration of larvae through tissues.

clozeText: Schistosoma japonicum is the only species for which {{c1::domestic animals}} (e.g., water buffalo and pigs) act as significant reservoirs.
extraNote: This species is found specifically in Asia.

clozeText: Acute schistosomiasis may present with {{c1::itching and dermatitis}} immediately following cercarial penetration.
extraNote: Commonly referred to as swimmer's itch.

clozeText: Schistosoma mansoni is endemic in {{c1::Africa and Latin America}} (including Puerto Rico).
extraNote: Its distribution is limited by the range of its specific intermediate snail hosts.

clozeText: Schistosoma haematobium is primarily found in {{c1::Africa and the Middle East}}.
extraNote: Associated with freshwater sources containing specific intermediate snail hosts.

clozeText: During the life cycle, the adult Schistosoma worms migrate against the {{c1::portal flow}} to reach the mesenteric venules.
extraNote: Mature flukes move from the liver to their final residence in the veins.

clozeText: Portal hypertension caused by Schistosoma infection leads directly to {{c1::splenomegaly::organ enlargement}}.
extraNote: Enlargement of the spleen is common in S. mansoni and S. japonicum infections.

clozeText: Schistosoma transmission occurs via {{c1::penetration of the skin}} by larvae, rather than ingestion of eggs or cysts.
extraNote: Avoiding bathing or swimming in contaminated freshwater is a key preventive measure.

clozeText: In the definitive host (humans), the {{c1::sexual cycle}} of Schistosoma occurs.
extraNote: Adult flukes mate and the female produces fertilized eggs within the venous system.

clozeText: Diagnostic examination for Schistosoma involves looking for {{c1::ova::eggs}} in the stool or urine.
extraNote: The presence of eggs with characteristic spines is definitive for diagnosis.

clozeText: Acute Schistosoma infection symptoms like fever, chills, and lymphadenopathy typically appear {{c1::2 to 3 weeks}} after cercarial penetration.
extraNote: This stage represents the host reaction to migrating larvae and early egg production.

clozeText: Schistosoma adults are often called {{c1::blood flukes}} because they live within human veins.
extraNote: They are specifically found in the mesenteric or bladder venous plexuses.

clozeText: The larval stage of Schistosoma that is carried via the veins to the lungs and eventually the liver is the {{c1::schistosomula}}.
extraNote: These are the transformed cercariae that have lost their tails and entered the circulatory system.

clozeText: Humans are infected with Schistosoma when free-swimming, fork-tailed {{c1::cercariae}} penetrate the skin.
extraNote: Cercariae are found in freshwater; once they penetrate the skin, they differentiate into schistosomula and enter the blood.

clozeText: Schistosoma {{c1::mansoni}} eggs are characterized by having a prominent lateral spine.
extraNote: These eggs are typically found in the stool of infected patients.

clozeText: Schistosoma {{c1::haematobium}} eggs are characterized by having a large terminal spine.
extraNote: These eggs are typically found in the urine and are associated with bladder disease.

clozeText: Schistosoma {{c1::japonicum}} eggs are characterized by having a very small lateral spine.
extraNote: This species is primarily found in Asia and is the only one with significant animal reservoirs like water buffalo.

clozeText: Adult Schistosoma mansoni and S. japonicum reside in the {{c1::mesenteric veins}}, whereas S. haematobium resides in the veins of the bladder.
extraNote: Because of their location, they are commonly referred to as blood flukes.

clozeText: Pathological findings in schistosomiasis are primarily caused by {{c1::eggs}} in the liver, spleen, or organ walls inducing granulomas.
extraNote: Granulomas form in response to antigens secreted by the eggs, leading to fibrosis and portal hypertension.

clozeText: The most common cause of death in chronic Schistosoma mansoni or S. japonicum infection is exsanguination from {{c1::ruptured esophageal varices}}.
extraNote: Portal hypertension from liver fibrosis leads to the development of these varices.

clozeText: Schistosoma haematobium infection is a known risk factor for the development of {{c1::carcinoma of the bladder}}.
extraNote: Chronic inflammation and granulomas in the bladder wall lead to this malignancy.

clozeText: The acute stage of schistosomiasis, occurring shortly after cercarial penetration, often presents with {{c1::itching and dermatitis}}.
extraNote: This is followed 2 to 3 weeks later by fever, chills, diarrhea, and lymphadenopathy.

clozeText: The early chief complaint of patients infected with Schistosoma haematobium is {{c1::hematuria}}.
extraNote: This is often accompanied by frequent superimposed bacterial urinary tract infections.

clozeText: In contrast to other trematodes which are hermaphrodites, Schistosoma species exist as {{c1::separate sexes}}.
extraNote: The female lives in the gynecophoric canal of the male where continuous fertilization occurs.

clozeText: Schistosoma infections elicit {{c1::eosinophilia}} and elevated levels of Immunoglobulin E (IgE).
extraNote: Eosinophils are a critical component of host defense against these helminths.

clozeText: The free-swimming ciliated larvae that hatch from Schistosoma eggs in freshwater are called {{c1::miracidia}}.
extraNote: Miracidia must find and penetrate a snail to continue the life cycle.

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating all three major Schistosoma species is {{c1::praziquantel}}.
extraNote: Treatment targets the adult flukes in the venous circulation.

clozeText: In the liver, Schistosoma eggs cause {{c1::portal hypertension}}, but usually leave hepatocytes undamaged with normal liver function tests.
extraNote: The damage is perisinusoidal, leading to fibrosis and subsequent splenomegaly.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri is a free-living {{c1::ameba}} that causes meningoencephalitis.
extraNote: It is categorized as a minor protozoan of the blood and tissue.

clozeText: The organisms are found in warm {{c1::freshwater}} lakes and in soil.
extraNote: Stagnant or warm fresh water is the classic environmental source for infection.

clozeText: The life cycle of Naegleria fowleri involves {{c1::trophozoite}} and {{c1::cyst::non-trophozoite}} stages.
extraNote: The trophozoite is the active, infectious form in humans.

clozeText: Naegleria cysts are quite resistant and are not killed by {{c1::chlorination}}.
extraNote: This resistance makes them difficult to eliminate from certain water sources.

clozeText: Naegleria trophozoites usually enter the body through mucous membranes while an individual is {{c1::swimming}}.
extraNote: The organism is often associated with water activities in warm climates.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri penetrates the {{c1::nasal mucosa}} and {{c2::cribriform plate}} to reach the central nervous system.
extraNote: This pathway allows the ameba direct access to the brain from the nasal cavity.

clozeText: The infection caused by Naegleria fowleri is usually {{c1::rapidly fatal}}.
extraNote: The disease progression from initial symptoms to death is very fast.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri produces a {{c1::purulent}} meningitis and encephalitis.
extraNote: This is often referred to as primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM).

clozeText: Unlike Acanthamoeba, Naegleria infections typically occur in otherwise {{c1::healthy}} persons.
extraNote: It does not require an immunocompromised state to cause severe disease.

clozeText: In the United States, Naegleria fowleri infections occur mainly in the {{c1::southern}} states and California.
extraNote: Warm environmental temperatures in these regions facilitate the growth of the ameba.

clozeText: Diagnosis is made by finding {{c1::amebas}} in the spinal fluid.
extraNote: CSF examination is critical for identifying the motile organisms.

clozeText: {{c1::Amphotericin B}} is the drug of choice that may be effective in Naegleria infections.
extraNote: Despite treatment, the prognosis remains extremely poor.

clozeText: The stage of Naegleria fowleri that infects humans is the {{c1::trophozoite}}.
extraNote: The trophozoite is also the stage most associated with disease in the meninges.

clozeText: The important stage of Naegleria fowleri outside of humans is the {{c1::cyst}}.
extraNote: Cysts allow the organism to survive in soil and water when conditions are unfavorable.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri has {{c1::no insect vector::vector?}}.
extraNote: Transmission is via direct contact with contaminated water, not through arthropods.

clozeText: Microscopic examination of a wet mount of spinal fluid reveals {{c1::motile}} trophozoites.
extraNote: The movement of the amebas is a key diagnostic feature in fresh CSF samples.

clozeText: In a patient with Naegleria fowleri, the spinal fluid white blood cell count is often highly elevated with a predominance of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
extraNote: This neutrophil predominance can mimic acute bacterial meningitis.

clozeText: A classic clinical presentation of Naegleria fowleri includes a severe headache, fever, and {{c1::nuchal rigidity}}.
extraNote: Nuchal rigidity is a hallmark sign of meningeal irritation.

clozeText: Infections with Naegleria fowleri most commonly affect {{c1::children}}.
extraNote: Younger populations are frequently exposed via recreational water activities.

clozeText: The ameba-shaped trophozoites of Naegleria fowleri can be found within {{c1::brain tissue}}.
extraNote: The organism causes extensive damage to the parenchyma and meninges.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri is classified as a {{c1::free-living}} ameba that causes meningoencephalitis.
extraNote: It is found primarily in warm freshwater lakes and soil.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri causes a severe brain infection known as {{c1::meningoencephalitis}}.
extraNote: This condition involves inflammation of both the meninges and the brain parenchyma.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri is typically found in {{c1::warm freshwater}} lakes and in soil.
extraNote: Infections are often associated with recreational water activities in these environments.

clozeText: The life cycle of Naegleria fowleri involves both {{c1::trophozoite}} and {{c2::cyst}} stages.
extraNote: Both stages are critical for survival in the environment and pathogenesis in humans.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri {{c1::cysts}} are resistant to environmental stressors and are not killed by {{c2::chlorination}}.
extraNote: This resistance allows the organism to survive standard water treatment processes.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri trophozoites penetrate the {{c1::nasal mucosa}} and {{c2::cribriform plate}} to reach the central nervous system.
extraNote: This direct pathway allows rapid access to the brain from the nasal cavity.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri produces a {{c1::purulent}} meningitis and encephalitis that is usually rapidly fatal.
extraNote: The infection progresses quickly, often leading to death within days of symptom onset.

clozeText: Unlike Acanthamoeba, Naegleria fowleri infections typically occur in {{c1::otherwise healthy}} persons, usually children.
extraNote: Immunocompetence does not protect against this specific amebic infection.

clozeText: In the United States, rare Naegleria fowleri infections occur mainly in the {{c1::southern states}} and California.
extraNote: The geographic distribution is linked to warmer water temperatures required for the organism to thrive.

clozeText: Diagnosis of Naegleria fowleri is made by finding {{c1::amebas}} in the {{c2::spinal fluid (CSF)}}.
extraNote: A wet mount of CSF can reveal the motile trophozoites.

clozeText: The drug {{c1::Amphotericin B}} may be effective in treating Naegleria fowleri infections.
extraNote: Despite treatment, the prognosis remains very poor for infected individuals.

clozeText: The {{c1::trophozoite}} stage of Naegleria fowleri is the stage that infects humans.
extraNote: This motile form is responsible for tissue invasion and destruction.

clozeText: The stage of Naegleria fowleri most associated with disease in the meninges is the {{c1::trophozoite}}.
extraNote: These are the ameboid forms seen infiltrating brain tissue.

clozeText: The important stage of Naegleria fowleri found outside of humans in the environment is the {{c1::cyst}}.
extraNote: The cyst stage allows the organism to persist in soil and water under harsh conditions.

clozeText: Microscopic examination of a {{c1::wet mount}} of spinal fluid in Naegleria fowleri infection reveals {{c2::motile}} trophozoites.
extraNote: Observing the characteristic movement of the ameba is a key diagnostic step.

clozeText: In a clinical case of Naegleria fowleri, the spinal fluid white blood cell count can be very high, with a predominance of {{c1::neutrophils::cell type}}.
extraNote: Values as high as 12,200 WBCs with 80% neutrophils have been observed in acute cases.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri is categorized as a minor protozoan of the {{c1::blood and tissue}}.
extraNote: It specifically targets the central nervous system after entering through nasal tissues.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri trophozoites in brain tissue can be identified by their distinct {{c1::ameba}} shape.
extraNote: Histological examination of brain tissue often reveals these organisms near sites of necrosis.

clozeText: The prognosis for Naegleria fowleri infection is {{c1::poor}} even in treated cases.
extraNote: Rapid progression to death is the typical clinical course.

clozeText: Entry of Naegleria fowleri into the brain occurs following exposure to contaminated water, often during the month of {{c1::August::month}} in temperate regions.
extraNote: The peak of infections coincides with the warmest summer months when water temperatures are highest.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri is one of the {{c1::free-living}} amebas, distinguishing it from obligate parasites like Entamoeba histolytica.
extraNote: It can complete its life cycle in the environment without a host.

clozeText: A critical step in the pathogenesis of Naegleria fowleri is the invasion of the {{c1::nasal mucosa}}.
extraNote: This occurs before the ameba traverses the cribriform plate.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri infections are characterized by a purulent {{c1::meningitis}}.
extraNote: This mimics acute bacterial meningitis in its clinical presentation and CSF findings.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri is found in soil and {{c1::freshwater::water type}}.
extraNote: Saltwater does not typically harbor this organism.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for Naegleria fowleri is the {{c1::environment::reservoir type}}.
extraNote: There is no known animal reservoir; humans are accidental hosts.

clozeText: In Naegleria fowleri infections, the {{c1::trophozoite}} is the stage found in the meninges and brain tissue.
extraNote: Direct visualization of this stage in CSF or tissue is diagnostic.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri is a cause of {{c1::primary::classification}} amebic meningoencephalitis.
extraNote: This distinguishes it from secondary infections that might spread from other sites in the body.

clozeText: Environmental Naegleria fowleri {{c1::cysts}} are notoriously resistant to standard {{c2::chlorine}} levels in swimming pools.
extraNote: This resistance is a major factor in the risk associated with warm freshwater bodies.

clozeText: The typical patient profile for Naegleria fowleri infection is a {{c1::child}} or young adult with a recent history of swimming in freshwater.
extraNote: Vigorous water activities that force water into the nose increase the risk of infection.

clozeText: The primary clinical manifestation of Naegleria fowleri is {{c1::meningoencephalitis}}.
extraNote: The infection involves both the meninges and the brain parenchyma.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri is found in {{c1::warm freshwater}} lakes and in soil.
extraNote: The organism thrives in higher temperatures and is not typically found in saltwater.

clozeText: The life cycle of Naegleria fowleri involves two stages: the {{c1::trophozoite}} and the cyst.
extraNote: The trophozoite is the stage that infects humans and is associated with disease.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri cysts are resistant and are not killed by {{c1::chlorination}}.
extraNote: This resistance allows the organism to survive in treated water systems if not properly managed.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri trophozoites usually enter the body through {{c1::mucous membranes::tissue type}} while an individual is swimming.
extraNote: The nasal mucosa is the primary point of entry.

clozeText: The organism penetrates the {{c1::nasal mucosa}} and the {{c2::cribriform plate}} to reach the brain.
extraNote: The proximity of the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulbs provides a direct route to the CNS.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri infections are usually {{c1::rapidly fatal}}.
extraNote: Progression from symptom onset to death typically occurs within a few days.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri infections primarily occur in {{c1::otherwise healthy persons}}, usually children.
extraNote: This contrasts with Acanthamoeba, which usually affects immunocompromised individuals.

clozeText: Diagnosis of Naegleria fowleri is made by finding {{c1::amebas}} in the spinal fluid.
extraNote: Motile trophozoites can sometimes be seen on a wet mount of the CSF.

clozeText: The important stage of Naegleria fowleri found outside of humans is the {{c1::cyst}}.
extraNote: The cyst stage allows the organism to survive environmental stressors.

clozeText: A lumbar puncture in a Naegleria fowleri patient typically reveals a high white blood cell count with a predominance of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
extraNote: One clinical case showed a WBC count of 12,200 with 80% neutrophils.

clozeText: Microscopic examination of a {{c1::wet mount}} of spinal fluid may reveal motile Naegleria fowleri trophozoites.
extraNote: Direct visualization is a key diagnostic method for identifying the motile amebas.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri does not utilize an {{c1::insect vector}} for transmission.
extraNote: Infection is acquired directly from the environment, primarily through water contact.

clozeText: Clinical history for Naegleria fowleri often involves swimming in a pond or lake during the month of {{c1::August}}.
extraNote: Infections are most common during the hottest summer months when water temperatures peak.

clozeText: The infective stage of Naegleria fowleri that enters the human host is the {{c1::trophozoite}}.
extraNote: The trophozoite enters the nasal cavity and migrates to the brain.

clozeText: Primary symptoms of Naegleria fowleri infection include {{c1::fever}} and a severe {{c2::headache}}.
extraNote: These symptoms typically appear within 2 days of initial presentation and progress rapidly.

clozeText: Physical examination of a patient with Naegleria fowleri often reveals {{c1::nuchal rigidity}}.
extraNote: This sign of meningeal irritation is characteristic of the infection.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri is often identified in {{c1::brain tissue::biopsy location}} during autopsy or biopsy.
extraNote: Ameba-shaped trophozoites can be seen infiltrating the tissue.

clozeText: The prognosis for Naegleria fowleri is described as {{c1::poor}} even in treated cases.
extraNote: The fatality rate exceeds 95% for this infection.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri can be found in {{c1::soil}} in addition to freshwater environments.
extraNote: It is a widely distributed free-living organism in the environment.

clozeText: The clinical presentation of Naegleria fowleri can be confused with {{c1::acute bacterial meningitis}}.
extraNote: Both present with purulent spinal fluid and high neutrophil counts.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri trophozoites are {{c1::motile}}.
