extraNote: This motility is a distinguishing feature when observed in a wet mount of CSF.

clozeText: The presence of {{c1::ameba-shaped trophozoites}} in brain tissue is diagnostic for Naegleria fowleri.
extraNote: Histological examination can confirm the presence of the parasite in the parenchyma.

clozeText: In the United States, rural areas of {{c1::California}} have been identified as sites for Naegleria fowleri cases.
extraNote: The organism's presence is noted in both the southern states and the western US.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri {{c1::cysts}} are quite resistant and are not killed by chlorination.
extraNote: This resistance allows the organism to survive in various water environments.

clozeText: Naegleria fowleri trophozoites usually enter the body through the {{c1::nasal mucosa}} while an individual is swimming.
extraNote: Entry occurs specifically during activities in warm freshwater lakes.

clozeText: In patients with AIDS, {{c1::Cryptosporidium parvum}} is a causative organism for {{c2::diarrhea}} in the intestinal tract.
extraNote: It is listed as a major opportunistic infection in late-stage HIV, alongside other pathogens like Salmonella and cytomegalovirus.

clozeText: Protozoa such as {{c1::Cryptosporidium::genus}} species are recognized as causes of {{c2::traveler’s diarrhea}}, alongside norovirus and Various bacteria.
extraNote: While ETEC is the most common cause of traveler's diarrhea, Cryptosporidium is a significant protozoan contributor.

clozeText: The genus {{c1::Cryptosporidium}} is biologically classified as a(n) {{c2::sporozoan}} pathogen within the intestinal tract.
extraNote: Other intestinal protozoa mentioned in the text include the ameba Entamoeba histolytica and the flagellate Giardia lamblia.

clozeText: In patients with AIDS, the {{c1::intestinal tract}} is the primary site of infection for the protozoan {{c2::Cryptosporidium parvum}}.
extraNote: Infections at this site frequently cause symptomatic diarrhea in immunocompromised hosts.

clozeText: {{c1::Cryptosporidium parvum}} is categorized as an opportunistic pathogen that causes disease during the late stage of {{c2::HIV}} infection.
extraNote: The late stage is defined by a decline in CD4 cells below 200/ΑL and the onset of opportunistic infections.

clozeText: The major protozoan pathogens, such as {{c1::Cryptosporidium}}, are grouped according to the {{c2::location in the body}} where they most frequently cause disease.
extraNote: Categories include intestinal, urogenital, blood, and tissue protozoa.

clozeText: Opportunistic infections including {{c1::Cryptosporidium parvum}} significantly increase in severity when the CD4 count falls below {{c2::200 cells/ μ L}}.
extraNote: This threshold is used to define an AIDS-defining condition and to guide chemoprophylaxis decisions.

clozeText: {{c1::Cryptosporidium}} is listed as the causative agent for the intestinal disease known as {{c2::cryptosporidiosis}}.
extraNote: It is categorized as a major intestinal protozoan alongside Giardia and Entamoeba.

clozeText: {{c1::Cryptosporidium parvum}} is a protozoan pathogen that causes {{c2::diarrhea}} in the intestinal tract of patients with AIDS.
extraNote: It is listed as a common opportunistic infection in the late stage of HIV infection.

clozeText: In patients with AIDS, infection with {{c1::Cryptosporidium parvum}} is localized to the {{c2::intestinal tract}}.
extraNote: Other pathogens causing diarrhea in this population include Salmonella species, Shigella species, and cytomegalovirus.

clozeText: {{c1::Cryptosporidium}} species are recognized as protozoan causes of {{c2::traveler’s diarrhea}}, although enterotoxigenic E. coli is the most common cause.
extraNote: Other involved organisms include norovirus and Giardia.

clozeText: The frequency and severity of opportunistic infections like {{c1::Cryptosporidium parvum}} increase significantly when the CD4 count falls below {{c2::200::number}} cells/μL.
extraNote: A CD4 count of 200 cells/μL or below is considered an AIDS-defining condition.

clozeText: In the late stage of HIV infection, {{c1::Cryptosporidium parvum}} is classified as an {{c2::opportunistic}} infection.
extraNote: This stage is manifested by a decline in CD4 cells and an increase in the severity of such infections.

clozeText: Along with *Giardia lamblia*, the organism {{c1::Cryptosporidium parvum}} is a protozoan identified as a cause of {{c2::diarrhea}} in the intestinal tract of AIDS patients.
extraNote: These infections are part of the common opportunistic pathogens seen in late-stage HIV.

clozeText: Along with viruses like norovirus and bacteria like *Salmonella*, {{c1::Cryptosporidium::organism}} species are protozoan causes of traveler’s diarrhea.
extraNote: While *Enterotoxigenic E. coli* (ETEC) is the most common cause of traveler’s diarrhea, protozoa like *Cryptosporidium* and *Giardia* are also significant causes.

clozeText: In patients with AIDS, {{c1::Cryptosporidium parvum}} is a causative organism of diarrhea in the intestinal tract.
extraNote: Other opportunistic causes of diarrhea in AIDS patients include *Salmonella* species, *Shigella* species, and cytomegalovirus (CMV).

clozeText: Within the intestinal tract, {{c1::Cryptosporidium hominis::organism}} is classified biologically as a sporozoan.
extraNote: It is one of the three most important intestinal protozoa, alongside *Entamoeba histolytica* (an ameba) and *Giardia lamblia* (a flagellate).

clozeText: The disease caused by *Cryptosporidium hominis* in the intestinal tract is known as {{c1::cryptosporidiosis}}.
extraNote: It is categorized as a major protozoan pathogen within the intestinal tract.

clozeText: *Cryptosporidium parvum* is an opportunistic infection that manifests during the {{c1::late stage::HIV stage}} of HIV infection, also known as AIDS.
extraNote: This stage is defined by a decline in CD4 cells and an increase in opportunistic pathogens.

clozeText: The frequency and severity of opportunistic infections like *Cryptosporidium parvum* significantly increase when the CD4 count falls below {{c1::200::number}} cells/μL.
extraNote: A CD4 count of 200 cells/μL or below is an AIDS-defining condition.

clozeText: *Cryptosporidium parvum* is listed as a major cause of {{c1::diarrhea}} in the intestinal tract of immunocompromised patients.
extraNote: In AIDS patients, it is frequently grouped with other enteric pathogens such as *Giardia lamblia* and *Shigella* species.

clozeText: In the categorization of protozoan pathogens, *Cryptosporidium hominis* is identified as a(n) {{c1::major}} intestinal protozoan.
extraNote: It is distinguished from minor intestinal protozoa such as *Balantidium coli*, *Isospora belli*, and *Cyclospora cayetanensis*.

clozeText: The primary site of infection for *Cryptosporidium parvum* in patients with HIV/AIDS is the {{c1::intestinal tract}}.
extraNote: This organism is part of the 'intestinal and urogenital protozoa' grouping based on its most frequent site of disease.

clozeText: {{c1::Cryptosporidium hominis}} is one of the three most important protozoa found within the intestinal tract, along with the ameba *Entamoeba histolytica* and the flagellate *Giardia lamblia*.
extraNote: These three organisms are the primary focus of intestinal protozoology.

clozeText: *Cryptosporidium parvum* is considered a(n) {{c1::opportunistic}} pathogen, particularly in the context of advanced HIV infection.
extraNote: Opportunistic infections are those that take advantage of a weakened immune system, specifically a decline in CD4-positive T cells.

clozeText: Among the sporozoans infecting the intestinal tract, {{c1::Cryptosporidium hominis}} is noted as a major pathogen causing cryptosporidiosis.
extraNote: Other sporozoans mentioned in medical microbiology include *Plasmodium* and *Toxoplasma*, which are blood and tissue pathogens.

clozeText: In patients with AIDS, {{c1::Cryptosporidium parvum}} is a common causative agent of {{c2::diarrhea}} in the intestinal tract.
extraNote: It is grouped with other intestinal pathogens such as Salmonella, Shigella, and Cytomegalovirus in the context of late-stage HIV.

clozeText: Along with viruses and bacteria, protozoa such as {{c1::Cryptosporidium}} species are potential causes of {{c2::traveler's diarrhea::"turista"}}.
extraNote: While Enterotoxigenic E. coli is the most common cause, protozoa like Cryptosporidium and Giardia are also involved.

clozeText: {{c1::Cryptosporidium parvum}} is an opportunistic pathogen that targets the {{c2::intestinal tract}} in HIV-infected individuals.
extraNote: Other intestinal pathogens in this group include Giardia lamblia and Salmonella species.

clozeText: A CD4 count of {{c1::200}} cells/μ L or below is used to determine if a patient requires {{c2::chemoprophylaxis}} against opportunistic organisms like {{c3::Cryptosporidium parvum}}.
extraNote: Chemoprophylaxis is indicated in patients with significantly reduced T-cell counts to prevent opportunistic infections.

clozeText: In the context of AIDS, {{c1::Cryptosporidium parvum}} is classified as a(n) {{c2::opportunistic}} infection.
extraNote: Opportunistic infections become frequent and severe when the immune system is significantly compromised.

clozeText: {{c1::Cryptosporidium parvum}} is listed alongside the flagellate {{c2::Giardia lamblia}} as a common protozoan cause of diarrhea in the intestinal tract of AIDS patients.
extraNote: Both are protozoan pathogens that take advantage of declining CD4-positive T cells.

clozeText: Diarrhea associated with {{c1::Cryptosporidium}} in traveler's diarrhea is generally described as {{c2::watery}} and {{c3::nonbloody}}.
extraNote: This presentation is characteristic of traveler's diarrhea (turista) caused by protozoa and ETEC.

clozeText: Late-stage HIV infection (AIDS) is manifested by a decline in the number of {{c1::CD4}} cells to below {{c2::200}}/μ L and a resulting increase in infections like {{c3::Cryptosporidium parvum}}.
extraNote: The lower limit of a normal CD4 count is 500 cells/μ L.

clozeText: The primary symptom caused by {{c1::Cryptosporidium parvum}} in the intestinal tract of immunocompromised patients is {{c2::diarrhea}}.
extraNote: Diarrhea in these patients can be severe and is often associated with a decline in immune function.

clozeText: Protozoa such as {{c1::Cryptosporidium}} are grouped with bacterial species like {{c2::Salmonella}}, {{c3::Shigella}}, and {{c4::Campylobacter}} as causes of diarrhea in travelers.
extraNote: While ETEC is the most common cause, a variety of bacteria, viruses, and protozoa can be involved.

clozeText: The risk of developing intestinal disease from {{c1::Cryptosporidium parvum}} increases during the {{c2::late stage}} of HIV infection.
extraNote: This stage is characterized by a CD4 count below 200/μ L and symptomatic AIDS.

clozeText: {{c1::Cryptosporidium parvum}} is one of the specific causative organisms identified as a source of diarrhea in the intestinal tract of {{c2::AIDS}} patients.
extraNote: Its presence is a clinical marker often associated with the progression of HIV to AIDS.

clozeText: Management of HIV-infected patients involves monitoring the {{c1::CD4-positive T cell}} count to guide decisions regarding prophylaxis for opportunistic pathogens like {{c2::Cryptosporidium parvum}}.
extraNote: The CD4 count is a critical measure for determining when anti-HIV therapy or chemoprophylaxis is needed.

clozeText: In traveler's diarrhea, organisms like {{c1::Cryptosporidium}} are considered {{c2::protozoan}} pathogens, distinguishing them from viral and bacterial causes like norovirus and ETEC.
extraNote: Giardia lamblia is another protozoan listed as a cause of traveler's diarrhea.

clozeText: Ancylostoma duodenale is a member of the phylum {{c1::Nemathelminthes}} (roundworms).
extraNote: Nemathelminthes are characterized as roundworms with cylindrical bodies and complete digestive tracts.

clozeText: The body of Ancylostoma duodenale is covered by a noncellular, highly resistant coating called a {{c1::cuticle}}.
extraNote: The cuticle provides protection for the roundworm within the host environment.

clozeText: In Ancylostoma duodenale, the {{c1::female}} worm is typically larger than the male.
extraNote: This sexual dimorphism is common among nematodes; the male typically has a coiled tail.

clozeText: Human infection by Ancylostoma duodenale occurs through the {{c1::penetration of the skin}} by larvae.
extraNote: This differs from other intestinal nematodes like Ascaris, which are acquired by ingestion of eggs.

clozeText: The infectious, nonfeeding stage of Ancylostoma duodenale is the third-stage {{c1::filariform}} larva.
extraNote: This stage is responsible for penetrating human skin to initiate infection.

clozeText: The first- and second-stage larvae of Ancylostoma duodenale, known as {{c1::rhabditiform}} larvae, are noninfectious feeding forms.
extraNote: Rhabditiform larvae develop from eggs in the environment before maturing into the infectious filariform stage.

clozeText: During the life cycle of Ancylostoma duodenale, larvae pass through the {{c1::lungs}}, potentially causing symptoms of pneumonitis.
extraNote: Pneumonitis occurs as larvae migrate through the tissue toward the respiratory tract before being swallowed.

clozeText: Adult Ancylostoma duodenale worms reside and mate within the {{c1::small intestine}} of the host.
extraNote: Once in the small intestine, they attach to the wall and begin feeding.

clozeText: The primary clinical consequence of adult Ancylostoma duodenale worms in the small intestine is {{c1::blood loss (anemia)}}.
extraNote: Hookworms consume host blood, leading to iron-deficiency anemia in chronic or heavy infections.

clozeText: Laboratory diagnosis of Ancylostoma duodenale is typically made by finding {{c1::eggs::stage}} in the stool.
extraNote: Stool examination for ova and parasites (O&P) is the standard diagnostic method.

clozeText: The drugs of choice for treating intestinal Ancylostoma duodenale infections include {{c1::albendazole}}, mebendazole, or pyrantel pamoate.
extraNote: These medications target the adult worms residing in the intestinal tract.

clozeText: Ancylostoma duodenale infection often results in a striking increase in the number of {{c1::eosinophils}}.
extraNote: Eosinophilia is a hallmark of helminth infections, especially during the tissue-migration phase of the larvae.

clozeText: Host defenses against Ancylostoma duodenale involve eosinophils attaching to the parasite via {{c1::IgE::immunoglobulin}}.
extraNote: Eosinophils then secrete cytotoxic enzymes from their granules to damage the parasite.

clozeText: A key preventive measure against Ancylostoma duodenale infection is {{c1::wearing shoes}}.
extraNote: This prevents filariform larvae in the soil from coming into contact with and penetrating the skin of the feet.

clozeText: The environmental life cycle of Ancylostoma duodenale progresses from egg to rhabditiform larva to {{c1::filariform}} larva.
extraNote: The filariform larva is the final environmental stage that must penetrate human skin to continue the cycle.

clozeText: In hookworm infections, the number of eosinophils is increased by the cytokine {{c1::IL-5}}.
extraNote: IL-5 is synthesized by the Th-2 subset of helper T cells in response to helminth antigens.

clozeText: Ancylostoma larvae can cause a localized skin condition known as {{c1::cutaneous larva migrans}}.
extraNote: This occurs when larvae penetrate the skin but are unable to complete their migration to the intestines.

clozeText: The male Ancylostoma duodenale typically has a {{c1::coiled tail}}.
extraNote: This is a characteristic morphological feature used to distinguish male nematodes.

clozeText: Host defenses against helminths like Ancylostoma are stimulated by interleukins synthesized by the {{c1::Th-2}} subset of helper T cells.
extraNote: The Th-2 response is characterized by the production of IL-4 and IL-5, leading to IgE production and eosinophilia.

clozeText: Cysteine proteases produced by Ancylostoma worms facilitate their {{c1::migration}} through tissue.
extraNote: These enzymes act as stimuli for the production of IL-5 by Th-2 cells.

clozeText: Ancylostoma duodenale possesses a complete digestive tract, including a {{c1::mouth and an anus}}.
extraNote: This distinguishes roundworms (nematodes) from flatworms (platyhelminths).

clozeText: The production of IgE in response to Ancylostoma duodenale is increased by the cytokine {{c1::IL-4}}.
extraNote: IL-4 is a key cytokine produced by Th-2 cells that promotes B-cell class switching to IgE.

clozeText: Hookworms like Ancylostoma are characterized by a {{c1::cylindrical}} body shape.
extraNote: This shape is the defining feature of the phylum Nemathelminthes.

clozeText: For cutaneous larva migrans caused by Ancylostoma larvae, the recommended drugs are {{c1::albendazole}} or ivermectin.
extraNote: Ivermectin is an alternative to albendazole specifically for the larval skin infection.

clozeText: Ancylostoma duodenale is especially endemic in {{c1::tropical}} areas.
extraNote: Warm, moist soil in these regions facilitates the survival and development of larvae.

clozeText: Hookworms are classified as {{c1::intestinal}} nematodes because the adult worms reside in the gut.
extraNote: While larvae migrate through tissue and lungs, the primary site of disease and reproduction is the intestine.

clozeText: The nonfeeding, infectious stage of the hookworm life cycle is the {{c1::third}}-stage larva.
extraNote: This is the filariform stage that survives in the soil waiting for a host.

clozeText: Eosinophils do not ingest Ancylostoma duodenale; instead, they secrete {{c1::cytotoxic enzymes}} to kill the parasite.
extraNote: These enzymes are stored within eosinophilic granules and are released upon attachment to the worm.

clozeText: In the laboratory diagnosis of hookworm, the term {{c1::ova}} specifically refers to the parasite's eggs.
extraNote: Ova are typically detected in stool samples using microscopic examination.

clozeText: Ancylostoma duodenale belongs to the class {{c1::Nematoda}}.
extraNote: Nematodes are the medically important roundworms described in parasitology.

clozeText: Ancylostoma duodenale is classified as an {{c1::intestinal}} nematode.
extraNote: Nematodes are roundworms with a cylindrical body and a complete digestive tract.

clozeText: The common name for Ancylostoma duodenale is the {{c1::hookworm}}.
extraNote: It is one of the two main hookworm species infecting humans, the other being Necator americanus.

clozeText: Transmission of Ancylostoma duodenale occurs via {{c1::penetration of the skin}} by larvae.
extraNote: This differentiates it from other nematodes like Ascaris which are acquired by ingestion of eggs.

clozeText: The infectious stage of Ancylostoma duodenale is the {{c1::filariform}} larva.
extraNote: Filariform larvae are the third-stage, nonfeeding forms of the parasite.

clozeText: The first- and second-stage larvae of Ancylostoma duodenale, which are noninfectious and feeding forms, are called {{c1::rhabditiform}} larvae.
extraNote: The life cycle progresses from egg to rhabditiform larva to filariform larva.

clozeText: Adult Ancylostoma duodenale worms live within the {{c1::small intestine}} of the human host.
extraNote: They attach to the intestinal wall and cause significant morbidity.

clozeText: The presence of adult Ancylostoma duodenale in the small intestine primarily causes {{c1::blood loss}}, leading to anemia.
extraNote: Iron-deficiency anemia is a major clinical finding in hookworm infections.

clozeText: During their life cycle, Ancylostoma duodenale larvae pass through the {{c1::lungs}}, which can cause symptoms of pneumonitis.
extraNote: This migration through the respiratory system is common to Ascaris, Strongyloides, and hookworms.

clozeText: A striking increase in the number of {{c1::eosinophils::cell type}} occurs during infections where Ancylostoma duodenale larvae migrate through tissue.
extraNote: Eosinophilia is a hallmark of many helminth infections, especially during larval migration.

clozeText: Host defense against Ancylostoma duodenale involves {{c1::IgE::immunoglobulin}}, which allows eosinophils to attach to the parasite surface.
extraNote: Eosinophils then secrete cytotoxic enzymes to damage the worm.

clozeText: The cytokine {{c1::IL-5}}, synthesized by Th-2 helper T cells, is responsible for increasing the number of eosinophils during a hookworm infection.
extraNote: Interleukin-5 is the primary factor for eosinophil growth and activation.

clozeText: Ancylostoma duodenale produces {{c1::cysteine proteases}} to facilitate its migration through host tissue.
extraNote: These enzymes act as the stimuli for IL-5 production by the host.

clozeText: Laboratory diagnosis of Ancylostoma duodenale is typically confirmed by finding {{c1::eggs}} in the stool.
extraNote: Microscopic examination for ova and parasites (O&P) is the standard diagnostic procedure.

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating Ancylostoma duodenale is {{c1::albendazole::name one of three}}.
extraNote: Alternative treatments include mebendazole or pyrantel pamoate.

clozeText: A key personal protection measure to prevent Ancylostoma duodenale infection is {{c1::wearing shoes}}.
extraNote: This prevents the filariform larvae in the soil from penetrating the skin of the feet.

clozeText: Ancylostoma duodenale belongs to the phylum {{c1::Nemathelminthes}}.
extraNote: This phylum consists of the roundworms.

clozeText: The body of Ancylostoma duodenale is covered with a noncellular, highly resistant coating called a {{c1::cuticle}}.
extraNote: The cuticle provides protection against host immune responses and environmental stress.

clozeText: In Ancylostoma duodenale, the {{c1::female}} is usually larger than the male.
extraNote: Nematodes generally have separate sexes with distinct size differences.

clozeText: Ancylostoma duodenale is primarily endemic in {{c1::tropical}} areas.
extraNote: It is found worldwide but thrives in warm, moist climates where larvae can survive in the soil.

clozeText: The hookworm Ancylostoma duodenale has a complete digestive tract including a {{c1::mouth and an anus}}.
extraNote: This differentiates nematodes from some other helminth classes.

clozeText: Eosinophils do not ingest Ancylostoma duodenale; instead, they attach to the surface and secrete {{c1::cytotoxic enzymes}}.
extraNote: These enzymes are contained within the eosinophilic granules.

clozeText: The {{c1::Th-2}} subset of helper T cells is responsible for the synthesis of interleukins that stimulate host defenses against Ancylostoma duodenale.
extraNote: The Th-2 response is characteristically associated with anti-helminth immunity.

clozeText: In the laboratory diagnosis of hookworms, the term 'ova' refers specifically to the {{c1::eggs}}.
extraNote: Stool examination for Ova & Parasites (O&P) is the primary diagnostic tool.

clozeText: Ancylostoma duodenale larvae entering the skin can cause symptoms of {{c1::pneumonitis}} as they migrate toward the intestines.
extraNote: This is often referred to as eosinophilic pneumonia when larvae pass through the lungs.

clozeText: Proper {{c1::sewage disposal}} is a critical public health measure for preventing the spread of Ancylostoma duodenale.
extraNote: This prevents soil contamination with eggs and subsequent larval development.

clozeText: The infectious larvae of Ancylostoma duodenale are the {{c1::third}}-stage larvae.
extraNote: These are also known as filariform larvae and are nonfeeding.

clozeText: Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus are the two medically important types of {{c1::hookworms}}.
extraNote: They share similar life cycles and clinical presentations of blood loss and anemia.

clozeText: The diagnosis of Ancylostoma duodenale infection involves finding eggs in the stool, as part of an {{c1::O&P::abbreviation}} exam.
extraNote: O&P stands for Ova and Parasites.

clozeText: Ancylostoma duodenale belongs to the phylum {{c1::Nemathelminthes}}, which comprises the roundworms.
extraNote: Nematodes are multicellular metazoa characterized by cylindrical bodies and complete digestive tracts.

clozeText: The common name for the intestinal nematode Ancylostoma duodenale is the {{c1::hookworm}}.
extraNote: Ancylostoma and Necator are the two primary hookworm species infecting humans.

clozeText: Ancylostoma duodenale is primarily transmitted to humans through the {{c1::penetration of the skin::mode}} by larvae.
extraNote: This transmission route is shared with Strongyloides and Schistosoma.

clozeText: The specific infectious stage of Ancylostoma duodenale that enters the skin is the {{c1::filariform}} larva.
extraNote: Filariform larvae are the third-stage, nonfeeding, infectious form of the parasite.

clozeText: In the life cycle of Ancylostoma duodenale, the first- and second-stage larvae are known as {{c1::rhabditiform}} larvae.
extraNote: Rhabditiform larvae are the noninfectious, feeding forms found in the environment.

clozeText: Adult Ancylostoma duodenale worms reside and cause disease within the human {{c1::small intestine}}.
extraNote: They are categorized as intestinal nematodes based on this primary site of infection.

clozeText: The hallmark clinical manifestation of adult Ancylostoma duodenale infection in the small intestine is {{c1::blood loss::symptom}}, which leads to anemia.
extraNote: Hookworms attach to the intestinal wall and feed on host blood.

clozeText: During the migration phase of infection, Ancylostoma duodenale larvae pass through the {{c1::lungs}}, potentially causing symptoms of pneumonitis.

clozeText: Infections with Ancylostoma duodenale are associated with a striking increase in {{c1::eosinophils::cell type}} (eosinophilia).

clozeText: A critical preventative measure against Ancylostoma duodenale infection is {{c1::wearing shoes}}.

clozeText: The drugs of choice for treating Ancylostoma duodenale infection include albendazole, mebendazole, or {{c1::pyrantel pamoate}}.

clozeText: Ancylostoma duodenale is particularly endemic to {{c1::tropical::climate}} areas.

clozeText: Host defense against helminths like Ancylostoma duodenale is stimulated by interleukins synthesized by the {{c1::Th-2}} subset of helper T cells.

clozeText: Necator americanus is a(n) {{c1::nematode}} (roundworm) that belongs to the group of hookworms.

clozeText: Necator americanus possesses a complete digestive tract, which includes a(n) {{c1::mouth and an anus}}.
extraNote: This is a distinguishing feature of nematodes compared to other helminths.

clozeText: Necator americanus has separate sexes, and the {{c1::female}} is usually the larger of the two.
extraNote: Sexual dimorphism is common in nematodes, where males typically have a coiled tail.

clozeText: The adult male of Necator americanus typically has a(n) {{c1::coiled tail}}.
extraNote: The coiled tail is a characteristic morphological feature of male nematodes.

clozeText: Necator americanus is primarily transmitted to humans through the {{c1::penetration of the skin}} by larvae.

clozeText: In the United States, {{c1::Necator::organism name}} is the most common hookworm species.

clozeText: The infectious, nonfeeding larval form of Necator americanus is the {{c1::filariform::specific stage}} larva.

clozeText: The noninfectious, feeding larval forms of Necator americanus are the {{c1::rhabditiform::specific stage}} larvae.
extraNote: These are the first- and second-stage larvae that exist in the soil.

clozeText: Adult Necator americanus worms live within the human {{c1::small intestine}}.
extraNote: Adult hookworms attach to the intestinal wall and feed on blood.

clozeText: The primary clinical finding associated with adult Necator americanus in the small intestine is {{c1::blood loss (anemia)}}.
extraNote: The chronic loss of blood due to worm attachment leads to iron-deficiency anemia.

clozeText: During their migration, Necator americanus larvae pass through the {{c1::lungs}}, which can cause symptoms of pneumonitis.

clozeText: Infections with Necator americanus are associated with a striking increase in the number of {{c1::eosinophils}} (eosinophilia).

clozeText: Host defense against Necator americanus involves the elevation of immunoglobulin {{c1::IgE}}.

clozeText: Eosinophilia in Necator americanus infections is stimulated by the production of {{c1::IL-5}} by Th-2 cells.

clozeText: The production of IgE in response to Necator americanus is increased by the cytokine {{c1::IL-4}}.

clozeText: Eosinophils damage Necator americanus by secreting cytotoxic enzymes from their granules after attaching via {{c1::IgE}}.

clozeText: Necator americanus infection can be prevented by {{c1::wearing shoes}}.

clozeText: The standard laboratory diagnosis of Necator americanus involves finding {{c1::eggs}} in the stool.

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating Necator americanus is {{c1::albendazole}} (or mebendazole/pyrantel pamoate).

clozeText: Besides albendazole, {{c1::pyrantel pamoate}} is a common treatment for hookworms like Necator americanus.

clozeText: The life cycle outside of humans for Necator americanus follows the sequence: Egg to {{c1::rhabditiform}} larva to filariform larva.

clozeText: Because the sexual cycle of Necator americanus occurs in humans, humans are considered the {{c1::definitive}} host.

clozeText: Necator americanus is classified as a(n) {{c1::intestinal}} nematode.

clozeText: Proper {{c1::sewage disposal}} is a key method for interrupting the transmission chain of Necator americanus.

clozeText: The larva of Necator americanus that is infectious and does NOT feed is the {{c1::third::stage number}}-stage larva.

clozeText: Necator americanus is a member of the phylum {{c1::Nemathelminthes}} (roundworms).

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating Necator americanus infection is {{c1::albendazole}} (or mebendazole).

clozeText: Necator americanus belongs to the group of {{c1::intestinal}} nematodes.

clozeText: The noninfectious, feeding stage of the hookworm life cycle is the {{c1::rhabditiform}} larva.

clozeText: Necator americanus and Ancylostoma differ from Strongyloides because hookworms are only transmitted as larvae and lack a {{c1::free-living}} cycle in the soil.

clozeText: A common clinical sign of larval migration in hookworm infection is {{c1::eosinophilic pneumonia}}.

clozeText: Unlike many intestinal protozoa, the transmission of Necator americanus does not typically involve the {{c1::ingestion of eggs}}.
