clozeText: Rectal prolapse in Trichuris trichiura infection is caused by increased {{c1::peristalsis}} as the body attempts to expel the worms.
extraNote: The mechanical effort of the colon to rid itself of the worms leads to the prolapse.

clozeText: During a rectal prolapse caused by Trichuris trichiura, {{c1::whitish worms}} may be visible on the prolapsed mucosa.
extraNote: Direct visualization of the worms on the mucosa is a diagnostic finding in heavy pediatric infections.

clozeText: Trichuris trichiura eggs are found in the {{c1::stool}} and are described as being {{c2::barrel}}-shaped or lemon-shaped.
extraNote: Microscopic examination of feces is the standard diagnostic method.

clozeText: Trichuris trichiura eggs become infectious only after they form embryos in {{c1::warm, moist soil}}.
extraNote: Environmental conditions are crucial for the development of the infective embryonated egg.

clozeText: Trichuris trichiura is found worldwide but is especially prevalent in the {{c1::tropics}}, affecting more than 500 million people.
extraNote: In the United States, it is most commonly found in the southern states.

clozeText: Like other nematodes, Trichuris trichiura has separate sexes, and the {{c1::female}} is usually larger than the {{c2::male}}.
extraNote: Sexual dimorphism is a common trait among roundworms.

clozeText: The body of Trichuris trichiura is covered with a highly resistant, noncellular coating known as a {{c1::cuticle}}.
extraNote: The cuticle protects the worm from the host's digestive enzymes.

clozeText: Diagnosis of Trichuris trichiura is strictly based on stool samples, unlike {{c1::Enterobius}} (pinworm), which requires the Scotch tape technique.
extraNote: Whipworm eggs are passed in the feces, whereas pinworm eggs are typically laid on perianal skin.

clozeText: In the life cycle of Trichuris trichiura, the {{c1::embryonated egg}} is the specific stage that infects humans.
extraNote: Unembryonated eggs passed in the stool are not yet infectious to the next host.

clozeText: {{c1::Trichinella}} is the nematode responsible for the disease known as trichinosis.
extraNote: Trichinella is a medically important roundworm categorized as an intestinal nematode.

clozeText: Humans are considered {{c1::dead-end}} hosts for Trichinella, as the larvae are not transmitted further to other hosts.
extraNote: In dead-end hosts, the parasite cannot complete its natural life cycle or be transmitted to a new host.

clozeText: Transmission of Trichinella occurs by the ingestion of larvae in {{c1::undercooked meat}}.
extraNote: Unlike some other nematodes that are transmitted via egg ingestion, Trichinella is acquired via larval ingestion.

clozeText: A striking increase in the number of eosinophils, or {{c1::eosinophilia}}, is a characteristic finding in Trichinella infections.
extraNote: Eosinophilia is particularly prominent when roundworm larvae migrate through tissue.

clozeText: Eosinophils attach to the surface of Trichinella via {{c1::IgE}} antibodies.
extraNote: IgE levels are typically elevated in helminthic infections.

clozeText: Upon attaching to the parasite, eosinophils secrete {{c1::cytotoxic enzymes}} from their granules to defend against Trichinella.
extraNote: Eosinophils do not ingest the organism; they release contents that damage the parasite surface.

clozeText: Host defenses against Trichinella are stimulated by interleukins from the {{c1::Th-2}} subset of helper T cells.
extraNote: The Th-2 response is the primary arm of adaptive immunity against helminths.

clozeText: In Trichinella infection, the interleukin {{c1::IL-5}} is responsible for increasing the number of eosinophils.
extraNote: IL-5 is a key cytokine for eosinophil recruitment and activation.

clozeText: The interleukin {{c1::IL-4}} increases the production of IgE during a Trichinella infection.
extraNote: IL-4 promotes B-cell class switching to IgE.

clozeText: Trichinella worms produce {{c1::cysteine proteases}} to facilitate migration through tissue, which also stimulates IL-5 production.
extraNote: These enzymes help the parasite move through host tissues and trigger the eosinophilic response.

clozeText: The laboratory diagnosis of Trichinella is often confirmed by finding larvae {{c1::encysted}} in muscle.
extraNote: Muscle biopsy is a definitive diagnostic tool for identifying the larval stage.

clozeText: In addition to muscle biopsy, {{c1::serology}} can be used to diagnose trichinosis.
extraNote: Serologic testing detects specific antibodies against Trichinella antigens.

clozeText: Treatment for Trichinella larvae involves the use of {{c1::albendazole}} plus prednisone.
extraNote: Prednisone is added as an anti-inflammatory to manage the reaction to dying larvae.

clozeText: In the treatment of trichinosis, {{c1::prednisone}} is used alongside albendazole specifically to target larvae.
extraNote: Corticosteroids help reduce inflammation during the systemic larval phase.

clozeText: The drug {{c1::mebendazole}} is used to treat the adult Trichinella worms located in the intestine.
extraNote: Adult worms reside in the GI tract before larvae migrate to muscle.

clozeText: Trichinella belongs to the phylum {{c1::Nemathelminthes}}, which contains the roundworms.
extraNote: Nematodes (roundworms) are characterized by cylindrical bodies and a complete digestive tract.

clozeText: Like other nematodes, Trichinella has a complete digestive tract that includes a {{c1::mouth}} and an {{c1::anus}}.
extraNote: This distinguishes roundworms from flatworms, which may have incomplete tracts.

clozeText: The body of Trichinella is protected by a noncellular, highly resistant coating called a {{c1::cuticle}}.
extraNote: The cuticle is a hallmark feature of the nematode phylum.

clozeText: Trichinella nematodes have separate sexes; the {{c1::female}} is usually larger than the male.
extraNote: Sexual dimorphism is common in nematodes.

clozeText: The male Trichinella worm typically possesses a {{c1::coiled tail}}.
extraNote: This is a characteristic morphological feature used to identify male nematodes.

clozeText: Trichinella is classified as an {{c1::intestinal}} nematode because the adult worms live within the human intestines.
extraNote: Other members of this group include Enterobius, Ascaris, and Strongyloides.

clozeText: In the Trichinella life cycle, the {{c1::larva}} is the stage that infects humans.
extraNote: Transmission occurs when infectious larvae are consumed.

clozeText: Trichinella has a {{c1::worldwide}} geographic distribution.
extraNote: It is not restricted to tropical regions, unlike many other helminths.

clozeText: The symptoms of trichinosis are caused by the migration and encystment of {{c1::larvae}} in tissue.
extraNote: While adults are in the intestine, the systemic disease is primarily due to the larval stage.

clozeText: Trichinella is one of the nematodes that can be diagnosed by examining {{c1::muscle tissue}} rather than stool.
extraNote: While many intestinal nematodes are diagnosed via eggs in stool, Trichinella requires muscle examination for larvae.

clozeText: Along with Trichinella, the roundworms Ascaris, Strongyloides, and hookworms are associated with high {{c1::eosinophil}} counts.
extraNote: Eosinophilia is a hallmark of roundworms that migrate through host tissues.

clozeText: Nematodes like Trichinella that migrate through tissue induce the production of {{c1::IgE}}, which is important for host defense.
extraNote: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation and eosinophil attachment are critical against helminths.

clozeText: The primary mode of transmission for Trichinella is {{c1::ingestion}}.
extraNote: Transmission is specifically via ingestion of larval-containing meat, not skin penetration.

clozeText: Unlike Enterobius and Ascaris, which are transmitted by eggs, Trichinella is transmitted as {{c1::larvae}}.
extraNote: This distinction is important for understanding the source of infection (meat vs. fecal-contaminated environment).

clozeText: The life cycle of most helminths, including Trichinella, progresses from {{c1::egg}} to larva to adult.
extraNote: The adult form is the stage that produces eggs to continue the cycle.

clozeText: Trichinella spiralis is a medically important nematode that causes the disease {{c1::trichinosis}}.
extraNote: Trichinella is classified as an intestinal nematode even though its larvae cause significant tissue-related pathology in muscles.

clozeText: Humans serve as {{c1::dead-end}} hosts for Trichinella, meaning the larvae are not transmitted from humans to other hosts.
extraNote: A dead-end host is one where the parasite cannot continue its life cycle to another organism.

clozeText: Transmission of Trichinella occurs via the {{c1::ingestion}} of larvae found in undercooked meat.
extraNote: This differentiates Trichinella from other nematodes like Enterobius or Ascaris, which are typically transmitted via eggs.

clozeText: Infections with Trichinella spiralis are characterized by a striking increase in the number of {{c1::eosinophils}} (eosinophilia).
extraNote: Eosinophilia is especially prominent when roundworm larvae migrate through tissue.

clozeText: Host defense against Trichinella involves eosinophils attaching to the parasite surface via {{c1::immunoglobulin E::antibody type}} (IgE).
extraNote: IgE is characteristically elevated in helminthic infections to facilitate eosinophil-mediated destruction.

clozeText: During host defense, eosinophils do not ingest Trichinella; instead, they secrete {{c1::cytotoxic enzymes}} from their granules onto the parasite.
extraNote: These granules contain toxic proteins that damage the parasite's cuticle during tissue migration.

clozeText: The production of IgE in Trichinella infections is increased by the cytokine {{c1::interleukin-4}} (IL-4).
extraNote: IL-4 is synthesized by the Th-2 subset of helper T cells to stimulate the allergic/parasitic immune response.

clozeText: The number of eosinophils in Trichinella infections is increased by the cytokine {{c1::interleukin-5}} (IL-5).
extraNote: IL-5 is a key driver of eosinophil production and activation in the bone marrow and tissues.

clozeText: {{c1::Cysteine proteases}} produced by Trichinella worms facilitate tissue migration and serve as the stimulus for IL-5 production.
extraNote: These enzymes are critical virulence factors that allow the worm to traverse host tissues.

clozeText: In addition to biopsy, {{c1::serology}} is a primary method for the laboratory diagnosis of Trichinella.
extraNote: Serologic testing detects host antibodies against Trichinella antigens.

clozeText: To treat Trichinella larvae, clinicians use a combination of {{c1::albendazole}} and {{c2::prednisone}}.
extraNote: Prednisone is added to reduce the inflammatory response triggered by dying larvae in the muscle.

clozeText: The drug used specifically against the adult Trichinella worms in the intestine is {{c1::mebendazole}}.
extraNote: Mebendazole targets the intestinal phase of the infection.

clozeText: Trichinella is covered with a noncellular, highly resistant coating called a(n) {{c1::cuticle}}.
extraNote: The cuticle is a common feature among nematodes, providing protection against host immune defenses and digestive enzymes.

clozeText: Host defenses against Trichinella are primarily stimulated by interleukins synthesized by the {{c1::Th-2}} subset of helper T cells.
extraNote: Th-2 responses are the hallmark of the immune response against helminthic parasites.

clozeText: Trichinella is unique among many intestinal nematodes because it is transmitted by the ingestion of {{c1::larvae}} rather than eggs.
extraNote: While Enterobius, Trichuris, and Ascaris are egg-transmitted, Trichinella larvae are found in muscle tissue of the host meat.

clozeText: In the nematode life cycle, the noninfectious, feeding forms are called {{c1::rhabditiform}} larvae.
extraNote: This stage precedes the infectious filariform stage in most nematode lifecycles.

clozeText: The infectious, nonfeeding larval stage of nematodes is known as the {{c1::filariform}} larvae.
extraNote: Although Trichinella is acquired via larvae in meat, this terminology applies generally to the roundworm group.

clozeText: Trichinella spiralis is categorized as an {{c1::intestinal}} nematode based on the primary location of the adult worms.
extraNote: Adult worms mate and reside in the small intestine of the host.

clozeText: In Trichinella infections, both IgE and {{c1::cell-mediated immunity}} (CMI) play roles in the host defense.
extraNote: CMI is particularly important for controlling infections and preventing dissemination in immunocompromised individuals.

clozeText: The male Trichinella worm typically has a(n) {{c1::coiled tail}}, a characteristic feature of many male nematodes.
extraNote: Females are generally larger than males in the Trichinella species.

clozeText: Trichinella is categorized under the class {{c1::Nematoda}} within the phylum Nemathelminthes.
extraNote: Nematodes are distinct from Platyhelminthes (flatworms) such as flukes and tapeworms.

clozeText: Humans acquire trichinosis by eating undercooked meat containing {{c1::encysted}} larvae.
extraNote: The larvae remain viable within the muscle tissue of the animal source until consumed.

clozeText: The definitive host for a parasite like Trichinella is defined as the host in which the {{c1::sexual cycle}} occurs.
extraNote: In Trichinella, humans act as both definitive hosts (adults in gut) and intermediate hosts (larvae in muscle), but are ultimately dead-end hosts.

clozeText: An intermediate host is one in which the {{c1::asexual cycle}} occurs or the larvae are present.
extraNote: In Trichinella infections, the larvae reside in the muscle tissue, representing the intermediate phase.

clozeText: Eosinophils utilize {{c1::IgE}} to attach to Trichinella larvae during the tissue migration phase of the infection.
extraNote: This attachment triggers the degranulation and release of cytotoxic proteins.

clozeText: Unlike many other nematodes, Trichinella infections are diagnosed by serology or muscle biopsy rather than {{c1::ova}} in the stool.
extraNote: Trichinella does not typically present with eggs (ova) in the stool of the host.

clozeText: Trichinella is found {{c1::worldwide}}, appearing in many regions where undercooked meat is consumed.
extraNote: While some parasites are restricted to the tropics, Trichinella has a global distribution.

clozeText: In Trichinella infections, the adult worms reside in the {{c1::intestine}}, whereas the larvae reside in the muscle.
extraNote: The presence of adults in the intestine precedes the migration of larvae to the musculature.

clozeText: Trichinella is classified as a {{c1::Nemathelminthes::phylum}}, which is the phylum containing roundworms.
extraNote: Nematodes are roundworms with a cylindrical body and a complete digestive tract.

clozeText: Humans are considered {{c1::dead-end::host type}} hosts for Trichinella because the larval form is not transmitted to other humans or animals.
extraNote: A dead-end host is one where the parasite cannot be transmitted further from that host.

clozeText: The clinical condition caused by Trichinella infection is known as {{c1::trichinosis}}.
extraNote: Trichinella is a medically important nematode that migrates through tissue.

clozeText: Transmission of Trichinella occurs primarily by the {{c1::ingestion}} of larvae found in {{c2::undercooked meat}}.
extraNote: Unlike some other nematodes that are transmitted via eggs, Trichinella is transmitted in its larval stage.

clozeText: During the laboratory diagnosis of Trichinella, larvae may be found {{c1::encysted in muscle::location}}.
extraNote: Muscle biopsy for encysted larvae is a key diagnostic finding for this parasite.

clozeText: Besides muscle biopsy, Trichinella infection can be diagnosed through {{c1::serology}}.
extraNote: Serologic testing is an alternative or adjunctive diagnostic method for trichinosis.

clozeText: Infections with Trichinella are associated with a striking increase in {{c1::eosinophils::cell type}}, a condition called eosinophilia.
extraNote: Eosinophilia is common when roundworm larvae migrate through tissue.

clozeText: The treatment for Trichinella larvae involves the use of {{c1::albendazole}} combined with {{c2::prednisone}}.
extraNote: Prednisone is typically added to albendazole when targeting the larval stage in tissue.

clozeText: {{c1::Mebendazole}} is the drug specifically used against the adult form of the Trichinella worm.
extraNote: Different medications are used depending on whether the target is the adult worm in the intestine or the larvae in the muscle.

clozeText: The number of eosinophils in a Trichinella infection is increased by the cytokine {{c1::IL-5}}.
extraNote: IL-5 is synthesized by the Th-2 subset of helper T cells.

clozeText: During host defense against Trichinella, {{c1::IgE::immunoglobulin}} production is increased by the cytokine {{c2::IL-4}}.
extraNote: IgE and eosinophils work together to defend against helminthic infections.

clozeText: Eosinophils attach to the surface of Trichinella via {{c1::IgE::immunoglobulin}} and secrete {{c2::cytotoxic enzymes}} to destroy the parasite.
extraNote: Eosinophils do not ingest the organism but rather use antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.

clozeText: The stimulus for IL-5 production during Trichinella migration is the release of {{c1::cysteine proteases}} by the worms.
extraNote: These proteases facilitate the migration of the parasite through host tissue.

clozeText: Trichinella belongs to the group of {{c1::intestinal::location}} nematodes, although its larvae cause significant disease in tissue.
extraNote: It is categorized with other intestinal nematodes like Enterobius and Ascaris.

clozeText: Nematodes like Trichinella have a highly resistant, noncellular outer coating called a {{c1::cuticle}}.
extraNote: The cuticle provides protection for the roundworm within the host environment.

clozeText: In the nematode life cycle, including that of Trichinella, the adult female is usually {{c1::larger}} than the adult male.
extraNote: Nematodes have separate sexes and exhibit sexual dimorphism.

clozeText: Male nematodes, such as Trichinella, typically possess a {{c1::coiled tail}}.
extraNote: The coiled tail is a characteristic morphological feature of the male roundworm.

clozeText: Entamoeba histolytica causes amebic {{c1::dysentery}} and liver abscess.
extraNote: Amebic dysentery is characterized by bloody, mucus-containing diarrhea.

clozeText: The life cycle of E. histolytica has two stages: the motile {{c1::trophozoite}} and the nonmotile cyst.
extraNote: Trophozoites are found in lesions and diarrheal stools, while cysts predominate in formed (non-diarrheal) stools.

clozeText: Entamoeba cysts are resistant to {{c1::chlorination}} of water supplies but are killed by {{c2::boiling}}.
extraNote: Cysts are also effectively removed from water supplies by filtration.

clozeText: The Entamoeba histolytica cyst is characterized by having {{c1::four}} nuclei, which is a key diagnostic criterion.
extraNote: Upon excystation, the four-nucleated ameba eventually divides to form eight trophozoites.

clozeText: The mature Entamoeba trophozoite has a single nucleus with an even lining of peripheral chromatin and a prominent {{c1::central nucleolus (karyosome)}}.
extraNote: This nuclear morphology helps distinguish it from other nonpathogenic amebas.

clozeText: The infective stage of Entamoeba histolytica for humans is the {{c1::cyst}}.
extraNote: Ingestion of cysts usually occurs via contaminated food or water.

clozeText: Entamoeba trophozoites invade the colonic epithelium and secrete enzymes that create a typical {{c1::flask-shaped}} ulcer.
extraNote: The ulcer can undermine and destroy large areas of the intestinal epithelium.

clozeText: The most frequent site of extraintestinal disease in amebiasis is the {{c1::liver}}.
extraNote: Trophozoites reach the liver via the portal circulation, forming abscesses.

clozeText: Entamoeba infection has {{c1::no animal reservoir}}.
extraNote: The organism is primarily transmitted by the fecal-oral route between humans.

clozeText: In the colon, Entamoeba may form a granulomatous lesion called an {{c1::ameboma}}, which can be mistaken for adenocarcinoma.
extraNote: These typically form in the cecal or rectosigmoid areas.

clozeText: Aspiration of an amebic liver abscess typically yields brownish-yellow pus described as {{c1::anchovy paste}}.
extraNote: Most patients with amebic liver abscess do not have concurrent overt intestinal amebiasis.

clozeText: To observe ameboid motility, diarrheal stool specimens containing Entamoeba trophozoites should be examined within {{c1::1 hour}} of collection.
extraNote: Trophozoites are fragile and lose motility quickly outside the body.

clozeText: The presence of ingested {{c1::red blood cells}} within the trophozoite is a diagnostic feature of E. histolytica.
extraNote: Fecal leukocytes are the most common error when identifying trophozoites in stool.

clozeText: E. histolytica cysts are distinguished from Entamoeba coli cysts because E. coli cysts contain {{c1::eight}} nuclei.
extraNote: E. histolytica cysts are smaller and only have four nuclei.

clozeText: {{c1::Entamoeba dispar}} is a nonpathogenic species that is morphologically indistinguishable from E. histolytica.
extraNote: PCR or antigen detection is required to differentiate the two species specifically.

clozeText: A complete stool examination for Entamoeba cysts includes a saline wet mount, an iodine-stained wet mount, and a fixed {{c1::trichrome}}-stained preparation.
extraNote: These different preparations highlight various aspects of cyst and trophozoite morphology.

clozeText: Unlike bacillary dysentery, stool from patients with amebic dysentery lacks {{c1::polymorphonuclear leukocytes (inflammatory cells)}}.
extraNote: Little inflammation occurs at the site of the amebic lesion despite mucosal destruction.

clozeText: The {{c1::indirect hemagglutination}} test is a serologic assay useful for the diagnosis of invasive amebiasis.
extraNote: This test is usually positive in invasive disease but negative in asymptomatic cyst carriers.

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating symptomatic intestinal amebiasis or hepatic abscesses is {{c1::metronidazole}} or tinidazole.
extraNote: Hepatic abscesses generally do not need to be surgically drained.

clozeText: Asymptomatic carriers of Entamoeba histolytica should be treated with {{c1::iodoquinol}} or paromomycin.
extraNote: These are luminal amebicides used to eliminate the cyst stage from the gut.

clozeText: Entamoeba liver abscesses can penetrate the diaphragm and lead to disease in the {{c1::lung}}.
extraNote: This occurs most commonly with abscesses located in the right lobe of the liver.

clozeText: Following excystation in the ileum, Entamoeba trophozoites typically colonize the {{c1::cecum}} and colon.
extraNote: This colonization precedes the invasion of the epithelium.

clozeText: The stool O&P (ova and parasite) test for Entamoeba is often {{c1::insensitive}}, frequently resulting in false negatives.
extraNote: Because cysts are passed intermittently, at least three specimens should be examined.

clozeText: Antibodies formed against trophozoite antigens are useful for diagnosis but are {{c1::not protective}} against reinfection.
extraNote: Previous infection does not confer immunity.

clozeText: Transmission of Entamoeba among men who have sex with men is often via the {{c1::anal–oral}} route.
extraNote: This represents a significant transmission pathway in some populations in the United States.

clozeText: In areas where Entamoeba is endemic, the use of {{c1::human feces (night soil)}} for fertilization should be prohibited to prevent transmission.
extraNote: Cooking vegetables is also a recommended preventive measure in these regions.

clozeText: Acute amebiasis is characterized by {{c1::tenesmus}} and lower abdominal discomfort.
extraNote: Tenesmus refers to the constant feeling of needing to pass stool.

clozeText: Chronic amebiasis can present with low-grade symptoms such as weight loss, fatigue, and {{c1::occasional diarrhea}}.
extraNote: It may persist for years if left untreated.

clozeText: The diagnostic PCR-based assay for Entamoeba stool samples detects the {{c1::nucleic acids}} of the organism.
extraNote: PCR and antigen tests are highly specific for E. histolytica compared to microscopy.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::90}}% of individuals infected with E. histolytica have asymptomatic infections.
extraNote: These individuals act as carriers and can transmit the infection to others via cysts.

clozeText: E. histolytica causes {{c1::amebic dysentery}} and {{c2::liver abscess}}.
extraNote: Amebiasis is a major protozoan disease of the intestinal tract.

clozeText: Entamoeba cysts are readily killed by {{c1::boiling}} but are resistant to {{c2::chlorination}} of water supplies.
extraNote: Filtration is required to remove cysts from municipal water.

clozeText: The E. histolytica cyst has {{c1::four}} nuclei, which serves as a critical diagnostic criterion.
extraNote: Upon excystation, an ameba with four nuclei emerges and divides to form eight trophozoites.

clozeText: The mature trophozoite of Entamoeba has a single nucleus with a prominent {{c1::central nucleolus::karyosome}} and an even lining of peripheral chromatin.
extraNote: Nuclear morphology distinguishes E. histolytica from other amebas.

clozeText: In invasive amebiasis, antibodies are formed against {{c1::trophozoite}} antigens, but they are {{c2::not protective}}.
extraNote: Previous infection does not prevent reinfection; however, antibodies are useful for serologic diagnosis.

clozeText: Entamoeba is acquired by ingestion of cysts via the {{c1::fecal–oral}} route and has {{c2::no animal reservoir}}.
extraNote: Transmission occurs through contaminated food, water, or anal-oral contact.

clozeText: E. histolytica trophozoites invade the colonic epithelium and secrete enzymes causing localized {{c1::necrosis::cell death}}.
extraNote: Initial invasion occurs with little inflammation at the site.

clozeText: As Entamoeba lesions reach the muscularis layer of the colon, a typical {{c1::flask-shaped}} ulcer forms.
extraNote: These ulcers can undermine and destroy large areas of the intestinal epithelium.

clozeText: The most frequent site of systemic amebiasis is the {{c1::liver}}, where abscesses containing trophozoites form.
extraNote: Trophozoites reach the liver by invading the portal circulation.

clozeText: Acute intestinal amebiasis presents as {{c1::dysentery}}, which is characterized by bloody, mucus-containing diarrhea.
extraNote: Symptoms also include lower abdominal discomfort, flatulence, and tenesmus.

clozeText: In some patients, a granulomatous lesion called an {{c1::ameboma}} may form in the cecal or rectosigmoid areas.
extraNote: These lesions can resemble adenocarcinoma of the colon.

clozeText: Amebic liver abscess is characterized by {{c1::right-upper-quadrant}} pain, weight loss, fever, and a tender, enlarged liver.
extraNote: Right-lobe abscesses can penetrate the diaphragm to cause lung disease.

clozeText: Aspiration of an amebic liver abscess yields brownish-yellow pus described as having the appearance of {{c1::anchovy paste}}.
extraNote: Most cases of liver abscess occur in patients without overt intestinal amebiasis.

clozeText: Diarrheal stools should be examined within {{c1::1 hour}} of collection to observe the ameboid motility of the trophozoite.
extraNote: Rapid examination is necessary as trophozoites are labile.

clozeText: E. histolytica trophozoites characteristically contain ingested {{c1::red blood cells::RBCs}}.
extraNote: Presence of ingested erythrocytes helps identify the pathogenic trophozoite.

clozeText: The most common error in laboratory diagnosis of amebiasis is mistaking {{c1::fecal leukocytes}} for trophozoites.
extraNote: Accurate microscopic identification is vital as O&P tests can be insensitive.

clozeText: Mature cysts of E. histolytica contain {{c1::four}} nuclei, whereas cysts of the nonpathogenic Entamoeba coli have {{c2::eight}}.
extraNote: Cyst size and number of nuclei are major criteria for species differentiation.

clozeText: The nonpathogenic {{c1::Entamoeba dispar}} is morphologically indistinguishable from E. histolytica.
extraNote: Highly specific antigen or PCR-based assays are required to differentiate these species.

clozeText: Two highly specific tests for E. histolytica in stool include detection of {{c1::antigen}} and {{c2::nucleic acids (PCR)}}.
extraNote: These tests are superior to routine microscopy for distinguishing pathogenic from nonpathogenic species.

clozeText: In the diagnosis of amebic dysentery, the stool typically lacks {{c1::inflammatory cells (leukocytes)}}, unlike in bacillary dysentery.
extraNote: Microscopic examination of wet mounts helps distinguish amebic from bacterial causes.

clozeText: The {{c1::indirect hemagglutination}} test is a serologic assay usually positive in invasive amebiasis but negative in asymptomatic cyst carriers.
extraNote: Serology is particularly useful for diagnosing extraintestinal disease.

clozeText: The treatment of choice for symptomatic intestinal amebiasis or hepatic abscesses is {{c1::metronidazole}} or {{c2::tinidazole}}.
extraNote: Hepatic abscesses generally do not require surgical drainage.

clozeText: Asymptomatic cyst carriers of Entamoeba should be treated with {{c1::iodoquinol}} or {{c2::paromomycin}}.
extraNote: Carriers can transmit infection to others through fecal-oral spread.

clozeText: Entamoeba trophozoites differentiate from cysts in the {{c1::ileum}} and primarily colonize the cecum and colon.
extraNote: Excystation occurs following ingestion of the cyst.

clozeText: Infection with E. histolytica is common in men who {{c1::have sex with men}} due to anal–oral transmission.
extraNote: Epidemiology in the United States includes immigrants and returning travelers.

clozeText: E. histolytica is grouped as an {{c1::intestinal}} protozoan along with Giardia and Cryptosporidium.
extraNote: These organisms are the most important pathogens within the intestinal tract.

clozeText: Chronic amebiasis symptoms include low-grade symptoms like occasional diarrhea, {{c1::weight loss}}, and fatigue.
extraNote: Roughly 90% of infected individuals remain asymptomatic.

clozeText: A complete stool examination for Entamoeba cysts includes a wet mount in saline, an {{c1::iodine}}-stained wet mount, and a fixed, {{c2::trichrome}}-stained preparation.
extraNote: Each preparation technique highlights different aspects of cyst morphology.

clozeText: Entamoeba histolytica primarily causes {{c1::amebic dysentery}} and {{c2::liver abscess}}.
extraNote: These are the two hallmark manifestations of symptomatic infection.

clozeText: The {{c1::cyst}} stage of E. histolytica is nonmotile and predominates in {{c2::non-diarrheal (formed)}} stools.
extraNote: The cyst is the infective stage transmitted via the fecal-oral route.

clozeText: E. histolytica cysts are resistant to {{c1::chlorination}} of water supplies but are killed by {{c2::boiling}}.
extraNote: Filtration is also effective at removing cysts from water.

clozeText: A mature E. histolytica cyst is characterized by having {{c1::four}} nuclei, which is a key diagnostic criterion.
extraNote: This distinguishes it from Entamoeba coli, which typically has eight nuclei.

clozeText: The {{c1::trophozoite}} is the motile stage of E. histolytica found in intestinal lesions and diarrheal stools.
extraNote: It is the stage responsible for causing tissue damage and symptoms.

clozeText: The E. histolytica trophozoite nucleus contains a prominent {{c1::central nucleolus (karyosome)}} and an even lining of peripheral chromatin.
extraNote: This morphology is diagnostic during stool examination.

clozeText: E. histolytica trophozoites invade the colonic epithelium to create a characteristic {{c1::flask-shaped}} ulcer.
extraNote: The ulcer forms as the organism reaches the muscularis layer and undermines the epithelium.

clozeText: Invasion of the {{c1::portal circulation}} by trophozoites leads to systemic spread, most commonly to the liver.
extraNote: The liver is the most frequent site of extraintestinal amebiasis.

clozeText: Acute intestinal amebiasis presents as dysentery, which is defined by {{c1::bloody, mucus-containing}} diarrhea.
extraNote: It is often accompanied by lower abdominal discomfort and tenesmus.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::90}}% of individuals infected with E. histolytica are asymptomatic carriers.
extraNote: These individuals still pass infectious cysts in their feces.

clozeText: An {{c1::ameboma}} is a granulomatous lesion in the colon that can mimic {{c2::adenocarcinoma}}.
extraNote: It typically forms in the cecal or rectosigmoid areas.

clozeText: Amebic liver abscess is characterized by {{c1::right-upper-quadrant}} pain, weight loss, fever, and a tender liver.
extraNote: Most patients with liver abscesses do not have concurrent overt intestinal symptoms.

clozeText: Aspiration of an amebic liver abscess yields pus with the appearance of {{c1::anchovy paste}}.
extraNote: The pus is typically brownish-yellow and thick.

clozeText: Liver abscesses located in the {{c1::right lobe}} can penetrate the diaphragm and cause lung disease.
extraNote: This represents a common secondary site for extraintestinal spread.

clozeText: E. histolytica trophozoites in diarrheal stools characteristically contain {{c1::ingested red blood cells}}.
extraNote: This is a key feature used to distinguish it from nonpathogenic amebas.

clozeText: The most common error in stool diagnosis is mistaking {{c1::fecal leukocytes}} for trophozoites.
extraNote: True amebic dysentery typically shows few inflammatory cells compared to bacillary dysentery.

clozeText: Mature cysts of E. histolytica contain {{c1::4}} nuclei, while Entamoeba coli cysts contain {{c2::8}} nuclei.
extraNote: Nuclei count is a primary criterion for species differentiation.

clozeText: Humans are considered {{c1::dead-end}} hosts for Echinococcus because the larval form is not transmitted to other humans or animals.
extraNote: In this context, the human is an incidental host where the parasite cannot complete its life cycle for further transmission.

clozeText: Echinococcus granulosus is transmitted to humans via the ingestion of {{c1::eggs}} in food or water contaminated with {{c2::dog}} feces.
extraNote: Dogs are the definitive hosts harboring the adult tapeworms in their intestines.

clozeText: The natural intermediate host for Echinococcus granulosus, where the asexual cycle occurs, is {{c1::sheep}}.
extraNote: Humans act as accidental intermediate hosts in place of sheep.

clozeText: The definitive host for Echinococcus is the {{c1::dog}}, which harbors the {{c2::adult}} stage of the worm.
extraNote: The adult tapeworm in the dog's intestine produces the eggs that are infectious to humans.

clozeText: In humans, Echinococcus infection results in the formation of {{c1::hydatid cysts}}.
extraNote: This condition is specifically known as hydatid cyst disease.

clozeText: The most common site in the human body affected by Echinococcus hydatid cysts is the {{c1::liver}}.
extraNote: Other frequent sites include the lungs and the brain.

clozeText: Besides the liver, Echinococcus granulosus often affects the {{c1::lungs}} and the {{c2::brain}}.
extraNote: Larvae disseminate to these organs to form space-occupying hydatid cysts.

clozeText: The drug of choice for the treatment of Echinococcus granulosus is {{c1::albendazole}}.
extraNote: Treatment may also involve surgical removal of the cysts.

clozeText: Diagnosis of Echinococcus hydatid disease typically involves {{c1::imaging::modality}} such as a CT scan, as well as serology or biopsy.
extraNote: Imaging helps identify the location and size of cysts in internal organs.

clozeText: Microscopically, the eggs of Echinococcus species appear identical to the eggs of {{c1::Taenia}} species.
extraNote: This similarity makes it difficult to differentiate these genera based on stool egg morphology alone.

clozeText: The scolex of Echinococcus is characterized by having {{c1::hooks::attachment structure}} and suckers for attachment.
extraNote: The presence of hooks distinguishes it from other cestodes like Diphyllobothrium latum.

clozeText: Echinococcus belongs to the class {{c1::Cestoda}}, which are commonly known as tapeworms.
extraNote: Tapeworms are characterized by a flat body and a specialized head called a scolex.

clozeText: Like other tapeworms, Echinococcus consists of a scolex and a body made of segments called {{c1::proglottids}}.
extraNote: The worm grows by adding new proglottids from its germinal center.

clozeText: A medically important species of lesser prevalence than E. granulosus is {{c1::Echinococcus multilocularis}}.
extraNote: This is categorized as a cestode of minor importance in human pathology.

clozeText: In the human host, Echinococcus is found in the {{c1::larval::stage}} stage, which causes disease.
extraNote: Humans do not harbor the adult tapeworm; they only harbor the larvae in the form of cysts.

clozeText: Echinococcus is classified under the phylum {{c1::Platyhelminthes}}, which includes all flatworms.
extraNote: This phylum is divided into Cestodes (tapeworms) and Trematodes (flukes).

clozeText: Hydatid cysts of Echinococcus can be diagnosed through {{c1::serology}} tests that detect specific antibodies.
extraNote: Serology is often used in conjunction with imaging like CT scans.

clozeText: The growth of Echinococcus proglottids occurs from the {{c1::germinal center}}, which is located next to the scolex.
extraNote: This is the primary site of segment multiplication in tapeworms.

clozeText: Hydatid disease is considered a {{c1::helminthic}} infection because Echinococcus is a parasitic worm.
extraNote: Helminths often induce eosinophilia and elevated IgE levels in the host.

clozeText: In contrast to many intestinal helminths, Echinococcus is a {{c1::tissue}} parasite in humans.
extraNote: While the adult lives in the dog's intestine, the larvae encyst in human tissues.

clozeText: Humans serve as {{c1::dead-end}} hosts for Echinococcus, meaning the larval form in the human is not transmitted to other humans or animals.
extraNote: In dead-end hosts, the parasite cannot complete its life cycle by moving to another host.

clozeText: Echinococcus granulosus is the causative agent of {{c1::hydatid cyst}} disease.
extraNote: This condition is characterized by the formation of large cysts in various organs.

clozeText: The primary mode of transmission for Echinococcus granulosus is the ingestion of {{c1::eggs::stage}} in food contaminated with {{c2::dog}} feces.
extraNote: Unlike some other tapeworms where larvae are ingested in meat, Echinococcus is acquired through egg ingestion.

clozeText: The natural {{c1::intermediate}} host for Echinococcus granulosus is {{c2::sheep}}.
extraNote: Humans accidentally enter the cycle as intermediate hosts by ingesting eggs.

clozeText: Hydatid cysts caused by Echinococcus granulosus are most commonly found in the {{c1::liver}}, {{c2::lungs}}, and brain.
extraNote: These cysts represent the larval stage of the parasite within the human body.

clozeText: Diagnosis of Echinococcus granulosus often relies on {{c1::serology}}, biopsy, and {{c2::CT scan::imaging}}.
extraNote: Serologic tests detect antibodies against Echinococcus antigens.

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating Echinococcus granulosus infection is {{c1::albendazole}}.
extraNote: Surgical removal of the cyst is also a common treatment modality.

clozeText: While Echinococcus granulosus is more common, {{c1::Echinococcus multilocularis}} is a cestode of minor importance that also infects humans.
extraNote: Both species belong to the genus Echinococcus and cause different forms of hydatid disease.

clozeText: Microscopically, the eggs of Echinococcus species appear the same as those of {{c1::Taenia solium}} and Taenia saginata.
extraNote: Because the eggs are indistinguishable, species identification often depends on the clinical context or adult worm morphology.

clozeText: The {{c1::dog}} serves as the definitive host for Echinococcus granulosus, as the adult tapeworm resides in its {{c2::intestine}}.
extraNote: The definitive host is the organism in which the sexual cycle occurs or the adult form is present.

clozeText: Echinococcus belongs to the class {{c1::Cestoda}}, which is characterized by flat, segmented bodies.
extraNote: Cestodes are commonly known as tapeworms.

clozeText: The scolex of Echinococcus contains {{c1::hooks}} and suckers for attachment to the host intestinal wall.
extraNote: This distinguishes it from Diphyllobothrium, which uses sucking grooves and lacks hooks.

clozeText: In the human life cycle of Echinococcus, the {{c1::larvae::life stage}} are the form most associated with disease, typically presenting as cysts.
extraNote: Disease occurs when the ingested eggs hatch and the larvae migrate to tissues.

clozeText: Echinococcus is a member of the phylum {{c1::Platyhelminthes}}, which comprises the flatworms.
extraNote: This phylum is further divided into cestodes (tapeworms) and trematodes (flukes).

clozeText: The body of a tapeworm like Echinococcus consists of a head called a scolex and segments called {{c1::proglottids}}.
extraNote: New proglottids are added from a germinal center next to the scolex.

clozeText: Distal proglottids in Echinococcus are {{c1::gravid}}, meaning they produce many eggs which are eventually excreted.
extraNote: These eggs are transmitted to intermediate hosts to continue the life cycle.

clozeText: Humans are infected with Echinococcus when they ingest eggs in water or food contaminated with {{c1::human}} or {{c2::dog}} feces.
extraNote: While the text specifies dog feces for E. granulosus, contamination of water and food is a general route for egg transmission.

clozeText: Unlike Taenia saginata which is transmitted via beef, Echinococcus granulosus transmission involves {{c1::sheep}} as the intermediate host.
extraNote: Human infection occurs through contact with the definitive host (dog) rather than eating the intermediate host.

clozeText: In some helminthic infections like Echinococcus, {{c1::eosinophilia}} may be associated with the migration of larvae through tissue.
extraNote: Eosinophils and IgE are important components of the host defense against parasitic worms.

clozeText: One method for managing Echinococcus hydatid cysts, besides medication, is {{c1::surgical removal}}.
extraNote: Care must be taken during surgery to avoid spilling cyst contents, which can cause an allergic reaction.

clozeText: Prevention of Echinococcus involves interrupting the chain of transmission by improving {{c1::sewage disposal}} and water purification.
extraNote: This prevents the eggs from contaminating food or water sources used by humans.

clozeText: The {{c1::asexual}} cycle of Echinococcus occurs in the intermediate host, where the larvae are present.
extraNote: In humans (the intermediate host), this cycle results in the development of hydatid cysts.

clozeText: The eggs of Echinococcus species contain an {{c1::embryo}} that differentiates into a larval form upon hatching.
extraNote: This larval form then migrates to organs to form cysts.

clozeText: Echinococcus is categorized as a {{c1::tissue::habitat}} helminth because its larvae cause disease in organs rather than the intestinal lumen of humans.
extraNote: This is in contrast to intestinal tapeworms like adult Taenia saginata.

clozeText: Diagnostic identification of Echinococcus in tissue is often accomplished by demonstrating the presence of the {{c1::cyst}}.
extraNote: Imaging like CT scans is vital for localizing these lesions in the liver or lungs.

clozeText: Echinococcus granulosus is classified as one of the four medically important {{c1::cestodes::class of parasite}}.
extraNote: Cestodes are tapeworms belonging to the phylum Platyhelminthes.

clozeText: The disease caused by Echinococcus is primarily known as {{c1::hydatid cyst disease}}.
extraNote: This disease is characterized by the formation of slow-growing cysts in various organs.

clozeText: Humans acquire Echinococcus infection through the ingestion of {{c1::eggs::stage of parasite}} in food or water.
extraNote: In hydatid disease, humans are infected by eggs rather than larvae in meat.

clozeText: The eggs of Echinococcus granulosus that infect humans are typically found in food or water contaminated with {{c1::dog feces}}.
extraNote: The adult tapeworm lives in the dog's intestine and produces the eggs.

clozeText: In the life cycle of Echinococcus granulosus, the {{c1::sheep}} serves as the natural intermediate host.
extraNote: The intermediate host harbors the asexual cycle or the larval stage.

clozeText: Humans are considered {{c1::dead-end}} hosts for Echinococcus because the larvae are not transmitted to other humans or animals.
extraNote: This occurs because the human cycle does not naturally lead back to the definitive host.

clozeText: The most common site affected by Echinococcus hydatid cysts in the human body is the {{c1::liver}}.
extraNote: The liver is the first major organ encountered by embryos entering the portal circulation.

clozeText: After the liver, the {{c1::lungs}} are the second most common site for Echinococcus hydatid cyst formation.
extraNote: Cysts in the lungs can cause respiratory symptoms and are a major manifestation of the disease.

clozeText: Echinococcus hydatid cysts can also develop in the {{c1::brain}}, where they may act as space-occupying lesions.
extraNote: Brain involvement is a serious complication of hydatid disease.

clozeText: The laboratory diagnosis of Echinococcus often utilizes {{c1::serology}} to detect specific antibodies.
extraNote: Serologic testing is a key diagnostic tool alongside imaging.

clozeText: A common imaging modality used to identify hydatid cysts in organs such as the liver or brain is the {{c1::CT scan}}.
extraNote: Imaging helps visualize the size, location, and structure of the cysts.

clozeText: The primary medical treatment for Echinococcus granulosus infection is {{c1::albendazole}}.
extraNote: Albendazole is the drug of choice for treating hydatid cysts.

clozeText: In addition to medical therapy, the management of Echinococcus cysts often involves {{c1::surgical removal}}.
extraNote: Surgery is frequently used for large or symptomatic hydatid cysts.

clozeText: In the Echinococcus life cycle, the {{c1::dog}} is the definitive host, harboring the adult tapeworm in its intestine.
extraNote: The definitive host is the one in which the sexual cycle occurs.

clozeText: The eggs of Echinococcus species appear microscopically similar to those of the genus {{c1::Taenia}}.
extraNote: This similarity makes it difficult to distinguish them by egg morphology alone.

clozeText: The scolex (head) of Echinococcus is equipped with {{c1::hooks}} for attachment, unlike Diphyllobothrium latum.
extraNote: Hooks and suckers are specialized attachment organs in several medically important cestodes.

clozeText: While Echinococcus granulosus is the primary cause of hydatid disease, {{c1::Echinococcus multilocularis}} is another medically relevant species of lesser importance.
extraNote: Both species cause different forms of hydatid disease.

clozeText: The adult Echinococcus worm grows by adding new segments, called {{c1::proglottids}}, from its germinal center.
extraNote: The germinal center is located next to the scolex.

clozeText: The mature, distal segments of the Echinococcus worm that produce many eggs are known as {{c1::gravid}} proglottids.
extraNote: Gravid proglottids eventually detach and release eggs into the feces.

clozeText: Echinococcus belongs to the class Cestoda, within the phylum {{c1::Platyhelminthes}}.
extraNote: Platyhelminthes are known as flatworms and include both tapeworms and flukes.

clozeText: In the intermediate host, the Echinococcus parasite undergoes its {{c1::asexual}} cycle.
extraNote: The larval stage or asexual reproduction characterizes the intermediate host stage.

clozeText: The Echinococcus scolex is a rounded head that uses {{c1::suckers::attachment mechanism}} in addition to hooks for intestinal attachment.
extraNote: The scolex is the specialized part of the tapeworm used to anchor to the host wall.

clozeText: According to specific microscopic features, Echinococcus granulosus eggs are very similar to Taenia solium eggs but do not have {{c1::hooklets}}.
extraNote: This distinguishes them from the T. solium oncosphere embryo as stated in descriptions of the egg stage.

clozeText: Diagnosis of Echinococcus can be achieved through tissue analysis, specifically via {{c1::biopsy}}.
extraNote: Demonstration of the cyst in tissue is a definitive diagnostic step.

clozeText: Hydatid disease occurs when the {{c1::larvae::stage of parasite}} of Echinococcus encyst in human tissue.
extraNote: The larvae develop after the human ingests the eggs.

clozeText: In humans, the life cycle of Echinococcus progresses from the ingested egg to the {{c1::larval}} form that creates cysts.
extraNote: The adult stage of Echinococcus is not found in humans.

clozeText: Preventing Echinococcus infection involves proper disposal of waste to ensure that dogs cannot ingest {{c1::sheep}} carcasses or infected tissue.
extraNote: Interrupting the chain between the definitive and intermediate hosts is essential for prevention.

clozeText: The adult form of Echinococcus granulosus is much smaller than other tapeworms, measuring only about {{c1::3 to 6 mm::length}} in total.
extraNote: Despite its small size as an adult, the hydatid cysts it causes can grow quite large.

clozeText: In the human body, the Echinococcus embryo emerges from the egg in the {{c1::small intestine}} before burrowing into blood vessels.
extraNote: This is the initial site of entry before dissemination to organs like the liver.

clozeText: The germinal center of Echinococcus, which produces new segments, is located immediately adjacent to the {{c1::scolex}}.
extraNote: Growth occurs by the addition of proglottids from this proximal region.

clozeText: Dermatophytes infect only {{c1::superficial keratinized}} structures such as the skin, hair, and nails.
extraNote: Dermatophytes do not infect deeper tissues.

clozeText: The three most important genera of dermatophytes are {{c1::Trichophyton}}, {{c1::Epidermophyton}}, and {{c1::Microsporum}}.
extraNote: These three genera are the primary causative agents of dermatophytoses.

clozeText: All dermatophytes are characterized as {{c1::molds}} and are not {{c2::dimorphic}}.
extraNote: This distinguishes them from systemic fungi that can exist as both yeasts and molds.

clozeText: Dermatophytes are primarily spread from person to person by {{c1::direct contact}}.
extraNote: Direct contact is the primary transmission pathway for these fungi.

clozeText: The genus {{c1::Microsporum}} can be spread from animals such as dogs and cats to humans.
extraNote: This zoonotic transmission means the animal must be treated to prevent reinfection.

clozeText: {{c1::Fatty acids}} in the skin serve as a host defense by inhibiting the growth of dermatophytes.
extraNote: Chemical barriers like fatty acids complement the physical barrier of intact skin.

clozeText: In the treatment of dermatophyte infections of the skin, fingernails, and toenails, {{c1::terbinafine}} is used.
extraNote: Terbinafine is a common drug of choice for onychomycosis.

clozeText: Terbinafine acts by inhibiting {{c1::squalene epoxidase}}, which blocks ergosterol synthesis.
extraNote: Squalene epoxidase inhibition is the specific mechanism of action for terbinafine.

clozeText: {{c1::Griseofulvin}} is an antifungal drug specifically useful for hair and nail infections caused by dermatophytes.
extraNote: It is often used when topical treatments are insufficient for hair or nails.

clozeText: Griseofulvin functions by binding to {{c1::tubulin}} in microtubules, preventing the formation of the mitotic spindle.
extraNote: Disrupting the mitotic spindle prevents the fungus from reproducing via cell division.

clozeText: Azole drugs used topically for dermatophytoses include {{c1::miconazole}} and {{c2::clotrimazole}}.
extraNote: These imidazoles are too toxic for systemic use and are reserved for topical therapy.

clozeText: {{c1::Ketoconazole}} is an azole useful in treating skin infections caused by dermatophytes.
extraNote: Ketoconazole is part of the azole class that inhibits ergosterol synthesis.

clozeText: Tinea corporis, or {{c1::ringworm}}, typically presents as an oval, ring-shaped inflamed lesion with {{c2::central clearing}}.
extraNote: The classic 'ring' appearance gives the infection its common name.

clozeText: The fungal cell wall of dermatophytes is composed of {{c1::chitin}}.
extraNote: This distinguishes fungi from bacteria, which have peptidoglycan cell walls.

clozeText: Antibiotics like {{c1::penicillins}} or cephalosporins are ineffective against dermatophytes because they lack {{c2::peptidoglycan}}.
extraNote: Fungal cell walls contain chitin instead of the bacterial target for these antibiotics.

clozeText: Dermatophyte cell membranes contain {{c1::ergosterol}}, which is the target for many antifungal drugs.
extraNote: Ergosterol is the fungal equivalent of cholesterol found in human cell membranes.

clozeText: Azoles inhibit ergosterol synthesis by blocking the cytochrome P450-dependent {{c1::demethylation of lanosterol}}.
extraNote: Lanosterol is the precursor that is modified to create ergosterol.

clozeText: Microsporum species produce asexual spores known as {{c1::microconidia}} and {{c2::macroconidia}}.
extraNote: The shape and arrangement of these conidia assist in laboratory identification.

clozeText: Dermatophytoses are categorized as {{c1::cutaneous}} mycoses.
extraNote: This category involves infections limited to the epidermis and its appendages.

clozeText: If {{c1::intact skin}} is damaged, dermatophytes can more easily become established and cause infection.
extraNote: Mechanical integrity of the skin is a primary host defense.

clozeText: Fungi like dermatophytes propagate asexually by forming {{c1::conidia}} from specialized structures.
extraNote: Conidia are asexual spores that aid in identification based on shape and color.

clozeText: Dermatophytes are {{c1::eukaryotic}} organisms.
extraNote: As eukaryotes, they contain mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum, unlike bacteria.

clozeText: The diameter of a typical fungal cell is approximately {{c1::4}} μm, which is larger than most bacteria.
extraNote: Bacteria are typically closer to 1 μm in diameter.

clozeText: Dermatophytes, being molds, consist of long filaments of cells called {{c1::hyphae}}.
extraNote: Hyphae are the structural units of molds.

clozeText: Molds like dermatophytes reproduce by {{c1::cell division}}, where the resulting daughter cells are equal in size.
extraNote: This contrasts with yeasts, which reproduce by budding and produce unequal daughter cells.

clozeText: Like all fungi of medical interest, dermatophytes require {{c1::organic carbon}} for metabolism.
extraNote: Fungi are heterotrophic and do not include obligate anaerobes.

clozeText: Fungi that do not form sexual spores are termed {{c1::fungi imperfecti}}.
extraNote: Dermatophytes are typically classified this way as they reproduce asexually.

clozeText: In the classification of seriousness, dermatophytoses are generally considered {{c1::moderately}} serious (2+).
extraNote: Treatment is often given, though the illness is rarely life-threatening.

clozeText: Dermatophyte growth can be inhibited by {{c1::hormone-associated}} skin changes.
extraNote: Changes in skin chemistry or structure due to hormones can impact susceptibility.

clozeText: A common mechanism of drug resistance in fungi is the export of the drug by {{c1::efflux pump}} transporters.
extraNote: These transporters are located in the fungal cell membrane.

clozeText: Dermatophytes are unique among pathogenic fungi as they infect only {{c1::superficial keratinized}} structures such as the skin, hair, and nails.
extraNote: Dermatophytes do not invade deeper tissues, remaining restricted to the dead layers of the epidermis and its appendages.

clozeText: Unlike many systemic fungal pathogens, dermatophytes are classified as {{c1::molds}} and are {{c2::not::dimorphism status}} dimorphic.
extraNote: Dermatophytes maintain a filamentous (mold) morphology regardless of temperature.

clozeText: Growth of dermatophytes is inhibited by {{c1::fatty acids}} found naturally in the skin.
extraNote: This is a key chemical host defense mechanism against cutaneous fungal colonization.

clozeText: {{c1::Microsporum::Genus}} can be transmitted to humans from animals such as dogs and cats.
extraNote: Preventing reinfection requires treating the source animal in addition to the human patient.

clozeText: {{c1::Terbinafine}} is an antifungal drug used for dermatophyte infections that acts by inhibiting the enzyme {{c2::squalene epoxidase}}.
extraNote: This drug is specifically indicated for infections involving the skin, fingernails, and toenails.

clozeText: {{c1::Griseofulvin}} is an antifungal agent useful for dermatophyte infections of the hair and nails that acts by binding to {{c2::tubulin}}.
extraNote: By binding to tubulin, the drug prevents the formation of the mitotic spindle, inhibiting fungal cell division.

clozeText: The clinical lesion of tinea corporis (ringworm) is characterized by a(n) {{c1::oval, ring-shaped}} appearance with {{c2::central clearing}}.
extraNote: The inflamed border represents the active site of fungal growth.

clozeText: Topical therapy for dermatophytoses often involves imidazole drugs such as {{c1::miconazole}} or {{c2::clotrimazole}}.
extraNote: These drugs are generally too toxic for systemic use but are effective when applied to the skin.

clozeText: Dermatophytes, like all fungi, contain {{c1::ergosterol}} in their cell membranes, which is the primary target for many antifungal drugs.
extraNote: Bacteria lack ergosterol, making these drugs selective for fungal cells.

clozeText: The cell wall of dermatophytes is composed of {{c1::chitin}}, while bacterial cell walls are composed of peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This structural difference explains why antibiotics like penicillins are ineffective against dermatophytes.

clozeText: Azole drugs used against dermatophytes block the synthesis of ergosterol by inhibiting the {{c1::cytochrome P450-dependent demethylation}} of lanosterol.
extraNote: Lanosterol is the direct precursor to ergosterol in the fungal membrane synthesis pathway.

clozeText: Transmission of dermatophytes occurs primarily through {{c1::direct contact::method}}.
extraNote: Person-to-person spread is a major route for these cutaneous infections.

clozeText: Dermatophytes propagate asexually by forming {{c1::conidia::spores}} from specialized structures.
extraNote: The shape, color, and arrangement of these asexual spores are used for laboratory identification.

clozeText: {{c1::Ketoconazole::Drug}} is a specific azole mentioned as useful for treating skin infections caused by dermatophytes.
extraNote: It is part of the broader azole class that inhibits ergosterol synthesis.

clozeText: In the categorization of medical mycoses, dermatophytoses are classified as {{c1::cutaneous}} mycoses.
extraNote: They are specifically restricted to the dead layer of the skin (epidermis).

clozeText: Dermatophytes do not produce {{c1::bacterial-type exotoxins}} and their cell walls lack {{c2::endotoxin}}.
extraNote: Fungal pathogenesis differs significantly from bacterial pathogenesis in this regard.

clozeText: Host defense against dermatophytes is primarily mediated by {{c1::intact skin}}.
extraNote: Damage to the skin barrier is often required for these organisms to become established.

clozeText: The genus {{c1::Microsporum}} is identified in part by the production of both microconidia and {{c2::macroconidia}}.
extraNote: The morphology of these spores is diagnostic for the genus.

clozeText: Griseofulvin is used for dermatophyte infections because it specifically targets the {{c1::mitotic spindle}}.
extraNote: This action occurs by binding to tubulin, a component of microtubules.

clozeText: Fungi like dermatophytes require {{c1::organic carbon}} for metabolism.
extraNote: Unlike some bacteria, they are never obligate anaerobes.

clozeText: Dermatophyte spores are used for {{c1::reproduction}}, whereas bacterial endospores are used for survival.
extraNote: Fungal spores (conidia) can be sexual or asexual.

clozeText: The term {{c1::ringworm}} is the common name for dermatophytosis.
extraNote: This refers to the circular nature of the clinical lesions.

clozeText: In cutaneous mycoses like dermatophytoses, the fungi reside in the {{c1::epidermis}}.
extraNote: This is the outermost, dead layer of the skin.

clozeText: Dermatophytes are described as having a {{c1::2+::rating}} seriousness of illness, meaning they are moderately serious and treatment is often given.
extraNote: This distinguishes them from 1+ infections (like Tinea versicolor) or 4+ systemic infections.

clozeText: The genus {{c1::Epidermophyton::Genus}} is one of the three main causes of ringworm.
extraNote: It is grouped with Trichophyton and Microsporum.

clozeText: The genus {{c1::Trichophyton::Genus}} is one of the three main causes of ringworm.
extraNote: It is grouped with Epidermophyton and Microsporum.

clozeText: Because dermatophytes are eukaryotic, their cytoplasm contains {{c1::mitochondria}} and endoplasmic reticulum.
extraNote: These structures are absent in bacteria.

clozeText: Resistance to antifungal drugs in fungi can occur via {{c1::efflux pump transporters}} that export the drug from the cell.
extraNote: These transporters are located in the fungal cell membrane.

clozeText: The drug {{c1::Terbinafine::drug}} is specifically noted for its use in treating dermatophyte infections of the {{c2::fingernails and toenails}}.
extraNote: Nail infections often require systemic therapy with terbinafine.

clozeText: Dermatophytes are fungi that infect only {{c1::superficial keratinized structures::anatomic depth}} such as skin, hair, and nails.
extraNote: Dermatophytes do not infect deeper tissues.

clozeText: The most important dermatophytes are classified into three genera: {{c1::Trichophyton}}, {{c1::Epidermophyton}}, and {{c1::Microsporum}}.
extraNote: All three genera are classified as molds and are not dimorphic.

clozeText: Dermatophytes exist strictly as {{c1::molds}} and are not dimorphic.
extraNote: Molds consist of long filaments of cells called hyphae.

clozeText: Tinea corporis (ringworm) typically presents as an oval, {{c1::ring-shaped}} inflamed lesion.
extraNote: The clinical presentation often involves central clearing.

clozeText: A classic clinical finding in tinea corporis is an inflamed lesion characterized by {{c1::central clearing}}.
extraNote: This gives the lesion its characteristic 'ringworm' appearance.

clozeText: In addition to person-to-person contact, {{c1::Microsporum}} is also spread from animals such as dogs and cats.
extraNote: Treating the animal is necessary to prevent reinfection in humans.

clozeText: The growth of dermatophytes on the skin is inhibited by {{c1::fatty acids::chemical factor}}.
extraNote: Fatty acids along with intact skin serve as effective host defenses.

clozeText: Dermatophyte growth is inhibited by hormone-associated skin changes that occur at {{c1::puberty}}.
extraNote: This specifically affects susceptibility to infections like those on the scalp.

clozeText: {{c1::Terbinafine}} is an antifungal drug used to treat dermatophyte infections of the skin, fingernails, and toenails by inhibiting squalene epoxidase.
extraNote: It blocks ergosterol synthesis by targeting the squalene epoxidase enzyme.

clozeText: Terbinafine blocks ergosterol synthesis by inhibiting the enzyme {{c1::squalene epoxidase}}.
extraNote: This mechanism is distinct from the azole drugs which target a different step in the ergosterol pathway.

clozeText: The antifungal drug {{c1::Griseofulvin}} is used for hair and nail infections caused by dermatophytes.
extraNote: It acts by binding to tubulin in microtubules.

clozeText: Griseofulvin interferes with fungal growth by binding to {{c1::tubulin::protein}} and preventing the formation of the mitotic spindle.
extraNote: This mechanism targets the microtubules within the fungal cell.

clozeText: The azole drugs {{c1::clotrimazole}} and {{c1::miconazole}} are used only topically for dermatophytoses because they are too toxic for systemic use.
extraNote: These are imidazoles useful for treating Candida and dermatophyte skin infections.

clozeText: {{c1::Ketoconazole::Azole drug}} is useful in the treatment of blastomycosis, chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, and skin infections caused by dermatophytes.
extraNote: It acts by inhibiting ergosterol synthesis via cytochrome P450-dependent demethylation of lanosterol.

clozeText: Dermatophytes are transmitted primarily via {{c1::direct contact}}.
extraNote: Transmission can occur from person to person or animal to person.

clozeText: The genus {{c1::Microsporum}} can be identified by the presence of both microconidia and macroconidia.
extraNote: Identification is based on the shape, color, and arrangement of these asexual spores.

clozeText: Malassezia species cause {{c1::tinea versicolor}} (pityriasis versicolor), a superficial skin infection.
extraNote: The condition is often of cosmetic importance only and is typically asymptomatic.

clozeText: Malassezia is categorized as a {{c1::cutaneous}} mycosis because it infects the dead layer of the skin.
extraNote: Cutaneous mycoses involve the epidermis and its structures without invading deeper tissues.

clozeText: In tissue, Malassezia is seen as a mixture of {{c1::hyphae}} and {{c1::yeasts}}.
extraNote: This dual morphology (mixture of both forms) is a key identifier during microscopic examination.

clozeText: The lesions of tinea versicolor are usually noticed as {{c1::hypopigmented}} areas, especially on tanned skin.
extraNote: The contrast between infected and healthy skin is most apparent during the summer months.

clozeText: Malassezia is transmitted from {{c1::human to human}}.
extraNote: Transmission occurs through direct contact between individuals.

clozeText: Laboratory diagnosis of Malassezia is usually performed using {{c1::KOH (potassium hydroxide)}} preparations of skin scrapings.
extraNote: The KOH preparation dissolves skin cells to reveal the fungal elements.

clozeText: Clinical findings for Malassezia include {{c1::scaly plaques}} on the trunk.
extraNote: These plaques are typically nonpruritic, distinguishing them from the itchy lesions of dermatophytes.

clozeText: Tinea versicolor occurs more frequently in {{c1::hot, humid}} weather.
extraNote: Environmental conditions like high temperature and humidity facilitate the growth of Malassezia.

clozeText: For Malassezia infections, {{c1::culture}} is not usually done.
extraNote: Diagnosis relies primarily on the visual observation of fungal elements in skin scrapings.

clozeText: The treatment of choice for tinea versicolor is topical {{c1::miconazole}}.
extraNote: Antifungal creams are effective for primary infections, though the condition tends to recur.

clozeText: Recurrences of Malassezia infection can be treated with oral antifungal drugs such as {{c1::fluconazole}} or {{c1::itraconazole}}.
extraNote: Systemic treatment is used when topical therapy fails or the infection returns frequently.

clozeText: On the seriousness scale, Malassezia infections are rated as {{c1::1+}}, meaning they are not serious.
extraNote: Treatment may or may not be given depending on the patient's cosmetic concerns.

clozeText: Malassezia specifically infects the {{c1::dead layer}} of the skin.
extraNote: This superficial localization distinguishes it from subcutaneous mycoses like sporotrichosis.

clozeText: While often asymptomatic, tinea versicolor may cause slight {{c1::scaling}} or itching.
extraNote: Pruritus is much less common in Malassezia infections compared to dermatophytoses.

clozeText: Malassezia is also known as the causative agent of {{c1::pityriasis versicolor}}.
extraNote: This is a synonymous term for tinea versicolor used in clinical dermatology.

clozeText: In tissue scrapings, Malassezia hyphae and {{c1::budding yeast}} cells are found together.
extraNote: The presence of both forms simultaneously is characteristic of this organism's appearance in KOH prep.

clozeText: Malassezia is classified separately from dermatophytes like {{c1::Trichophyton}} or Microsporum.
extraNote: Unlike dermatophytes, Malassezia typically produces nonpruritic, hypopigmented lesions rather than ringworm-like inflammation.

clozeText: The primary clinical location for Malassezia lesions is the {{c1::trunk}}.
extraNote: Scaly, hypopigmented plaques are most frequently found on the chest and back.

clozeText: A significant clinical challenge with Malassezia infections is their tendency to {{c1::recur}}.
extraNote: Despite effective initial treatment with topical azoles, many patients experience repeat infections.

clozeText: Malassezia is a fungus that causes disease characterized as {{c1::asymptomatic}} in most cases.
extraNote: The lack of significant inflammation or pain is a hallmark of tinea versicolor.

clozeText: Unlike Microsporum, Malassezia is transmitted via {{c1::human to human}} contact rather than from animals.
extraNote: Animal-to-human transmission is not a feature of tinea versicolor epidemiology.

clozeText: Diagnosis of tinea versicolor is confirmed by seeing a mixture of {{c1::hyphae and yeasts}} in skin scrapings.
extraNote: This visual finding is definitive for Malassezia species in a KOH preparation.

clozeText: Treatment for Malassezia with {{c1::itraconazole}} is typically reserved for {{c2::recurrences}}.
extraNote: Topical miconazole is generally the first-line treatment for an initial episode.

clozeText: Malassezia is distinguished from systemic mycoses because it does not infect {{c1::internal organs}}.
extraNote: It is restricted to the most superficial layers of the skin.

clozeText: Hypopigmented areas in Malassezia infections are most common in the {{c1::summer}}.
extraNote: This seasonality is due to the lack of tanning in infected skin compared to surrounding healthy skin.

clozeText: Malassezia's anatomical location is described specifically as the {{c1::dead layer of skin}}.
extraNote: This excludes the deeper epidermis or dermis, which are involved in other types of mycoses.

clozeText: The lesions of Malassezia are often described as {{c1::nonpruritic::pruritic or nonpruritic?}}.
extraNote: The absence of itching helps distinguish tinea versicolor from dermatophytoses like tinea corporis.

clozeText: Tinea versicolor is a {{c1::superficial}} infection, meaning it does not penetrate into the subcutis.

clozeText: KOH preparation of Malassezia skin scrapings reveals the fungus without the need for {{c1::culture}}.

clozeText: Oral {{c1::fluconazole}} is a systemic option for managing Malassezia when topical creams fail.
extraNote: Azoles are effective against the fungal growth that causes pityriasis versicolor.

clozeText: Tinea versicolor (pityriasis versicolor) is a superficial skin infection of {{c1::cosmetic}} importance only.

clozeText: Malassezia lesions are typically more noticeable in the {{c1::summer}} due to skin tanning.

clozeText: Malassezia is categorized under {{c1::cutaneous}} mycoses in medical mycology.

clozeText: Malassezia plaques are frequently found on the {{c1::trunk::anatomic site}}.

clozeText: Malassezia is a {{c1::fungus}} that causes skin infections in humans.

clozeText: The serological response or skin test for Malassezia is not typically used; diagnosis is {{c1::microscopic}}.

clozeText: In Malassezia infections, the fungal elements are found in the {{c1::stratum corneum}}.

clozeText: Malassezia species are the causative agents of {{c1::tinea versicolor}} (also known as pityriasis versicolor).

clozeText: Sporothrix schenckii is classified as a {{c1::subcutaneous}} mycosis based on its anatomic location.
extraNote: Subcutaneous mycoses are typically introduced into the skin via trauma.

clozeText: Sporothrix schenckii is a {{c1::dimorphic}} fungus, existing as a mold on plants and a yeast in human tissue.
extraNote: Dimorphic fungi change their growth form based on temperature; mold at room temperature and yeast at body temperature.

clozeText: In human tissue, Sporothrix schenckii exists as round or {{c1::cigar-shaped}} budding yeasts.
extraNote: The unique shape seen in tissue specimens is a hallmark diagnostic feature.

clozeText: The mold form of Sporothrix schenckii is typically introduced into the skin via a {{c1::thorn::injury type}}, such as from a rose bush.
extraNote: This leads to the common name 'rose gardener's disease'.

clozeText: Sporotrichosis is characterized by a local pustule or ulcer that often develops {{c1::nodules}} along the draining {{c2::lymphatics}}.
extraNote: This pattern of spread is a classic presentation of the infection.

clozeText: Unlike systemic fungi like Histoplasma, infection with Sporothrix elicits a {{c1::pyogenic}} host defense response.
extraNote: A pyogenic response is primarily composed of neutrophils.

clozeText: The host defense response to Sporothrix schenckii is primarily composed of {{c1::neutrophils}}.
extraNote: This is characteristic of a pyogenic response rather than a granulomatous one.

clozeText: Sporotrichosis occurs most frequently in {{c1::gardeners}}, especially those who prune roses.
extraNote: Occupational exposure to contaminated plant material is the primary risk factor.

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating skin lesions caused by Sporothrix schenckii is {{c1::itraconazole}}.
extraNote: Itraconazole (Sporanox) is the standard antifungal for cutaneous sporotrichosis.

clozeText: In culture at room temperature, Sporothrix schenckii produces hyphae with oval conidia arranged in {{c1::daisy-like}} clusters.
extraNote: The conidia are found at the tips of slender conidiophores.

clozeText: Disseminated sporotrichosis is a potential complication in patients with {{c1::HIV}} and low CD4 counts.
extraNote: While usually local, the disease can spread systemically in immunocompromised hosts.

clozeText: Clinical findings of sporotrichosis often include a pustule or ulcer on the {{c1::hands}} with nodules extending up the arm.
extraNote: The site of inoculation is usually the hand, followed by lymphatic spread.

clozeText: The lesions associated with Sporothrix schenckii infection are typically {{c1::painless}}.
extraNote: Despite their appearance, the pustules and nodules do not usually cause significant pain.

clozeText: Laboratory diagnosis using a potassium hydroxide (KOH) prep of a Sporothrix specimen reveals {{c1::cigar-shaped}} yeasts.
extraNote: KOH preparation is used to visualize fungal elements in clinical specimens.

clozeText: At room temperature (25°C), Sporothrix schenckii grows as a {{c1::mold}}.
extraNote: Dimorphic fungi are molds at room temperature and yeasts at body temperature.

clozeText: The fungal cell wall of Sporothrix schenckii is composed of {{c1::chitin}}.
extraNote: This distinguishes fungi from bacteria, which have peptidoglycan cell walls.

clozeText: The cell membrane of Sporothrix schenckii contains {{c1::ergosterol}}, which is the target of azole drugs and amphotericin B.
extraNote: Ergosterol is the fungal equivalent of cholesterol in animal cell membranes.

clozeText: Sporothrix schenckii is found in the {{c1::soil}} and on various types of vegetation.
extraNote: The organism is naturally occurring in the environment.

clozeText: Sporotrichosis can be prevented by protecting the skin when handling plants, {{c1::moss}}, and wood.
extraNote: Protective clothing prevents the traumatic inoculation of spores.

clozeText: In its yeast form, Sporothrix schenckii reproduces by {{c1::budding}}, where daughter cells are unequal in size.
extraNote: This is the characteristic asexual reproduction method for yeasts.

clozeText: Untreated lesions of sporotrichosis may {{c1::wax and wane}} for many years.
extraNote: The infection is chronic and may persist for long periods without intervention.

clozeText: On the seriousness scale, sporotrichosis is categorized as {{c1::2+}}, meaning it is moderately serious and treatment is often given.
extraNote: It is less serious than systemic mycoses like Coccidioidomycosis (4+).

clozeText: The anatomic location of infection for Sporothrix schenckii is the {{c1::subcutis}}.
extraNote: It primarily affects the tissue layer immediately beneath the skin.

clozeText: In culture at room temperature, Sporothrix schenckii conidia are described as being {{c1::oval}} in shape.
extraNote: These conidia form the characteristic daisy-like clusters on conidiophores.

clozeText: The primary mode of transmission for Sporothrix involves the implantation of fungal {{c1::spores}}.
extraNote: The spores from the mold form are what enter the tissue through trauma.

clozeText: Antibiotics such as {{c1::penicillins}} are ineffective against Sporothrix because they target peptidoglycan synthesis.
extraNote: Fungal cell walls do not contain peptidoglycan.

clozeText: Sporothrix schenckii is a {{c1::eukaryotic}} organism, which distinguishes it from bacteria.
extraNote: Like all fungi, Sporothrix has a defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

clozeText: At body temperature (37°C), Sporothrix schenckii exists in the {{c1::yeast}} form.
extraNote: This transition is essential for survival within the human host.

clozeText: In culture, Sporothrix conidia are borne on slender stalks known as {{c1::conidiophores}}.
extraNote: The arrangement of conidia on these stalks is used for identification.

clozeText: The inflammatory response to Sporothrix is classified as {{c1::pyogenic::type}}.
extraNote: This response is characterized by the accumulation of pus and neutrophils.

clozeText: Unlike Histoplasma, infection with {{c1::Sporothrix}} elicits a {{c2::pyogenic::type}} response composed of neutrophils.
extraNote: Most systemic fungi cause granulomatous responses; Sporothrix is a notable exception that triggers a pyogenic response.

clozeText: The primary host defense cell type found in the response to Sporothrix schenckii is {{c1::neutrophils}}.
extraNote: This is contrasted with Histoplasma and Coccidioides, which elicit responses from macrophages and helper T cells.

clozeText: Sporothrix schenckii is classified as a {{c1::dimorphic}} fungus, existing as a mold in nature and a yeast in human tissue.

clozeText: In the clinical laboratory, tissue specimens of Sporothrix schenckii show {{c1::round}} or {{c2::cigar-shaped}} budding yeasts.

clozeText: Sporothrix schenckii is the representative genus for {{c1::subcutaneous::category}} mycoses, which typically affect the {{c2::subcutis}}.

clozeText: The most common mode of transmission for Sporothrix schenckii is a {{c1::penetrating lesion::mechanism}}, such as a rose thorn.

clozeText: Sporotrichosis is an occupational hazard often associated with {{c1::gardeners::profession}}, especially those who prune roses.

clozeText: A characteristic clinical finding of sporotrichosis is a local pustule or ulcer with {{c1::nodules}} along the {{c2::draining lymphatics}}.
