clozeText: The Reovirus virion polymerase is an {{c1::RNA-dependent RNA polymerase}}.
extraNote: It transcribes the negative strand of the dsRNA into mRNA.

clozeText: One of the key distinguishing features of Reoviruses is that their genome is {{c1::RNA}} based.
extraNote: Despite being double-stranded like most DNA viruses, its chemical composition is RNA.

clozeText: Reoviruses, specifically Rotavirus, exhibit a {{c1::segmented}} genome structure.
extraNote: This allows for high genetic diversity and specific mRNA regulation.

clozeText: The {{c1::virion RNA polymerase}} of Reoviruses is essential for the initial synthesis of viral proteins.
extraNote: Without this enzyme, the double-stranded RNA cannot be translated by host ribosomes.

clozeText: Reoviruses are defined by their (±) RNA genome, where (±) stands for {{c1::double-stranded}}.
extraNote: This terminology is standard in virological classification.

clozeText: In Reoviruses, transcription of mRNA is the {{c1::first}} step of gene expression after entry.
extraNote: This must occur before any viral proteins can be produced.

clozeText: All viruses have one copy of their genome (haploid) except {{c1::retroviruses}}, which have {{c2::two}} copies (diploid).
extraNote: Retroviruses are the only family of viruses that are diploid.

clozeText: Retroviruses have a genome consisting of {{c1::single-stranded::strand type}} {{c2::RNA}} of {{c3::positive}} polarity.
extraNote: This positive-polarity RNA is transcribed into double-stranded DNA by reverse transcriptase.

clozeText: Retroviruses carry a virion-encoded enzyme called {{c1::reverse transcriptase}} (RNA-dependent DNA polymerase).
extraNote: This enzyme allows the virus to synthesize a DNA copy from its RNA genome.

clozeText: Unlike most RNA viruses that replicate in the cytoplasm, retroviruses have an important replicative step in the {{c1::nucleus}}.
extraNote: Retroviruses must integrate a DNA copy of their genome into the host cell DNA within the nucleus.

clozeText: Retroviruses integrate a {{c1::DNA}} copy of their genome into the host cell DNA.
extraNote: This integration is a defining step of the retroviral life cycle.

clozeText: The viral mRNA of retroviruses is transcribed from the integrated DNA intermediate by the host cell {{c1::RNA polymerase II}}.
extraNote: The virus uses the regular host cell machinery for mRNA synthesis after integration.

clozeText: The purified {{c1::RNA}} genome of retroviruses is not infectious because it requires a {{c2::virion-carried polymerase}} to initiate the replicative cycle.
extraNote: Viruses that require a polymerase in the virion, like retroviruses, do not have infectious purified genomic RNA.

clozeText: Although the retroviral genome RNA is not infectious, the {{c1::DNA intermediate}} is infectious.
extraNote: The DNA intermediate can be transcribed by host cell machinery directly.

clozeText: Prototype human retroviruses include {{c1::HIV::Acronym}} and {{c2::HTLV::Acronym}}.
extraNote: HIV stands for human immunodeficiency virus; HTLV stands for human T-cell leukemia virus.

clozeText: The drug {{c1::lamivudine}} is effective against both HIV and HBV because it inhibits the {{c2::reverse transcriptase}} found in both viruses.
extraNote: Lamivudine acts on the RNA-dependent DNA polymerase activity shared by these distinct virus families.

clozeText: Retroviruses are {{c1::enveloped}} viruses, which makes them less stable and more easily inactivated than naked viruses.
extraNote: Enveloped viruses generally survive for shorter periods in the environment.

clozeText: Retroviruses are generally transmitted by direct contact via {{c1::blood and body fluids}}.
extraNote: This is a common characteristic of enveloped viruses that are less stable in the environment.

clozeText: The retroviral envelope is typically acquired as the virus exits the cell in a process called {{c1::budding}}.
extraNote: The envelope contains lipids derived from the host cell and proteins encoded by the virus.

clozeText: The {{c1::matrix protein}} in retroviruses mediates the interaction between the viral nucleocapsid proteins and the envelope proteins.
extraNote: This protein acts as a bridge during virus assembly and structure maintenance.

clozeText: Retroviral {{c1::surface proteins}} mediate attachment to host cell receptors, determining host and organ specificity.
extraNote: These proteins are the primary targets for neutralizing antibodies.

clozeText: Antibody bound to retroviral surface proteins {{c1::neutralizes}} viral replication by preventing attachment to the cell receptor.
extraNote: Neutralization is the primary mechanism by which antibodies inhibit viral infection.

clozeText: Retroviruses use their genome RNA as the template to synthesize a DNA copy {{c1::early}} in the replicative cycle.
extraNote: This contrasts with hepadnaviruses (like HBV), which synthesize DNA late in the cycle.

clozeText: Some retroviruses produce {{c1::antigenic variants}} of their surface proteins to evade host immune defenses.
extraNote: Antibody against one serotype will not necessarily neutralize a different variant.

clozeText: The interaction between retroviral surface proteins and host cell receptors determines {{c1::host specificity}} and {{c2::organ specificity}}.
extraNote: Receptor-ligand binding is a critical determinant of viral tropism.

clozeText: Retroviruses are classified as viruses that contain a {{c1::polymerase}} within the virion particle.
extraNote: This virion-associated enzyme is essential because host cells lack the mechanism to transcribe RNA into DNA.

clozeText: The retroviral envelope consists of a membrane containing {{c1::lipid}} derived from the host cell and {{c2::proteins}} encoded by the virus.
extraNote: The composition of the envelope is a hybrid of host and viral components.

clozeText: Retroviruses have a protein coat called a {{c1::capsid}} which is composed of repeating subunits called {{c2::capsomers}}.
extraNote: The capsid covers the viral genome and forms the nucleocapsid when combined with nucleic acids.

clozeText: In the retroviral life cycle, the synthesis of a DNA copy from the RNA genome occurs {{c1::before}} the synthesis of viral mRNA.
extraNote: The DNA intermediate is a required template for subsequent mRNA production by host RNA polymerase II.

clozeText: The genome of retroviruses is {{c1::diploid}}, meaning it contains two copies of {{c2::single-stranded RNA}}.
extraNote: This is a unique genetic feature among all known virus families.

clozeText: Retroviruses require an {{c1::RNA-dependent DNA polymerase}} to replicate their genome.
extraNote: This enzyme is commonly known as reverse transcriptase.

clozeText: Because they are enveloped, retroviruses are primarily transmitted by {{c1::direct contact}} rather than the fecal-oral route.
extraNote: Naked viruses are more likely to survive the environment for transmission via the fecal-oral route.

clozeText: The structure composed of the retroviral nucleic acid genome and the capsid proteins is called the {{c1::nucleocapsid}}.
extraNote: In retroviruses, this structure is surrounded by a matrix and an outer envelope.

clozeText: Antibodies against one {{c1::serotype}} of a retrovirus will not neutralize a different serotype.
extraNote: This is why antigenic variation is an effective method for immune evasion.

clozeText: Retroviral mRNA is generated by the host cell {{c1::RNA polymerase II::specific enzyme}} from the integrated proviral DNA.
extraNote: The integrated DNA acts as a template for host transcription machinery.

clozeText: The {{c1::diploid}} nature of retroviruses distinguishes them from all other virus families, which are {{c2::haploid}}.
extraNote: Having two copies of the RNA genome is a characteristic unique to Retroviridae.

clozeText: Retroviruses follow a replication strategy where they integrate a {{c1::DNA copy}} of their genome into the host cell DNA.
extraNote: This integration step is a hallmark of the retroviral life cycle and requires entry into the nucleus.

clozeText: Retroviruses use a virion-encoded {{c1::RNA-dependent DNA polymerase}} (reverse transcriptase) to synthesize a DNA copy of their RNA genome.
extraNote: This enzyme is carried within the viral particle because host cells lack the machinery to synthesize DNA from an RNA template.

clozeText: The genome of a retrovirus consists of {{c1::single-stranded RNA}} of {{c2::positive}} polarity.
extraNote: Despite being positive-polarity, the RNA itself is not immediately used as mRNA; it must first be reverse-transcribed.

clozeText: Retroviruses do not yield {{c1::infectious}} nucleic acid because they require a virion polymerase for their replicative cycle.
extraNote: Purified retroviral RNA cannot initiate infection alone because the cell does not contain reverse transcriptase.

clozeText: The viral mRNA of retroviruses is transcribed from the integrated DNA intermediate by the {{c1::host cell RNA polymerase}}.
extraNote: Specifically, the regular host cell RNA polymerase II is utilized for this transcription step.

clozeText: Retroviruses, such as HIV, utilize reverse transcriptase {{c1::early}} in the replicative cycle.
extraNote: This contrasts with hepadnaviruses (like HBV), which utilize reverse transcriptase late in the cycle to produce the DNA genome.

clozeText: The drug {{c1::lamivudine}} is effective against both HIV and HBV because it inhibits the {{c2::reverse transcriptase}} of both viruses.
extraNote: This shared target exists despite the different roles reverse transcriptase plays in the life cycles of these two virus families.

clozeText: The two prototype human pathogens in the retrovirus family are {{c1::HIV}} and {{c2::HTLV::Human T-cell leukemia virus}}.
extraNote: HIV is the human immunodeficiency virus, and HTLV is the human T-cell leukemia virus.

clozeText: Retroviral surface proteins mediate attachment to host cell receptors, which determines the {{c1::host}} and {{c2::organ}} specificity of the virus.
extraNote: Antibodies targeting these surface proteins can neutralize the virus by blocking attachment.

clozeText: The {{c1::matrix protein}} of retroviruses mediates the interaction between the viral nucleocapsid proteins and the envelope proteins.
extraNote: This protein acts as a bridge during viral assembly and structure maintenance.

clozeText: Some retroviruses produce {{c1::antigenic variants}} of their surface proteins, allowing them to evade host antibody responses.
extraNote: Antibody against one serotype will often not neutralize a different antigenic variant.

clozeText: The retroviral envelope is typically acquired as the virus exits from the cell in a process called {{c1::budding}}.
extraNote: The envelope consists of a host cell-derived lipid membrane and virus-encoded proteins.

clozeText: Because retroviruses possess an envelope, they are {{c1::less stable}} and more easily inactivated compared to naked viruses.
extraNote: Enveloped viruses generally require direct contact (blood/body fluids) for transmission because they cannot survive long in the environment.

clozeText: Retroviruses are classified as having {{c1::spherical::icosahedral}} symmetry of their nucleocapsids.
extraNote: Most viruses appear as either spheres or rods under electron microscopy; retroviruses fall into the spherical category.

clozeText: Retroviruses belong to the group of RNA viruses that utilize a {{c1::DNA intermediate}} for mRNA synthesis.
extraNote: The flow of genetic information is RNA → DNA → mRNA.

clozeText: Host cell {{c1::RNA polymerase II}} is the specific enzyme that transcribes the integrated retroviral provirus into mRNA.
extraNote: The provirus is the term for the viral DNA integrated into the host genome.

clozeText: Retroviruses are obligate {{c1::intracellular}} parasites that must utilize host cell ribosomes for protein synthesis.
extraNote: Like all viruses, they lack their own machinery for translating viral mRNAs into proteins.

clozeText: The process where {{c1::antibody}} bound to retroviral surface proteins prevents attachment is known as {{c2::neutralization}}.
extraNote: This inhibition of viral replication is a key mechanism of the immune response.

clozeText: Retroviruses carry {{c1::two}} copies of their genome, which makes them the only known viruses to be diploid.
extraNote: All other known human viruses are haploid.

clozeText: The enzyme reverse transcriptase possesses {{c1::RNA-dependent DNA polymerase}} activity.
extraNote: This enzyme is critical for converting the single-stranded RNA genome into double-stranded DNA.

clozeText: Retroviruses are characterized as enveloped viruses that are transmitted via {{c1::blood}} and {{c2::body fluids}}.
extraNote: The envelope makes them too fragile for fecal-oral (indirect) transmission routes.

clozeText: In retroviral replication, the genome is transcribed into DNA {{c1::before}} it integrates into the host chromosome.
extraNote: The reverse transcription occurs in the cytoplasm before the DNA intermediate enters the nucleus.

clozeText: The protein coat of a retrovirus that covers the genome is called the {{c1::capsid}}.
extraNote: The capsid is composed of repeating subunits called capsomers.

clozeText: Retroviruses have a genome composed of {{c1::RNA}}, which differentiates them from Hepadnaviruses that have a DNA genome.
extraNote: Both utilize reverse transcriptase, but they start with different nucleic acids in the virion.

clozeText: Retroviruses cannot initiate an infection by their purified RNA alone because they lack a host cell enzyme to perform {{c1::reverse transcription}}.
extraNote: The virion must bring its own polymerase into the cell to begin the replicative cycle.

clozeText: The retrovirus {{c1::HIV}} uses its genome RNA as a template for DNA synthesis in the {{c2::early}} stage of infection.
extraNote: Synthesis of the DNA copy is one of the first events following uncoating.

clozeText: Most RNA viruses undergo their entire replicative cycle in the cytoplasm; the two principal exceptions are {{c1::retroviruses}} and {{c2::influenza viruses::other virus family}}, both of which have an important replicative step in the {{c3::nucleus}}.
extraNote: Retroviruses require a nuclear step to integrate their DNA intermediate into the host cell DNA.

clozeText: The genome of retroviruses consists of {{c1::single-stranded RNA::ssRNA/dsRNA}} of {{c2::positive}} polarity.
extraNote: Despite having positive polarity, the RNA itself does not act directly as mRNA; it must first be reverse transcribed.

clozeText: Retroviruses contain an {{c1::RNA-dependent DNA polymerase}} (also known as {{c2::reverse transcriptase}}).
extraNote: This enzyme is carried within the virion to synthesize a DNA copy from the RNA genome.

clozeText: Unlike most other positive-strand RNA viruses, purified retroviral {{c1::genome RNA}} is {{c2::not infectious::infectivity status}}.
extraNote: The genome RNA is not infectious because it requires the virion-associated reverse transcriptase to initiate the replicative cycle.

clozeText: In retroviruses, mRNA is transcribed from the DNA intermediate by the regular host cell {{c1::RNA polymerase II::specific enzyme}}.
extraNote: The virus utilizes the host's transcriptional machinery once the DNA intermediate is formed.

clozeText: Retroviruses, such as HIV, use their genome RNA as a template to synthesize a DNA copy {{c1::early}} in the replicative cycle.
extraNote: This distinguishes them from hepadnaviruses (like HBV), which synthesize their DNA genome late in the cycle.

clozeText: The antiviral drug {{c1::lamivudine}} is effective against both HIV and HBV because it inhibits the {{c2::reverse transcriptase}} of both viruses.
extraNote: Both Retroviridae (HIV) and Hepadnaviridae (HBV) utilize a reverse transcriptase enzyme.

clozeText: Prototype human retroviruses include {{c1::HTLV::leukemia-associated}} and {{c2::HIV::immunodeficiency-associated}}.
extraNote: HTLV stands for human T-cell leukemia virus; HIV stands for human immunodeficiency virus.

clozeText: Viruses such as retroviruses, which require a {{c1::virion polymerase}}, cannot yield infectious purified nucleic acid.
extraNote: The absence of the packaged enzyme prevents the purified RNA from initiating a successful infection cycle.

clozeText: The strategy for retroviruses involves transcribing {{c1::single-stranded RNA::genome type}} into {{c2::double-stranded DNA::intermediate}}.
extraNote: This conversion is mediated by the viral reverse transcriptase carried in the particle.

clozeText: Hepadnaviruses (HBV) and retroviruses (HIV) are similar in that they both utilize {{c1::reverse transcriptase}}, but they use it at {{c2::different}} stages of the replicative cycle.
extraNote: HIV uses it early to create a DNA intermediate; HBV uses it late to produce the DNA genome for the virion.

clozeText: In the retrovirus lifecycle, the {{c1::DNA copy}} is transcribed into viral mRNA by the host cell {{c2::RNA polymerase}}.
extraNote: The integrated provirus acts as a template for host enzymes to produce viral transcripts.

clozeText: All human viruses have one copy of their genome (haploid) except {{c1::retroviruses}}, which have two copies (diploid).
extraNote: Retroviruses are the only family of viruses that are diploid.

clozeText: While most RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm, {{c1::retroviruses}} and influenza viruses are the two principal exceptions that have an important replicative step in the nucleus.
extraNote: Retroviruses integrate a DNA copy of their genome into the host cell DNA within the nucleus.

clozeText: Retroviruses possess a {{c1::diploid}} genome, meaning they carry two copies of their RNA.
extraNote: This is a unique feature among human viruses.

clozeText: The enzyme carried by retroviruses that transcribes single-stranded RNA into double-stranded DNA is called {{c1::reverse transcriptase::RNA-dependent DNA polymerase}}.
extraNote: This enzyme is also known as RNA-dependent DNA polymerase.

clozeText: Retroviruses utilize the host cell {{c1::RNA polymerase II}} to transcribe their integrated DNA copy into viral mRNA.
extraNote: This occurs after the DNA copy has been integrated into the host genome.

extraNote: By contrast, viruses that do not require a virion polymerase can produce infectious nucleic acid.

clozeText: Although the retroviral RNA genome itself is not infectious, the {{c1::DNA intermediate}} is infectious.
extraNote: The DNA intermediate is synthesized by reverse transcriptase before being integrated.

clozeText: Flaviviruses are characterized by an {{c1::enveloped}} virion and an {{c2::icosahedral}} capsid.
extraNote: Unlike Picornaviruses, Flaviviruses possess a lipid envelope surrounding their icosahedral nucleocapsid.

clozeText: The Flavivirus genome consists of {{c1::single-stranded::number of strands}}, {{c2::positive-polarity::polarity}} RNA.
extraNote: The positive polarity allows the genome to function directly as mRNA upon entering the host cell.

clozeText: The RNA genome of Flaviviruses is {{c1::linear}} and {{c2::nonsegmented::segmented or nonsegmented}}.
extraNote: Nonsegmented genomes typically encode a single polyprotein, whereas segmented genomes (like influenza) encode separate proteins per segment.

clozeText: Flaviviruses translate their entire genome into a {{c1::single polypeptide::structure}} that is subsequently cleaved.
extraNote: This large precursor protein must be processed into individual functional proteins by proteases.

clozeText: The precursor polypeptide of Flaviviruses is cleaved into functional proteins by a {{c1::virus-encoded protease}}.
extraNote: Proteolytic cleavage is a mandatory step for the maturation of viral proteins in Flaviviruses, Coronaviruses, and Picornaviruses.

clozeText: The proteolytic cleavage of the Flavivirus polyprotein occurs in the {{c1::cytoplasm}} of the host cell.
extraNote: This matches the location of translation for most positive-strand RNA viruses.

clozeText: During replication, Flaviviruses use a {{c1::negative-strand::polarity}} RNA intermediate to produce progeny genomes.
extraNote: The parental (+) ssRNA serves as a template for (-) ssRNA, which then serves as a template for new (+) ssRNA genomes.

clozeText: The genome of Flaviviruses is considered {{c1::infective}} when purified and introduced into a susceptible cell.
extraNote: Positive-strand RNA genomes are inherently infectious because they can be directly translated by host ribosomes without a virion-associated polymerase.

clozeText: Flaviviruses do {{c1::NOT}} contain a polymerase within the mature virion.
extraNote: Because they are (+) RNA viruses, they use the host's machinery to first translate their own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

clozeText: {{c1::Hepatitis C virus}} is a medically important Flavivirus that causes chronic liver disease.
extraNote: Other members include Yellow Fever and Dengue viruses.

clozeText: The Flavivirus family includes {{c1::Yellow fever virus}}, which is a classic cause of viral hemorrhagic fever.
extraNote: Yellow fever is characterized by jaundice and hemorrhagic symptoms.

clozeText: {{c1::Dengue virus}} and {{c2::West Nile virus}} are prominent members of the Flavivirus family transmitted by arthropod vectors.
extraNote: Most flaviviruses are arboviruses (arthropod-borne), though Hepatitis C is a notable exception.

clozeText: Encephalitis-causing members of the Flavivirus family include {{c1::St. Louis encephalitis}} and {{c2::Japanese encephalitis}} viruses.
extraNote: These viruses are significant causes of neuroinvasive disease globally.

clozeText: {{c1::Zika virus}} is an enveloped, icosahedral virus belonging to the Flavivirus family.
extraNote: Zika virus gained prominence for its association with microcephaly and Guillain-Barré syndrome.

clozeText: In Flavivirus replication, the source of viral mRNA is the {{c1::parental genome itself}}.
extraNote: The virion RNA is identical to the mRNA that will be translated into the viral polyprotein.

clozeText: Flaviviruses and {{c1::Coronaviruses}} both utilize a strategy of synthesizing large precursor polypeptides that require proteolytic cleavage.
extraNote: In contrast, viruses like influenza or rotaviruses use segmented genomes to produce distinct proteins.

clozeText: The replication of Flaviviruses follows the principle of {{c1::complementarity}} for genome synthesis.
extraNote: This requires the synthesis of a strand with a complementary base sequence to serve as a template.

clozeText: Unlike Togaviruses, which may use subgenomic mRNAs, Flaviviruses translate their {{c1::entire}} genome into a single polyprotein.
extraNote: Togaviruses like Rubella translate more than one polypeptide from subgenomic mRNAs.

clozeText: Flaviviruses are distinguished from Picornaviruses by the presence of a viral {{c1::envelope}}.
extraNote: Both are (+) ssRNA viruses with icosahedral symmetry, but Picornaviruses are naked (non-enveloped).

clozeText: The intermediate form during the replication of the Flavivirus genome is {{c1::ssRNA::nucleic acid type}} of {{c2::negative::polarity}} polarity.
extraNote: The positive-strand genome produces a negative-strand intermediate, which then templates new positive-strand progeny.

clozeText: Flaviviruses possess a {{c1::single-stranded::strand count}} linear RNA genome.
extraNote: The genome is a single molecule of RNA rather than multiple segments.

clozeText: The polarity of the Flavivirus RNA genome is {{c1::positive (+)}}.
