clozeText: In the viral growth cycle of coronaviruses, the process of {{c1::uncoating}} refers to the removal of capsid proteins to free the genome.
extraNote: Once uncoated, the positive-strand RNA is free to function as mRNA.

clozeText: Coronaviruses, like picornaviruses, have an {{c1::infective}} genome because the purified RNA can initiate the full replicative cycle.
extraNote: This is a characteristic of many positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses.

clozeText: Coronavirus {{c1::assembly}} involves combining the newly replicated genetic material with structural capsid proteins.
extraNote: This occurs during the late events of the viral growth cycle.

clozeText: The mRNA of coronaviruses is produced directly from the {{c1::genome::template source}}.
extraNote: Because the genome is (+) RNA, it functions as the initial mRNA for early protein synthesis.

clozeText: The {{c1::fusion protein}} of coronaviruses is only revealed after the spike protein is processed by host proteases.
extraNote: This protein is responsible for the actual merging of the viral and cellular membranes.

clozeText: For coronaviruses, {{c1::cell surface proteases}} are required to cleave the spike protein to reveal a fusion protein.
extraNote: This cleavage is a critical step for the virus to mediate entry into the host cell.

clozeText: Cleavage of the coronavirus {{c1::spike protein}} reveals a fusion protein that mediates entry into the host cell.
extraNote: The spike protein is the primary attachment and entry protein for the virus.

clozeText: The genome of a coronavirus is described as {{c1::single-stranded::strand type}} and {{c2::nonsegmented::segmentation}}.
extraNote: Coronaviruses possess one of the largest nonsegmented RNA genomes.

clozeText: Coronaviruses have a genome with {{c1::positive::polarity}} polarity.
extraNote: Positive polarity means the genomic RNA has the same polarity as mRNA and can be translated directly.

clozeText: Coronaviruses do not contain a {{c1::polymerase}} within the mature virion.
extraNote: Because their genome is positive-sense RNA, it can be translated directly into the necessary replication enzymes by host ribosomes.

clozeText: The purified genome of a coronavirus is {{c1::infective::infectious?}}.
extraNote: Purified positive-strand RNA can initiate the entire viral growth cycle when introduced into a cell because it acts directly as mRNA.

clozeText: Coronaviruses synthesize {{c1::precursor polypeptides::intermediate proteins}} that must be cleaved to form functional proteins.
extraNote: These are also known as polyproteins which are processed post-translationally.

clozeText: The cleavage of coronavirus precursor polypeptides is performed by a {{c1::virus-encoded protease}}.
extraNote: Functional viral proteins are only produced after the polyprotein is cut into smaller, active units.

clozeText: In coronaviruses, two polyproteins are formed by the translation of {{c1::two-thirds}} of the genome RNA.
extraNote: The remaining third of the genome typically encodes structural proteins.

clozeText: The site of proteolytic cleavage for coronavirus polyproteins is the {{c1::cytoplasm}}.
extraNote: RNA virus replication and protein processing typically occur in the host cell cytoplasm.

clozeText: The parental {{c1::+ssRNA}} genome of a coronavirus uses a {{c2::−ssRNA}} intermediate for replication.
extraNote: The negative-strand intermediate serves as the template for producing new positive-strand progeny genomes.

clozeText: The source of mRNA for coronaviruses is the {{c1::viral genome}} itself.
extraNote: The positive-sense RNA genome functions as the initial messenger RNA for early protein synthesis.

clozeText: The prototype human coronavirus mentioned for single-strand, positive-polarity, nonsegmented viruses is {{c1::SARS-CoV-2}}.
extraNote: SARS-CoV-2 follows the standard replication pattern of the Coronaviridae family.

clozeText: Coronavirus entry into the host cell is mediated by a process called {{c1::fusion}}.
extraNote: Fusion occurs between the viral envelope and the host cell membrane.

clozeText: The specificity of coronavirus {{c1::attachment}} determines the host range and organ specificity of the virus.
extraNote: This is governed by the interaction between the viral spike protein and specific host cell receptors.

clozeText: Viral genome replication in coronaviruses is governed by the principle of {{c1::complementarity}}.
extraNote: This requires the synthesis of a strand with a complementary base sequence to act as a template.

clozeText: In the coronavirus growth cycle, {{c1::early}} proteins are enzymes used to replicate the viral genome.
extraNote: Early proteins are synthesized before genome replication occurs.

clozeText: In the coronavirus growth cycle, {{c1::late}} proteins are the structural, capsid proteins.
extraNote: Late proteins are synthesized after or during genome replication to assemble progeny virions.

clozeText: The {{c1::uncoating}} process in coronaviruses refers to the removal of capsid proteins to free the viral genome.
extraNote: Uncoating allows the genome to function and begin the replication cycle.

clozeText: During the growth cycle of coronaviruses, a {{c1::low pH}} within the endocytic vesicle often favors the uncoating process.
extraNote: Acidification of the vesicle is a common trigger for the release of viral genomes.

clozeText: The progeny genome of a coronavirus has {{c1::positive}} polarity.
extraNote: The progeny must match the parental positive-strand RNA to be packaged into new virions.

clozeText: The attachment of coronaviruses to cell surface receptors occurs through {{c1::weak, noncovalent}} bonding.
extraNote: This initial binding is the first step of the infection process before fusion.

clozeText: In coronaviruses, newly replicated viral genomes can serve as templates for {{c1::late mRNA}} to produce capsid proteins.
extraNote: This temporal control ensures structural proteins are available when genomes are ready for assembly.

clozeText: Coronaviruses belong to the group of viruses that produce {{c1::two}} distinct polyproteins during translation.
extraNote: These polyproteins are cleaved into individual functional enzymes and components.

clozeText: Unlike influenza, coronaviruses do not have a {{c1::segmented}} genome.
extraNote: Influenza has segments that each encode specific proteins, while coronaviruses use polyprotein cleavage from a single nonsegmented strand.

clozeText: The process of {{c1::penetration}} involves the coronavirus particle being engulfed in a vesicle.
extraNote: This follows attachment and precedes the completion of uncoating.

clozeText: The assembly of progeny coronavirus virions occurs after the synthesis of {{c1::structural capsid proteins}}.
extraNote: Assembly is a 'late event' in the viral growth cycle.

clozeText: Coronaviruses use their genome RNA directly as {{c1::mRNA::functional RNA type}}.
extraNote: Being positive-sense RNA, the genome is functionally equivalent to mRNA.

clozeText: The synthesis of the negative-strand template in coronavirus replication is carried out in the {{c1::cytoplasm}}.
extraNote: All steps of the RNA replication cycle for coronaviruses are localized to the cytoplasm.

clozeText: Cleavage of the spike protein is required to reveal the {{c1::fusion protein}}, which allows the virus to enter the cell.
extraNote: Without this proteolytic step, the virus cannot successfully fuse with the host membrane.

clozeText: The {{c1::spike protein}} of coronaviruses must be cleaved by cell surface proteases to reveal a fusion protein for entry.
extraNote: This cleavage is a mandatory step to activate the viral fusion mechanism.

clozeText: Cleavage of the coronavirus spike protein by cell surface proteases reveals a {{c1::fusion protein}} that mediates entry into the host cell.
extraNote: The fusion protein allows the viral envelope to merge with the host cell membrane.

clozeText: Coronaviruses possess a single-strand RNA genome of {{c1::positive}} polarity.
extraNote: Positive polarity means the genome can act directly as messenger RNA (mRNA).

clozeText: The coronavirus genome is described as {{c1::nonsegmented}}, meaning it consists of a single continuous piece of RNA.
extraNote: This is in contrast to viruses like influenza, which have segmented genomes.

clozeText: Unlike many other RNA viruses, coronaviruses do not contain a {{c1::polymerase}} within the virion.
extraNote: They do not need to carry a polymerase because their positive-strand genome is translated immediately upon entry to produce one.

clozeText: The purified genome of coronaviruses is considered {{c1::infectious}} because it can initiate the entire growth cycle without viral proteins.
extraNote: Infectious nucleic acid can bypass host range specificity if it successfully enters a cell.

clozeText: Coronaviruses synthesize precursor {{c1::polyproteins::polypeptides}} that must be cleaved by a virus-encoded protease to form functional units.
extraNote: These large polypeptides are the initial products of genome translation.

clozeText: In coronaviruses like SARS-CoV-2, {{c1::two}} polyproteins are formed by the translation of approximately {{c2::two-thirds}} of the genome RNA.
extraNote: The remaining third of the genome typically encodes structural proteins.

clozeText: The proteolytic cleavage of coronavirus polyproteins occurs within the {{c1::cytoplasm}} of the host cell.
extraNote: This contrasts with some other viruses where cleavage might occur during budding.

clozeText: Coronaviruses utilize a {{c1::virus-encoded protease}} to cleave their precursor polyproteins into functional proteins.
extraNote: Virus-encoded proteases are high-yield targets for antiviral drug development.

clozeText: During replication, the parental {{c1::positive-strand}} coronavirus RNA is used as a template to synthesize a {{c2::negative-strand}} intermediate.
extraNote: This negative-strand intermediate then serves as the template for progeny genomes.

clozeText: The replication of the coronavirus genome is governed by the principle of {{c1::complementarity}}, requiring a template with a complementary base sequence.
extraNote: Base pairing (A-U, G-C) ensures the fidelity of the progeny genome sequence.

clozeText: The coronavirus genome is functionally equivalent to {{c1::mRNA}}, allowing it to be translated directly by host ribosomes.
extraNote: This direct translation is characteristic of positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses.

clozeText: Attachment, penetration, and uncoating of coronaviruses are collectively categorized as {{c1::early}} events of the growth cycle.
extraNote: These steps occur before the replication of the viral genome begins.

clozeText: Synthesis of viral mRNA, protein processing, and genome replication are categorized as the {{c1::middle}} events of the coronavirus growth cycle.
extraNote: These events follow uncoating and precede virion assembly.

clozeText: Paramyxoviruses have a {{c1::single-stranded::number of strands}} RNA genome.
extraNote: They are classified among the RNA viruses with linear, nonsegmented genomes.

clozeText: The RNA genome of Paramyxoviruses has {{c1::negative::polarity}} polarity.
extraNote: Negative-polarity RNA is complementary to mRNA and cannot be directly translated by host ribosomes.

clozeText: Paramyxoviruses possess a(n) {{c1::helical::symmetry}} nucleocapsid symmetry.
extraNote: The helical nucleocapsid is typical for enveloped, negative-strand RNA viruses.

clozeText: Unlike Orthomyxoviruses, the genome of Paramyxoviruses is {{c1::nonsegmented}}.
extraNote: Nonsegmented genomes consist of a single continuous piece of RNA.

clozeText: Paramyxoviruses are {{c1::enveloped::enveloped or naked}} viruses.
extraNote: The envelope is a lipid bilayer usually derived from the host cell membrane during budding.

clozeText: Paramyxoviruses carry a(n) {{c1::virion RNA polymerase}} within their particles to synthesize viral mRNA.
extraNote: Because their genome is negative-polarity, they must provide their own polymerase to transcribe mRNA upon entry.

clozeText: The purified genome of Paramyxoviruses is {{c1::not infectious}} when injected into cells.
extraNote: Negative-strand RNA genomes require the virion-associated polymerase to initiate the infection cycle.

clozeText: A prototype human virus for the Paramyxovirus family is {{c1::measles virus}}.
extraNote: Measles virus is a classic example of a nonsegmented, negative-strand RNA virus.

clozeText: Important human pathogens in the Paramyxovirus family include measles, {{c1::mumps}}, parainfluenza, and RSV.
extraNote: All four are major causes of respiratory or systemic illness in humans.

clozeText: Infection with Paramyxoviruses characteristically produces {{c1::multinucleated giant}} cells.
extraNote: This occurs via the fusion of infected cells with neighboring uninfected cells.

clozeText: Cell fusion in Paramyxovirus infections is caused by the insertion of {{c1::viral proteins}} into the host cell membrane.
extraNote: These proteins promote the fusion of adjacent cell membranes, leading to syncytia formation.

clozeText: Paramyxoviruses synthesize their mRNA through the process of {{c1::transcription}}.
extraNote: The negative-strand genome serves as a template for the virion RNA polymerase.

clozeText: The genome of Paramyxoviruses is {{c1::linear}} in structure.
extraNote: This distinguishes them from other negative-strand RNA viruses that may have circular genomes.

clozeText: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a member of the {{c1::Paramyxovirus::family}} family.
extraNote: RSV is a leading cause of lower respiratory tract infections in infants.

clozeText: Paramyxoviruses belong to the group of {{c1::enveloped helical}} RNA viruses.
extraNote: This classification is based on the presence of a lipid envelope and the symmetry of the protein capsid.

clozeText: The formation of giant cells (syncytia) is a hallmark of infection by Paramyxoviruses and {{c1::Herpesviruses}}.
extraNote: Both virus families induce cell-to-cell fusion as part of their cytopathic effect.

clozeText: In the replication of Paramyxoviruses, mRNA is transcribed from the genome into {{c1::positive}} polarity RNA.
extraNote: Positive polarity RNA has the same sequence as mRNA and can be translated by ribosomes.

clozeText: The {{c1::cytopathic effect (CPE)}} of Paramyxoviruses often culminates in giant cell formation or lysis.
extraNote: CPE is the visible change in cell appearance used by laboratories to detect viral infection.

clozeText: Paramyxoviruses utilize a {{c1::virion}} polymerase because human cells lack an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
extraNote: Host cells can only synthesize RNA from a DNA template.

clozeText: The virus family that includes parainfluenza and RSV is {{c1::Paramyxoviridae}}.
extraNote: These viruses are nonsegmented and possess single-stranded negative RNA.

clozeText: Negative-strand RNA viruses like Paramyxoviruses must first produce {{c1::mRNA::intermediate}} before protein synthesis can occur.
extraNote: The genome itself cannot serve as mRNA because it has the incorrect polarity.

clozeText: Paramyxoviruses are distinguished from orthomyxoviruses by the lack of {{c1::segmentation}} in their genome.
extraNote: Orthomyxoviruses (like influenza) have 8 segments, while Paramyxoviruses have only one.

clozeText: Death of cells infected by Paramyxoviruses is often due to the inhibition of {{c1::macromolecular::general term}} synthesis.
extraNote: This primarily includes the shutdown of host cell protein synthesis.

clozeText: Infected cells may contain {{c1::inclusion bodies}}, which are discrete areas of viral proteins or particles.
extraNote: These can be used for laboratory diagnosis, appearing in specific locations depending on the virus.

clozeText: Paramyxoviruses cause fusion of cells by changing the host cell {{c1::membrane}}.
extraNote: Insertion of viral proteins into the membrane facilitates this process.

clozeText: The {{c1::measles}} virus is a prototype for nonsegmented, negative-polarity RNA viruses.
extraNote: It follows the standard replication strategy of the Paramyxovirus family.

clozeText: The helical nucleocapsid of Paramyxoviruses is surrounded by a(n) {{c1::envelope::outer layer}}.
extraNote: The presence of this lipid layer makes the virus susceptible to detergents and heat.

clozeText: Paramyxoviruses are categorized as {{c1::negative-strand}} RNA viruses.
extraNote: This category requires a virion RNA-dependent RNA polymerase for replication.

clozeText: The fusion of cells in Paramyxovirus infection produces large cells with multiple {{c1::nuclei}}.
extraNote: These are known as multinucleated giant cells or syncytia.

clozeText: Paramyxoviruses use a(n) {{c1::RNA-dependent RNA polymerase}} to replicate their genome.
extraNote: This enzyme is contained within the virion to initiate transcription immediately upon infection.

clozeText: Paramyxoviruses are {{c1::enveloped}} viruses with a {{c2::helical}} nucleocapsid.
extraNote: These viruses are classified as enveloped helical viruses with a single-stranded linear RNA genome.

clozeText: The genome of Paramyxoviruses is composed of {{c1::single-stranded}}, {{c2::negative-polarity}} RNA.
extraNote: Negative-polarity RNA is complementary to the mRNA and cannot be directly translated by host ribosomes.

clozeText: Paramyxoviruses possess a genome that is {{c1::linear}} and {{c2::nonsegmented}}.
extraNote: The nonsegmented nature of the Paramyxovirus genome distinguishes it from the segmented genome of Orthomyxoviruses.

clozeText: Important human pathogens in the Paramyxovirus family include {{c1::measles}}, {{c1::mumps}}, {{c1::parainfluenza}}, and {{c1::respiratory syncytial}} viruses.
extraNote: These viruses are significant causes of respiratory and systemic illness in humans.

clozeText: Paramyxoviruses must contain a {{c1::virion RNA polymerase}} within the virion to synthesize viral mRNA.
extraNote: Since the genome is negative-polarity, it must be transcribed into positive-polarity mRNA by the virus's own polymerase.

clozeText: The fusion of cells in Paramyxovirus infections is caused by the insertion of {{c1::viral proteins}} into the cell membrane.
extraNote: These protein insertions lead to cell membrane changes that facilitate fusion with adjacent cells.

clozeText: The purified genome of Paramyxoviruses is {{c1::not infective}} on its own.
extraNote: The genome is non-infective because it is negative-polarity and requires the virion-associated polymerase to initiate the replication cycle.

clozeText: In Paramyxoviruses, the source of mRNA is {{c1::transcription}} of the negative-strand genome.
extraNote: mRNA synthesis involves transcription of the negative-polarity RNA into positive-polarity mRNA strands.

clozeText: Paramyxoviruses are distinguished from {{c1::Orthomyxoviruses}} because Paramyxoviruses have a nonsegmented genome.
extraNote: Orthomyxoviruses, such as influenza virus, have an eight-segment genome.

clozeText: The {{c1::capsid symmetry::structure}} of Paramyxoviruses is helical.
extraNote: This is a primary morphologic criterion used for the classification of medically important RNA viruses.

clozeText: Measles virus is a prototype human virus for the {{c1::Paramyxovirus::family}} family.
extraNote: Measles is a major pathogen within the group of nonsegmented, negative-strand RNA viruses.

clozeText: {{c1::Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)}} is a medically important Paramyxovirus that causes respiratory infections.
extraNote: RSV is one of the four key human pathogens identified in the Paramyxovirus family.

clozeText: The term negative-polarity (–) indicates that the viral RNA strand is {{c1::complementary}} to the mRNA.
extraNote: Positive-polarity (+) strands have the same polarity as mRNA.

clozeText: The {{c1::cytopathic effect (CPE)}} of Paramyxoviruses typically culminates in either lysis or giant cell formation.
extraNote: CPE refers to the change in appearance of an infected cell, often starting with rounding and darkening.

clozeText: The fusion of cells into multinucleated giant cells is a characteristic shared by Paramyxoviruses and {{c1::herpesviruses}}.
extraNote: Both virus families cause these distinctive cell membrane changes during infection.

clozeText: In the classification of viruses, Paramyxoviruses are categorized by their {{c1::nucleic acid}} structure and {{c2::capsid}} symmetry.
extraNote: Chemical and morphologic criteria are the foundations of viral classification.

clozeText: Paramyxoviruses are part of the group of eight RNA virus families that are {{c1::enveloped}} and have {{c2::helical}} capsids.
extraNote: These viruses are also characterized by having single-stranded linear RNA.

clozeText: The virion of Paramyxoviruses is described as having a {{c1::helical nucleocapsid}}.
extraNote: The nucleocapsid contains the linear, single-stranded, negative-polarity RNA.

clozeText: In Paramyxovirus replication, the virion RNA polymerase synthesizes {{c1::viral mRNA}}.
extraNote: This occurs during the synthesis phase of the replication cycle for negative-strand RNA viruses.

clozeText: {{c1::Mumps virus}} is one of the important human pathogens within the Paramyxovirus family.
extraNote: The family consists of measles, mumps, parainfluenza, and respiratory syncytial viruses.

clozeText: Unlike Paramyxoviruses, {{c1::Picornaviruses}} have a naked icosahedral capsid and positive-polarity RNA.
extraNote: Paramyxoviruses are enveloped with helical capsids and negative-polarity RNA.

clozeText: Infection with Paramyxoviruses is classified as involving a {{c1::negative-strand RNA}} genome.
extraNote: Viruses with this genome type require a virion polymerase for transcription into positive-strand mRNA.

clozeText: Formation of multinucleated giant cells is a hallmark of infection for viruses that insert {{c1::viral proteins}} into the host cell membrane.
extraNote: This process is specifically mentioned as a characteristic of Paramyxoviruses.

clozeText: Paramyxoviruses possess a {{c1::nonsegmented}} genome, which means all viral genes are on a single piece of RNA.
extraNote: This contrasts with segmented viruses like influenza or rotavirus.

clozeText: The diameter of the helical nucleocapsid in Paramyxoviruses is distinct from the {{c1::envelope}}, which is acquired from the host cell.
extraNote: Paramyxoviruses are defined as enveloped viruses in major classification schemes.

clozeText: {{c1::Parainfluenza}} virus is a member of the Paramyxovirus family.
extraNote: It is one of the four primary medically important viruses listed in this family.

clozeText: The mRNA produced during Paramyxovirus infection is of {{c1::positive}} polarity.
extraNote: The negative-polarity genome serves as the template for the synthesis of this positive-polarity mRNA.

clozeText: Paramyxoviruses use {{c1::virion RNA polymerase}} to transcribe their genome into mRNA.
extraNote: Host cell RNA polymerase is generally used by DNA viruses, not negative-strand RNA viruses like Paramyxoviruses.

clozeText: The appearance of {{c1::multinucleated giant cells}} in a patient specimen can aid in the diagnosis of Paramyxovirus infection.
extraNote: This is part of the cytopathic effect observed in clinical laboratories.

clozeText: The genome of Paramyxoviruses consists of {{c1::single-stranded, linear, nonsegmented, negative-polarity RNA}}.
extraNote: Unlike Orthomyxoviruses, the Paramyxovirus genome is nonsegmented.

clozeText: Paramyxoviruses are characterized by having a {{c1::helical}} nucleocapsid symmetry.
extraNote: This is a key morphologic criterion for classification among RNA viruses.

clozeText: Because they have a negative-polarity RNA genome, Paramyxoviruses must carry a {{c1::virion RNA polymerase}} to synthesize viral mRNA.
extraNote: The virion-associated polymerase is essential because host cells do not have enzymes to transcribe RNA from an RNA template.

clozeText: Major human pathogens in the Paramyxovirus family include {{c1::measles}}, mumps, parainfluenza, and respiratory syncytial viruses.
extraNote: Measles virus is the prototype for nonsegmented, negative-polarity RNA viruses.

clozeText: Major human pathogens in the Paramyxovirus family include measles, mumps, parainfluenza, and {{c1::respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)}}.
extraNote: RSV is a leading cause of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants.

clozeText: Paramyxovirus infection characteristically results in the formation of {{c1::multinucleated giant cells}}.
extraNote: This is a hallmark cytopathic effect (CPE) used for clinical diagnosis.

clozeText: The formation of giant cells in Paramyxovirus infections is caused by the {{c1::fusion}} of virus-infected cells.
extraNote: This fusion is triggered by changes in the host cell membrane.

clozeText: Cell membrane fusion during Paramyxovirus infection is likely caused by the insertion of {{c1::viral proteins}} into the host cell membrane.
extraNote: Insertion of these proteins alters the membrane, allowing adjacent cells to merge.

clozeText: The {{c1::purified genome RNA}} of Paramyxoviruses is not infectious.
extraNote: Negative-polarity RNA cannot be directly translated by host ribosomes; it must first be transcribed into positive-polarity mRNA by a virion polymerase.

clozeText: The term {{c1::myxo}} refers to the affinity of viruses like Paramyxoviruses for mucins.
extraNote: The prefix 'para-' was added to distinguish them from the Orthomyxoviruses.

clozeText: The mRNA produced by Paramyxoviruses has a {{c1::positive-polarity}} to allow for translation by host ribosomes.
extraNote: By definition, the (+) strand has the same polarity as mRNA.

clozeText: The source of mRNA for Paramyxoviruses is {{c1::transcription}} from the negative-strand genome.
extraNote: This transcription is mediated by the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase carried within the virion.

clozeText: The {{c1::cytopathic effect (CPE)}} of Paramyxoviruses frequently begins with a rounding and darkening of the cell and culminates in either lysis or giant cell formation.
extraNote: CPE is the basis for the plaque assay and laboratory detection in cell culture.

clozeText: In the laboratory, detection of Paramyxoviruses in a patient specimen is often based on the appearance of {{c1::CPE::abbreviation}} in cell culture.
extraNote: CPE stands for cytopathic effect, which describes morphologic changes in infected cells.

clozeText: Paramyxoviruses are classified as having a {{c1::linear}} RNA structure.
extraNote: This contrasts with some other negative-strand RNA viruses that have circular genomes.

clozeText: Viruses with a single-stranded, negative-polarity RNA genome, such as Paramyxoviruses, are always {{c1::enveloped}}.
extraNote: This is a consistent structural feature for this group of viruses.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses are characterized by a unique {{c1::bullet-shaped}} morphology.
extraNote: The term 'rhabdo' refers specifically to this bullet shape.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses possess a {{c1::helical}} nucleocapsid symmetry.
extraNote: This is a key structural feature shared with other negative-strand RNA viruses like paramyxoviruses.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses are {{c1::enveloped::enveloped or naked}} viruses.
extraNote: The envelope surrounds the helical nucleocapsid.

clozeText: The genome of Rhabdoviruses consists of {{c1::single-stranded::ss or ds}} RNA.
extraNote: It is a linear, nonsegmented molecule.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses have a {{c1::negative}}-polarity RNA genome.
extraNote: Negative polarity means the genomic RNA is complementary to the mRNA.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses must carry a(n) {{c1::virion polymerase}} to synthesize viral mRNA.
extraNote: Specifically, they contain an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase because the negative-strand genome is not infectious on its own.

clozeText: The RNA genome of Rhabdoviruses is {{c1::nonsegmented::segmented or nonsegmented}}.
extraNote: This differentiates them from segmented negative-strand viruses like orthomyxoviruses.

clozeText: The only important human pathogen in the Rhabdovirus family is {{c1::rabies virus}}.
extraNote: Rabies is the prototype human virus for this family.

clozeText: The Rhabdovirus genome is described as {{c1::not infective}} because it requires a virion polymerase for transcription.
extraNote: Unlike positive-strand RNA genomes, the negative-strand cannot be directly translated by host ribosomes.

clozeText: In the Rhabdovirus life cycle, viral mRNA is produced via {{c1::transcription}} from the negative-strand genome.
extraNote: This step requires the virion-encoded RNA polymerase.

clozeText: Worldwide, the most common animal reservoir for the rabies virus is {{c1::dogs}}.
extraNote: Domestic dogs remain the primary vector globally.

clozeText: In the United States, common animal reservoirs for rabies include {{c1::bats}}, skunks, and raccoons.
extraNote: These wild animals maintain the virus in the US population.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses like {{c1::vesicular stomatitis virus}} are classified as arboviruses because they are transmitted by arthropods.
extraNote: While the prototype (rabies) is not an arbovirus, other family members can be arthropod-borne.

clozeText: {{c1::Kern Canyon virus}} is an example of a Rhabdovirus that belongs to the group of arboviruses.
extraNote: Arbovirus is an acronym for arthropod-borne virus.

clozeText: The RNA genome of Rhabdoviruses is {{c1::linear::linear or circular}} in structure.
extraNote: This linear structure is common among the nonsegmented negative-strand RNA viruses.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses fall into the category of viruses that replicate within both {{c1::animal}} and human cells.
extraNote: This wide host range is characteristic of viruses with significant animal reservoirs.

clozeText: The virion polymerase in Rhabdoviruses is an {{c1::RNA-dependent RNA polymerase}}.
extraNote: This enzyme is essential for initiating the replication cycle by creating mRNA.

clozeText: The term 'Rhabdo' in Rhabdoviruses is derived from the Greek word for {{c1::rod or bullet}}.
extraNote: The morphology is a defining characteristic of the family.

clozeText: The Rhabdovirus envelope contains the {{c1::attachment}} proteins that interact with host cell receptors.
extraNote: Viral attachment is restricted to host cells that possess specific receptors.

clozeText: Many {{c1::mammals}} serve as a reservoir for rabies virus, the most significant Rhabdovirus.
extraNote: This includes both wild and domestic species.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses are categorized alongside {{c1::Paramyxoviruses}} and Filoviruses as enveloped helical viruses with negative-strand RNA.
extraNote: These families share similar morphologic and genomic features.

clozeText: The mRNA produced by Rhabdoviruses is a {{c1::positive}}-polarity strand.
extraNote: The positive-polarity mRNA is translated by host cell ribosomes into viral proteins.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses are distinguished from Picornaviruses by having an {{c1::envelope}} and negative-strand RNA.
extraNote: Picornaviruses are naked and have positive-strand RNA.

clozeText: The Rhabdovirus genome size is approximately {{c1::13::molecular weight}} x 10^6 daltons.
extraNote: This value reflects the molecular weight of the single-stranded linear RNA.

clozeText: The Rhabdovirus capsid has {{c1::helical}} symmetry.
extraNote: Helical capsids are typical for enveloped RNA viruses with negative polarity.

clozeText: For Rhabdoviruses, the {{c1::virion}} contains the polymerase required for initial transcription.
extraNote: Without this pre-packaged enzyme, the virus cannot initiate infection.

clozeText: Unlike Parvoviruses which use host DNA polymerase, Rhabdoviruses use a {{c1::viral-encoded}} polymerase for genome replication.
extraNote: All RNA viruses (except retroviruses) must encode their own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

clozeText: Rabies virus, a prototype Rhabdovirus, is primarily transmitted to humans through the {{c1::bite}} of an infected animal.
extraNote: The virus is typically present in the saliva of the reservoir host.

clozeText: The Rhabdovirus life cycle involves the synthesis of {{c1::mRNA}} as an obligatory first step after entry.
extraNote: Because the negative-strand genome cannot be translated, mRNA synthesis is required before viral proteins can be made.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses are listed as {{c1::medically important}} viruses due to the fatal nature of rabies infection.
extraNote: Despite the family having many members, rabies virus is the primary medical concern for humans.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses are structurally characterized as {{c1::bullet-shaped}} enveloped viruses.
extraNote: The term 'rhabdo' is derived from the Greek word for rod, reflecting this unique morphology.

clozeText: The Rhabdovirus genome consists of {{c1::single-stranded}} RNA.
extraNote: This genomic structure is a primary criterion for its classification among RNA viruses.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses possess a genome with {{c1::negative}} polarity.
extraNote: Negative-polarity RNA is complementary to mRNA and cannot be directly translated by host ribosomes.

clozeText: The nucleocapsid of Rhabdoviruses has {{c1::helical}} symmetry.
extraNote: This symmetry type is common among several families of enveloped RNA viruses.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses are {{c1::enveloped}} viruses, meaning they have a lipid bilayer surrounding the nucleocapsid.
extraNote: Enveloped viruses are generally more susceptible to environmental factors like detergents than naked viruses.

clozeText: The Rhabdovirus genome is {{c1::nonsegmented}}, consisting of a single piece of RNA.
extraNote: This distinguishes them from viruses like influenza or rotavirus which have segmented genomes.

clozeText: {{c1::Rabies virus}} is the only important human pathogen within the Rhabdovirus family.
extraNote: It causes a nearly 100% fatal encephalitis if not treated before symptoms appear.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses must contain a(n) {{c1::RNA polymerase}} within the virion to initiate replication.
extraNote: Since the negative-strand genome cannot act as mRNA, the virus must provide its own enzyme to transcribe mRNA upon entry.

clozeText: In Rhabdoviruses, the source of viral mRNA is {{c1::transcription}} of the genome.
extraNote: This process is catalyzed by the virion-associated RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

clozeText: The purified genome of a Rhabdovirus is {{c1::not infective}} when introduced into a host cell.
extraNote: Infectivity requires the presence of the virion-associated polymerase to generate mRNA.

clozeText: Many {{c1::mammals}} serve as natural reservoirs for the rabies virus.
extraNote: The virus can replicate within both the cells of the host animal and human cells.

clozeText: In the United States, common reservoirs for rabies virus include bats, {{c1::skunks}}, and raccoons.
extraNote: The relative importance of different reservoir species varies by geographic region within the US.

clozeText: Worldwide, the most common reservoir for rabies virus is {{c1::dogs}}.
extraNote: Canine rabies is responsible for the vast majority of human rabies deaths globally.

clozeText: Two Rhabdoviruses categorized as arboviruses are Kern Canyon virus and {{c1::vesicular stomatitis virus}}.
extraNote: These are exceptions to the general rule that Rhabdoviruses are transmitted by animal bites.

clozeText: {{c1::Kern Canyon virus}} is a Rhabdovirus that is classified as an arbovirus.
extraNote: Arboviruses are defined by their transmission via arthropod vectors.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses are classified based on the {{c1::nucleic acid}} structure and the capsid symmetry.
extraNote: These chemical and morphologic criteria are standard for viral taxonomy.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses utilize a(n) {{c1::virion RNA polymerase}} to synthesize viral mRNA from their negative-polarity genome.
extraNote: This enzyme is an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase packaged inside the bullet-shaped virion.

clozeText: The term 'Rhabdo' in Rhabdoviruses specifically refers to their {{c1::bullet}} shape.
extraNote: This morphology is diagnostic and can be visualized using electron microscopy.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses are grouped with other {{c1::enveloped helical}} viruses, such as Paramyxoviruses and Filoviruses.
extraNote: These families all share a similar structural arrangement of the nucleocapsid and envelope.

clozeText: The genomic RNA of Rhabdoviruses has the same polarity as {{c1::strand complementary to mRNA::mRNA or strand complementary to mRNA}}.
extraNote: This is the definition of negative-polarity RNA.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses can replicate in human cells because their surface proteins can interact with {{c1::receptors}} on the surface of human cells.
extraNote: The animal reservoir also maintains the virus by providing host cells with compatible receptors.

clozeText: One of the two major components used in the classification of Rhabdoviruses is the {{c1::capsid}}, specifically its size and symmetry.
extraNote: The symmetry of the Rhabdovirus capsid is helical.

clozeText: Medically important Rhabdoviruses are distinguished from Picornaviruses by having a {{c1::negative-polarity}} genome and an envelope.
extraNote: Picornaviruses are naked viruses with positive-polarity RNA.

clozeText: The genome of Rhabdoviruses is nonsegmented, unlike the {{c1::segmented}} genome of Orthomyxoviruses.
extraNote: Nonsegmented viruses do not undergo the same high rates of reassortment as segmented viruses like influenza.

clozeText: Viral mRNA synthesis in Rhabdoviruses is essential for the production of {{c1::viral proteins}}.
extraNote: The mRNA must be transcribed first because the negative-strand genome cannot be translated directly.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses belong to the class of viruses that have an animal {{c1::reservoir}}.
extraNote: This animal host allows the virus to persist in the environment and occasionally cross into human populations.

clozeText: The Rhabdovirus virion size is significant for classification, specifically the {{c1::capsid}} size and its symmetry.
extraNote: In helical viruses like Rhabdoviruses, the capsid interacts closely with the RNA genome.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses possess a(n) {{c1::enveloped}} virion with a {{c2::helical}} nucleocapsid.
extraNote: They are categorized among the enveloped helical viruses with single-stranded linear RNA.

clozeText: The genome of Rhabdoviruses consists of {{c1::negative-polarity::polarity}} single-stranded RNA.
extraNote: Negative-polarity means the RNA strand is complementary to the viral mRNA.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses have a genome that is both {{c1::linear}} and {{c2::nonsegmented}}.
extraNote: This distinguishes them from other negative-strand RNA viruses like Orthomyxoviruses, which have segmented genomes.

clozeText: Because their genome is negative-polarity, Rhabdoviruses must carry a(n) {{c1::virion RNA polymerase}} to synthesize mRNA.
extraNote: The host cell lacks the enzymes necessary to transcribe mRNA from a negative-strand RNA template.

clozeText: In Rhabdoviruses, the source of viral mRNA is {{c1::transcription}} from the negative-strand genome.
extraNote: The virion polymerase performs this transcription step.

clozeText: The purified genome of Rhabdoviruses is considered {{c1::non-infective::infective/non-infective}}.
extraNote: Purified negative-strand RNA cannot be translated directly and requires the virion-associated polymerase to initiate the life cycle.

clozeText: The only medically important human pathogen within the Rhabdovirus family is {{c1::rabies virus}}.
extraNote: Rabies is the primary cause of human rhabdovirus infection.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses such as rabies virus are maintained in {{c1::animal}} reservoirs.
extraNote: These viruses can replicate in both the cells of host animals and human cells.

clozeText: In the United States, common animal reservoirs for rabies virus include {{c1::bats, skunks, and raccoons}}.
extraNote: These animals are the primary source of domestic rabies transmission in the US.

clozeText: Worldwide, the most common animal reservoir for rabies virus is {{c1::dogs}}.
extraNote: Domestic dogs are the leading cause of rabies transmission to humans globally.

clozeText: The host range of Rhabdoviruses is determined by the interaction between viral attachment proteins and {{c1::receptors}} on the surface of host cells.
extraNote: Specificity for these receptors usually limits most human viruses, but rabies can interact with various mammalian receptors.

clozeText: {{c1::Vesicular stomatitis virus}} is an example of a rhabdovirus that is classified as an arbovirus.
extraNote: Arboviruses are typically arthropod-borne, and this rhabdovirus can be transmitted by arthropod vectors.

clozeText: {{c1::Kern Canyon virus}} is a member of the Rhabdovirus family that is listed as an arbovirus.
extraNote: It is one of the few rhabdoviruses besides rabies and vesicular stomatitis virus mentioned.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses, like all negative-strand RNA viruses, have a genome with polarity {{c1::complementary}} to their mRNA.
extraNote: Positive polarity denotes a strand with the same polarity as mRNA.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses are categorized as {{c1::enveloped}} viruses, similar to Paramyxoviruses and Orthomyxoviruses.
extraNote: This envelope is acquired during the budding process.

clozeText: The symmetry of the Rhabdovirus capsid is {{c1::helical}}.
extraNote: Capsid symmetry (icosahedral vs. helical) is a major criterion for viral classification.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses are classified under medically important {{c1::RNA}} viruses.
extraNote: Their classification is based on nucleic acid type, capsid symmetry, and envelope presence.

clozeText: Unlike Picornaviruses, the Rhabdovirus genome {{c1::cannot}} function directly as mRNA.
extraNote: Picornaviruses are positive-sense and their genome is immediately infectious and translatable.

clozeText: Orthomyxoviruses have a {{c1::segmented}} single-stranded RNA genome.
extraNote: This segmentation is a key distinction from paramyxoviruses which have nonsegmented genomes.

clozeText: The RNA genome of Orthomyxoviruses is of {{c1::negative}} polarity.
extraNote: Negative-polarity RNA cannot be directly translated and requires a virion polymerase.

clozeText: Orthomyxoviruses possess a(n) {{c1::helical}} nucleocapsid symmetry.
extraNote: Most enveloped RNA viruses with negative polarity exhibit helical symmetry.

clozeText: Orthomyxoviruses are {{c1::enveloped}} viruses.
extraNote: The presence of an envelope makes them more susceptible to detergents and environmental heat.

clozeText: Orthomyxoviruses contain a(n) {{c1::RNA polymerase}} within the virion.
extraNote: This enzyme is necessary to transcribe the negative-strand RNA into mRNA.

clozeText: The Orthomyxovirus genome typically consists of {{c1::eight::number}} linear RNA segments.
extraNote: Influenza virus is the primary example of this segmented arrangement.

clozeText: Because their genome is negative-polarity, Orthomyxoviruses use a virion RNA polymerase to synthesize viral {{c1::mRNA}}.
extraNote: The viral mRNA has the same polarity as the host cell's messenger RNA.

clozeText: The term "myxo" in Orthomyxovirus refers to the affinity of these viruses for {{c1::mucins}}.
extraNote: Mucins are glycoproteins found on the surface of host cells.

clozeText: The main human pathogen within the Orthomyxovirus family is {{c1::influenza virus}}.
extraNote: It is the only member of the Orthomyxovirus family.

clozeText: The genome of Orthomyxoviruses is {{c1::not}} infectious when purified.
extraNote: Purified negative-strand RNA cannot be translated by host machinery without the virion-associated polymerase.

clozeText: {{c1::Influenza A}} virus is the only type that causes worldwide pandemics.
extraNote: Pandemics occur when new hemagglutinin variants are introduced.

clozeText: {{c1::Influenza B}} virus causes major outbreaks of influenza but does not cause pandemics.
extraNote: Outbreaks occur frequently but are less geographically widespread than pandemics.

clozeText: {{c1::Influenza C}} virus causes mild respiratory tract infections but does not cause outbreaks.
extraNote: It is generally less clinically significant than types A and B.

clozeText: Laboratory diagnosis of serious influenza virus infections is made using {{c1::PCR::method}}-based assays.
extraNote: These assays are typically performed on respiratory tract secretions.

clozeText: Influenza virus affects the mucosal cells of the {{c1::upper and lower}} respiratory tracts.
extraNote: Symptoms manifest in the pharynx, larynx, trachea, and bronchi.

clozeText: A(n) {{c1::H5N1}} strain of influenza A virus is responsible for outbreaks of avian influenza (bird flu).
extraNote: These outbreaks involve direct or indirect transmission from birds to humans.

clozeText: The 2009 pandemic was caused by a(n) {{c1::H1N1}} strain of swine-origin influenza virus.
extraNote: This was a novel variant that spread rapidly worldwide.

clozeText: The 1918 influenza pandemic was caused by an H1N1 strain containing genes of {{c1::avian}} origin.
extraNote: This pandemic killed more Americans than several major wars combined.

clozeText: Pandemics occur when a variant of influenza A contains a new {{c1::hemagglutinin}} to which the population has no antibodies.
extraNote: This surface protein is critical for viral entry and host immune recognition.

clozeText: In some cases, influenza virus infection can progress to {{c1::pneumonia}}.
extraNote: This is a serious complication involving the lower respiratory tract.

clozeText: A bird-related strain of influenza virus that caused an outbreak in 2013 is {{c1::H7N9}}.
extraNote: This demonstrates the ongoing threat of zoonotic influenza transmission.

clozeText: Most human influenza cases are currently caused by the {{c1::H1N1}} and {{c2::H3N2}} strains.
extraNote: These represent the common circulating seasonal influenza A subtypes.

clozeText: The prefix "ortho" is added to the family name to distinguish these viruses from the {{c1::paramyxoviruses}}.
extraNote: Both families are enveloped RNA viruses but differ in genome segmentation.

clozeText: Orthomyxoviruses use the process of {{c1::transcription}} as the source of their mRNA.
extraNote: The virion RNA polymerase transcribes the negative-sense genome into positive-sense mRNA.

clozeText: Influenza symptoms occur in the pharynx, larynx, trachea, and {{c1::bronchi}}.
extraNote: These areas constitute the primary sites of infection in the respiratory tree.

clozeText: PCR panels used for diagnosis include influenza, {{c1::parainfluenza}}, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).
extraNote: Multiplex PCR allows for the simultaneous detection of multiple respiratory pathogens.

clozeText: Viral classification for Orthomyxoviruses is based on {{c1::chemical}} and morphologic criteria.
extraNote: The structure and molecular weight of the nucleic acid are primary factors.

clozeText: In the United States, influenza is the most common cause of respiratory infections resulting in {{c1::hospitalizations}}.
extraNote: This highlights the significant public health burden of the virus annually.

clozeText: Unlike Paramyxoviruses, which have a single piece of RNA, Orthomyxoviruses have a(n) {{c1::segmented}} genome.
extraNote: This segmentation allows for genetic reassortment.

clozeText: PCR-based assays for influenza use {{c1::respiratory}} tract secretions for diagnosis.
extraNote: Common samples include nasopharyngeal swabs or throat washings.

clozeText: Orthomyxoviruses possess a {{c1::segmented}} RNA genome, typically consisting of {{c2::eight}} pieces.
extraNote: The segmented nature of the genome allows for reassortment, leading to antigenic shifts.

clozeText: The RNA genome of Orthomyxoviruses is characterized as {{c1::single-stranded}} and {{c2::negative-polarity}}.
extraNote: Negative-polarity RNA cannot be directly translated and must first be transcribed into mRNA.

clozeText: Orthomyxoviruses are {{c1::enveloped}} viruses with a(n) {{c2::helical}} nucleocapsid.
extraNote: The presence of an envelope makes these viruses susceptible to detergents and environmental heat.

clozeText: Because their genome is negative-polarity RNA, Orthomyxoviruses must carry a(n) {{c1::RNA polymerase}} within the virion to synthesize mRNA.
extraNote: This virion polymerase is essential for initiating the replication cycle upon entering a host cell.

clozeText: The term "myxo" in Orthomyxovirus refers to the affinity these viruses have for {{c1::mucins::target substance}} (glycoproteins) on the surface of cells.
extraNote: This interaction is critical for the initial binding and infection of host cells.

clozeText: Unlike paramyxoviruses, which have a single piece of RNA, Orthomyxoviruses are distinguished by their {{c1::segmented}} genome.
extraNote: Segmentation is the primary genetic difference used to distinguish orthomyxoviruses from paramyxoviruses.

clozeText: {{c1::Influenza A}} virus is the specific member of the Orthomyxovirus family known for causing worldwide pandemics.
extraNote: Influenza A can infect multiple species, facilitating the emergence of new pandemic strains.

clozeText: {{c1::Influenza B}} virus causes major outbreaks of influenza but is not associated with worldwide pandemics.
extraNote: Outbreaks from this virus type occur less frequently than those caused by Influenza A.

clozeText: {{c1::Influenza C}} virus causes mild respiratory tract infections and does not cause major outbreaks.
extraNote: This type is generally less severe and less clinically significant than types A and B.

clozeText: Pandemics occur when a variant of influenza A virus containing a new {{c1::hemagglutinin}} is introduced into a population lacking antibodies.
extraNote: The introduction of a novel hemagglutinin subtype is the key driver of pandemic influenza.

clozeText: In humans, most cases of influenza are caused by the {{c1::H1N1}} and {{c2::H3N2}} strains of influenza A.
extraNote: These two subtypes are the primary circulating seasonal strains in the human population.

clozeText: The 1997 human outbreak of avian influenza (bird flu) was caused by the {{c1::H5N1}} strain of influenza A.
extraNote: Avian strains typically require specific genetic changes to transmit efficiently between humans.

clozeText: The 2009 influenza pandemic was caused by a(n) {{c1::swine-origin::source species}} H1N1 strain.
extraNote: This strain (S-OIV) represented a significant shift from previous seasonal H1N1 viruses.

clozeText: Influenza virus causes clinical symptoms in the upper respiratory tract as well as the {{c1::pharynx}}, {{c2::larynx}}, trachea, and bronchi.
extraNote: The virus infects mucosal cells throughout the respiratory system.

clozeText: Laboratory diagnosis of Orthomyxovirus infections is frequently performed using {{c1::PCR}}-based assays on respiratory tract secretions.
extraNote: PCR panels are used to distinguish influenza from other respiratory viruses like RSV or adenovirus.

clozeText: Molecular evidence suggests that the devastating 1918 influenza pandemic was caused by an H1N1 strain with genes of {{c1::avian}} origin.
extraNote: This pandemic was exceptionally lethal, killing more Americans than several major wars combined.

clozeText: Orthomyxoviruses use a(n) {{c1::virion RNA polymerase}} to synthesize viral mRNA from their negative-strand RNA template.
extraNote: This replication step occurs because the negative-strand genome cannot be read directly by host ribosomes.

clozeText: An outbreak of bird-related influenza that occurred in 2013 was caused by the {{c1::H7N9}} strain.
extraNote: Like H5N1, H7N9 is an example of an avian influenza virus that has crossed the species barrier to infect humans.

clozeText: In severe cases, Orthomyxovirus infections can progress to cause {{c1::pneumonia}}.
extraNote: Influenza affects both the upper and lower respiratory tracts, with pneumonia being a serious lower tract complication.

clozeText: The genome of Orthomyxoviruses is considered {{c1::non-infective}} because it requires a virion-associated polymerase to initiate transcription.
extraNote: In contrast, the genomes of positive-polarity RNA viruses (like picornaviruses) are often directly infective.

clozeText: Orthomyxoviruses are part of a group of enveloped respiratory viruses that also includes {{c1::paramyxoviruses}} and {{c2::coronaviruses}}.
extraNote: These three families represent the major enveloped RNA viruses infecting the respiratory tract.

clozeText: The term {{c1::ortho}} was added to the family name to distinguish these viruses from paramyxoviruses.
extraNote: Both families are "myxoviruses" but differ significantly in genome segmentation.

clozeText: Influenza virus is noted as the {{c1::only}} medically important member of the Orthomyxovirus family.
extraNote: While other viruses may exist in the family, influenza remains the primary human pathogen.

clozeText: The source of mRNA for Orthomyxoviruses is {{c1::transcription}} of the viral genome using a virion polymerase.
extraNote: Because the genome is negative-sense, it must be transcribed into a positive-sense mRNA strand.

clozeText: Orthomyxoviruses interact specifically with cell surface {{c1::glycoproteins}}.
extraNote: This interaction with mucins (glycoproteins) is the basis for the name "myxovirus."

clozeText: The capsid symmetry of Orthomyxoviruses is {{c1::helical}}.
extraNote: This symmetry is characteristic of all the enveloped RNA viruses with negative polarity mentioned in the text.

clozeText: Influenza viruses are classified into Types A, B, and C; of these, Type {{c1::A}} is the most common cause of hospitalizations in the United States.
extraNote: Influenza A outbreaks occur virtually every year and result in significant morbidity.

clozeText: A diagnostic panel for respiratory viruses often tests for influenza alongside {{c1::parainfluenza}} virus and {{c2::respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)}}.
extraNote: PCR assays allow for the simultaneous detection of multiple pathogens causing similar respiratory symptoms.

clozeText: The segmented nature of the Orthomyxovirus genome typically includes {{c1::8::number}} segments of linear RNA.
extraNote: This specific number of segments is a defining characteristic of the influenza genome structure.

clozeText: Before the 2009 pandemic, the last worldwide pandemic caused by an influenza A variant occurred in {{c1::1968}}.
extraNote: Pandemics are infrequent events compared to the annual major outbreaks caused by circulating strains.

clozeText: Orthomyxoviruses are {{c1::enveloped}} viruses with a {{c2::helical}} nucleocapsid symmetry.
extraNote: These viruses are categorized as enveloped helical RNA viruses with linear, single-stranded genomes.

clozeText: The genome of an Orthomyxovirus consists of {{c1::eight}} segments of linear, single-stranded, {{c2::negative}}-polarity RNA.
extraNote: The segmented nature of the genome distinguishes Orthomyxoviruses from Paramyxoviruses and allows for genetic reassortment.

clozeText: Orthomyxoviruses must carry a {{c1::virion RNA polymerase}} within their capsid to synthesize viral mRNA.
extraNote: Because the genome is negative-polarity, it cannot be directly translated by host ribosomes and requires a virion-encoded enzyme for transcription.

clozeText: The name Orthomyxovirus is derived from the term "myxo," which refers to the virus's affinity for {{c1::mucins::glycoproteins}}.
extraNote: Mucins are glycoproteins found on the surface of host cells.

clozeText: Influenza virus causes symptoms in the upper and lower respiratory tract, specifically affecting the {{c1::pharynx, larynx, trachea, and bronchi}}.
extraNote: The virus infects mucosal cells throughout these specific anatomical sites.

clozeText: Worldwide epidemics, known as {{c1::pandemics}}, are exclusively caused by {{c2::Influenza A}} virus.
extraNote: Influenza B causes major outbreaks, while Influenza C causes only mild respiratory infections without outbreaks.

clozeText: Pandemics occur when an Influenza A variant introduces a new {{c1::hemagglutinin}} to which the human population has no preexisting antibodies.
extraNote: The introduction of novel surface proteins is the primary driver of devastating global outbreaks.

clozeText: Most human cases of influenza are caused by the {{c1::H1N1 and H3N2}} strains of Influenza A.
extraNote: These represent the most common circulating subtypes in the human population.

clozeText: The {{c1::H5N1}} strain of Influenza A is the primary cause of avian influenza, also known as {{c2::bird flu}}.
extraNote: Outbreaks of H5N1 started in 1997 and involve transmission from birds to humans.

clozeText: The 2009 influenza pandemic was caused by an H1N1 strain of {{c1::swine}} origin.
extraNote: This is often referred to as swine-origin influenza virus (S-OIV).

clozeText: Molecular evidence indicates the 1918 influenza pandemic was caused by an {{c1::H1N1}} strain containing genes of {{c2::avian}} origin.
extraNote: This pandemic was historically significant, killing more Americans than several major wars combined.

clozeText: A serious complication of influenza virus infection involving the lower respiratory tract is {{c1::pneumonia}}.
extraNote: Influenza can progress from standard respiratory symptoms to severe lung involvement.

clozeText: Laboratory diagnosis of serious influenza is typically achieved via {{c1::PCR (polymerase chain reaction)}} based assays.
extraNote: PCR assays are performed on respiratory tract secretions to detect viral genetic material.

clozeText: Influenza virus is the only member of the {{c1::Orthomyxovirus}} family.
extraNote: Unlike other respiratory virus families like Paramyxoviridae, it is characterized by a segmented genome.

clozeText: In the United States, {{c1::influenza}} is the most common cause of respiratory tract infections that result in hospitalizations.
extraNote: It causes significant annual morbidity and mortality beyond pandemic years.

clozeText: Filoviruses are {{c1::enveloped}} viruses characterized by a {{c2::helical}} nucleocapsid.
extraNote: The presence of an envelope and helical symmetry are common features of many negative-strand RNA viruses.

clozeText: The genome of Filoviruses consists of {{c1::single-stranded::number of strands}} RNA with {{c2::negative::polarity}} polarity.
extraNote: Negative-polarity RNA viruses must carry their own RNA polymerase because host cells cannot translate negative-strand RNA directly.

clozeText: Filoviruses possess a {{c1::linear::shape}}, {{c2::nonsegmented::segments}} RNA genome.
extraNote: Linear, nonsegmented genomes are a key structural feature used in the classification of RNA virus families like Filoviridae.

clozeText: Morphologically, Filoviruses are highly {{c1::pleomorphic}} and typically appear as long {{c2::filaments}}.
extraNote: Filamentous morphology is a hallmark identifying feature of viruses like Ebola.

clozeText: Filoviruses have a consistent diameter of {{c1::80}} nm, though they can be thousands of nanometers long.
extraNote: The extreme length variability is a defining characteristic of the Filoviridae family.

clozeText: Filoviruses contain a {{c1::virion RNA polymerase}} within the particle to facilitate replication.
extraNote: This enzyme is necessary to synthesize mRNA from the negative-sense RNA genome upon entry into the host cell.

clozeText: {{c1::Ebola virus}} is the primary medically important member of the Filovirus family.
extraNote: Ebola virus is a major cause of severe hemorrhagic fever.

clozeText: There are {{c1::five}} recognized strains of Ebola virus (a filovirus), which are described as being {{c2::cross-reactive}}.
extraNote: Cross-reactivity indicates that antibodies to one strain may recognize antigens from another strain.

clozeText: The nucleocapsid of Filoviruses exhibits {{c1::helical}} symmetry.
extraNote: Helical symmetry involves the viral genome being wound in a spiral with the protein subunits.

clozeText: Filoviruses are categorized as {{c1::RNA}} viruses according to the classification scheme based on chemical and morphologic criteria.
extraNote: The two major components used for classification are the nucleic acid and the capsid symmetry.

clozeText: Unlike some other RNA viruses, the Filovirus genome is {{c1::nonsegmented}}.
extraNote: This distinguishes them from families like Orthomyxoviruses or Reoviruses which have segmented genomes.

clozeText: Filoviruses are described as being thousands of nanometers long while maintaining a diameter of {{c1::80}} nm.
extraNote: The high aspect ratio of these filaments is a key diagnostic feature in electron microscopy.

clozeText: The Filovirus virion is surrounded by a lipoprotein {{c1::envelope}}.

clozeText: The genome of the Ebola virus is characterized as {{c1::single-stranded}} RNA.

clozeText: Filoviruses are classified as {{c1::negative}}-polarity RNA viruses, meaning their genome cannot be directly translated by host ribosomes.
extraNote: The virus must first transcribe the negative-sense genome into a positive-sense mRNA.

clozeText: The structural classification of Filoviruses is determined by the symmetry of the {{c1::capsid}} and the nature of the {{c2::nucleic acid}}.

clozeText: The Ebola virus, a filovirus, possesses a {{c1::helical}} nucleocapsid enclosed within its envelope.
extraNote: The nucleocapsid structure protects the single-stranded RNA genome.

clozeText: The virion of the Filovirus family includes a(n) {{c1::RNA polymerase}}, which is an obligatory requirement for negative-strand RNA viruses.

clozeText: Filoviruses are {{c1::enveloped}} viruses with a helical nucleocapsid.
extraNote: Filoviruses are categorized among the eight families of enveloped helical RNA viruses.

clozeText: The nucleocapsid of a Filovirus has {{c1::helical}} symmetry.
extraNote: Filoviruses possess a helical nucleocapsid and are highly pleomorphic.

clozeText: Filoviruses possess a genome consisting of {{c1::single-stranded::ss or ds}} RNA.

clozeText: The genome of Filoviruses is {{c1::linear::linear or circular}} in structure.

clozeText: The RNA genome of Filoviruses is {{c1::nonsegmented::segmented or nonsegmented}}.

clozeText: Filoviruses appear as highly {{c1::pleomorphic}}, long filaments.

clozeText: There are {{c1::five}} strains of Ebola virus mentioned in classification.

clozeText: Filoviruses are described morphologically as long {{c1::filaments}}.
