clozeText: Filoviruses fall under the category of viruses that acquire a(n) {{c1::envelope}} as they bud.
extraNote: They are classified strictly as enveloped RNA viruses.

clozeText: The genome of Ebola virus (a Filovirus) consists of {{c1::negative}}-polarity RNA.
extraNote: Negative-polarity RNA genomes serve as a template for mRNA synthesis via virion RNA polymerase.

clozeText: The Filovirus genome is {{c1::single}}-stranded, distinguishing it from Reoviruses.
extraNote: Reoviruses have double-stranded segments, while Filoviruses have a single linear strand.

clozeText: Filoviruses are classified as having {{c1::helical::icosahedral or helical}} capsid symmetry.
extraNote: This is a key morphologic criterion used in the classification of RNA viruses.

clozeText: The diameter of Filoviruses is {{c1::80}} nm.
extraNote: Their unique structure combines a small diameter with extraordinary length.

clozeText: Filoviruses require a(n) {{c1::RNA-dependent RNA polymerase::specific enzyme}} for the initial steps of replication.
extraNote: This enzyme is also referred to as a virion RNA polymerase in the source text.

clozeText: Filoviruses are highly {{c1::pleomorphic}} viruses, meaning they can take on many shapes.
extraNote: Their filamentous structure allows for significant pleomorphism.

clozeText: In the classification of RNA viruses, Filoviruses are grouped with {{c1::Rhabdoviruses}} as they both have negative polarity and envelopes.
extraNote: Both families (Filoviruses and Rhabdoviruses) contain an RNA polymerase in the virion.

clozeText: Filoviruses possess a {{c1::nonsegmented}} genome, unlike the segmented Orthomyxoviruses.
extraNote: The genome is one continuous single strand of negative-polarity RNA.

clozeText: The five strains of Ebola virus show significant {{c1::cross-reactivity}}.
extraNote: Serological testing may be affected by the cross-reactivity between these strains.

clozeText: The structure of Filoviruses is defined by a {{c1::helical}} nucleocapsid inside an envelope.
extraNote: This structural combination is found in many medically important negative-strand RNA viruses.

clozeText: A Filovirus virion contains a(n) {{c1::RNA polymerase::enzyme}} within its structure.
extraNote: This enzyme is part of the infectious virion and is essential for the viral life cycle.

clozeText: Filoviruses have a {{c1::linear}} genome, differing from the circular genomes of Arenaviruses.
extraNote: The RNA structure is linear and nonsegmented.

clozeText: Filoviruses are categorized as {{c1::RNA}} viruses, not DNA viruses.
extraNote: They are specifically enveloped helical negative-strand RNA viruses.

clozeText: Ebola virus is classified within the family of {{c1::Filoviruses}}.
extraNote: Ebola is the most medically significant representative of this family in the provided text.

clozeText: Filoviruses are distinct for their potential length, which can be {{c1::thousands}} of nanometers long.
extraNote: This filamentous property is unique among most other virus families.

clozeText: Filoviruses are categorized as {{c1::enveloped}} viruses with a {{c2::helical}} nucleocapsid.
extraNote: Filoviruses share these structural features with other RNA virus families like Rhabdoviruses and Paramyxoviruses.

clozeText: The genome of Filoviruses consists of {{c1::single-stranded::ss or ds?}} RNA.
extraNote: Like many medically important RNA viruses, filoviruses utilize a single-stranded genome structure.

clozeText: Filoviruses possess a genome with {{c1::negative::positive or negative?}} polarity.
extraNote: Because the RNA is negative-polarity, the virion must carry its own RNA polymerase to initiate transcription.

clozeText: The RNA genome of a Filovirus is described as {{c1::linear}} and {{c2::nonsegmented::segmented or nonsegmented?}}.
extraNote: This differentiates them from segmented RNA viruses like Orthomyxoviruses or Reoviruses.

clozeText: Morphologically, Filoviruses are highly {{c1::pleomorphic::diverse in shape}} and appear as long filaments.
extraNote: The name 'filovirus' is derived from their characteristic filamentous appearance.

clozeText: Filoviruses have a diameter of approximately {{c1::80}} nm.
extraNote: While the diameter is consistent, the length of the filaments can vary significantly.

clozeText: Filoviruses can be as long as {{c1::thousands}} of nanometers.
extraNote: This extreme length relative to their 80 nm diameter gives them their filament-like appearance.

clozeText: Because their genome is negative-polarity RNA, filoviruses must contain a(n) {{c1::RNA polymerase}} within the virion.
extraNote: This enzyme is necessary to synthesize mRNA upon entry into the host cell.

clozeText: Ebola virus is a prominent member of the {{c1::Filovirus}} family.
extraNote: Ebola and Marburg are the primary medically significant filoviruses.

clozeText: There are {{c1::five}} identified strains of Ebola virus.
extraNote: These strains are distinguished by their genetic and antigenic properties.

clozeText: The capsid symmetry of the Filovirus family is {{c1::helical}}.
extraNote: This helical nucleocapsid is contained within a lipoprotein envelope.

clozeText: Filoviruses are classified as {{c1::RNA::DNA or RNA?}} viruses.
extraNote: They are specifically enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses.

clozeText: The {{c1::lipoprotein}} envelope of Filoviruses is a defining characteristic of their structure.
extraNote: Enveloped viruses are generally more susceptible to environmental factors like detergents.

clozeText: In the classification scheme of RNA viruses, Filoviruses are grouped with {{c1::Rhabdoviruses}} and Paramyxoviruses based on their helical nucleocapsid.
extraNote: This group consists of enveloped viruses with single-stranded linear RNA genomes.

clozeText: The term 'Filovirus' refers to the virus's appearance as {{c1::long filaments}}.
extraNote: This characteristic shape is distinct among human viral pathogens.

clozeText: The filovirus genome is {{c1::linear::linear or circular?}}.
extraNote: This is a standard feature for the Mononegavirales order, which includes filoviruses.

clozeText: Filoviruses are approximately {{c1::80::size?}} nm in diameter.
extraNote: Their long filamentous structure can make them appear much larger under electron microscopy.

clozeText: A virion {{c1::RNA-dependent RNA polymerase}} is an obligatory component of Filoviruses for successful replication.
extraNote: Negative-sense viruses cannot be directly translated by host ribosomes.

clozeText: Filoviruses possess a {{c1::single-stranded::ss or ds?}} RNA genome of {{c2::negative}} polarity.
extraNote: This genome structure requires the virion to package its own replication machinery.

clozeText: Regarding Ebola virus strains, the {{c1::five}} variants show significant antigenic {{c2::cross-reactivity}}.
extraNote: This is a key property used in laboratory identification and serological studies.

clozeText: The structure of Filoviruses is noted for being {{c1::highly pleomorphic}}.
extraNote: Individual virions may appear as branched, circular, or 'U-shaped' filaments.

clozeText: Filoviruses are categorized as {{c1::enveloped}} viruses.
extraNote: Loss of the envelope typically leads to loss of viral infectivity.

clozeText: The nucleocapsid of the Ebola virus (a filovirus) has {{c1::helical}} symmetry.
extraNote: The nucleocapsid contains the negative-strand RNA genome and viral polymerase.

clozeText: Filoviruses have a {{c1::nonsegmented}} genome.
extraNote: All genetic information is contained on a single molecule of RNA.

clozeText: Enteroviruses are members of the {{c1::Picornavirus}} family, which are the smallest RNA viruses at 28 nm in diameter.
extraNote: The name picorna is derived from 'pico' (small) and RNA.

clozeText: The genome of enteroviruses consists of {{c1::single-stranded}}, {{c2::linear}}, nonsegmented, {{c3::positive-polarity}} RNA.
extraNote: This genomic structure is typical for all members of the Picornaviridae family.

clozeText: Enteroviruses are characterized by a(n) {{c1::naked icosahedral}} capsid structure.
extraNote: Naked viruses lack a lipid envelope, making them more resistant to environmental conditions.

clozeText: Human pathogens within the enterovirus group include {{c1::poliovirus}}, {{c2::Coxsackie virus}}, {{c3::echovirus}}, and {{c4::hepatitis A virus}}.
extraNote: These are the four primary examples of enteroviruses mentioned as human pathogens.

clozeText: Certain enteroviruses can be detected in culture by a decrease in acid production, causing the {{c1::phenol red}} indicator to remain {{c2::red::color}}.
extraNote: Normal metabolizing cells produce acid that turns the indicator yellow; infected, dying cells do not, leaving the medium alkaline (red).

clozeText: The {{c1::interference}} technique can detect viruses like rubella by showing they prevent the formation of a {{c2::cytopathic effect (CPE)}} by enteroviruses like echovirus or Coxsackie virus.
extraNote: This is used for viruses that do not produce their own visible CPE in culture.

clozeText: A definitive identification of an enterovirus grown in cell culture is frequently made using {{c1::neutralization}} tests with known antibodies.
extraNote: Neutralization blocks viral infectivity and prevents subsequent CPE formation.

clozeText: Enteroviruses are classified as {{c1::RNA nonenveloped}} viruses based on their structural characteristics.
extraNote: This classification distinguishes them from enveloped RNA viruses like orthomyxoviruses or paramyxoviruses.

clozeText: In enterovirus cell culture, the {{c1::cytopathic effect (CPE)}} is usually a manifestation of virus-infected cells that are {{c2::dying or dead}}.
extraNote: Changes in size, shape, and cell fusion are important clues for presumptive identification.

clozeText: For serologic diagnosis of an enterovirus infection, a significant rise in antibody titer is defined as at least a(n) {{c1::fourfold}} increase between acute and convalescent samples.
extraNote: A single sample titer cannot distinguish between past and current infection.

clozeText: When diagnosing enteroviruses via serology, the convalescent-phase serum sample is typically obtained {{c1::10 to 14}} days after the acute-phase sample.
extraNote: This timeframe allows for a detectable rise in antibody levels (seroconversion).

clozeText: Detection of enterovirus {{c1::nucleic acids}} in a patient's blood or cells is often performed using {{c2::PCR}}, which offers high sensitivity and speed.
extraNote: Polymerase Chain Reaction is faster than traditional viral culture for detection.

clozeText: Enteroviruses require {{c1::cell cultures}} for growth because they can only replicate within living cells, not on cell-free media.
extraNote: This differentiates viral growth requirements from most bacteria.

clozeText: In cell culture, normal metabolizing cells turn the pH indicator yellow through the production of {{c1::acid}}.
extraNote: Enterovirus-infected cells fail to produce this acid as they die, maintaining an alkaline environment.

clozeText: Enteroviruses like {{c1::Coxsackie virus}} or {{c2::echovirus}} are often used in interference assays to detect the presence of {{c3::rubella}} virus.
extraNote: Rubella virus lacks its own CPE and is detected by its ability to block the CPE of the enterovirus.

clozeText: The use of fluorescein-tagged antibodies to identify enteroviruses in infected cells by UV microscopy is known as a(n) {{c1::fluorescent antibody assay}}.
extraNote: A positive result typically shows an apple-green fluorescence.

clozeText: Identification of enteroviruses via {{c1::complement fixation}} involves binding complement to an antigen-antibody complex, preventing the lysis of sensitized red blood cells.
extraNote: This is one of several tests used to definitively identify a virus grown in culture.

clozeText: If an antibody is homologous to an enterovirus, it can block the virus from attaching to erythrocytes, a test known as {{c1::hemagglutination inhibition}}.
extraNote: This test is only applicable to viruses that naturally agglutinate red blood cells.

clozeText: Direct microscopic identification of enterovirus particles in clinical specimens can be achieved using {{c1::electron microscopy}} to determine size and morphology.
extraNote: This method allows for visualization of the characteristic 28 nm icosahedral structure.

clozeText: The term {{c1::seroconversion}} describes the transition of a patient's serum from antibody-negative to antibody-positive regarding an enterovirus.
extraNote: This indicates a recent or current infection.

clozeText: Clinical specimens suspected of containing enteroviruses should be stored at {{c1::4°C}} if they cannot be inoculated into cell culture immediately.
extraNote: Many viruses are inactivated at room temperature.

clozeText: The Picornavirus name is partially derived from the word {{c1::pico}}, meaning small.
extraNote: Enteroviruses are among the smallest known RNA viruses (28 nm).

clozeText: Enteroviruses have a genome that is described as {{c1::nonsegmented}}, meaning the entire genome is on a single piece of RNA.
extraNote: This contrasts with viruses like orthomyxoviruses (influenza), which have segmented genomes.

clozeText: In the phenol red culture test, the indicator remains {{c1::red}} in the presence of enterovirus-infected cells, indicating an {{c2::alkaline}} state.
extraNote: The red color signifies that the cells are no longer metabolizing and producing acid.

clozeText: Enteroviruses possess {{c1::positive-polarity}} RNA, which can serve directly as messenger RNA (mRNA).
extraNote: This is a key characteristic of the Picornaviridae family.

clozeText: The {{c1::neutralization}} of a cytopathic effect (CPE) is a definitive test for enteroviruses using {{c2::known antibody}}.
extraNote: Homologous antibody prevents the virus from replicating and causing visible cell damage.

clozeText: Enteroviruses are grouped with {{c1::rhinoviruses}} as the two main groups of human pathogens in the Picornavirus family.
extraNote: Both groups share the naked icosahedral, small RNA virus structure.

clozeText: Aggregates of enterovirus-antibody complexes seen via an electron microscope indicate a positive {{c1::immunoelectron microscopy}} test.
extraNote: This requires an antibody homologous to the virus.

clozeText: Viral antigens from enteroviruses are most often detected in blood or body fluids using an {{c1::ELISA}}.
extraNote: Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) is a common method for antigen detection.

clozeText: While hepatitis B is a DNA enveloped virus, {{c1::hepatitis A}} is an RNA nucleocapsid (nonenveloped) virus belonging to the enteroviruses.
extraNote: This distinction is important for classification and clinical presentation.

clozeText: Enteroviruses are members of the {{c1::Picornavirus}} family, which are the smallest RNA viruses.
extraNote: Picornaviruses measure approximately 28 nm in diameter and contain single-stranded RNA.

clozeText: The genome of Enteroviruses consists of {{c1::single-stranded}}, {{c2::positive-polarity}} RNA.
extraNote: Positive-polarity RNA can be directly translated by the host cell machinery.

clozeText: Enteroviruses possess a {{c1::naked icosahedral}} capsid structure.
extraNote: Being 'naked' means they lack a lipid envelope, which typically makes them more resistant to environmental conditions.

clozeText: The Enterovirus genome is described as {{c1::linear}} and {{c2::nonsegmented}}.
extraNote: This distinguishes them from viruses with circular or segmented genomes (like Orthomyxoviruses or Reoviruses).

clozeText: Common human pathogens in the Enterovirus group include poliovirus, {{c1::Coxsackie virus}}, {{c2::echovirus}}, and hepatitis A virus.
extraNote: These are the four primary groups of human pathogens categorized as enteroviruses within the Picornavirus family.

clozeText: The name "picorna" is derived from {{c1::pico}} (meaning small) and {{c2::RNA}}.
extraNote: This reflects their small size (28 nm) and genetic material.

clozeText: The presence of rubella virus can be detected by its {{c1::interference}} with the formation of a cytopathic effect (CPE) by {{c2::echovirus}} or Coxsackie virus.
extraNote: This is a diagnostic technique used when a virus does not produce its own CPE in cell culture.

clozeText: A decrease in {{c1::acid}} production by infected, dying cells can be used to detect certain enteroviruses in cell culture.
extraNote: Normal metabolizing cells produce acid, whereas virus-infected dying cells do not.

clozeText: To detect enteroviruses, the pH indicator {{c1::phenol red}} is added to the culture medium.
extraNote: Metabolic changes in the cell culture result in color changes of this indicator.

clozeText: In enterovirus-infected cell cultures, the phenol red indicator remains {{c1::red::color}}, which indicates {{c2::alkaline}} conditions.
extraNote: The indicator remains red because the dying, infected cells fail to produce acid.

clozeText: In normal metabolizing cell cultures, the phenol red indicator turns {{c1::yellow}}.
extraNote: The yellow color is the result of acid production by healthy cells, contrasting with enterovirus-infected cultures.

clozeText: Enteroviruses are approximately {{c1::28}} nm in diameter.
extraNote: This size classification makes them some of the smallest medically important viruses.

clozeText: Unlike Hepatitis B, which is a DNA virus, {{c1::Hepatitis A}} is an enterovirus with an RNA nucleocapsid.
extraNote: Hepatitis A is specifically classified as an enterovirus within the Picornavirus family.

clozeText: The {{c1::cytopathic effect (CPE)}} is used as a presumptive identification tool for many viruses, including enteroviruses like {{c2::poliovirus}}.
extraNote: CPE refers to observable changes in the appearance of virus-infected cells, such as changes in size or shape.

clozeText: Neutralization of the {{c1::cytopathic effect (CPE)}} using known antibodies is a method for definitive identification of {{c2::enteroviruses}} grown in cell culture.
extraNote: Homologous antibodies block viral entry and prevent replication/CPE formation.

clozeText: Enteroviruses are categorized under the broader grouping of {{c1::RNA nonenveloped}} viruses.
extraNote: The absence of an envelope is a key structural feature for environmental stability.

clozeText: Identification of an unknown enterovirus in culture can be achieved via {{c1::complement fixation}}, where complement is bound to the antigen–antibody complex.
extraNote: If the virus (antigen) and antibody are homologous, complement is fixed and unavailable to lyse indicator red blood cells.

clozeText: In the diagnosis of enteroviral infections, {{c1::seroconversion}} is defined as a significant rise in antibody titer between acute-phase and convalescent-phase sera.
extraNote: A significant rise is typically considered at least a fourfold increase in titer.

clozeText: Convalescent-phase serum for enterovirus testing should be obtained {{c1::10 to 14}} days after the acute-phase sample.
extraNote: This timing allows for the development of a detectable antibody response.

clozeText: A significant rise in antibody titer for an enterovirus infection is defined as a {{c1::fourfold}} or greater increase.
extraNote: For example, a jump from a titer of 1/4 to 1/16 indicates recent infection.

clozeText: The {{c1::icosahedral}} capsid of enteroviruses is composed of proteins and contains the viral genome without a surrounding lipid layer.
extraNote: This structure is characteristic of all Picornaviruses.

clozeText: Enteroviruses replicate strictly in {{c1::living cells}}, and cannot be grown on cell-free media.
extraNote: This is a universal property of viruses, including the Picornaviridae.

clozeText: Because many enteroviruses are inactivated at room temperature, specimens should be transported or stored at {{c1::4°C}} if immediate inoculation is not possible.
extraNote: Maintaining the cold chain is critical for successful viral culture.

clozeText: The {{c1::positive-polarity}} of the enterovirus RNA genome means it is the same sense as messenger RNA (mRNA).
extraNote: This allows the viral genome to be translated into a polyprotein immediately upon entering the host cell cytoplasm.

clozeText: Within the Picornavirus family, {{c1::rhinoviruses}} represent the second major group of human pathogens alongside enteroviruses.
extraNote: Though related, rhinoviruses are typically associated with the common cold, while enteroviruses have a broader clinical range.

clozeText: Detection of viral {{c1::nucleic acids}} in blood or patient cells is a standard approach for diagnosing infections caused by enteroviruses.
extraNote: This is often achieved via Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR).

clozeText: The time taken for a {{c1::cytopathic effect (CPE)}} to appear in cell culture is a diagnostic clue for identifying the specific {{c2::enterovirus}} present.
extraNote: Different viruses produce characteristic changes in specific cell types over varying durations.

clozeText: Definitive identification of an enterovirus can be performed using an {{c1::ELISA::acronym}}, where known antibody is bound to a surface to capture the virus.
extraNote: The amount of bound enzyme-linked antibody determines the presence of the virus in the specimen.

clozeText: Enteroviruses are linear, nonsegmented viruses, which contrasts with {{c1::Reoviruses}}, which have 10 or 11 segments of double-stranded RNA.
extraNote: Enteroviruses possess single-stranded RNA and are much smaller (28 nm vs 75 nm).

clozeText: If an enterovirus and its homologous antibody are mixed, the antibody blocks entry into the cell, a process known as {{c1::neutralization}}.
extraNote: This test confirms the identity of the virus by preventing subsequent replication and CPE formation.

clozeText: Enteroviruses are members of the Picornavirus family, which are the smallest RNA viruses with a diameter of {{c1::28}} nm.
extraNote: The name picorna is derived from pico (small) and RNA-containing.

clozeText: Enteroviruses are characterized by a(n) {{c1::naked icosahedral}} capsid.
extraNote: Being naked (nonenveloped) makes them more resistant to environmental conditions compared to enveloped viruses.

clozeText: The four main groups of human pathogens within the enteroviruses are {{c1::poliovirus}}, {{c2::Coxsackie virus}}, {{c3::echovirus}}, and {{c4::hepatitis A virus}}.
extraNote: These are all members of the Picornavirus family.

clozeText: Certain enteroviruses can be detected in cell culture because infected, dying cells show a(n) {{c1::decrease}} in acid production.
extraNote: Normal metabolizing cells produce acid that changes the pH of the medium.

clozeText: In enterovirus cell cultures, the pH indicator {{c1::phenol red}} remains red (alkaline) in the presence of infected cells.
extraNote: In normal cultures, the indicator turns yellow due to acid produced by metabolizing cells.

clozeText: The presence of rubella virus is often detected by its ability to {{c1::interfere}} with the formation of a cytopathic effect (CPE) by enteroviruses.
extraNote: This is a classic diagnostic technique for viruses that do not produce their own CPE.

clozeText: Two specific enteroviruses used in rubella interference assays are {{c1::echovirus}} and {{c2::Coxsackie virus}}.
extraNote: Rubella prevents these enteroviruses from producing their characteristic CPE.

clozeText: Definitive identification of enteroviruses grown in cell culture is frequently performed using {{c1::neutralization}} of the cytopathic effect (CPE).
extraNote: Homologous antibodies bind the virus surface and block entry into the cell.

clozeText: In a neutralization test, the antibody blocks viral {{c1::entry into the cell}}, which prevents subsequent replication and CPE formation.
extraNote: This confirms the identity of the virus if the known antibody matches the isolated virus.

clozeText: Serologic diagnosis of enteroviral infection requires an acute-phase serum sample and a convalescent-phase sample taken {{c1::10 to 14}} days later.
extraNote: Comparing the two samples allows for the detection of a rise in antibody titer.

clozeText: A diagnostic rise in antibody titer for enteroviruses is defined as a(n) {{c1::fourfold}} or greater increase between acute and convalescent samples.
extraNote: For example, a rise from a titer of 1/4 to 1/16 is considered significant.

clozeText: {{c1::Seroconversion}} is the term used when a patient's serum changes from antibody-negative to antibody-positive during an infection.
extraNote: This indicates a current or very recent primary infection.

clozeText: Enteroviruses are grouped medically as {{c1::RNA nonenveloped}} viruses.
extraNote: This group also includes hepeviruses, caliciviruses, and reoviruses.

clozeText: Hepatitis A virus is specifically described as a(n) {{c1::RNA nucleocapsid}} virus, whereas Hepatitis B is a DNA enveloped virus.
extraNote: Hepatitis A belongs to the Enterovirus group of Picornaviruses.

clozeText: The Enterovirus genome is {{c1::linear}} and {{c2::nonsegmented}}.
extraNote: This distinguishes it from segmented RNA viruses like orthomyxoviruses or reoviruses.

clozeText: Poliovirus has {{c1::three}} distinct serotypes based on its surface antigens.
extraNote: In contrast, measles virus has only one serotype, while rhinoviruses have over 100.

clozeText: Polioviruses have three different {{c1::antigenic determinants}} on their surface proteins, which define their specific serotypes.
extraNote: Poliovirus type 1, type 2, and type 3 each have unique determinants that induce specific neutralizing antibodies.

clozeText: A person immune to poliovirus type 1 can still develop {{c1::poliomyelitis}} if infected by poliovirus types 2 or 3.
extraNote: Immunity is type-specific; antibodies against one serotype do not protect against the others.

clozeText: The polio vaccine must contain {{c1::all three serotypes}} to be completely protective against the disease.
extraNote: This is a direct implication of the virus having multiple distinct antigenic types.

clozeText: Poliovirus is a {{c1::nonenveloped::envelope status}} virus, which means it is composed only of nucleic acid and capsid proteins.
extraNote: Nonenveloped viruses are also referred to as naked nucleocapsid viruses.

clozeText: Poliovirus is transmitted by the {{c1::fecal–oral}} route because it lacks an envelope and can survive in the environment.
extraNote: Viruses transmitted this way must be stable enough to survive external conditions and the digestive tract.

clozeText: Because it is nonenveloped, poliovirus is {{c1::resistant::sensitivity}} to lipid solvents such as alcohol and ether.
extraNote: Enveloped viruses are sensitive to these agents, whereas naked viruses like poliovirus are more stable.

clozeText: Poliovirus exhibits high stability against {{c1::heat}}, drying, and detergents compared to enveloped viruses.
extraNote: The lack of a lipoprotein envelope confers environmental instability to many other viruses, but not poliovirus.

clozeText: Intact poliovirus has a narrow host range and can enter the cells of only {{c1::humans}} and other {{c2::primates}}.
extraNote: This specificity is governed by the interaction between viral surface proteins and specific cell receptors.

clozeText: Purified {{c1::poliovirus RNA}} is considered infectious nucleic acid because it can carry out the entire growth cycle in a cell without viral proteins.
extraNote: The purified genome can bypass the host range specificity normally provided by the viral capsid.

clozeText: Purified poliovirus RNA can enter {{c1::nonprimate}} cells and produce normal progeny, even though the intact virus cannot.
extraNote: This demonstrates that the internal machinery of nonprimate cells can support poliovirus replication once entry is achieved.

clozeText: Poliovirus progeny produced in nonprimate cells can only infect {{c1::primate}} cells because they possess their original {{c2::capsid proteins}}.
extraNote: The viral protein-cell receptor interaction dictates the host range for the complete virus particle.

clozeText: The infectious nature of purified poliovirus RNA provides definitive proof that {{c1::nucleic acid}} is the genetic material.
extraNote: This shows that the genome alone carries all the necessary information for viral replication.

clozeText: Surface proteins of poliovirus act as the antigens against which {{c1::neutralizing antibodies}} are formed.
extraNote: These antibodies are the primary defense that prevents the virus from infecting cells.

clozeText: Poliovirus is an {{c1::RNA}} virus, as evidenced by its infectious purified RNA genome.
extraNote: Most RNA viruses undergo their entire replicative cycle in the cytoplasm.

clozeText: The specific attachment of poliovirus to host cells is mediated by {{c1::weak, noncovalent}} bonding to receptor proteins.
extraNote: The presence or absence of these receptors determines the organ and host specificity.

clozeText: During the middle events of the poliovirus growth cycle, the {{c1::viral genome}} is replicated and viral mRNA is synthesized.
extraNote: Early events involve attachment, penetration, and uncoating.

clozeText: In the poliovirus life cycle, {{c1::late proteins}} correspond to the structural capsid proteins.
extraNote: Early proteins typically function as enzymes (e.g., polymerases) used to replicate the genome.

clozeText: The term {{c1::uncoating}} refers to the removal of poliovirus capsid proteins, freeing the genome to function within the host cell.
extraNote: This typically occurs after penetration into the cell.

clozeText: Poliovirus is grouped with other fecal-oral viruses like {{c1::Hepatitis A}} and {{c2::Norovirus}} because they all lack an envelope.
extraNote: Nonenveloped viruses are generally more resistant to environmental stressors.

clozeText: The surface proteins of poliovirus determine its {{c1::host range}} by binding to specific receptors.
extraNote: Rabies virus has a broad range (all mammals), whereas poliovirus has a narrow range (primates only).

clozeText: Poliovirus undergoes {{c1::penetration}} into the host cell by being engulfed in a vesicle.
extraNote: Low pH within the vesicle often favors the subsequent uncoating process.

clozeText: Poliovirus {{c1::type 1}}, type 2, and type 3 are the three primary serotypes that cause disease.
extraNote: Vaccine development must account for all three to ensure immunity against poliomyelitis.

clozeText: Unlike influenza or HIV, poliovirus does not {{c1::change rapidly::antigenic stability}} in its antigenicity, though it still has three distinct serotypes.
extraNote: Viruses like influenza require frequent vaccine updates because new antigens appear constantly.

clozeText: The lack of an envelope in poliovirus means it does not acquire a {{c1::lipoprotein}} membrane from the host cell during release.
extraNote: Enveloped viruses typically acquire their membrane by budding through the cell's outer or nuclear membrane.

clozeText: Poliovirus lacks {{c1::glycoprotein spikes}} which are typically found on the surface of enveloped viruses.
extraNote: Instead, its attachment is mediated by the proteins of its icosahedral capsid.

clozeText: Once poliovirus RNA is released into the cytoplasm during {{c1::uncoating}}, it can begin the replication process.
extraNote: The genome must be freed from the capsid to serve as a template for protein synthesis and replication.

clozeText: The {{c1::capsid}} of poliovirus protects its nucleic acid from the harsh acidic environment of the stomach.
extraNote: This protection is essential for viruses following the fecal-oral transmission pathway.

clozeText: Specific {{c1::receptor interaction}} governs the organ specificity of poliovirus infection.
extraNote: This dictates which tissues within a primate host the virus can successfully infect.

clozeText: Poliovirus is a medically important example of a {{c1::naked nucleocapsid}} virus that causes human disease.
extraNote: Naked viruses are generally more resistant to detergents and lipid solvents than enveloped viruses.

clozeText: Polioviruses have {{c1::three}} distinct serotypes based on their surface antigens.
extraNote: Each serotype has a different antigenic determinant on its surface protein, necessitating a trivalent vaccine for full protection.

clozeText: Polioviruses have different {{c1::antigenic determinants}} on their surface proteins, meaning immunity to one type does not prevent infection by another.
extraNote: Type 1, type 2, and type 3 each possess unique surface proteins that induce specific neutralizing antibodies.

clozeText: The polio vaccine must contain all three {{c1::serotypes}} to provide complete protection against the disease.
extraNote: This requirement stems from the fact that poliovirus surface antigens are distinct and do not provide cross-neutralization.

clozeText: The capsid of rotavirus is constructed from identical protein subunits, which promotes {{c1::self-assembly}}.
extraNote: Self-assembly is efficient because it requires no extra genetic information, energy, or enzymes.

clozeText: The combination of the rotavirus nucleic acid and its capsid proteins is referred to as the {{c1::nucleocapsid}}.
extraNote: For naked viruses like rotavirus, the nucleocapsid and the virion are essentially the same structure.

clozeText: Rotavirus falls within the typical viral size range of {{c1::20 to 300 nm}} in diameter.
extraNote: This range spans from the size of a large protein to the smallest known cells.

clozeText: The shape of rotavirus is determined by the arrangement of repeating subunits in its {{c1::protein coat::capsid}}.
extraNote: The geometry of these subunits gives the virus its precise symmetry.

clozeText: Because rotavirus has multiple serotypes, a vaccine must ideally contain {{c1::all}} relevant serotypes to be fully protective.
extraNote: Immunity to one serotype does not necessarily prevent infection by others.

clozeText: The antigenic determinants on the {{c1::surface proteins}} of rotavirus are what induce neutralizing antibodies.
extraNote: Changes in these surface antigens can lead to the formation of new serotypes.

clozeText: The {{c1::nonenveloped}} structure of rotavirus allows it to remain infectious even after exposure to environmental drying.
extraNote: Enveloped viruses are typically inactivated when they dry out.

clozeText: Rotavirus genome pieces are composed of {{c1::double-stranded}} or single-stranded RNA (Context: Page 218 notes RNA genomes can be either).
extraNote: While the text mentions RNA can be either, it highlights that both influenza and rotavirus specifically have segmented RNA.

clozeText: The environmental persistence of rotavirus is a key factor in its {{c1::fecal–oral::transmission route}} transmission.
extraNote: Lack of an envelope is the structural basis for this environmental persistence.

clozeText: Structural proteins of rotavirus include those that form the {{c1::capsid}}, whereas non-structural proteins include enzymes.
extraNote: Capsid proteins protect the genome, while internal enzymes like polymerases assist in replication.

clozeText: Compared to {{c1::herpes simplex}} virus, rotavirus is significantly more resistant to lipid solvents.
extraNote: Herpesviruses are enveloped and therefore highly sensitive to solvents like alcohol and ether.

clozeText: {{c1::Rotavirus}} has a segmented RNA genome.
extraNote: Both influenza virus and rotavirus possess genomes that exist in several pieces rather than a single molecule.

clozeText: Rotavirus is transmitted primarily by the {{c1::fecal–oral}} route.
extraNote: Naked nucleocapsid viruses are generally transmitted this way to survive environmental conditions and the gastrointestinal tract.

clozeText: Rotavirus is classified as a {{c1::naked}} (nonenveloped) nucleocapsid virus.
extraNote: The absence of a lipoprotein envelope allows these viruses to survive longer in the environment.

clozeText: The genome of Rotavirus is composed of {{c1::segmented}} RNA.
extraNote: Segmentation allows for potential reassortment, though the text primarily focuses on its structural classification.

clozeText: Because it lacks an envelope, Rotavirus is {{c1::resistant}} to lipid solvents such as alcohol and ether.
extraNote: Enveloped viruses are sensitive to these agents, whereas naked viruses like rotavirus are not.

clozeText: Rotavirus is {{c1::less}} sensitive to detergents and heat compared to enveloped viruses like Herpes simplex virus.
extraNote: The lack of a lipid-containing envelope confers greater stability against chemical and physical inactivation.

clozeText: The Rotavirus genome is surrounded by a protein coat called a(n) {{c1::capsid}}.
extraNote: The capsid is made of repeating subunits called capsomers and protects the internal nucleic acid.

clozeText: Rotavirus has {{c1::icosahedral}} symmetry, characterized by capsomers arranged in 20 triangles.
extraNote: All naked human viruses described in the text have icosahedral symmetry.

clozeText: Rotavirus is considered {{c1::haploid}} because it contains a single copy of its genome.
extraNote: Retroviruses are the only exception, being diploid (two copies).

clozeText: The surface proteins of Rotavirus are the primary targets of {{c1::neutralizing}} antibodies.
extraNote: Antibody binding to these surface proteins prevents the virus from attaching to host cell receptors.

clozeText: The interaction between Rotavirus surface proteins and host cell receptors determines {{c1::organ}} specificity.
extraNote: Surface proteins mediate attachment, which is the first step in determining which tissues the virus can infect.

clozeText: Rotavirus ranges in size between {{c1::20 and 300::range}} nm in diameter.
extraNote: This range spans from the size of the largest protein to the smallest cell.

clozeText: The repeating subunits that form the Rotavirus capsid are called {{c1::capsomers}}.
extraNote: Capsomers can be seen under an electron microscope as spherical particles.

clozeText: The structure consisting of the Rotavirus RNA genome and its protein coat is the {{c1::nucleocapsid}}.
extraNote: In naked viruses like rotavirus, the nucleocapsid is synonymous with the entire virus particle.

clozeText: Rotavirus can {{c1::survive}} longer in the environment compared to enveloped viruses like HIV.
extraNote: Environmental stability is a hallmark of nonenveloped viruses transmitted via the fecal-oral route.

clozeText: Rotavirus does {{c1::not}} have a lipoprotein envelope derived from the host cell membrane.
extraNote: Naked viruses consist only of nucleic acid and a protein capsid.

clozeText: Specific subcategories of Rotavirus based on surface antigens are referred to as {{c1::serotypes}}.
extraNote: Antibodies against one serotype may not neutralize a different serotype of the same virus.

clozeText: The Rotavirus genome consists of {{c1::RNA}} rather than DNA.
extraNote: While some viruses use DNA, rotavirus uses a segmented RNA genome.

clozeText: Rotavirus symmetry is described as a symmetric figure with the approximate outline of a {{c1::sphere}}.
extraNote: This is characteristic of icosahedral viruses where capsomers form 20 triangles.

clozeText: Unlike helical viruses, icosahedral viruses like Rotavirus can be {{c1::naked}} or enveloped.
extraNote: All human helical viruses are enveloped, but icosahedral ones vary.

clozeText: The assembly of the Rotavirus particle from protein subunits is a process of {{c1::self-assembly}} requiring no energy.
extraNote: This efficiency reduces the need for extensive genetic information.

clozeText: Rotavirus surface proteins serve as {{c1::antigens}} against which the host forms a protective immune response.
extraNote: These proteins are the specific components recognized by the immune system to inhibit viral replication.

clozeText: Rotavirus is grouped with {{c1::Norovirus}} and Poliovirus as a common naked virus transmitted via contaminated food or water.
extraNote: These viruses are all characterized by their lack of an envelope and fecal-oral transmission.

clozeText: The Rotavirus capsid functions to {{c1::protect}} the segmented RNA genome from environmental degradation.
extraNote: The protein shell is robust enough to survive the acidic environment of the stomach.

clozeText: Rotavirus lacks a(n) {{c1::matrix}} protein because it does not possess an envelope.
extraNote: The matrix protein's role is to mediate the interaction between the capsid and the envelope.

clozeText: The {{c1::segmented}} nature of the Rotavirus genome distinguishes it from other nonenveloped RNA viruses like Poliovirus.
extraNote: Poliovirus has a single molecule of RNA, whereas rotavirus has several pieces.

clozeText: A booster dose of {{c1::Pneumovax (23-valent polysaccharide vaccine)}} is recommended for people between the ages of 19 and 64 years who are infected with {{c2::human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)}}.
extraNote: HIV infection is an indication for a pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine booster in adults under age 65 because these patients are considered immunocompromised.

clozeText: The {{c1::conjugate meningococcal vaccine}} is recommended for children younger than {{c2::11}} years with high-risk conditions such as HIV infection.
extraNote: While standard meningococcal conjugate vaccination occurs at age 11-12, high-risk conditions like HIV require earlier administration.

clozeText: Immunocompromised patients, such as those infected with {{c1::human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)}}, should be immunized with the {{c2::13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (Prevnar 13)}} due to high mortality rates.
extraNote: HIV-infected individuals have a high mortality rate from pneumococcal infections and require the conjugate vaccine (Prevnar 13).

clozeText: People between the ages of {{c1::19 and 64}} years who are infected with {{c2::HIV}} are indicated for a booster dose of the unconjugated 23-valent pneumococcal vaccine.
extraNote: Standard 23-valent vaccination is for age 65+, but HIV status makes it recommended for the 19-64 age group as a booster.

clozeText: {{c1::HIV infection}} is classified as a high-risk condition that warrants the use of the {{c2::conjugate meningococcal vaccine}} in children under age 11.
extraNote: HIV and asplenia are the primary high-risk conditions listed for pediatric meningococcal vaccination prior to the standard age.

clozeText: A booster dose of {{c1::Pneumovax}} is recommended for individuals between the ages of 19 and 64 who are immunocompromised, including those infected with {{c2::human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)}}.
extraNote: Pneumovax is the 23-valent unconjugated polysaccharide vaccine.

clozeText: Individuals infected with {{c1::HIV}} are recommended to receive a booster dose of the 23-valent pneumococcal vaccine between the ages of {{c2::19 and 64}} years.
extraNote: This is recommended for those classified as immunocompromised.

clozeText: The {{c1::meningococcal conjugate vaccine}} is recommended for children younger than 11 years who have high-risk conditions, such as {{c2::HIV}} infection.
extraNote: HIV is categorized alongside conditions like asplenia as a high-risk factor for meningococcal disease.

clozeText: The mortality rate of pneumococcal infections is particularly high in {{c1::immunocompromised}} patients, such as those with {{c2::HIV}} infection.
extraNote: Splenectomized patients and children under 5 are also at increased risk for high mortality.

clozeText: Children younger than {{c1::11}} years with high-risk conditions like {{c2::HIV}} infection should receive the conjugate vaccine against groups A, C, Y, and W-135 meningococci.
extraNote: Under normal circumstances, the conjugate vaccine is recommended at age 11 to 12 years.

clozeText: Immunocompromised patients, such as those with {{c1::HIV}}, should be immunized with the {{c2::13-valent pneumococcal conjugate}} vaccine (Prevnar 13).
extraNote: The 13-valent vaccine uses a carrier protein (diphtheria toxoid) conjugated to the polysaccharide immunogens.

clozeText: A booster dose of {{c1::Pneumovax 23::23-valent polysaccharide vaccine}} is recommended for people between the ages of 19 and 64 years who are immunocompromised due to {{c2::HIV}} infection.
extraNote: Patients with HIV are at increased risk for invasive pneumococcal disease and require additional immunization beyond the standard schedule.

clozeText: Individuals with {{c1::HIV}} infection who are between 19 and 64 years of age should receive a booster dose of the {{c2::unconjugated polysaccharide}} pneumococcal vaccine.
extraNote: This booster is also recommended for other immunocompromised states like asplenia or those receiving cancer chemotherapy.

clozeText: The {{c1::conjugate}} meningococcal vaccine is recommended for children younger than 11 years who have high-risk conditions, such as {{c2::HIV}} infection.
extraNote: The conjugate vaccine covers meningococcal groups A, C, Y, and W-135.

clozeText: In children with {{c1::HIV}}, the conjugate meningococcal vaccine is preferred over the unconjugated version because it induces {{c2::higher titers}} of antibodies.
extraNote: Conjugate vaccines involve coupling a polysaccharide to a carrier protein to enhance the immune response in pediatric populations.

clozeText: {{c1::HIV infection}} is categorized as a high-risk condition that justifies the administration of the conjugate meningococcal vaccine in children under the age of {{c2::11}} years.
extraNote: Standard administration is usually at age 11 to 12, but high-risk conditions like HIV or asplenia require earlier dosing.

clozeText: For patients with {{c1::HIV}}, a booster dose of the 23-valent pneumococcal vaccine is indicated for those in the {{c2::19 to 64}} year age range.
extraNote: Immunocompromised status is a primary indication for this booster prior to the standard age of 65.

clozeText: The conjugate meningococcal vaccine administered to children with {{c1::HIV}} provides protection against serogroups {{c2::A, C, Y, and W-135}}.
extraNote: Group B meningococcus is not included in these conjugate vaccines because its polysaccharide is not immunogenic in humans.

clozeText: Adults between the ages of 19 and 64 years who are immunocompromised, specifically those infected with {{c1::human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)}}, are recommended to receive a booster dose of {{c2::Pneumovax 23::vaccine name}}.
extraNote: Pneumovax 23 is the 23-valent unconjugated polysaccharide vaccine used to prevent pneumococcal disease in high-risk adult populations.

clozeText: In children younger than 11 years of age, {{c1::HIV infection}} is classified as a high-risk condition that warrants immunization with the {{c2::meningococcal conjugate vaccine}}.
extraNote: The conjugate vaccine provides critical protection against Neisseria meningitidis in children with immunocompromising conditions.

clozeText: Because the mortality rate of {{c1::pneumococcal}} infections is high in immunocompromised individuals such as those with {{c2::HIV}}, these patients should be immunized with the {{c3::13-valent conjugate vaccine::Prevnar 13}}.
extraNote: Prevnar 13 contains pneumococcal polysaccharides from 13 serotypes conjugated to a carrier protein (diphtheria toxoid) to enhance immunogenicity.
